tagline: The largest land animal, talking in rumbles too deep for us to hear
summary: The biggest animal on land lives in family herds led by an older female, the matriarch. Much of its conversation happens in low rumbles, many of them below the range of human hearing, that can carry for kilometres across the savanna — and part of that sound may travel through the ground to be felt by other elephants' feet.

stats.size: Males weigh 4,500–6,100 kg and stand 3.2–4 m at the shoulder; females are smaller
stats.habitat: Savanna, grassland, woodland and semi-desert, wherever water is within reach
stats.range: Patchily across eastern and southern Africa, with scattered populations further north and west
stats.diet: Grasses, leaves, bark, roots and fruit; drinks large amounts of water every day

facts.title: Rumbles below our hearing
facts.text: The fundamental frequency of an adult elephant's rumble typically lies between 12 and 20 Hz — mostly below the roughly 20 Hz lower limit of human hearing — with calves rumbling higher, at about 20–35 Hz. Field recordings have caught rumbles as low as 8 Hz.

facts.title: Heard at least 4 km away
facts.text: In 58 playback experiments in Etosha National Park, Namibia, wild elephants responded to recorded calls played 1.2 and 2.0 km away, freezing, spreading their ears and scanning; some males walked 1 km or more towards the loudspeaker. Because the speaker played calls at only half the strongest recorded sound pressure, the researchers estimated the calls are audible to elephants at least 4 km from the source.

facts.title: Ten kilometres on a still night
facts.text: Measurements of the air over Etosha fed into a sound model suggest that on clear, cold, calm nights, 1–2 hours after sunset, temperature inversions more than double the range of elephant calls, to over 10 km.

facts.title: Listening with their feet
facts.text: Some of a rumble's energy travels through the ground. When alarm calls were played to wild family groups as vibrations through the ground, elephants responded to the calls of familiar herds but not to those of unfamiliar herds or to control signals, showing they can tell seismic calls apart.

facts.title: Led by the matriarch
facts.text: Herds are made up of females and their young, led by an older female. Pregnancy lasts about 22 months, and wild elephants live on average 60–70 years.

facts.title: Its own species since 2021
facts.text: Until 2021 Africa's elephants were assessed together as one Vulnerable species. That year the IUCN assessed the savanna (bush) and forest elephants separately for the first time, listing the savanna elephant as Endangered after its numbers fell by at least 60% over the last 50 years; the forest elephant was listed as Critically Endangered.

notes: signatureData: rumbleHzMin/Max 12–20 Hz is ElephantVoices' 'typical' fundamental frequency for adult rumbles (calves ~20–35 Hz; as low as 8 Hz in field recordings). The brief suggested Payne, Langbauer & Thomas 1986 (Behav Ecol Sociobiol 18:297–301) for the rumble range, but that paper is titled 'Infrasonic calls of the Asian elephant (Elephas maximus)' and reports 14–24 Hz from captive Asian elephants, so it was not used for this species. rangeKm 10 is from Garstang et al. 1995 (modelled: 'ranges of over 10 km are likely' 1–2 h after sunset under temperature inversions; marked 'hypothesis'). The measured-playback basis is Langbauer et al. 1991 (responses at 2.0 km; audible 'at least 4 km'), and Larom et al. 1997 (J Exp Biol 200:421) also models ranges exceeding 10 km; ElephantVoices gives 2–4 km by day and 7–10 km under evening inversions. Seismic: O'Connell-Rodwell et al. 2007 (wild Namibian family groups discriminate familiar vs unfamiliar seismic alarm calls); their 2006 Behav Ecol Sociobiol 59:842 paper (doi 10.1007/s00265-005-0136-2) showed the first responses to seismic playback but its abstract could not be read, so it is not cited. Detection specifically via foot receptors is described by ElephantVoices as 'may be detected ... through vibration-sensitive receptors in their feet and trunk'; the summary says 'may' accordingly. Size, elevation (0–4,000 m), gestation and lifespan from Animal Diversity Web, whose L. africana account may predate the 2021 forest/savanna split. Conservation: IUCN 2021 assessment, amended 2022 (e.T181008073A223031019, Gobush et al.; URL confirmed via GBIF's IUCN checklist, iucnredlist.org returns 403 to scripted requests); reference 0 is the IUCN news release, which resolves. Regions: namib-kalahari for the desert-dwelling elephants of north-west Namibia (gallery photo) and the Kalahari populations of Botswana. Categories: endangered (IUCN EN). Hero swapped to the mother and calf; the two gallery images both show dust/sand-spraying, but in contrasting habitats (Namibian desert vs Kruger riverbed).

anatomy.lede: The largest animal on land is built around a few extraordinary tools: a trunk that is both nose and hand, ears that work as radiators, and teeth that are replaced from the back of the jaw like a conveyor belt.

hotspots.label: Ear
hotspots.text: The huge triangular ears help the elephant keep cool in the hottest months.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Long lashes guard the small eyes from dust and debris. Elephants see in two colour channels, much like a red–green colour-blind person.

hotspots.label: Tusk
hotspots.text: Tusks are enlarged incisor teeth made of ivory. Calves are born without them; the tusk-forming incisors replace small milk teeth at about a year old.

hotspots.label: Trunk
hotspots.text: The muscular trunk is used for breathing, smelling and grabbing objects, and as a temporary container to suck up water and squirt it into the mouth.

hotspots.label: Cracked skin
hotspots.text: A network of tiny cracks covers the skin. These channels hold water and mud, helping the elephant stay cool and protecting it from parasites and sun.

hotspots.label: Foot
hotspots.text: Some of a rumble's energy travels through the ground. Elephants detect these seismic calls and can tell those of familiar and unfamiliar herds apart.

hotspots.label: Calf
hotspots.text: A newborn weighs about 100 kg. It stays close at its mother's side for its first four years or so.

senses.lede: An elephant lives in a world of smell and sound — much of it below the range of human hearing — and even feels distant calls through the ground.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: African elephants carry about 2,000 working smell-receptor genes, packed into enlarged gene clusters — an extreme expansion compared with the other mammals studied.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Much of an adult's rumble lies below about 20 Hz, under the lower limit of human hearing, yet elephants respond to such calls played from kilometres away.

senses.name: Seismic sense
senses.text: Part of a rumble's energy travels through the ground. In playback trials, wild elephants reacted to seismic alarm calls of familiar herds but ignored those of strangers.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Elephants have two colour pigments in daylight, sensitive to blue and yellow-green light, giving them dichromatic vision like a red–green colour-blind person.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: Touch matters most between mother and calf and between mating pairs; courting elephants stroke each other with their trunks.

body.lede: Keeping a six-tonne body fed, cool and working for 60 years or more takes some unusual engineering.

systems.title: Six sets of molars
systems.text: Elephants grow six molars on each side of each jaw in turn. Each new tooth moves forward as the one in front wears away; when the sixth is worn down there is no replacement, and the elephant can no longer chew its food.

systems.title: Skin that cracks on purpose
systems.text: The outer layer of elephant skin is thick, brittle and slow to shed. As it thickens on the skin's tiny bumps it fractures, creating micrometre-wide channels that hold water and mud.

systems.title: Ears as radiators
systems.text: The large ears help keep the body cool. Elephants also use their trunks to coat themselves with mud or water, which helps them stay hydrated.

systems.title: A trunk for drinking
systems.text: An elephant needs around 50 gallons (about 190 litres) of water every day. It sucks water into its trunk and squirts it into its mouth rather than drinking directly.

genome.lede: A first draft of the African elephant genome was released in 2009, and a chromosome-level assembly followed in 2023. It has helped explain why such a large, long-lived animal rarely gets cancer.

findings.title: Twenty copies of a cancer guard
findings.text: Humans have one copy of the tumour-suppressor gene TP53; African elephants have at least 20, most of them extra copies called retrogenes. Elephant cells exposed to DNA damage self-destruct more readily than human cells, and elephants' estimated cancer mortality is about 5%, against 11–25% in people.

findings.title: A zombie gene comes back to life
findings.text: Elephants revived a dead copy of a gene called LIF6. Switched on by TP53 when DNA is damaged, it helps kill the damaged cell — a change that appeared as elephants' ancestors grew large.

findings.title: Two species, long apart
findings.text: Genomes from living and extinct elephants show the ancestors of savanna and forest elephants were almost completely isolated from each other for about 500,000 years, supporting their treatment as separate species.

mind.lede: Long lives, long memories and close family ties make elephants some of the most socially skilled animals studied.

studies.title: The wisdom of the matriarch
studies.text: Playback experiments in Amboseli, Kenya, showed that families led by older matriarchs were better at telling familiar callers from strangers, and these groups may raise more calves.

studies.title: Reading a pointing finger
studies.text: Eleven captive African elephants, without prior training, found hidden food by following a person's pointing gesture, even when the gesture was subtle.

studies.title: Telling people apart by voice
studies.text: In Amboseli, family groups bunched defensively and sniffed the air more after hearing recorded voices of Maasai men, who pose a greater threat to them, than voices of another ethnic group — and reacted less to Maasai women and boys.

studies.title: Calling each other by name
studies.text: Machine-learning analysis of wild elephant rumbles found calls specific to the elephant being addressed, and elephants reacted more strongly to playbacks of calls originally aimed at them.

survival.lede: A healthy adult has little to fear from other animals. The danger is to calves that stray — and, above all, from people.

tactics.title: Safety in the herd
tactics.text: Females live in family herds of 6 to 70 animals that guard the young. Predators mostly take calves that lag behind the group.

tactics.title: Sheer size
tactics.text: Males can weigh over six tonnes. Few predators will risk attacking a full-grown elephant.

tactics.title: Long-distance warning
tactics.text: Elephants call to warn or gather members of their herd, and their low-frequency calls can be heard by other elephants at least 4 km away.

threats.title: Poaching for ivory
threats.text: Despite an international ban on the ivory trade since 1989, illegal ivory trading doubled between 2007 and 2014.

threats.title: Losing the oldest
threats.text: Hunters often target the largest elephants. Because older females hold the herd's social knowledge, losing them may harm the whole family.

threats.title: Shrinking, unprotected range
threats.text: About 70% of the elephant's remaining range lies outside protected land, and human development continues to take habitat.

life.lede: Elephants grow up slowly, with the longest pregnancy of any land mammal and years of learning within the family.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: A single calf, rarely twins, develops for almost two years. Females breed only once every 3 to 9 years.

stages.name: Newborn
stages.text: The calf weighs 90–120 kg at birth. It may suckle for up to three years and keeps close to its mother, who helps it past obstacles.

stages.name: Youngster
stages.text: The whole herd teaches the young elephant to use its trunk, find food and move safely, until it becomes independent at around eight.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature at about 11 and stay with their family; males mature at about 20 and live alone or with a few other bulls.

lifespan.value: 60–70 years on average in the wild

tagline: The heaviest soaring bird, which almost never needs to flap
summary: A huge black-and-white vulture of the Andes, with a white neck ruff and wings spanning about 3.2 m. Flight recorders fitted to wild condors in Patagonia showed they flap for only 1% of their time in the air, riding thermals and mountain winds instead. One bird flew for more than five hours without a single wingbeat.

stats.size: 97.5–128 cm long with a wingspan of about 3.2 m; 7.7–15 kg, males larger than females
stats.habitat: Open mountains, high canyons, cliffs, steppe and desert, where carrion can be spotted from the air
stats.range: The Andes and Pacific side of South America, from Colombia and north-western Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego
stats.diet: Mainly carrion; occasionally newborn animals

facts.title: One wingbeat in a hundred
facts.text: Custom 'flight recorders' that logged every wingbeat across more than 216 hours of flight showed that young wild condors in Patagonia flapped for only 1% of their flight time. More than 75% of that flapping came during take-off.

facts.title: 172 km on still wings
facts.text: One tagged condor flew for more than five hours without flapping, covering about 172 km. Even in winter, when thermals are weak, the researchers predict condors need to flap for only about two seconds per kilometre.

facts.title: Wings of a glider
facts.text: At around 3.2 m, the Andean condor's wingspan is the longest of any land bird. Gaps between its spread primary feathers help it soar, and it rides the thermals rising off cliff faces for hours with very little effort.

facts.title: Searching by sight
facts.text: Andean condors find carrion by sight, scanning the ground from thousands of feet up. They mostly scavenge, but sometimes take small animals such as marmots and rabbits.

facts.title: Comb and eye colour
facts.text: Males are larger than females and have a fleshy comb on the head, which females lack. Males have yellow eyes, while females' eyes are red.

facts.title: A slow start in life
facts.text: Andean condors breed only every two to three years, laying a single egg on a bare cliff ledge, and both parents share the 54–58 days of incubation. For a bird that breeds so slowly, lead from ammunition and persecution by farmers are serious threats.

notes: Flight figures (1% flapping, >216 h, >75% at take-off, >5 h and ~172 km without flapping, ~2 s per km in winter) are verbatim from the Williams et al. 2020 abstract and significance statement, read in full text via Europe PMC (PMC7395523). The tagged birds were immatures (eight condors) from Bariloche, Argentina, 2013–2018. Williams et al. call it the 'world's heaviest soaring bird'. The wingspan, mass, elevation (up to 5,500 m), diet, incubation and 'breed every 2 to 3 years' are from Animal Diversity Web. ADW still lists the species as Near Threatened, which is outdated; status is taken from IUCN (VU, 2020, confirmed via GBIF's IUCN checklist and the DOI handle). The range, comb, eye colour, 'one chick every other year' and 'shot and poisoned' are from the Peregrine Fund; ADW also lists lead ammunition and persecution by farmers. Order: Cathartiformes is used, as in most current bird checklists; the GBIF backbone places Cathartidae in Accipitriformes. Regions: andes-patagonia only (the Venezuelan and Colombian Andes are not a separate region). Categories: fliers only. It is a scavenger, not an apex predator, and VU does not meet the EN/CR bar for 'endangered'. Image alt-1: the Commons file name says 'male in flight Torres del Paine', but its description reads 'immature in flight, Farellones, Andes Mountains, Chile' (apparently copied from a sister upload). The caption therefore says only 'Chilean Andes' and does not give an age or sex. Only one gallery image is used; the others found were zoo birds or near-duplicates. iucnredlist.org and gbif.org web pages return 403 to scripted requests, so they were checked through the DOI handle API and the GBIF API.

anatomy.lede: The Andean condor is a glider first and foremost: enormous wings, a bare head for feeding inside carcasses, and feet made for walking rather than killing.

hotspots.label: Bill
hotspots.text: The hooked bill, dark at the base and ivory towards the tip, is used to tear open and strip carcasses.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Sight is the condor's main sense for finding food, scanning the ground from high above.

hotspots.label: Bare head
hotspots.text: The head and neck have no feathers. Bare skin is thought to stay cleaner after feeding on carcasses, and condors can change its colour to signal their mood.

hotspots.label: Neck ruff
hotspots.text: A collar of white down circles the base of the neck in adults; young birds are olive-grey and brown.

hotspots.label: White wing panel
hotspots.text: Adults have white flight feathers on the upper wing, more pronounced in males.

hotspots.label: Wing
hotspots.text: A wingspan of about 3.2 m — the largest of any land bird — lets the condor ride rising air for hours with barely a flap.

senses.lede: Soaring for hours over mountains and steppe, a condor relies on its eyes — and sometimes on other birds — to find a meal.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Condors find carrion mainly by sight, spotting it from high altitude as they soar.

senses.name: Watching other vultures
senses.text: Turkey and black vultures find food by smell. Condors may follow these smaller birds to a carcass they could not have located themselves.

body.lede: The heaviest soaring bird has some unusual ways of coping with heat, carrion and a life on the wing.

systems.title: Cooling with its own droppings
systems.text: Condors excrete onto their own legs so that evaporation cools them — a habit called urohidrosis that leaves the legs streaked white with uric acid.

systems.title: Walking feet
systems.text: Unlike hunting raptors, condors have relatively weak feet with short, blunt talons and a small hind toe, suited to standing on carcasses rather than gripping prey.

systems.title: A voice without a voice box
systems.text: Condors lack a syrinx, the bird's sound-making organ, so they cannot sing or call in the usual way. They communicate mainly with hisses and clicks.

genome.lede: The first chromosome-scale Andean condor genome was published in 2025, allowing a close comparison with its critically endangered cousin, the California condor.

findings.title: A close cousin
findings.text: The assembly contains 29 autosomes and the Z sex chromosome, and its gene order closely matches that of the California condor genome.

findings.title: Less inbred than California condors
findings.text: Andean condors carry less genetic diversity than California condors, yet far less of their genome lies in long identical stretches inherited from related parents — about 1.4% versus 7.3% for the longest stretches.

findings.title: Genes of a scavenger
findings.text: Gene families linked to detoxification, high-altitude living and immunity have expanded or shrunk differently in the two condors. Avian scavengers share some of these trends, suggesting similar adaptations evolved independently.

mind.lede: Condors are long-lived social birds with ranks, displays and partnerships that can last for life.

studies.title: A pecking order
studies.text: Condors roost together on cliff ledges. Males dominate females and adults dominate juveniles, which affects who gets the best roost sites.

studies.title: Courtship
studies.text: A courting male spreads his wings, inflates his neck and flushes its skin bright yellow, then approaches the female with arched neck, swaying from side to side. Pairs nibble each other and click their bills together.

studies.title: Partners at the carcass
studies.text: Condors can tear open tough hides that smaller vultures cannot, while those vultures are better at finding carcasses by smell; each benefits from the other.

survival.lede: A healthy adult condor has no natural predators. Its risks come from slow breeding and from people.

tactics.title: Fierce nest defence
tactics.text: Condors are not territorial away from the nest, but they defend it vigorously — even against zookeepers in captivity.

tactics.title: Liver first
tactics.text: Condors often open a carcass near the tail end and eat the liver first, then the muscle.

predators: Large birds of prey (eggs and chicks)

threats.title: Lead poisoning
threats.text: Wild condors in Argentina showed high lead levels across more than 4,000 km of their range; exposure has also been found in Chile, Ecuador and Peru. Captive-bred birds had far lower levels.

threats.title: Poison and persecution
threats.text: Condors are persecuted by farmers and lose habitat, and their slow breeding makes every loss hard to replace.

life.lede: A pair raises at most one chick every two to three years, and that chick takes many years to grow up.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: A single egg of about 280 g is laid on a bare cliff ledge, and both parents take turns incubating it.

stages.name: Nestling
stages.text: The helpless chick, covered in grey down, is fed by both parents — the male more often than the female — until it fledges.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Young condors stay with their parents for about two years, in olive-grey and brown plumage.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Condors reach breeding age at 6 to 11 years and are thought to mate for life.

lifespan.value: Estimated about 50 years in the wild; nearly 80 years in captivity

tagline: The fish that looks up through its own forehead
summary: A small twilight-zone fish whose glowing green, tube-shaped eyes sit inside a transparent, fluid-filled shield on its head. It hovers almost motionless, scanning the faint light above for the silhouettes of prey, then rotates its eyes forward to feed.
ability: rotating tubular eyes inside a see-through head

stats.size: Up to about 15 cm
stats.depth: About 460–800 m
stats.range: North Pacific, from the Bering Sea to Japan and Baja California
stats.diet: Zooplankton, including small crustaceans and siphonophores

facts.title: A see-through head
facts.text: A transparent, fluid-filled shield covers the top of the head. It was missing from most older descriptions, probably because the fragile dome was destroyed when fish were hauled up in nets.

facts.title: Eyes that swivel
facts.text: Its tubular eyes were long thought to be fixed, staring only upward. Robison and Reisenbichler (2008) used ROV video and a live, net-caught fish to show the eyes rotate forward as the fish tilts to feed.

facts.title: Green sunglasses
facts.text: The tubular eyes are capped by bright green lenses. MBARI suggests the green pigment filters out direct sunlight, helping the fish pick out the bioluminescent glow of prey overhead.

facts.title: Hovering hunter
facts.text: Large, flat fins let it hang nearly motionless and manoeuvre precisely. Its pointed mouth is small, but its gut is large, and two net-caught fish had jelly fragments in their stomachs.

facts.title: Thief among tentacles?
facts.text: Researchers speculate it may pick prey out of the stinging tentacles of siphonophores (colonial jellies), with its clear shield protecting its eyes from stings — an idea still to be confirmed.

notes: Only one licence-compatible Commons image of M. microstoma exists (fresh trawl specimen held in a hand, NOAA public domain; Commons file description says 'a barreleye fish (Opisthoproctidae)' but it is filed in Category:Macropinna microstoma and the transparent head shield and tubular eyes match). MBARI's in-situ ROV images are copyrighted. 'Barreleye' is also used for other Opisthoproctidae. Conservation status per FishBase (IUCN Not Evaluated). WoRMS places the family in Argentiniformes; class given as Teleostei per WoRMS.

anatomy.lede: The barreleye is a small, dark fish built around its eyes: two green-lensed tubes inside a clear, fluid-filled dome.

hotspots.label: Transparent shield
hotspots.text: A tough, flexible, see-through skin covers the top of the head. It attaches to the scales behind the head and to clear bones that protect the eyes from the side.

hotspots.label: Tubular eye
hotspots.text: The tubular eyes sit in a fluid-filled chamber under the shield and can rotate through an arc of about 75 degrees, from looking up to looking forward.

hotspots.label: Small mouth
hotspots.text: Its name means 'large fins, small mouth'. The small, pointed mouth suggests it picks out prey precisely.

hotspots.label: Broad fins
hotspots.text: Large, flat fins let it hang nearly motionless and manoeuvre with precision.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: The dorsal fin has 11 soft rays and no spines.

hotspots.label: Dark body
hotspots.text: Adults are dark brown. Their digestive system is large, suggesting they can eat both small drifting animals and jellies.

senses.lede: In the twilight zone, the last of the sunlight comes from straight above, and the barreleye's senses are tuned to it.

senses.name: Light-gathering eyes
senses.text: The tubular shape concentrates light, letting the fish see the silhouettes of prey against the faint sunlight from above. The trade-off, in tubular eyes generally, is a very narrow field of view.

senses.name: Green filters
senses.text: Green pigment in the lenses may filter out direct sunlight, helping the fish tell it apart from the bioluminescent glow of prey overhead.

senses.name: Eyes that look sideways too?
senses.text: Other barreleyes in its family have light-sensitive pouches on their eyes that extend their view to the sides and below. The barreleye's own eyes have so far had only a preliminary description.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: The two spots above the mouth that look like eyes are actually its nares, olfactory organs comparable to our nostrils.

body.lede: Two features set this fish apart: a head you can see through, and eyes that are not fixed in place.

systems.title: A fluid-filled dome
systems.text: The eyes sit in a chamber of fluid under the clear shield. This fragile structure was missing from older descriptions, probably because it was destroyed when fish were hauled up in nets.

systems.title: Two ways to feed
systems.text: It can either tilt its whole body upwards while keeping its eyes locked on a target, or stay level and roll its eyes forward as food sinks towards its mouth.

mind.lede: Almost everything known about how the barreleye lives comes from a few encounters with underwater robots.

studies.title: Watching the eyes turn
studies.text: ROV video off central California, at 600 to 800 m, showed barreleyes hanging still with eyes glowing green in the lights. A net-caught fish kept alive for several hours on board confirmed that it rotated its eyes as it turned its body upright.

studies.title: A working hypothesis
studies.text: The researchers proposed that the fish waits horizontally with eyes up, then rotates its eyes forward and swims upwards when it spots prey such as a drifting jelly.

studies.title: A rare sighting in 4K
studies.text: A barreleye filmed about 600 m down, roughly 90 km off California, was only MBARI's eleventh observation of the species. The team spent about 20 minutes filming it, testing different lighting to show off its clear head.

tagline: By day a tight fist, by night a living plankton net
summary: A relative of brittle stars whose arms fork again and again into a fine, tangled mesh. By day it hides curled into a ball. At night it climbs to a high perch on a coral or sea fan and opens into a net close to a metre across to catch plankton drifting on the current.

stats.size: Arms spread to nearly 1 m across
stats.depth: Shallow water, down to about 30 m
stats.range: Western Atlantic, from North Carolina to Brazil, including the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico
stats.diet: Plankton, small shrimps and even juvenile fishes

facts.title: Branching arms
facts.text: Like other echinoderms it is built on five rays. In basket stars these arms split again and again into ever finer branches, a trait found only in the order Euryalida.

facts.title: A net that closes
facts.text: When a tiny branch touches food, the smallest branchlets curl around it to form a ball, which is passed to the mouth. Small shrimps and juvenile fish can be caught this way.

facts.title: Microscopic grabbers
facts.text: Its arms are ringed with bands of pedicellariae, tiny grasping structures that in this family help catch prey.

facts.title: Shy of torchlight
facts.text: Shine a light on a feeding basket star at night and it slowly curls up. Within several minutes it shrinks into a fist-sized bundle.

facts.title: Feeds facing the flow
facts.text: It feeds only when conditions suit. In moderate currents it spreads its arms and turns them toward the flow, but it keeps them folded when the current is too strong.

references.title: Astrophyton muricatum (Lamarck, 1816)
Astrophyton (giant basket star)
A Sister-Group Comparison of Branching and Pedicellariae in Brittlestars (Echinodermata: Ophiuroidea) — 2023

image.alt: Top view of a basket star on a black background. A small, spotted orange central disc gives rise to arms that fork repeatedly into fine, coiling, salmon-pink branches spreading across the whole frame.
image.caption: A giant basket star photographed by the Florida Museum of Natural History, showing its repeatedly forking arms.
image.creator: François Michonneau

gallery.alt: At night on a reef, a basket star perched on a boulder coral spreads a huge orange, lace-like fan of finely branching arms, with its coiled central body at the middle.
gallery.caption: Fully spread for night-time feeding on a reef in Panama.
gallery.creator: A H (via iNaturalist)

notes: We chose Astrophyton muricatum over Gorgonocephalus: Commons has very few live Gorgonocephalus photos and many good, correctly placed Astrophyton ones. Astrophyton is monotypic, which makes its ID easier. Two Diego Delso photos labelled A. muricatum from the Red Sea (Egypt; Jeddah, Saudi Arabia) were REJECTED as misidentified, because this species is western Atlantic only. The hero is a Florida Museum (FLMNH) photograph by echinoderm researcher F. Michonneau, probably a freshly collected animal; the setting is assumed to be 'specimen'. Gallery caveat: the iNaturalist image is from Panama, which has both Atlantic and Pacific coasts. The coral looks Caribbean, but please verify the observation locality before publishing. Wikipedia states 'eight arms'; we did not use that because basket stars have five branched rays (PMC 2023). The 'giants' category rests on the ~1 m arm spread and the common name 'giant basket star'; drop it if you want a stricter reading. Most behavioural facts come from Wikipedia, citing Jangoux 1990 (Echinoderm Research).

anatomy.lede: A basket star is a small central disc with arms that fork again and again, until the animal becomes a living net nearly a metre wide.

hotspots.label: Central disc
hotspots.text: All the arms grow out of a small central disc. Food caught by the arms is passed back here to the mouth.

hotspots.label: Arm base
hotspots.text: Near the disc the arms overlap one another. This may create turbulence that helps the outer branches catch food or brings more food within reach.

hotspots.label: Forking arm
hotspots.text: Each arm divides again and again into finer branches. Among brittle stars, only the order Euryalida has branching arms.

hotspots.label: Fine branchlets
hotspots.text: The finest branches make a small-meshed net that can catch a wide range of prey.

hotspots.label: Grasping bands
hotspots.text: Raised bands of pedicellariae, tiny grasping structures used for catching prey, ring the arms and give them a banded look.

hotspots.label: Coiled tip
hotspots.text: The tips can coil tightly. When a branchlet touches food, the smallest branches curl around it into a ball that is passed to the mouth.

senses.lede: A basket star responds to light, touch and the flow of water, and decides from moment to moment whether to feed.

senses.name: Light
senses.text: Shine a torch on a feeding basket star at night and it slowly curls up, taking several minutes to become a fist-sized bundle.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: When a branchlet touches a food particle, the smallest branches close around it, catching animals as large as small shrimps and juvenile fish.

senses.name: Current
senses.text: It feeds only when conditions suit, turning its arms to face the current at moderate speeds and keeping them folded when the flow is too strong.

body.lede: Branching arms and grasping bands are rare among brittle stars. In basket stars they work together as a net that catches food against the current.

systems.title: More arm, same five rays
systems.text: Echinoderms are built on five rays. Some increase the length of their food-gathering arms by adding extra rays, but basket stars branch the original five instead, as only suspension feeders do.

systems.title: Grabbers for catching prey
systems.text: Every member of the basket star's family, the Gorgonocephalidae, has pedicellariae on its arms, and in this family they are used mainly or only for catching prey.

systems.title: Why branch?
systems.text: Branching may help gorgonocephalid basket stars use their pedicellariae to catch zooplankton on the upstream side, unlike unbranched relatives that catch food downstream on mucus-covered tube feet.

mind.lede: The basket star follows a daily routine: hiding by day and climbing high to feed at night.

studies.title: A night-time climber
studies.text: It is nocturnal. At night it climbs to the top of large corals or sea fans, holding on with the lower parts of its arms, and spreads the rest in a bowl shape to catch plankton.

studies.title: Hiding by day
studies.text: By day it curls into a tight ball and retreats to the base of its coral or sea fan, or into a crevice, protecting itself from predators.

studies.title: A matching lodger
studies.text: The shrimp Periclimenes perryae often lives on the giant basket star, and larger shrimps are usually coloured to match their host.

tagline: A giant cape-wearing female and a walnut-sized male
summary: The violet blanket octopus drifts in warm open seas, never resting on the seafloor. Females unfurl a vast, colourful web of skin between their arms like a cape, and can grow to about 2 m, while males stay only a few centimetres long: one of the most extreme size gaps between the sexes in any large animal.

stats.size: Females up to about 2 m; males about 2.4 cm
stats.depth: Near-surface open ocean (epipelagic zone)
stats.range: Warm seas worldwide
stats.diet: Carnivore

facts.title: Extreme size gap
facts.text: Females can reach about 2 m long while males stay around 2.4 cm. By weight the sexes differ by a factor of at least 10,000; National Geographic puts it as high as 40,000.

facts.title: A cape for defence
facts.text: When threatened, a female spreads the sheets of webbing between her arms to look far bigger. The web can also tear away if a predator bites it, letting her escape.

facts.title: Borrowed stingers
facts.text: Small blanket octopuses have been seen carrying torn-off tentacles of the Portuguese man o' war, likely brandished as weapons. How they handle the stinging cells is not fully understood.

facts.title: A detachable arm
facts.text: The tiny male stores sperm in a special arm (the hectocotylus), which he detaches and gives to the female. She keeps it in her body until she is ready to fertilise her eggs.

facts.title: Males rarely seen
facts.text: Males are so small and elusive that the first live male was not seen by scientists until 2002, off the Great Barrier Reef.

notes: No freely licensed in-situ underwater photo of T. violaceus on Commons; available photos are beach-stranded/handheld specimens (South Padre Island), a museum jar, or multi-panel ZooKeys figures. Used Vérany's public-domain plate (portrait, includes plate margins/text). Tremoctopus robsoni photo rejected (different species). The NatGeo page covers the genus (Tremoctopus spp.); size ratio sources differ (10,000 vs 40,000 by weight) — both given. Wikipedia attributes the size/dimorphism and first-live-male facts to Norman et al. 2002 (NZ J. Mar. Freshw. Res.), and IUCN LC to Allcock 2014. Whether the octopus is immune to man o' war stings is disputed (NatGeo says immune; Wikipedia says unknown), so framed as hypothesis.

anatomy.lede: A mature female is mostly cape: two long arms joined by a broad web that she can unfurl, roll up or cut loose.

hotspots.label: Web
hotspots.text: Sheets of webbing stretch between the long dorsal arms of the female. She unfurls them to look bigger when threatened.

hotspots.label: Dorsal arm
hotspots.text: Young blanket octopuses have been found with fragments of Portuguese man o' war tentacles stuck to the suckers of these upper arms.

hotspots.label: Shorter arm
hotspots.text: The other arms are short and lined with suckers, and are not joined by the web.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Plates like this one were drawn from females in the 19th century. Scientists did not meet a live male until 2002.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The female stores the detached arms of males inside her mantle cavity until she is ready to fertilise her eggs.

body.lede: Male and female blanket octopuses are built for completely different lives, and their bodies show it.

systems.title: The most unequal pair
systems.text: Few large animals show a bigger size gap between the sexes. One idea is that big females can carry more eggs, while staying small lets males keep using stolen stinging tentacles, a defence that only works at small sizes.

systems.title: A detachable arm
systems.text: The male's third right arm, the hectocotylus, holds a sperm-filled pouch. When he is ready to mate, the pouch ruptures, he cuts the arm off and gives it to a female, who may store several from different males.

systems.title: A huge supply of eggs
systems.text: In a mature Mediterranean female, researchers estimated more than 105,000 oocytes (developing eggs).

genome.lede: No nuclear genome has been published for the blanket octopus. Most genetic work has used mitochondrial DNA to sort out which species is which.

findings.title: Mitochondrial genome
findings.text: Its complete mitochondrial genome is 16,015 base pairs long and holds 13 protein-coding genes, 2 rRNA genes and 22 tRNA genes.

findings.title: Two species, not one
findings.text: Genetic comparison of a Gulf of Mexico female with Pacific sequences suggests that blanket octopuses in the Pacific previously called T. violaceus are a separate species, T. gracilis.

mind.lede: Blanket octopuses live far out in the open ocean, so most of what is known comes from chance encounters.

studies.title: Armed with stingers
studies.text: Young blanket octopuses were found with many pieces of Portuguese man o' war tentacles attached to their upper arms, which they may use for attack and defence.

studies.title: The first living male
studies.text: Scientists encountered a live male for the first time, off the Great Barrier Reef, confirming how tiny males are compared with females.

studies.title: Dropping arms to save eggs
studies.text: A mature female found in the Gulf of Mexico showed evidence of autotomy, shedding parts of her body, as a way of protecting her egg mass.

survival.lede: With no seafloor to hide on, a blanket octopus defends itself by looking huge or carrying weapons it has stolen.

tactics.title: Unfurling the cape
tactics.text: When attacked, a female can roll up her web and then unfurl it, looking much larger and possibly scaring a predator away.

tactics.title: Cutting the cape loose
tactics.text: The web can tear away when a predator bites it, distracting the attacker while the octopus escapes.

tactics.title: Borrowed stingers
tactics.text: Males and females smaller than about 7 cm have been reported carrying man o' war tentacles. This defence works only at small sizes.

life.lede: Male and female lead very different lives. The male matures tiny and dies soon after mating, while the female keeps growing to lay a huge batch of eggs.

stages.name: Young octopus
stages.text: Small juveniles drift in the open ocean, where some carry pieces of man o' war tentacles for protection.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: The male detaches his sperm-filled arm and hands it to the female. Sperm packets found in a still-maturing female suggest females may mate with several males before they are fully mature.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: The female lays more than 100,000 eggs, then retrieves the stored arm and spreads the sperm over the egg mass.

tagline: Not ugly—just out of its depth
summary: Famous as the 'world's ugliest animal', the smooth-head blobfish only looks like a melted frown after being hauled up from the deep. At home on the seafloor 600–1,200 m down, its soft body is held in shape by the pressure and it looks like a plump, ordinary fish.

stats.size: Up to about 38 cm
stats.depth: About 600–1,200 m
stats.range: Continental slope off southern and south-eastern Australia, including Tasmania
stats.diet: Not well documented

facts.title: The famous face is damage
facts.text: The viral 'blob' photo shows a decompressed dead specimen. Hauled up rapidly from over a kilometre down, the fish's jelly-like body collapses at the surface, distorting its features.

facts.title: Built for pressure
facts.text: Blobfish have no swim bladder and very soft, barely hardened bones. That lets them withstand crushing deep-sea pressure without cracking—but leaves nothing to hold their shape in air.

facts.title: What it really looks like
facts.text: Alive and at the right pressure it is probably far more fish-like, as the original 1926 drawing shows: plump and soft-bodied, but with normal fins and a recognisable face.

facts.title: A 'withered' name
facts.text: Marcidus is Latin for withered or weak, probably because its head, body and fins are covered in loose, flabby skin that hides the features beneath.

facts.title: Which blob was 'Mr Blobby'?
facts.text: The famous 2003 specimen, nicknamed Mr Blobby and kept at the Australian Museum, was trawled off New Zealand. It is only 'possibly' this species; some sources assign it to a close relative.

references.title: Psychrolutes marcidus (McCulloch, 1926)
Smooth-head Blobfish, Psychrolutes marcidus
'World's ugliest animal' contest took a blobfish out of water
Psychrolutes marcidus – Smooth-head blobfish

image.alt: Black-and-white drawing of a soft-bodied fish with a large rounded head, big eye, wide mouth, broad fan-like pectoral fin, long dorsal and anal fins and a rounded tail.
image.caption: The original illustration from McCulloch's 1926 description of the species, drawn from a trawled specimen: far more fish-like than the famous 'blob' photo.
image.creator: Allan Riverstone McCulloch (Biological Results of the F.I.S. Endeavour)

notes: No licence-compatible photograph of P. marcidus exists on Commons; the famous 'Mr Blobby' photo (Kerryn Parkinson/NORFANZ) is copyrighted. Hero is the type illustration (McCulloch 1926, Endeavour results pl. LV fig. 2 — matches the citation in Fishes of Australia); it is only 1000×395 px and was NOT upscaled, so it needs a contained/letterboxed layout rather than a full-bleed crop. Rejected: 'Two Psychrolutes marcidus.jpg' (Rachel Caauwe, CC BY-SA 3.0) — a modern artist's imaginative painting labelled 'in situ', not a scientific record; 'Foul disease' (whiteboard graffiti); 'CBNMS Blob Sculpin' (different species, Psychrolutes phrictus). Diet: no fetched source documented it, hence 'Not well documented'. Mr Blobby's ID: Science News says 'possibly' P. marcidus; BBC Science Focus says P. microporos. Range per Fishes of Australia ('endemic'); some sources extend it to New Zealand. WoRMS order is Perciformes (older sources: Scorpaeniformes). 'Ugliest animal' title from the 2013 Ugly Animal Preservation Society vote.

anatomy.lede: Drawn from a specimen in 1926, the smooth-head blobfish looks like a plump, soft fish with a big head, not the collapsed blob of internet fame.

hotspots.label: Large head
hotspots.text: The head is big and rounded, about 40% of the body length, with a strongly curved profile from the blunt snout to the back of the head.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: The eyes are moderately large and set far apart: the space between them is more than twice the width of an eye.

hotspots.label: Mouth
hotspots.text: The large mouth reaches back to below the rear edge of the eyes, and both jaws carry a broad band of tiny, bristle-like teeth.

hotspots.label: Pectoral fin
hotspots.text: The pectoral fins are large and broadly angular, each with 24 or 25 rays.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fins
hotspots.text: There are two dorsal fins, but thick, fleshy skin wraps them so that they look like one, separated only by a shallow notch.

hotspots.label: Pelvic fin
hotspots.text: The small pelvic fins sit on the chest, beneath where the pectoral fins begin.

hotspots.label: Tail fin
hotspots.text: The rounded tail fin is moderately large, and the long anal and dorsal fins join the tail stalk by a membrane.

body.lede: The blobfish's soft body is not a flaw. It suits life on the continental slope, 600 to 1,200 m down, where the pressure is crushing.

systems.title: No swim bladder
systems.text: Many fish have a gas-filled swim bladder that expands violently when they are hauled up from depth. Blobfish have none.

systems.title: Barely bony bones
systems.text: Species of Psychrolutes have very weak, barely hardened bones, so they look somewhat blob-like even in life. Soft bones let the body compress under pressure without cracking.

systems.title: Loose, scaleless skin
systems.text: The skin is smooth, has no scales and hangs loose and flabby over the body and fins. Its lateral line, the sensory canal fish use to detect water movement, is obvious only on the head.

tagline: An upside-down sea slug that steals stingers from its prey
summary: A small nudibranch about 3 cm long that floats belly-up at the ocean surface, buoyed by a swallowed air bubble. It eats venomous drifters such as the Portuguese man o' war and stores their unfired stinging cells in its finger-like cerata, turning its prey's weapons into its own defence.

stats.size: Usually about 3 cm long
stats.depth: Floats at the sea surface
stats.range: Open ocean, tropical to temperate waters worldwide; often washed ashore
stats.diet: Floating cnidarians such as bluebottles/men o' war, by-the-wind sailors and blue buttons; also fish in lab trials

facts.title: Floats upside down
facts.text: Air swallowed into its stomach keeps it at the surface, belly-side up. Its blue underside faces the sky, while its silvery back faces the deep.

facts.title: Camouflage both ways
facts.text: Its colouring is countershading: from above, the blue blends with the sea, and from below, the silver-grey blends with the bright surface.

facts.title: Borrowed weapons
facts.text: It eats Physalia and other floating cnidarians and stores their stinging capsules, called nematocysts, in sacs at the tips of its cerata. This theft is called kleptocnidae. Handling one can cause a painful sting.

facts.title: Cerata used as hands
facts.text: In 2025 researchers filmed captive blue dragons using their front cerata like arms to grab whitebait and jellyfish. This suggests they are more generalist hunters than once thought.

facts.title: Look-alike species
facts.text: A similar blue dragon once lumped as Glaucus marginatus turned out to be four separate species. Genetic studies show that G. atlanticus populations are separated by ocean basins.

image.alt: Top-down view of a blue dragon sea slug in shallow water. Its slender body has a dark blue stripe and pale blue-white sides, and three pairs of fan-like clusters of pointed blue-and-white cerata spread out from it like wings, over a blurred olive-green rock.
image.caption: A blue dragon washed ashore at Bronte Beach, Sydney, photographed in a rock pool.
image.creator: Sylke Rohrlach

notes: Setting: a stranded animal photographed in a shallow rock pool, not its true open-ocean habitat. The photographer labels the animal G. atlanticus. Note that the G. marginatus complex also occurs off Sydney and looks similar, so photo IDs carry some uncertainty. Some Commons images show G. marginatus or G. bennettae alongside G. atlanticus; we avoided those. The 'venomous' category reflects its stolen nematocysts, which can sting humans; the slug itself does not make venom. We did NOT use the popular claim that it stings 'more powerfully than the man o' war' (Wikipedia), because it is weakly supported. Size, countershading and the cryptic-species details come from Wikipedia, which cites Churchill et al. 2014.

anatomy.lede: The blue dragon is a sea slug turned upside down: its foot faces the sky, and its six fans of cerata spread like wings.

hotspots.label: Head
hotspots.text: The head has dark blue stripes. Inside the mouth, a radula with serrated teeth and a strong jaw let it grasp prey and chip pieces off.

hotspots.label: Front cerata
hotspots.text: The first pair of cerata sits on short stalks. In aquaria, blue dragons use these front cerata like hands to grab fish and jellyfish.

hotspots.label: Cerata tips
hotspots.text: The tip of each ceras holds a cnidosac, a sac where stinging cells taken from its prey are stored.

hotspots.label: Blue foot
hotspots.text: What faces up is actually the foot, the underside in other slugs. Its blue colour blends with the sea when seen from above.

hotspots.label: Rear cerata
hotspots.text: The cerata are set in a single row in each group and can number up to 84 in total.

hotspots.label: Tapering tail
hotspots.text: The body is flat and tapers to a point behind.

body.lede: Unlike most sea slugs, which crawl on the seabed, blue dragons spend their whole lives at the sea surface.

systems.title: A bubble for a float
systems.text: All Glaucus species float on the surface using their cerata and air bubbles held in the stomach. Because of where the gas sits, they float upside down.

systems.title: A store of stolen stings
systems.text: Stinging capsules from swallowed prey pass through the gut to special cells in the cnidosacs at the cerata tips. They are fired off if the slug is attacked.

systems.title: Muscles for grasping
systems.text: A well-developed layer of muscle fibres lies under the skin of the cerata and at their bases, which may explain how the front cerata can move so skilfully.

mind.lede: Blue dragons are hard to keep alive in captivity, so their behaviour has only recently been watched closely.

studies.title: Eating from below
studies.text: In the Sargasso Sea, blue dragons showed no preference among their floating prey, but usually fed by crawling underneath and eating the prey's underside.

studies.title: Hands for hunting
studies.text: Captive blue dragons pointed their front cerata at live whitebait, grabbed them, twisted to aim their mouths and ate the fish from the gills to the tail. They caught every cnidarian jellyfish offered, but no comb jellies.

studies.title: Cannibals
studies.text: In captivity, individuals sometimes attack and eat each other.

survival.lede: Floating at the surface, the blue dragon cannot hide, so it relies on colour and borrowed weapons.

tactics.title: Countershading
tactics.text: The blue foot faces the sky and the silver-grey back faces the deep, hiding the slug from predators above and below.

tactics.title: Stolen stings
tactics.text: It keeps stinging cells from its prey, likely for defence against predators, and can give people a painful sting.

tactics.title: Washed ashore
tactics.text: Once over the continental shelf, winds and storms can push blue dragons towards land. Along the coast of Brazil, strandings happen in summer.

life.lede: Each blue dragon is both male and female, and after mating both partners can lay eggs.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: Blue dragons are hermaphrodites. Unlike most nudibranchs, which mate with their right sides together, they mate with their undersides facing.

stages.name: Egg strings
stages.text: Both partners can then lay strings of eggs. Blue dragons from the Sargasso Sea bred in the lab and laid large numbers of eggs, which may be an adaptation to heavy losses at sea.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults drift on winds and currents and feed on floating cnidarians such as bluebottles, by-the-wind sailors and blue buttons.

lifespan.value: Up to about a year under the right conditions

tagline: A pocket-sized octopus with a lethal warning sign
summary: Barely the size of a golf ball, the greater blue-ringed octopus hides camouflaged among reef rubble. Disturb it and about 60 electric-blue rings flash on its skin: a warning backed by tetrodotoxin, a nerve poison potent enough to kill a human.

stats.size: Up to about 10 cm, arms included
stats.depth: Shallow coastal waters
stats.range: Tropical and subtropical Indo-West Pacific, from Sri Lanka to the Philippines, Australia and Vanuatu
stats.diet: Small crabs, shrimps and molluscs

facts.title: Rings that switch on
facts.text: Its roughly 60 blue rings contain mirror-like layered reflectors. Muscles, under direct nerve control, open and close skin around each ring to flash it in a fraction of a second: a mechanism not known in other cephalopods.

facts.title: Tetrodotoxin venom
facts.text: Its bite can deliver tetrodotoxin (TTX), the same nerve poison found in pufferfish. TTX blocks the channels nerves use to fire, causing paralysis, and there is no known antidote.

facts.title: Who makes the poison?
facts.text: Bacteria living in the octopus's salivary glands have been proposed as the true source of its TTX, but early evidence was weak and the question remains open.

facts.title: Bluff first, bite last
facts.text: It spends most of its time hidden and well camouflaged. It flashes its rings when disturbed and bites only when strongly harassed, so it is dangerous mainly to people who handle it.

facts.title: A mother's last clutch
facts.text: The female carries her clutch of eggs beneath her arms until they hatch, not feeding during that time, and dies soon after.

notes: Venom confirmed as tetrodotoxin (TTX). The Mäthger et al. abstract (PubMed) states the neurotoxin can kill a human; the 'no antidote' and brooding details come from Wikipedia (secondary). Clutch size and brooding duration vary between sources (Wikipedia gives both 50–100 and 60–100 eggs, ~1 month and ~50 days), so no numbers used. Depth: sources say 'shallow waters'; depthRange 0–20 m is an approximation for the gauge. Rings in the alt photo: whether the eggs are visible is subtle in the frame; the Commons title states 'with eggs'.

anatomy.lede: The greater blue-ringed octopus is about the size of a golf ball, and its whole skin is a warning sign.

hotspots.label: Blue ring
hotspots.text: The rings are 7 to 8 mm across, larger than in other blue-ringed octopuses, which helps tell this species apart. Each is bordered by a black line that sharpens the contrast.

hotspots.label: Dark blotch
hotspots.text: Dark chromatophores sit beneath and around each ring to boost contrast. Unusually for a cephalopod, there are none on top of the ring.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Blue lines run through the eyes, a characteristic marking of this species.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The background colour changes with its surroundings and mood, from yellow ochre to light brown, or whitish when the octopus is inactive.

hotspots.label: Arms
hotspots.text: The eight arms are relatively short. It hunts by pouncing on prey, seizing it with its arms and pulling it to its beak.

body.lede: The blue-ringed octopus carries enough poison to kill a person, and it has evolved ways to show it off and to survive it.

systems.title: Rings on a switch
systems.text: Each ring contains inert multilayer reflectors tucked into a pouch of skin. Relaxing muscles above the reflectors and contracting muscles around the ring opens the pouch and flashes the blue.

systems.title: Poison throughout the body
systems.text: TTX is concentrated in the posterior salivary gland but also lies just under the skin of the mantle and arms and in channels through the dermis. Its presence in blood-rich organs such as the gills and hearts suggests it is carried in the blood.

systems.title: Immune to its own poison
systems.text: TTX works by blocking sodium channels in nerves. This octopus has three amino-acid changes in its sodium channel that reduce TTX binding, matching changes that evolved separately in TTX-bearing fish and salamanders.

systems.title: Two kinds of venom
systems.text: Its saliva carries the products of two kinds of venom glands: one used to subdue crustacean prey, and tetrodotoxin, thought to serve mainly for defence.

mind.lede: Most of the time this octopus is hidden and camouflaged. Its most dramatic behaviour, the ring flash, is reserved for emergencies.

studies.title: How the rings flash
studies.text: Bathing the skin in chemicals that act on colour cells did not change the rings, showing the blue comes from fixed reflectors. The fast flashes are driven by muscles under direct nerve control, a mechanism not reported before in cephalopods.

studies.title: Mating blind
studies.text: Whether one octopus touches another does not depend on sex, size or who lives there. Male–female matings last about 160 minutes, but male–male encounters about 30 seconds, suggesting a male cannot tell the sex of his partner until he inserts his mating arm.

studies.title: A tidy doorway
studies.text: Like other octopuses it lives in a den, and the entrance is easy to spot because it is littered with empty shells and crab legs from past meals.

survival.lede: The blue-ringed octopus hides first, warns second and bites only as a last resort.

tactics.title: Camouflage
tactics.text: It spends much of its time hidden, showing effective camouflage patterns.

tactics.title: Warning flash
tactics.text: When disturbed it flashes its rings, an exceptionally fast and conspicuous warning display.

tactics.title: A deadly bite
tactics.text: Strongly harassed, it bites and can deliver a neurotoxin able to kill a person. The bite is painless, and no antidote is known.

life.lede: A blue-ringed octopus lives fast: it hatches the size of a pea, is mating by the following autumn and dies after breeding.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays about 50 to 100 eggs and carries them under her arms until they hatch, without feeding.

stages.name: Paralarva
stages.text: Hatchlings are about the size of a pea and drift briefly in the plankton before settling on the seabed.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Young octopuses grow quickly on the reef, rubble and sand of shallow coasts, feeding on small crabs, shrimps and molluscs.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: They mature quickly and begin mating the following autumn. Males die after mating, and females die soon after their eggs hatch.

lifespan.value: About 2 years

tagline: The largest animal that has ever lived
summary: A slender, mottled blue-grey rorqual that can pass 30 metres and 150 tonnes, making it the largest animal known to have existed. It lives almost entirely on krill, gulping huge mouthfuls of water and straining them through baleen, and its low, powerful calls carry across ocean basins.
ability: lunge feeding: engulfing and filtering vast mouthfuls of krill

stats.size: Up to about 33 m and 150 tonnes in the Antarctic; about 27 m in the North Atlantic and North Pacific
stats.depth: Feeds in the upper ocean; tagged whales dived to 204 m
stats.range: All oceans except the Arctic; summers on polar feeding grounds, winters towards the tropics
stats.diet: Almost exclusively krill; occasionally fish and copepods

facts.title: Bigger than any dinosaur
facts.text: NOAA describes the blue whale as the largest animal ever to live on our planet. Antarctic blue whales are the biggest, reaching about 33 m and more than 150 tonnes; females are generally larger than males.

facts.title: A mouthful of krill
facts.text: It swims at a swarm of krill with its mouth open, inflating its pleated throat, then pushes the water out with its tongue while baleen plates hanging from the roof of the mouth hold the krill inside. The biggest whales may eat around 5 tonnes of krill a day.

facts.title: Two beats a minute
facts.text: An electrocardiogram tag on a whale feeding in Monterey Bay recorded heart rates of 4–8 beats a minute during dives, and as low as 2. Back at the surface the heart raced at 25–37 beats a minute.

facts.title: Short, shallow dives
facts.text: For such a big animal it does not dive for long. Seven tagged blue whales off California reached at most 204 m, and their longest dive lasted 14.7 minutes.

facts.title: Songs that are dropping in pitch
facts.text: Recordings going back to the 1960s show that blue whale songs worldwide are slowly getting lower. The song heard off California is now sung about 31% lower than in the 1960s, and no single explanation has been proved.

facts.title: Age written in earwax
facts.text: Scientists estimate a whale's age by counting the layers in the waxy earplugs of dead animals. On that basis blue whales are thought to live for around 80 to 90 years.

anatomy.lede: Seen from the air, a blue whale is mostly a long, slim back: the head glows turquoise just under the surface, and the tail lies more than twenty metres behind it.

hotspots.label: Head and baleen
hotspots.text: Inside the mouth, plates of baleen hang from the upper jaw and work like a sieve. After a gulp, the tongue pushes water out between them and the krill stay behind.

hotspots.label: Blowholes
hotspots.text: The whale breathes through blowholes on top of its head. Tagged blue whales came up to breathe after fairly short dives, the longest lasting 14.7 minutes.

hotspots.label: Blow
hotspots.text: The misty blow is the whale's breath. Between dives its heart speeds up to 25–37 beats a minute as it reloads oxygen.

hotspots.label: Mottled skin
hotspots.text: The blue-grey skin is mottled and looks light blue under water. Each whale's mottling is different, so researchers use it to identify individuals.

hotspots.label: Tail flukes
hotspots.text: The tail drives the whale at about 8 km/h while feeding and travelling, with short bursts of more than 30 km/h.

stats.label: Slowest heart rate recorded on a dive
Krill eaten a day by the largest whales

senses.lede: In a dim, wide ocean a blue whale lives largely by sound. Its calls are among the loudest of any animal, and it listens for other whales across enormous distances.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: NOAA describes blue whales as having excellent hearing. Under the right conditions their calls may be heard by other whales up to about 1,600 km away, and scientists think they may also use sound to find their way.

senses.name: Song
senses.text: Blue whale songs fall into at least ten regional types worldwide. Each type keeps the same units and phrasing for decades, and in any one year singers match each other's pitch to within 3%.

body.lede: Being this big changes how a body works, from a heart that beats only a few times a minute to a way of feeding that only pays off when krill are packed together.

systems.title: A slow heart and an elastic aorta
systems.text: During dives the heart beat only 4–8 times a minute, sometimes just twice. A wide, very stretchy aortic arch is thought to store blood from each beat and keep it flowing during the long pauses.

systems.title: The economics of a lunge
systems.text: Each lunge takes a lot of energy, but models based on tag data suggest blue whales feed nearly ten times more efficiently than other marine mammals. That only works when they target very dense swarms of krill.

systems.title: Dives cut short
systems.text: Tagged blue whales surfaced sooner than their oxygen stores would seem to allow, making at most six lunges per dive. The researchers suggest that costly lunge feeding uses up oxygen fast.

genome.lede: A reference-quality blue whale genome, built from long DNA reads and published in 2024, is being used to look for clues to the species' huge size and long life.

findings.title: A burst of duplicated genes
findings.text: Several genes have been copied many times in the blue whale genome after a recent burst of segmental duplications. Whether this is linked to its giant size still needs study.

findings.title: A growth-gene signal
findings.text: Comparing 11 whales and dolphins, the team found sites in and around the IGF1 growth-factor gene whose DNA letters track body size across cetaceans.

findings.title: Two oceans, long apart
findings.text: Pacific and Atlantic blue whale genomes are both highly varied, and their genetic separation dates back to the last interglacial period.

mind.lede: Blue whales are hard to follow, but long-term recordings and tracking show some patterns in their behaviour.

studies.title: A worldwide drop in pitch
studies.text: Song recordings from the 1960s onwards show that seven of the ten known song types are getting lower. One idea is that, as numbers recover after whaling, males no longer need to sing as loudly and can sing lower.

studies.title: Mostly alone
studies.text: Blue whales sometimes travel in small groups but are more often seen alone or in pairs.

studies.title: Following the krill
studies.text: Most spend summer feeding in polar waters and migrate towards the equator in winter, but some may not migrate at all. Where they go depends mostly on where krill are concentrated.

survival.lede: An adult blue whale has almost nothing to fear from other animals. Its real dangers have come from people.

tactics.title: Sheer size
tactics.text: Size is its main protection: adults reach about 33 m and 150 tonnes in the Antarctic.

tactics.title: Bursts of speed
tactics.text: Although it usually cruises at about 8 km/h, a blue whale can speed up to more than 30 km/h for short bursts.

threats.title: The legacy of whaling
threats.text: Commercial whaling in the early 1900s cut blue whale numbers to a small fraction of what they had been. Numbers are now rising, but the species is still listed as Endangered.

threats.title: Ship strikes
threats.text: Collisions with vessels injure and kill blue whales, especially near ports and in busy shipping lanes, and from large, fast ships.

threats.title: Entanglement
threats.text: Whales can become caught in traps, pots and nets and drag the gear for long distances, which can weaken, injure or kill them.

life.lede: Much of the blue whale's life history is still poorly known; most of what we have are estimates.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Mating and births mostly happen in winter, on or near the warmer breeding grounds.

stages.name: Calf
stages.text: The calf is probably weaned on, or on the way to, the summer feeding grounds. Mothers with young calves are regularly seen in the Gulf of California from December to March.

stages.name: Young whale
stages.text: Sexual maturity is thought to come at between 5 and 15 years old.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females are estimated to give birth about once every two to three years.

lifespan.value: Estimated at around 80–90 years

tagline: A buried ambush hunter with spring-loaded jaws
summary: A giant bristle worm that hides almost its whole body in a mucus-lined burrow, leaving only five striped antennae above the sand. When a fish touches them, its jaws snap shut and drag the prey underground. Recorded specimens approach 3 m long, which makes it a contender for the longest polychaete.

stats.size: Longest recorded specimen about 3 m (299 cm)
stats.depth: Shallow, warm coastal seabeds: intertidal to subtidal sand, rubble and rock
stats.range: Warm waters of the Indo-Pacific and Atlantic (identity of many records uncertain)
stats.diet: Fishes and other passing animals

facts.title: Antennae as bait
facts.text: By day it lies buried with five striped antennae poking out. These sense passing prey and may also work as a lure. Its jaws wait under tension like a sprung trap.

facts.title: Changes tactics at night
facts.text: After dark, it switches from waiting to actively hunting, pushing out of its burrow to snatch passing prey.

facts.title: Fish fight back
facts.text: In Indonesia's Lembeh Strait, groups of young monocle bream were seen 'mobbing' bobbit worms, squirting jets of water at the burrow until the worm sometimes retreated.

facts.title: A 20-million-year-old lair
facts.text: L-shaped fossil burrows up to 2 m long, found in Miocene rocks in Taiwan, closely resemble bobbit worm lairs. They suggest ambush-hunting worms like this were already present about 20 million years ago.

facts.title: Probably several species
facts.text: Many different giant worms have been lumped under this name. Taxonomists warn that some 'bobbit worms' worldwide may be other, even undescribed, species.

references.title: Eunice aphroditois (Pallas, 1788)
Novel mobbing strategies of a fish population against a sessile annelid predator — Lachat & Haag-Wackernagel 2016
A new species of giant Eunice (Eunicidae, Polychaeta, Annelida) from the east coast of Australia (2022)

image.alt: The head of a large worm rising from dark gravelly sand. Its tan, iridescent body segments shimmer blue and green, curved grey jaws spread open, and five striped antennae stick straight up.
image.caption: A bobbit worm with its jaws open, Anilao, Philippines.
image.creator: Rickard Zerpe

notes: WoRMS gives Eunice aphroditois (Pallas, 1788) as the accepted name. Its type locality is Sri Lanka and no type specimen exists. Per the ZooKeys 2022 paper, Indo-Pacific 'bobbit worms' are almost always identified as E. aphroditois, but this name has absorbed several giant species. The hero photo (Philippines) follows that convention; its true species identity cannot be confirmed from a photo. Commons iNaturalist images of slim reddish worms on rock, and a fish-like image ('Eunice aphroditois 33864655'), were rejected. The 299 cm figure is the record specimen cited in Lachat & Haag-Wackernagel 2016. We did not use the popular story that the name refers to females severing males' genitals: no source supports it. Depth is not given in the sources consulted; depthRange 0–40 m is an indicative value for shallow coastal habitat.

anatomy.lede: Almost all of a bobbit worm stays out of sight. What shows above the sand is a head built for one thing: seizing a fish in a fraction of a second.

hotspots.label: Antennae
hotspots.text: Five striped antennae stand up from the head. They are thought to detect prey, and some worms twitch an antenna in a worm-like way that may lure fish closer.

hotspots.label: Jaws
hotspots.text: The curved grey jaws are strong, toothed plates called maxillae, carried on a pharynx that the worm can turn inside out to grab prey.

hotspots.label: Jaw tip
hotspots.text: The jaws are armed with sharp teeth. Bobbit worms are known to bite people and can cause severe wounds.

hotspots.label: Iridescent skin
hotspots.text: The body surface shimmers blue and green in the light. Related giant Eunice worms are also described as iridescent when alive.

hotspots.label: Body segments
hotspots.text: The body is a long chain of segments. In a related giant species, one incomplete specimen nearly a metre long had 520 bristle-bearing segments.

hotspots.label: Side lobe
hotspots.text: Each segment carries a small fleshy side lobe, a parapodium, with bristles; further back, feathery gills grow from them.

hotspots.label: Burrow mouth
hotspots.text: The rest of the worm lies in a mucus-lined burrow. When it pulls back, sliding sand leaves a small crater that marks the spot.

senses.lede: A buried ambush hunter needs to know exactly when something edible is overhead. Touch and sight seem to do most of the work.

senses.name: Antennae
senses.text: By day the worm attacks when its antennae are touched by passing prey. In early field tests, only a lure that moved like a living fish set off a strike.

senses.name: Eyes
senses.text: Two eyes sit on the head. At night even a diver's torch beam can trigger an attack, which suggests sight plays a part.

senses.name: Vibration
senses.text: A closely related giant Eunice from Australia retreats quickly into its burrow when it senses vibration, which makes it very hard to collect.

body.lede: The bobbit worm's body is little more than a long, muscular tube with a deadly front end.

systems.title: A pharynx that turns inside out
systems.text: To feed, the worm shoots out its pharynx and closes its strong toothed maxillae on the prey, then drags it, still alive, down into the sediment.

systems.title: Mucus mortar
systems.text: The burrow is lined with mucus. Fossil burrows thought to be from similar worms are rich in iron, probably because bacteria feeding on the mucus left iron minerals behind.

systems.title: Moving by waves
systems.text: Burrowing worms like this move mainly by waves of muscle contraction along the body, which leaves a smooth-walled tunnel.

mind.lede: A worm has a simple nervous system, but the bobbit worm's ambush is precise, and some of its prey have learned to fight back.

studies.title: Mobbed by young fish
studies.text: Over 90 dives in Indonesia's Lembeh Strait, researchers recorded 54 encounters in which groups of up to seven young monocle bream harassed bobbit worms. The mobbing lasted from 4 to 62 seconds.

studies.title: Water jets at the burrow
studies.text: The fish squirted jets of water at the burrow. Most of the time the worm did not react, but in about a quarter of cases it pulled back completely, and it never caught a mobbing fish.

studies.title: Only moving bait works
studies.text: In preliminary trials, the worms struck only at a lure that moved like a living fish, not at still bait.

studies.title: Two ways to hunt
studies.text: Mature worms keep a permanent burrow and wait for prey, while some use an antenna to imitate a wriggling worm and draw fish within reach.

survival.lede: Little is known about what eats a bobbit worm. Its main defence is simply staying hidden.

tactics.title: Living underground
tactics.text: Keeping almost the whole body in the burrow protects the worm while it waits for prey.

tactics.title: Instant retreat
tactics.text: When harassed, the worm can pull its antennae, or its whole head, back into the sand.

tactics.title: Hard to spot
tactics.text: Bobbit worms are spread thinly: only four were found in 15,000 square metres of seabed at the Lembeh Strait study site.

tagline: A dolphin that calls its friends by name
summary: A big, sociable dolphin of warm and temperate seas, at home everywhere from estuaries and harbours to the open ocean. It hunts with sound, works in teams to trap fish, and each animal develops its own signature whistle that others recognise as an identity call.
ability: echolocation and individually distinctive signature whistles

stats.size: About 1.8–4 m (6–13 ft) long and 136–635 kg (300–1,400 lb); offshore animals are larger than coastal ones
stats.depth: Coastal animals stay shallow; offshore dolphins off Bermuda regularly dive below 200 m at night, to 1,000 m
stats.range: Temperate and tropical waters worldwide, from bays and estuaries to the open ocean
stats.diet: Fish, squid, and crustaceans such as crabs and shrimp

facts.title: A name of its own
facts.text: Each bottlenose dolphin develops a distinctive signature whistle, shaped by vocal learning. Playback experiments showed dolphins still recognise a familiar whistle after every feature of the caller's voice has been removed, so the identity lies in the whistle's shape.

facts.title: The dolphin in the mirror
facts.text: Two captive bottlenose dolphins marked with ink used a mirror to inspect the marked parts of their bodies. Mirror self-recognition was previously known only in humans and great apes.

facts.title: Teamwork at dinner
facts.text: Bottlenose dolphins hunt alone or together, herding fish into tight groups and taking turns to charge through the school, or pinning fish against sandbars and seawalls. They find prey by echolocation or simply by listening.

facts.title: Swallowed whole
facts.text: Despite a mouth full of teeth, a bottlenose dolphin does not chew. It grips a fish in its teeth and swallows it whole, head first.

facts.title: Deep divers offshore
facts.text: Satellite tags on offshore bottlenose dolphins near Bermuda recorded dives to 1,000 m and lasting up to 13.8 minutes, mostly at night. Coastal bottlenose dolphins, by contrast, are shallow divers.

facts.title: A long childhood
facts.text: After a pregnancy of about 12 months, a calf nurses for around 20 months and usually stays with its mother for three to six years. Females as old as 45 have given birth.
