notes: Taxonomy per WoRMS (AphiaID 137111; WoRMS places Delphinidae in order Cetartiodactyla). The IUCN assessment page blocks scripted access; the DOI was confirmed through Crossref (Wells, Natoli & Braulik; assessed 13 May 2018, published 2019) and the Least Concern category through the IUCN SSC Cetacean Specialist Group's March 2019 update. Size range converted from NOAA's 6–13 ft and 300–1,400 lb. The 1,000 m depth record comes from offshore dolphins off Bermuda that Fahlman et al. (2023) call 'Tursiops spp.'; they are the offshore ecotype long treated as T. truncatus. Bottlenose dolphin taxonomy is in flux (Tursiops aduncus and, more recently, Tamanend's bottlenose dolphin T. erebennus are now recognised), so famous studies of Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins, such as sponge-carrying at Shark Bay, were deliberately left out. The mirror-recognition study used two captive dolphins. Images are all NOAA/NPS public domain; the hero and pod photos carry no location in their NOAA captions (Commons files the hero under Stellwagen Bank NMS); the Everglades photo is from the Gulf coast of Florida.

anatomy.lede: Every part of a bottlenose dolphin is shaped for life in water: a smooth, torpedo-shaped body with no hair, no external ears and no hind limbs, steered by flippers and a tall fin.

hotspots.label: Beak (rostrum)
hotspots.text: Like all modern whales and dolphins, its skull is 'telescoped': the jaws are drawn out into a tapering beak and the nostrils have moved to the top of the head, so it can breathe while swimming.

hotspots.label: Toothed jaws
hotspots.text: The teeth grip slippery prey but do no chewing; fish are swallowed whole, head first.

hotspots.label: Flipper
hotspots.text: The front limbs are flippers, used with the dorsal fin and tail flukes for steering and swimming.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: The dorsal fin is tall and curved and sits near the middle of the back.

hotspots.label: Streamlined body
hotspots.text: A fusiform, hairless body reduces turbulence, letting the dolphin cruise at speed. The back is dark to light grey and the belly white, sometimes faintly pink.

senses.lede: In water that is often murky or dark, the bottlenose dolphin lives in a world of sound, and it keeps in close physical contact with its companions.

senses.name: Echolocation
senses.text: It sends out high-frequency clicks and listens for the echoes to find prey, a sense humans lack entirely.

senses.name: Passive listening
senses.text: Dolphins also find prey simply by listening for the sounds fish make, without clicking, and use sound to communicate with their group.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: Gentle body contact such as rubbing is a regular part of social life, alongside play and aggression.

body.lede: A warm-blooded, air-breathing mammal that lives its whole life at sea needs special plumbing for warmth, sleep and breath-holding.

systems.title: Keeping warm
systems.text: Blubber, a body large relative to its surface, and vascular shunts that cool chosen organs keep its temperature steady. Its metabolism rises if the water drops below about 13 °C or climbs above 28 °C.

systems.title: Half-asleep
systems.text: A dolphin must surface to breathe, so it rests one side of its brain at a time while slowing down, staying conscious enough to breathe and react.

systems.title: Holding its breath
systems.text: From thousands of tagged dives off Bermuda, researchers estimated that adults can stay down for about 9–11 minutes before needing extra recovery time near the surface.

genome.lede: The bottlenose dolphin has one of the best-studied genomes of any marine mammal, used in research on metabolism and ageing.

findings.title: Two parents, two genomes
findings.text: A 2019 assembly from a 36-year-old female improved on the earlier reference genome and was the first for the species to separate the copies inherited from each parent.

findings.title: Chromosome by chromosome
findings.text: The Vertebrate Genomes Project has since produced a chromosome-level assembly of about 2.38 billion base pairs.

findings.title: A conserved karyotype
findings.text: Bottlenose dolphins have 44 chromosomes, the same number as the related Burrunan dolphin and Risso's dolphin.

mind.lede: Experiments and decades of field study have made the bottlenose dolphin a standard example of animal intelligence.

studies.title: Recognising itself
studies.text: Two dolphins marked with ink went to a mirror and twisted to inspect the marks, evidence of mirror self-recognition.

studies.title: Names without voices
studies.text: Dolphins recognised synthetic versions of familiar signature whistles with every feature of the caller's voice removed, showing the whistle's shape alone carries identity.

studies.title: Twenty years of memory
studies.text: Playback of the whistles of former tank mates showed dolphins recognise companions they have not heard for at least 20 years.

studies.title: Hunting plans
studies.text: Wild dolphins herd fish into tight balls, take turns charging the school, and pin prey against sandbars and seawalls.

survival.lede: Safety for a bottlenose dolphin lies in its group.

tactics.title: Shifting groups
tactics.text: Dolphins live in fission–fusion societies: groups from a few animals to more than 100 split and re-form, and adult males often travel in strongly bonded pairs.

tactics.title: Shared babysitting
tactics.text: Females in a group help care for each other's calves and protect them from predators.

tactics.title: Helping the injured
tactics.text: Dolphins have been seen supporting injured companions at the surface and guarding them from threats.

threats.title: Fishing gear
threats.text: Bycatch and entanglement in gillnets, trawls, traps and recreational lines are major threats.

threats.title: Polluted coasts
threats.text: Harmful algal blooms, chemical contaminants such as PCBs and oil spills harm coastal dolphins.

threats.title: Boats and noise
threats.text: Vessel strikes, illegal feeding and harassment, and ocean noise also take a toll.

life.lede: A bottlenose dolphin grows up slowly, with one of the longest childhoods in the sea.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: A single calf is born after a year-long pregnancy, often in warmer months.

stages.name: Calf
stages.text: Newborns are 84–140 cm long and 14–20 kg. A calf swims in 'baby position' in its mother's slipstream, which makes nursing easier and reduces drag.

stages.name: Youngster
stages.text: Calves usually stay with their mothers for three to six years.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females can mature before males. Mothers calve every three to six years, and females as old as 45 have given birth.

lifespan.value: 40–60 years; females can outlive males

tagline: A slow-motion leaf-eater wearing its own garden
summary: A small, shaggy tree-dweller that spends most of its life hanging in the rainforest canopy, eating leaves. It runs on less energy than almost any other mammal, and its fur is home to algae and moths — a tiny ecosystem it may even snack on.

stats.size: About 60 cm long; 3.5–5.2 kg
stats.habitat: Rainforest canopy, semi-deciduous forest and swamp forest, favouring sunny treetops
stats.range: Southern Central America and much of tropical South America east to Brazil and south to Bolivia; possibly extinct in Argentina
stats.diet: Leaves, flowers and fruit, especially of Cecropia trees
stats.conservation: IUCN Red List: Least Concern (2022 assessment)

facts.title: A garden in its fur
facts.text: Algae grow in the sloth's coarse outer hair, often tinting it green and helping it blend into the canopy. A study in Costa Rica found that sloths eat these algae, which are easy to digest and rich in fats.

facts.title: Moths that ride along
facts.text: Three-toed sloths carry more fur-dwelling moths than two-toed sloths. Researchers propose a chain of partnerships: the moths lay eggs in sloth dung, the adults fertilise the fur with nitrogen, and the nitrogen feeds the algae the sloth eats.

facts.title: A dangerous trip to the toilet
facts.text: Every few days — roughly once a week — the sloth climbs all the way down its tree to urinate and defecate on the ground, where it is most exposed to predators.

facts.title: The lowest energy bill of any mammal
facts.text: Field measurements in Costa Rica found that three-toed sloths have the lowest field metabolic rate ever recorded for a mammal. They save energy by moving very little and letting their body temperature drift with the weather.

facts.title: Extra bones in the neck
facts.text: Most mammals have seven neck vertebrae; this sloth has about ten, letting it turn its head through as much as 270 degrees while its body hangs still.

facts.title: Slow in the trees, good in the water
facts.text: Though it barely manages to crawl on the ground, the brown-throated sloth is a capable swimmer and can cross rivers and flooded forest.

anatomy.lede: A sloth is a mammal rebuilt for hanging: long hooked arms, a neck that swivels, a coat that grows a garden, and internal organs strapped in place so they do not press on the lungs when upside down.

hotspots.label: Face
hotspots.text: The brown throat and head give the species its name. Its eyes lack a focusing muscle and have few nerve cells, so its eyesight is poor.

hotspots.label: Arm and claws
hotspots.text: Long forelimbs end in three clawed toes, which hook over branches so the sloth can hang with little effort.

hotspots.label: Neck
hotspots.text: About ten neck vertebrae, rather than the usual mammal seven, let the sloth turn its head through up to 270 degrees.

hotspots.label: Fur
hotspots.text: Its coat has a short, fine underfur and a thick, woolly outer layer, where algae grow and can tint the sloth green.

hotspots.label: Hind limb
hotspots.text: Sloths barely manage to crawl on the ground, and come down from the canopy only every 3–8 days to urinate and defecate.

senses.lede: Little is known about how sloths sense their world, but their eyes are among the poorest of any mammal studied.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Sloths lack the ciliary muscle that focuses the eye and have very few retinal nerve cells, so their vision is poor. It seems to work best in dim light.

senses.name: Colour
senses.text: Genetic studies of sloths indicate they have lost working cone cells, which leaves them colour-blind and likely to see poorly in bright light.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Mothers and young communicate a good deal by calls, and females call out to attract males in the breeding season.

body.lede: The sloth's whole body is organised around spending as little energy as possible on a diet of tough, low-energy leaves.

systems.title: Organs held in place
systems.text: Unique fibrous attachments anchor the liver and stomach to the lower ribs, so their weight does not press on the lungs when the sloth hangs upside down. This may cut its energy use by almost 13% whenever it is fully inverted.

systems.title: A many-chambered stomach
systems.text: Like many hoofed mammals, the sloth has a stomach divided into compartments, where microbes help digest the cellulose in leaves. Its teeth are peg-like and lack enamel.

systems.title: Barely keeping warm
systems.text: Sloths struggle to keep warm in cool weather, probably because of their sparse muscle, small heart and slow heart rate. They favour treetops exposed to the sun, which may help them warm up.

genome.lede: A draft genome of the brown-throated sloth was released in 2019, though it is still fragmentary. Measurements of its cells suggest about 4.2 picograms of DNA, roughly 4.1 billion base pairs.

findings.title: Colour vision switched off
findings.text: Sloths and anteaters share a broken gene, PDE6C, needed for cone cells to work. Their ancestors lost cone vision early on, perhaps while living underground.

findings.title: Fifty-four or fifty-five
findings.text: Most brown-throated sloths have 54 chromosomes, though a few individuals with 55 have been reported.

mind.lede: Sloths are famous for sleeping — but the first measurements from the wild suggest the reputation is exaggerated.

studies.title: Less sleepy than we thought
studies.text: Brain-wave recorders on wild sloths in the rainforest canopy showed they sleep about 9.6 hours a day — more than six hours less than had been reported for sloths in captivity.

studies.title: Solitary neighbours
studies.text: Adults have never been seen sharing a tree with another adult, and fights are rare, though they will defend territory and food.

studies.title: Help at the birth
studies.text: Other sloths have been reported cleaning the mother and newborn and making sure the infant does not fall.

survival.lede: A sloth cannot outrun anything. It survives by not being noticed.

tactics.title: Too slow to see
tactics.text: Moving very slowly and camouflaged by its fur, a sloth is hard for predators to spot.

tactics.title: A green disguise
tactics.text: Algae in the outer coat give it a greenish tint, which is thought to help it blend into the canopy.

tactics.title: Clinging infant
tactics.text: A newborn is carried on its mother's belly, which is thought to protect it from predators.

threats.title: Deforestation
threats.text: The species is not seriously threatened overall, but some populations in the Brazilian Amazon are thought to be declining as forest is cleared.

life.lede: A sloth has one baby a year and carries it everywhere until it can manage on its own.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: The mother makes no nest; she gives birth either in the trees or on the ground.

stages.name: Infant
stages.text: The newborn weighs under 1 kg and clings to its mother's front. She helps it learn posture, movement and how to explore.

stages.name: Independent young
stages.text: Most young become independent once they are weaned.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature by three years old, males between three and five.

lifespan.value: Reported as 30–40 years in the wild

tagline: A living link to the age before dinosaurs
summary: The chambered nautilus is a cephalopod that still carries its ancestors' coiled, striped shell, divided into gas-filled chambers that keep it afloat. It rises at night from deep reef slopes to hunt with more than 90 sticky tentacles, and lives for 20 years or more, which makes it slow to recover from shell collecting.

stats.size: Shell typically about 13–23 cm across
stats.depth: Down to about 700 m by day; up to about 70 m at night
stats.range: Western Pacific and coastal Indian Ocean
stats.diet: Fishes and crustaceans such as crabs and shrimps; also scavenges
stats.conservation: US Endangered Species Act: Threatened; CITES Appendix II (IUCN status not found)

facts.title: An ancient design
facts.text: Nautiluses have changed little over about 150 million years and were cruising deep reefs before the dinosaurs, earning them the label 'living fossil'.

facts.title: A shell that floats
facts.text: Its body sits in the outermost chamber. A tube called the siphuncle runs through the older chambers, letting the animal adjust the gas and liquid inside them to control buoyancy.

facts.title: Ninety-plus tentacles
facts.text: It has more than 90 tentacles, the most of any cephalopod. They have no suckers; instead, grooves, ridges and a sticky coating grip prey, and chemical sensors smell food in the water.

facts.title: Daily commute
facts.text: By day it lingers on deep reef slopes to avoid predators, as deep as about 700 m; at night it rises to around 70 m to feed and lay eggs.

facts.title: Slow life, real threat
facts.text: Nautiluses mature at roughly 10–15 years and lay few eggs. Fishing for the international shell trade is their main threat; the US listed the species as threatened in 2018.

MBA says ESA listing in 2017, NOAA Fisheries says 2018 (final rule was 2018) — used 2018. Shell size: MBA 16–21 cm diameter vs NOAA 5–9 in (13–23 cm) at maturity; used the NOAA range. Maturity: MBA 12–15 yr, NOAA 10–15 yr. The siphuncle fact is phrased from NOAA's description (which calls the tube the 'hyponome', a term usually used for the funnel; I used 'siphuncle', the standard anatomical term) — editor may wish to verify wording. anatomy.lede: The nautilus is a cephalopod in a coiled house: a soft, many-armed body living in the last and largest room of a shell it keeps adding to.

hotspots.label: Hood
hotspots.text: The tough, spotted hood works like a trapdoor. When the animal pulls back into its shell, the hood seals the opening.

hotspots.label: Pinhole eye
hotspots.text: The eye has no lens and works like a pinhole. It can sense only light and dark.

hotspots.label: Tentacles
hotspots.text: More than 90 suckerless tentacles feel, taste and grip. They are ridged and coated in a sticky secretion that holds prey.

hotspots.label: Striped shell
hotspots.text: Young shells are striped, and the stripes stretch as the animal grows. Each nautilus's pattern is distinctive enough to tell individuals apart.

hotspots.label: Living chamber
hotspots.text: The body occupies only the outermost chamber. Behind it, the older chambers hold the gas and liquid that keep the animal afloat.

senses.lede: In the dim deep reef, a nautilus finds food mainly by smell, with simple eyes adding a sense of light and shade.

senses.name: Rhinophores
senses.text: In experiments in the dark, nautiluses followed drifting odour plumes to their source from up to 10 m away. When two small smell organs, the rhinophores, were blocked, they could no longer find the source.

senses.name: Tentacles
senses.text: The thin tentacles can detect odour too, but in the same experiments they did not steer the animal. Instead they taste and touch as it feels along the reef.

senses.name: Pinhole eye
senses.text: The simple, lens-less eyes can only sense light and dark. They seem to play a smaller part than smell in finding food.

body.lede: A nautilus floats, steers and feeds with equipment that has served its ancestors for hundreds of millions of years.

systems.title: Buoyancy control
systems.text: A tube running back through the shell controls how much gas and liquid each chamber holds, letting the animal fine-tune its buoyancy as it rises and sinks.

systems.title: Jet propulsion
systems.text: It swims by squirting water from its mantle cavity through a flexible siphon near the head. Pointing the siphon lets it move forwards, backwards or sideways.

systems.title: Beak and radula
systems.text: Prey held by the tentacles is broken up by a hard, beak-like mouth and then shredded further by a radula, a ribbon lined with tiny teeth.

systems.title: Building the shell
systems.text: The genome contains a conserved molluscan toolkit for making shell, plus repetitive protein sections found only in this lineage, which together build its shell.

genome.lede: Two research teams published nautilus genomes in 2021, giving the first full genetic look at a shelled cephalopod.

findings.title: Compact and slow-changing
findings.text: Compared with other cephalopods, the nautilus genome is compact, has relatively few genes and has evolved slowly.

findings.title: Genes behind the pinhole eye
findings.text: Losses of certain genes, and changes in the size of gene families and their control networks, probably shaped the evolution of the lens-less pinhole eye.

findings.title: Jumping genes
findings.text: A chromosome-level assembly of about 785 million base pairs found recent activity of transposable elements, 'jumping genes' that may have helped the lineage adapt.

mind.lede: The nautilus has fewer brain lobes and neurons than octopuses or squid, yet it can still learn and remember.

studies.title: Light means food
studies.text: Nautiluses learned to link a blue light with the smell of food, and soon stretched out their tentacles at the light alone. Learning appeared within ten trials spread over 30 minutes.

studies.title: Two kinds of memory
studies.text: The trained response lasted under an hour, faded, then returned about six hours after training and lasted up to a day. This two-phase pattern resembles that of cuttlefish.

studies.title: Memory without a memory centre
studies.text: Nautiluses lack the vertical lobe that coleoid cephalopods use for learning, so their memory must rely on other parts of the brain.

survival.lede: With no ink and no colour-changing skin, the nautilus relies on its shell and on staying deep by day.

tactics.title: Retreat and seal
tactics.text: At any threat it can withdraw into its shell and close the hood over the opening.

tactics.title: Daytime refuge
tactics.text: It spends the day on deep reef slopes, away from predators, and rises to feed only at night.

tactics.title: No ink, no disguise
tactics.text: Unlike octopuses and squid, it has no ink sac and cannot camouflage itself, which may make learning to avoid danger especially valuable.

threats.title: Shell trade
threats.text: Overharvesting for souvenirs, jewellery and décor is the main threat. Targeted fishing continues in Indonesia, the Philippines and China despite bans.

threats.title: Slow to recover
threats.text: Because nautiluses mature late and produce few young, fished populations are prone to serious decline.

life.lede: A nautilus grows slowly, adding chamber after chamber over a decade or more before it can breed.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: A female lays only 10 to 18 eggs a year, each about the size and shape of a garlic bulb.

stages.name: Hatchling
stages.text: The young nautilus hatches with a striped shell that already has seven or eight small chambers.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: It keeps adding chambers as it grows, and reaches maturity at around 10 to 15 years old.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: A mature nautilus has about 30 chambers and continues to rise each night to feed and lay eggs.

lifespan.value: 20 years or more

tagline: The fastest land animal, built for a short, all-out sprint
summary: A slender, long-legged cat of open country that hunts by stalking close and then bursting into a sprint no other land mammal can match. Collars fitted to wild cheetahs in Botswana have clocked 93 km/h, but they also showed that most hunts are won by acceleration, braking and sharp turns rather than raw top speed.

stats.size: Adults weigh 34–64 kg; males are slightly larger than females
stats.habitat: Open savanna, grassland and dry scrub
stats.range: Patchy across eastern and southern Africa, with small populations in North Africa, the Sahel and Iran
stats.diet: Small to medium-sized mammals, hunted mainly in the early morning and late afternoon
stats.conservation: IUCN Red List: Vulnerable (2024 assessment version)

facts.title: 93 km/h, measured in the wild
facts.text: GPS and motion-sensor collars fitted to five wild cheetahs in Botswana recorded 367 runs, most of them hunts. The fastest reached 25.9 m/s (93 km/h, 58 mph) — yet most hunts involved only moderate speeds.

facts.title: Brakes and turns win the hunt
facts.text: The same collars recorded some of the highest sideways and forward acceleration, deceleration and power per kilogram of body weight measured for any land mammal.

facts.title: Seven metres a stride
facts.text: A classic study of filmed cheetahs found that at 25 m/s a cheetah completes a stride in 0.28 s, covering 7 m. Force-plate and high-speed video work found cheetahs raise their average stride frequency from 2.4 to 3.2 Hz as they speed up, using up to 3.9 Hz, and take longer, slower strides than racing greyhounds at the same speed.

facts.title: Claws that dig in
facts.text: Cheetahs have blunt, semi-retractable claws. At 18 m/s a galloping cheetah carries 70% of its body weight on its hind legs, and researchers suggest its substantial claws dig in to give the grip needed for acceleration and manoeuvring.

facts.title: A furry rudder
facts.text: Cheetahs swing their tails while turning and braking. Wind-tunnel tests showed the fur nearly doubles the tail's effective frontal area at little cost in weight, so the tail may steer the body through air resistance as well as through its swinging mass.

facts.title: Stalk first, then sprint
facts.text: Cheetahs usually creep to within about 90 m of their target before the final burst. A full sprint lasts only about 20 seconds, and about half of their chases succeed.

notes: signatureData: topSpeedMs 25.9 is verbatim from Wilson et al. 2013 (abstract). Stride values are from Hildebrand (1961, J Mammalogy), as quoted in the introduction of Hudson et al. 2012 (ref 2): 'at 25 m/s a cheetah completes a stride in 0.28 s with a stride length of 7 m'; strideFrequencyHz 3.57 is 1/0.28 s, my derivation, consistent with 7 m x 3.57 Hz = 25 m/s. Hudson et al.'s own measured values (mean 2.4 to 3.2 Hz, maximum 3.9 Hz; 'up to 4.0 Hz' in their summary) come from trials in which cheetahs galloped at 8.7–17.8 m/s, so they are given in a fact, not as the signature pair. Hudson et al. also cite a 29 m/s figure averaged over 200 m from another study; not used. The tail fact is marked 'hypothesis' because Patel et al. 2016 is a wind-tunnel and modelling study. Categories left empty: the cheetah is a predator but routinely loses kills to lions and hyenas, so I did not shelve it under apex-predators; IUCN status is Vulnerable, not EN/CR. Add apex-predators if the shelf is meant loosely. Regions: namib-kalahari for the Namibia/Botswana strongholds; sahara-arabia for the small Northwest African (Saharan) and Iranian (Asiatic) populations noted by the Smithsonian; India's reintroduced African cheetahs (Kuno, from 2022) are not counted. IUCN assessment: Durant et al., version e.T219A259025524 (2024 version per GBIF's IUCN checklist and its DOI 10.2305/IUCN.UK.2024-1.RLTS.T219A259025524.en); iucnredlist.org and gbif.org return 403 to scripted requests, so those two URLs were confirmed via the GBIF API rather than a page fetch. Smithsonian population estimate (7,500–10,000) not used as it may be dated. Hero swapped to the walking female (more typical profile); the stretching Masai Mara cheetah is a Featured Picture used in the gallery.

anatomy.lede: Everything about the cheetah is traded for speed: a light, greyhound-like frame, a spring-loaded spine, oversized airways and claws that grip like running spikes.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: High-set eyes with an elongated fovea give a sharp, wide-angle view of the plains. Cheetahs hunt by sight far more than by smell.

hotspots.label: Tear mark
hotspots.text: A black stripe runs from the inner corner of each eye to the mouth. It may cut glare from the sun, though this has not been proven.

hotspots.label: Nasal passages
hotspots.text: Large nostrils and nasal passages pull in air fast. They leave little room for long tooth roots, so a cheetah's teeth are small for a big cat.

hotspots.label: Spine
hotspots.text: The flexible spine works like a spring for the back legs, lengthening every stride — but it is physically taxing.

hotspots.label: Claws
hotspots.text: Its claws are only weakly retractile, with no protective skin folds, so they stay blunted from contact with the ground — and leave dog-like prints.

hotspots.label: Hind legs
hotspots.text: At high speed a galloping cheetah carries most of its weight on its powerful back legs.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The ringed tail, ending in a white tip, swings during turns and helps steer and balance the body.

stats.label: Top speed measured in the wild

senses.lede: A daytime hunter of the open plains, the cheetah relies on its eyes — and on an inner ear tuned to keep its gaze steady at full sprint.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Cheetahs scan the plains from termite mounds and rocky outcrops, picking out prey by eye before they begin to stalk.

senses.name: Balance
senses.text: Scans of cat skulls show the cheetah's balance organ in the inner ear is unusually large and differently shaped from other cats'. This probably helps keep its head and eyes steady while chasing prey at speed.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Cheetahs keep in touch with high-pitched chirps that can be heard about 1.6 km away. A study at the Smithsonian's National Zoo found each cheetah's chirp differs, so they may recognise one another by voice.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Because cheetahs are mostly solitary, scent marks of urine and droppings are an important way of passing on messages.

body.lede: A cheetah's body is tuned for a 20-second sprint, from its heart and lungs to the way its shoulders float free of the skeleton.

systems.title: Big heart, big lungs
systems.text: Large lungs and nostrils let air in quickly, while a large heart, liver and adrenal glands support a rapid physical response.

systems.title: Floating shoulders
systems.text: Its shoulder blades are vertical and not attached to the small collarbones, and its hips swivel on a flexible spine, all of which lengthens the stride.

systems.title: Not overheating after all
systems.text: Cheetahs were long said to give up chases because they overheat. Body-temperature loggers on four wild cheetahs showed they abandoned hunts at a normal 38.4 °C — and their temperature rose most after a successful hunt, perhaps from stress.

genome.lede: The cheetah genome, first published in 2015, reveals a species that passed through severe bottlenecks and now carries remarkably little genetic variety.

findings.title: Almost identical genomes
findings.text: Wild-born African cheetahs' genomes are on average 95% homozygous — far more than an outbred domestic cat (24%) or even a Virunga mountain gorilla (78%).

findings.title: Two ancient crashes
findings.text: Genetic models point to two population bottlenecks: one more than 100,000 years ago, and another about 11,000–12,600 years ago in Africa, when many large Ice Age mammals died out.

findings.title: Skin grafts that are not rejected
findings.text: Loss and low diversity of immune (MHC) genes would explain why unrelated cheetahs accept each other's skin grafts. Changes in a sperm gene may also help explain why most cheetah sperm are misshapen.

mind.lede: Cheetahs have one of the most unusual social lives among cats: solitary mothers, but brothers who stay together for life.

studies.title: Brothers for life
studies.text: Young males usually stay together in a coalition, often two or three littermates. Coalitions defend territories, and larger ones hold them longer than single males.

studies.title: Calling until reunited
studies.text: When members of a male coalition become separated, they may call with 'yipps' and 'churrs' for up to 20 minutes until they find each other again.

studies.title: Lessons in hunting
studies.text: When her cubs are about six months old, a mother brings them live prey so they can practise making a kill.

studies.title: A hunting partner for kings
studies.text: Cheetahs were semi-domesticated for hunting in ancient Egypt, Sumer and Assyria, and later by European and Indian royalty, who released them hooded, like falcons, when game was in sight.

survival.lede: The cheetah is a lightweight among big predators. It survives by speed and wariness rather than strength.

tactics.title: Flight, not fight
tactics.text: With small teeth and a light build, cheetahs are easily overwhelmed by lions, so they usually run rather than fight.

tactics.title: Eat fast
tactics.text: Cheetahs eat quickly because lions, hyenas and even vultures can drive them off a kill. They lose about half their food this way.

tactics.title: A cloak for cubs
tactics.text: Young cubs have a long, smoky-grey mantle down their backs that may camouflage them among dead grass. Mothers hide them for around eight weeks, moving them between hiding places.

threats.title: A shrinking range
threats.text: About 7,100 cheetahs remain, in just 9% of their historical range — and 77% of that range lies outside protected areas.

threats.title: Conflict with farmers
threats.text: In Namibia and elsewhere in southern Africa, cheetahs are treated as a threat to livestock and are shot.

life.lede: Few cheetah cubs survive to adulthood, and a mother raises them entirely alone.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: A female first gives birth at about 2.4 years old. Wild litters average 2–3 cubs.

stages.name: Hidden cub
stages.text: Cubs are born blind and weigh 250–300 g. Their eyes open after 4–11 days, and they are hidden in tall grass, marsh or rocks while their mother hunts.

stages.name: Following mother
stages.text: From about six weeks cubs follow the hunt, and they are weaned at 3–6 months. In the Serengeti about 90% of cubs die before they are three months old.

stages.name: Sibling group
stages.text: At around 18 months the mother leaves. Littermates stay together for about six more months; then sisters leave to live alone, while brothers often stay together.

lifespan.value: 8–10 years on average in the wild

tagline: Twin spiral crowns on a worm that lives inside living coral
summary: The colourful 'trees' are all most divers ever see of this worm. They are twin spiral crowns of feathery tentacles that strain food from the water and help it breathe. The rest of the worm stays hidden in a limy tube buried in living coral, and it snaps back inside and shuts a spiny trapdoor when danger approaches.
ability: spiral feeding crowns and trapdoor retreat

stats.size: Body about 3.8 cm; tube up to about 20 cm long
stats.depth: Shallow coral reefs
stats.range: Caribbean and tropical western Atlantic (similar worms in the Indo-Pacific are now often treated as separate species)
stats.diet: Plankton and other tiny particles filtered from the water

facts.title: Trees made of tentacles
facts.text: Each 'tree' is a spiral of feathery tentacles called radioles. Cilia on them carry trapped food to the mouth, and they double as gills.

facts.title: A spiny trapdoor
facts.text: When startled, the worm retreats into its tube and seals the entrance with an operculum: a hard, calcified lid armed with antler-shaped spines.

facts.title: Living inside coral
facts.text: Larvae settle on living coral and build a calcareous tube. The coral then grows around the tube until only the opening shows.

facts.title: Some live for decades
facts.text: By counting the host coral's annual growth bands, researchers estimated that some worms had lived more than 10 years and a few more than 40 years.

facts.title: Not always a good tenant
facts.text: Christmas tree worms' moving lids can rub and wound the coral around them, especially when algae grow on the lid. In a Thai survey of related Indo-Pacific species, about a fifth of the lids examined had caused visible injuries.

notes: TAXONOMY CAUTION: In the strict sense, S. giganteus is the Caribbean/western Atlantic Christmas tree worm. Indo-Pacific 'Christmas tree worms' are now mostly assigned to S. corniculatus and related species; the Thai survey (ref 2) found S. corniculatus, S. richardsmithi and S. cf. tetraceros. However, WoRMS distribution records and Wikipedia still list Indo-Pacific localities for S. giganteus. We therefore chose a Caribbean (Belize) photo and rejected the many Indo-Pacific Commons images filed under S. giganteus (Thailand, Philippines, Fiji, Red Sea, etc.) as doubtful IDs. A g. phua photo from Cuba was also good but carries a watermark. The age study (ref 3, Japanese authors, 1996) used the name S. giganteus before the Indo-Pacific split. It may concern an Indo-Pacific species of the complex; the abstract does not give the locality. CATEGORIES left empty: none of the allowed categories (deep-sea, bioluminescent, intelligent, camouflage, giants, venomous, transparent, reproduction, ancient) is sourced for this species; the editor may decide. Depth is not documented in the sources consulted; depthRange 0–30 m is an indicative value for shallow reef. Body and tube sizes come from Wikipedia.

anatomy.lede: The two 'trees' on top of the coral are one worm. Everything else, its body and its limy tube, is hidden inside the coral skeleton.

hotspots.label: Left crown
hotspots.text: Each crown is a spiral of feathery tentacles called radioles. The pair grow from the worm's head and are modified palps.

hotspots.label: Right crown
hotspots.text: Both crowns belong to the same animal. Most worms are only about 3.8 cm long, so the crowns are the largest visible part.

hotspots.label: Radioles
hotspots.text: The radioles are covered in beating cilia that carry trapped food particles down to the mouth.

hotspots.label: Host coral
hotspots.text: The worm's tube is buried in this brain coral. Larvae settle on bare patches of coral skeleton and grow their tubes towards the living tissue, which then hides them.

senses.lede: A worm that spends its life in one spot needs early warning. Christmas tree worms carry simple eyes on their feeding crowns.

senses.name: Radiolar eyes
senses.text: Serpulid worms have eyes on their feeding tentacles. In an Indo-Pacific Christmas tree worm, the light-sensitive pigment is tuned to 464 nm, matching the blue light on shallow reefs.

senses.name: Shadow alarm
senses.text: These eyes probably work as a 'burglar alarm': a passing shadow triggers the worm to snap back into its tube before a predator strikes.

senses.name: Larval eyes
senses.text: Larvae grow simple eyes within 24 hours of developing and swim towards light, responding to wavelengths shorter than 590 nm.

body.lede: The crowns do almost everything: they feed the worm, help it breathe and watch for danger.

systems.title: Gills that feed
systems.text: The radioles double as gills, taking up oxygen while they filter food from the water.

systems.title: Closed circulation
systems.text: Like other annelids, it has a well-developed closed circulatory system, with blood kept inside vessels, and it removes waste through organs called nephridia.

systems.title: A limy home
systems.text: The worm builds a hard calcareous tube that can reach 20 cm long, usually deep inside the coral skeleton. It is often mistaken for a boring animal, but the coral grows around it.

genome.lede: A chromosome-level genome of a Caribbean Christmas tree worm was released in 2026 by France's ATLASea marine genome programme. No paper describing it had been published at the time of writing.

findings.title: Eleven chromosomes
findings.text: The assembly, made from an adult collected off Guadeloupe and identified by DNA barcoding, spans about 1.66 billion base pairs arranged in 11 chromosomes.

findings.title: A fast-changing mitochondrion
findings.text: Its mitochondrial genome, sequenced in 2017, changes faster than that of other annelids studied.

survival.lede: A Christmas tree worm cannot run, so it hides: inside its tube, inside a coral.

tactics.title: Lightning retreat
tactics.text: When startled, the worm pulls its crowns back into its burrow in an instant.

tactics.title: A spiny lid
tactics.text: Once inside, it plugs the tube with its operculum, a modified radiole topped with sharp, antler-like spines.

tactics.title: Coral armour
tactics.text: Because the tube is usually buried deep in the coral skeleton, only the crowns are ever exposed.

life.lede: Christmas tree worms spawn in step with the corals they live on, and their young must find a coral home within days.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: Males and females release eggs and sperm in the evening during calm neap tides, when less turbulence lets more eggs be fertilised. In the Caribbean this coincides with spawning by their host corals.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: The larvae drift and feed in the plankton, swimming towards light with their newly formed eyes.

stages.name: Settler
stages.text: A larva settles on exposed coral skeleton and starts building its tube, which it extends towards the living coral tissue.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Counting the coral's annual growth bands around the tubes showed that some worms had lived more than 10 years, and a few more than 40.

lifespan.value: some more than 40 years

tagline: The fish that came back from extinction
summary: A large, slow-living fish with fleshy, limb-like fins, from a lineage thought extinct for 70 million years until a living specimen turned up in 1938. Dark metallic blue with pale spots, it shelters in deep rocky caves by day and drifts out to feed at night. It may live nearly a century.
ability: fleshy lobed fins and an ultra-slow life

stats.size: Up to about 2 m and 95 kg
stats.depth: About 150–700 m; often around 180–250 m
stats.range: Western Indian Ocean: the Comoros, with populations off South Africa, Madagascar and Mozambique
stats.diet: Fishes and squid

facts.title: Back from the dead
facts.text: Its lineage of lobe-finned fishes was thought to have died out 70 million years ago, until a living coelacanth was discovered in 1938. Modern coelacanths look remarkably like many fossil relatives.

facts.title: Not our closest fishy cousin
facts.text: Sequencing its genome in 2013 showed that lungfish, not the coelacanth, are the closest living relatives of four-limbed animals—though it still offers clues to how fins became limbs.

facts.title: A century-long life
facts.text: By counting tiny annual growth marks on scales, a 2021 study found the oldest specimen was 84 years old and estimated maturity at around 55. Earlier work had assumed lifespans of about 20 years.

facts.title: A five-year pregnancy
facts.text: Coelacanths give birth to live young. The same 2021 study suggests embryos develop for about five years inside the mother—earlier estimates were around three years, already among the longest of any vertebrate.

facts.title: Cave sleepers, night drifters
facts.text: By day they rest in caves on steep rocky slopes—up to 14 in one cave. At night they forage alone, drifting with currents and travelling up to about 8 km before retreating at dawn.

anatomy.lede: The coelacanth carries features that vanished from almost every other living animal long ago: fleshy limb-like fins, a hinged skull and a lung that no longer breathes.

hotspots.label: Snout
hotspots.text: Inside the snout lies the rostral organ, whose structure suggests it detects weak electric fields.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: The large eye is tuned to the narrow band of blue light, around 480 nm, that reaches the coelacanth's depths.

hotspots.label: Lobed pectoral fin
hotspots.text: The paired fins grow from fleshy, muscular lobes and move in an alternating pattern, like the legs of a walking four-limbed animal.

hotspots.label: Pelvic fin
hotspots.text: The pelvic fins are lobed too, and join in the same alternating, limb-like movements as the pectoral fins.

hotspots.label: Second dorsal fin
hotspots.text: The coelacanth usually swims slowly by sculling with its second dorsal fin and its anal fin.

hotspots.label: Armoured scales
hotspots.text: Tiny, nearly invisible yearly growth rings on the scales revealed that coelacanths live for around a century.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: Although it usually moves slowly, a sudden flip of the tail fin lets the fish make a quick lunge.

stats.label: Share of the braincase filled by the brain

senses.lede: Coelacanths hunt at night in near-darkness. Their senses are tuned to a deep, dim, blue world.

senses.name: Blue-tuned vision
senses.text: The coelacanth appears to see with just two visual pigments, a rod pigment and a cone pigment, most sensitive at 478 nm and 485 nm. Both are shifted to match the blue light near 200 m depth.

senses.name: Rostral organ
senses.text: The structure of the rostral organ in the snout points to an electroreceptive role, and the fish may use it to scan the seabed for hidden prey.

senses.name: The headstand
senses.text: Coelacanths have been seen standing on their heads for two or three minutes. This may be a way of scanning the bottom with the rostral organ, or simply a reaction to submersible lights.

body.lede: Under its armoured skin the coelacanth is a museum of early vertebrate design, adapted to a cold, deep, slow life.

systems.title: A hinged skull
systems.text: It is the only living vertebrate whose braincase is split in two by an intracranial joint. A unique muscle flexes the front of the skull at this joint and boosts its bite force.

systems.title: A lung that stopped growing
systems.text: The earliest known embryo has a well-developed lung, but its growth stalls and in adults it is vestigial. A fatty organ develops alongside it and controls buoyancy instead.

systems.title: Slow metabolism
systems.text: Coelacanths extract oxygen poorly and have a slow metabolism, which fits their slow growth and very long lives.

genome.lede: Sequencing the coelacanth in 2013 settled an old question about which fish are our closest cousins, and showed a genome that has changed unusually little.

findings.title: Slowly evolving genes
findings.text: Its protein-coding genes have changed at roughly half the rate of tetrapod genes since the two lineages split, which may help explain why it looks so like its fossil relatives.

findings.title: A switch for building limbs
findings.text: A stretch of DNA near the HoxD genes, shared with tetrapods but not ray-finned fish, drove limb-specific activity when tested in mice, suggesting a fin enhancer was later reused for building hands and feet.

findings.title: Missing antibody
findings.text: Despite extensive searching, no genes for IgM, an antibody found in almost all other jawed vertebrates, were found; it has two IgW genes instead.

mind.lede: Coelacanths are hard to watch: most of what is known about their behaviour comes from submersible and camera observations at depth.

studies.title: Drift hunting
studies.text: Coelacanths are slow, night-time drift hunters, riding currents close to the seabed and taking cephalopods, eels, cuttlefish and deep-water fishes.

studies.title: Known by their spots
studies.text: The pattern of white blotches on each fish is unique, so researchers can recognise individuals from photographs and video.

studies.title: Shared caves
studies.text: Up to 13 or 14 coelacanths have been found resting together in one cave by day, although each forages alone at night.

survival.lede: Coelacanths have few natural enemies but almost no capacity to recover from losses.

tactics.title: Cave shelter
tactics.text: Daytime caves and ledges on steep rocky slopes give them shelter from predators.

tactics.title: Living cheaply
tactics.text: A slow metabolism lets them live on little food in deep, cool water of about 13–25 °C.

threats.title: Shark gillnets
threats.text: Off Tanzania, coelacanths are caught as bycatch in deep-set shark gillnets, which NOAA calls historically the most significant threat. The fishery has expanded over the last decade.

threats.title: Coastal development
threats.text: Deep-water port building brings pollution, sediment, underwater blasting and dredging into coelacanth habitat.

threats.title: Slow life, high risk
threats.text: With maturity at 40 to 69 years and a five-year pregnancy, coelacanths may be more threatened than once thought.

life.lede: The coelacanth has one of the slowest life histories of any fish: decades to grow up, years to give birth.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Eggs are huge, about 9 cm across and over 325 g, and are fertilised and kept inside the mother.

stages.name: Embryo
stages.text: The young develop inside the mother for around five years, according to scale-based estimates, possibly the longest pregnancy of any animal with a backbone.

stages.name: Newborn
stages.text: Pups are born live at an estimated 35–38 cm long. One 179 cm female caught off Mozambique in 1991 carried 26 near-term pups.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Scale growth rings suggest sexual maturity comes very late, somewhere between 40 and 69 years of age.

lifespan.value: probably around 100 years

tagline: The heaviest invertebrate on Earth
summary: A giant of the icy Southern Ocean, the colossal squid is the heaviest known invertebrate, armed with rotating hooks on its tentacles and the largest eyes ever studied. For a century it was known almost only from whale stomachs and fishing catches, until a baby was filmed alive in 2025.

stats.size: Estimated up to about 7 m long and 500 kg
stats.depth: Adults about 1,000 m or deeper; juveniles shallower
stats.range: Antarctic waters, reaching north to southern New Zealand
stats.diet: Fishes, including Antarctic toothfish

facts.title: Heavyweight champion
facts.text: A colossal squid caught in the Ross Sea in 2007 weighed about 470–495 kg, and scientists estimate the species reaches about 500 kg, making it the heaviest invertebrate known.

facts.title: Hooks that turn
facts.text: The club-shaped tips of its two tentacles carry rotating hooks, and its arms bear hooks too. No other glass squid has them.

facts.title: Record-breaking eyes
facts.text: It has the largest animal eyes ever studied, possibly the largest of any animal in history, useful for spotting faint light in the deep.

facts.title: First seen alive in 2025
facts.text: In March 2025 a remotely operated vehicle filmed a see-through, 30 cm juvenile at 600 m near the South Sandwich Islands: the first confirmed footage of a live colossal squid in its habitat.

facts.title: Whale food
facts.text: Beaks pile up in sperm whale stomachs because they resist digestion. From these, scientists estimate colossal squid could make up a large share of some sperm whales' diet in the Southern Ocean.

anatomy.lede: The colossal squid is known mostly from a handful of dead or dying specimens. This one, caught in 2007, is the best studied of them all.

hotspots.label: Fin
hotspots.text: The body has three main parts: the mantle with its broad fin, the head, and a ring of arms and tentacles.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The mantle is the main body. The 2003 specimen, an immature female, had a mantle 2.5 m long and a total length of 5.4 m.

hotspots.label: Head
hotspots.text: The head holds the largest eyes ever studied, about 27 cm across, each with a lens 8–9 cm wide, about the size of an orange.

hotspots.label: Hooked arms
hotspots.text: The eight arms carry hooks partway along their length. These hooks tell young colossal squid apart from other glass squid.

hotspots.label: Tentacles
hotspots.text: The two longer tentacles end in clubs armed with rotating hooks that ensnare prey.

stats.label: Largest lower beak from a whale's stomach

senses.lede: At 1,000 m and below, there is almost no sunlight. The colossal squid's giant eyes seem built to catch the faintest glow.

senses.name: Headlights
senses.text: Each eyeball carries a light organ beside the lens that glows constantly. When the eyes turn forward, these light up prey in front of the arms.

senses.name: Judging distance
senses.text: The eyes face forward and can give overlapping, stereoscopic vision, helping the squid judge how far to reach with its tentacles. It probably cannot see colour.

senses.name: Whale warning
senses.text: Modelling suggests that eyes this large are best at spotting very large animals, such as sperm whales, lit by glowing plankton. A 27 cm eye below 600 m could detect a whale more than 120 m away.

body.lede: A giant body need not be a fast one. The colossal squid seems to live in the slow lane.

systems.title: Very slow metabolism
systems.text: Estimates based on its size and the near-freezing water suggest it burns only about 45 kcal a day.

systems.title: Two-piece lens
systems.text: As in other cephalopods, the lens of the eye is in two pieces. Its pupil is 8–9 cm across to gather as much light as possible.

systems.title: A beak that lasts
systems.text: The beak is the squid's mouth and the start of its digestive system. Beaks resist digestion, so they pile up in sperm whale stomachs and reveal how big the squid grow.

survival.lede: Rather than chasing prey at speed, the colossal squid probably waits for it in the dark.

tactics.title: Sit-and-float ambush
tactics.text: Researchers argue it is not a voracious, high-speed hunter but an ambush predator that uses its hooks to snag prey that drifts too close.

tactics.title: Early warning
tactics.text: Huge eyes may spot a hunting sperm whale from beyond 120 m, giving the squid early warning to prepare a powerful escape.

life.lede: Its life cycle is almost unknown. Only females have been found, and no one has seen it breed.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: It probably lays its eggs in a large, floating, jelly-like mass, as the giant squid does.

stages.name: Hatchling
stages.text: Eggs hatch into tiny versions of the adult.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: In 2025 a transparent juvenile about 30 cm long was filmed alive at 600 m, holding its arms in the 'cockatoo' pose typical of glass squid.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults live at 1,000 m or deeper. Males are thought to deliver sperm directly to the female, but none has been examined.

tagline: Rainbow-rippling, glass-clear and no relation to jellyfish
summary: Comb jellies are not jellyfish: they belong to their own ancient phylum, Ctenophora, and do not sting. The sea walnut swims by beating eight rows of tiny ciliary combs. These scatter light into shimmering rainbows, which is diffraction, not glowing. When disturbed it can also produce its own light.

stats.size: Up to roughly 7–12 cm long
stats.depth: Coastal and estuarine waters
stats.range: Native to the western Atlantic; invasive in the Black, Caspian, Baltic and North seas
stats.diet: Zooplankton, including crustaceans, other comb jellies, fish eggs and larvae

facts.title: Rainbows, not glowing
facts.text: The flickering rainbow colours come from light diffracting off the beating comb plates (fused cilia). It happens only in ambient light and is often mistaken for bioluminescence.

facts.title: It does make light too
facts.text: Mnemiopsis is genuinely bioluminescent. It uses a photoprotein, a single complex of light-making molecules, and its comb rows give off blue-green light when disturbed.

facts.title: An invader that crashed fisheries
facts.text: Carried in ships' ballast water, it reached the Black Sea in the early 1980s. There it ate fish eggs and larvae and competed with anchovy for food, contributing to a dramatic fall in catches.

facts.title: It can grow young again
facts.text: In 2024 researchers showed that stressed adults can revert to the earlier, two-tentacled cydippid larval form and later mature and spawn again. It is the first ctenophore known to do this.

facts.title: A now-you-see-it anus
facts.text: It has no permanent anus. When waste builds up, the gut fuses with the skin to open a temporary pore, which closes again after defecation. In adults this happens about once an hour.

image.caption: Sea walnut (Mnemiopsis leidyi). The rainbow streaks along its comb rows are diffracted light, not bioluminescence.
image.creator: Bruno C. Vellutini

notes: We chose Mnemiopsis leidyi because Commons has many correctly identified photos and it is documented as bioluminescent: the 2025 review lists it among photoprotein species. The hero was taken by ctenophore researcher Bruno Vellutini, filed under Category:Mnemiopsis leidyi. It is most likely a lab or aquarium shot against black (setting assumed). The animal fills most of the frame, so tight landscape crops may clip the lobes. The image is 1920×1493, uncropped. Wikipedia gives the first Black Sea record as 1982. Depth is not documented in the sources consulted; depthRange 0–30 m is an indicative value for coastal plankton. Size and the invasion history come from Wikipedia (last-resort source). The 2024 reverse-development finding is from the PNAS paper.

anatomy.lede: A sea walnut is a living bag of seawater with eight shimmering rows of paddles, two big feeding lobes and a balance organ at the top.

hotspots.label: Comb row
hotspots.text: Eight rows of comb plates, each made of fused cilia, beat in waves to row the animal along. They scatter light into rainbows.

hotspots.label: Rainbow combs
hotspots.text: The colours are diffracted light from the beating plates, not the animal's own glow, and they vanish in darkness.

hotspots.label: Oral lobe
hotspots.text: Two large lobes flank the mouth. Lobate comb jellies, the group this species belongs to, are named after them.

hotspots.label: Second lobe
hotspots.text: The lobes are among the features lost when a stressed adult reverts to its two-tentacled larval form.

hotspots.label: Aboral end
hotspots.text: At the end opposite the mouth sits the aboral organ, a sensory hub with a gravity-sensing statocyst.

hotspots.label: Clear body
hotspots.text: The body is about 97% water, which makes it almost invisible in the sea.

senses.lede: With no brain and no eyes, a comb jelly still knows which way is up and can sense light.

senses.name: Statocyst
senses.text: Four clusters of ciliated 'balancer' cells hold up a tiny weight called the statolith. When the animal tilts, the load on the balancers shifts and changes how the comb rows beat, turning it back on course.

senses.name: Light-sensing cells
senses.text: Mnemiopsis has three opsin genes, which make light-detecting proteins. Opsins are active in its apical sensory organ and in the cells that make light.

senses.name: Seeing its own light?
senses.text: One opsin absorbs light at wavelengths that overlap with the animal's own blue-green glow, raising the idea that light production and light sensing are linked.

body.lede: Comb jellies belong to one of the oldest branches of the animal tree, and their bodies work in ways found nowhere else.

systems.title: A fused nerve net
systems.text: Electron microscopy showed that neurons in its nerve net share one continuous cell membrane, forming a syncytium rather than separate cells linked by synapses.

systems.title: Light from a protein
systems.text: Its genome holds 10 full-length photoprotein genes, the light-making proteins in its photocytes, which line canals running through the body.

systems.title: Rebuilding the body
systems.text: A sea walnut can regenerate any missing organ, and can regrow a whole body from a fragment as small as about 15% of the original in a few days.

genome.lede: Mnemiopsis was the first comb jelly to have its genome sequenced, and the result reshaped ideas about the earliest animals.

findings.title: Sister to all other animals?
findings.text: The 2013 genome analysis suggested that comb jellies, not sponges, are the sister group of all other animals.

findings.title: Muscles invented twice?
findings.text: Mnemiopsis lacks many genes used by bilaterian muscle and other mesodermal cells, suggesting such cell types may have evolved independently in comb jellies.

findings.title: Thirteen chromosomes
findings.text: A 2025 chromosome-level assembly of about 248 million base pairs found 13 chromosomes and an unusual set of immune genes.

survival.lede: The sea walnut is a fragile animal that thrives through sheer numbers and flexibility.

tactics.title: Eating its own young
tactics.text: In the Baltic Sea, once adults have cleared the water of prey, they switch to eating their own larvae and keep building nutrient reserves for lean months.

tactics.title: Tough to kill
tactics.text: It tolerates salinity from 2 to 38 psu and temperatures from 2 to 32 °C.

tactics.title: Turning back time
tactics.text: Stressed adults can revert to the larval form and later grow up again, a possible way to ride out hard times.

life.lede: A sea walnut is hermaphroditic, so a single animal can fertilise its own eggs.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Spawning starts late in the evening or around 1–2 a.m. Eggs are released into the water, where they are fertilised.

stages.name: Cydippid larva
stages.text: The young hatch as rounded cydippid larvae with two tentacles, quite unlike the lobed adult.

stages.name: Lobate adult
stages.text: The larva grows lobes and becomes an adult. Egg-laying can begin at a body length of only about 15 mm.

stages.name: Reverse development
stages.text: Under stress, an adult can turn back into a cydippid larva, then mature and spawn again.

tagline: A dragonfly whose yearly migration takes three generations
summary: One of the largest and most familiar dragonflies in North America, the green darner patrols ponds and fields on long, clear wings. Each spring migrants fly north, and their offspring fly south in autumn. Radio tags and the chemistry of its wings have shown that one round trip takes three generations of dragonflies.

stats.size: Up to about 8 cm long
stats.habitat: Ponds, lakes and slow streams; hunts over fields, forest edges and desert near water
stats.range: Across the United States into southern Canada and Mexico; northern migrants winter as far as Central America; also Hawaii, the West Indies and parts of East Asia
stats.diet: Adults catch flying insects on the wing; nymphs hunt aquatic insects, tadpoles and even small fish

facts.title: Three generations, one round trip
facts.text: Hydrogen isotopes in 852 wings collected over 140 years, together with 21 years of citizen-science records, showed that the yearly cycle takes at least three generations. The first flies more than 650 km north in spring, breeds and dies. Its offspring fly more than 680 km south. A third, resident generation breeds in the south and produces the next spring's migrants.

facts.title: Followed by aeroplane
facts.text: Researchers attached radio transmitters weighing about 300 mg to the thoraxes of 14 migrating green darners. They followed them for up to 12 days with receiver-equipped Cessna aircraft and teams on the ground.

facts.title: Stop-and-go travel
facts.text: The tagged darners alternated stopover days with travel days, migrating on average every 2.9 days. On average they advanced 58 km south in 6.1 days, about 12 km a day.

facts.title: Rules of the road
facts.text: They flew only by day, and only when the wind was below 25 km/h, whatever its direction. They set off only after two nights of successively falling temperatures. These decision rules are strikingly similar to those of migrating songbirds.

facts.title: A darning needle in green and blue
facts.text: Green darners grow to about 8 cm long, among the larger dragonflies. Both sexes have a green thorax; males have a bright blue band near the base of the long, slender abdomen, which gives the group its name from its likeness to a darning needle.

facts.title: Laying in tandem
facts.text: After mating, the pair stays linked: the male keeps hold of the female while she lays eggs in floating stems and leaves. The aquatic nymphs live in shallow water near the shore and pass through 9 to 13 moults before climbing out to become adults.

The abstract of Wikelski et al. does not give the tracking year, so the fact text does not give one either. Regions: north-american-forests first (breeds widely across the US and southern Canada); north-american-deserts (ADW lists desert habitats near water, and the resident southern generation lives in the southern US and Mexico; alt-2 is from Arizona); central-america (ADW: northern migrants winter in Central America, including the Yucatán, Belize and Veracruz). Hawaii, the West Indies and East Asian records are mentioned in the range but not mapped. Biome: wetland, because the species breeds in ponds and still water. Images: hero (California, 2018) and alt-1 (Zelenko, 2008, location not stated) are CC BY-SA 4.0. alt-2 is CC0 (Alan Schmierer, Flickr); its title abbreviates 'pat lake state park, scc, az', read here as Patagonia Lake State Park, Santa Cruz County, Arizona. The alt-2 darner is a dull-blue individual in flight. Its sex is not stated, so the caption does not give one.

anatomy.lede: One of the larger dragonflies of North America: huge eyes, a short, muscular thorax that powers four independent wings, and a long abdomen like a darning needle.

hotspots.label: Compound eye
hotspots.text: The eyes are so large that they wrap around the head, giving an almost all-round view, though the dragonfly sees poorly directly above and below.

hotspots.label: Green face
hotspots.text: Males have a green face and dull green eyes.

hotspots.label: Thorax
hotspots.text: The short, robust thorax holds the flight muscles. Vibrating them warms the body.

hotspots.label: Four wings
hotspots.text: Each of the four wings can move independently, so the darner can fly forwards or backwards, hover and change direction in an instant.

hotspots.label: Blue abdomen
hotspots.text: In males, the second to sixth segments of the abdomen are bright blue. Most females are brown and grey-green here, though a minority resemble males.

hotspots.label: Tail appendages
hotspots.text: The male uses the claspers at the tip of his abdomen to grip a female by the head or the front of the thorax.

stats.label: Most a migrant can travel in a day

senses.lede: A dragonfly is a hunter of the eyes. Almost everything it does, from catching prey to finding a mate, starts with sight.

senses.name: Motion vision
senses.text: The great eyes detect movement easily, letting the darner spot flying and ground-dwelling prey as well as possible mates and predators.

senses.name: Colour and ultraviolet
senses.text: Dragonflies can see a wide range of colours, including ultraviolet light.

senses.name: Polarised light
senses.text: Migrating green darners may use the pattern of polarised light in the sky to work out which way is south.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: Sight identifies a mate, but touch matters too: the male holds the female with his claspers throughout mating.

body.lede: The green darner lives two lives, a hunter underwater and then in the air, with very different bodies for each.

systems.title: Making its own warmth
systems.text: Although it is an insect, the darner actively controls its temperature. It warms up by vibrating its wing muscles, and moves heat around the body by adjusting the flow of its blood-like haemolymph, letting it fly in cool weather and colder regions.

systems.title: A striking lower lip
systems.text: The nymph has a large, flat labium, or lower lip, that it shoots out to spear prey on pointed palps and then pulls back to the jaws.

systems.title: Breathing through the rear
systems.text: A nymph's gills sit in a chamber in its rectum. By squirting water out of the anus it can shoot forwards, away from danger.

mind.lede: The darner's behaviour follows consistent patterns: when to fly, where to rest and how to fight.

studies.title: Following the sun
studies.text: On autumn migrations, darners roost overnight on warm, west-facing vegetation. In the morning they flutter their wings to warm up, then move to east-facing perches in the sun.

studies.title: Weather watchers
studies.text: Cold fronts are a good sign that an autumn migration is about to start, while spring migrants often arrive on warm fronts. In flight they make use of thermals and updrafts.

studies.title: Fights over females
studies.text: Single males often attack a pair flying in tandem, landing on them, ramming, pulling and biting. The paired male fights back, and the struggle can split the pair or drown them.

studies.title: Raiders of the beehive
studies.text: Green darners have gathered in large numbers at bee yards to catch honey bees, especially queens and drones on their mating flights. A severe outbreak in 1941 cost beekeepers heavily.

survival.lede: In ponds without fish the darner nymph is the top predator, but in the air and the water there is always something larger.

tactics.title: Stab and jab
tactics.text: A threatened nymph twists its abdomen to jab at an attacker with its side spines and tail points. As a last resort it uses the hooks on its labium, at the risk of damaging its feeding apparatus.

tactics.title: Keep still, blend in
tactics.text: Nymphs may slow down or stop moving altogether when a predator is near. Their brown or green colours camouflage them, and green nymphs are more common in spring and summer, when water plants are thick.

tactics.title: Speed and sight
tactics.text: Adults fly fast and dodge predators easily, and their keen vision helps them see danger coming.

life.lede: Dragonflies have no pupal stage. The nymph that hatches from the egg grows through a series of moults and then climbs into the air as an adult.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The pair lays eggs in tandem on floating stems, leaves and branches. A lack of oxygen in the water triggers hatching.

stages.name: Nymph
stages.text: The aquatic nymph lives near the shore in water less than half a metre deep, moulting 9 to 13 times. Offspring of migrants develop fast; northern residents overwinter as nymphs.

stages.name: Emergence
stages.text: The full-grown nymph climbs out of the water, sometimes travelling far before scaling a plant stem. Its skin splits and the adult pulls free, expanding its wings.

stages.name: Teneral
stages.text: The newly emerged adult is soft, with little fat and immature reproductive organs; the tip of its abdomen is reddish-purple. It feeds heavily as its cuticle hardens and its colours develop, and migrants often set off at this stage.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Mature adults mate many times with many partners. Northern residents breed in July and August; migrants breed in the north in June and again in the south in late autumn.

lifespan.value: several weeks to a little over a month as an adult

tagline: A cigar-sized shark that bites cookies out of whales
summary: A glowing, cigar-shaped shark only about half a metre long that attacks animals far larger than itself. It latches on with sucker-like lips, spins, and carves out a neat round plug of flesh—leaving crater wounds on tunas, dolphins, whales and seals.
ability: suction-and-spin bite that cuts round plugs of flesh

stats.size: Females up to about 56 cm; males about 42 cm
stats.depth: Recorded from the surface to about 3,500–3,700 m; below about 1,000 m by day, rising at night
stats.range: Tropical to warm-temperate oceans worldwide
stats.diet: Plugs of flesh from large fishes, sharks and marine mammals; also whole squid and crustaceans

facts.title: The cookie-cutter bite
facts.text: It sucks onto its victim with fleshy lips and throat muscles, grips with slender upper teeth, then bites with its large lower teeth and spins, cutting out a deep, circular plug.

facts.title: A glowing belly
facts.text: Except for a dark collar around the throat, its underside is covered in tiny light organs that give an even greenish glow, hiding its silhouette from below (counter-illumination).

facts.title: A collar that lures?
facts.text: Biologist Edith Widder suggested that the unlit collar looks like a small fish against the glow, luring fast predators such as tunas and dolphins close enough to be bitten.

facts.title: Teeth replaced as a set
facts.text: Its lower teeth are joined at their bases and shed as a whole row rather than one by one. It swallows the old row—possibly a way to recycle calcium.

facts.title: Daily elevator ride
facts.text: It spends the day in deep water, below about 1,000 m, and migrates toward the surface at night to feed. There are even reports of its bite marks on submarine sonar domes.

Rejected: Smithsonian jar specimen (cluttered). The 'collar lure' fact cites Fishes of Australia's summary of Widder (1998). Fishes of Australia also reports a cookiecutter bite on a long-distance swimmer in Hawaii (Honebrink et al. 2011)—not used in facts. Depth: FishBase 0–3,700 m, Fishes of Australia 0–3,500 m.

anatomy.lede: A cookiecutter shark is small enough to hold in one hand, yet every part of its head is built for taking bites out of animals hundreds of times its size.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: The large green eyes face forwards but sit far enough back that the shark has little binocular vision.

hotspots.label: Sucking lips
hotspots.text: Fleshy, sucker-like lips and strong throat muscles let it seal onto the skin of its victim before it bites.

hotspots.label: Dark collar
hotspots.text: A dark brown band rings the gill region. It is the only part of the underside without light organs.

hotspots.label: Pectoral fin
hotspots.text: The pectoral fins sit just behind the collar. Further back, the pelvic fins are larger than the dorsal fins.

hotspots.label: Glowing belly
hotspots.text: The underside is densely covered in tiny light organs. They can keep glowing for up to three hours after the shark dies.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fins
hotspots.text: Two small, spineless dorsal fins of nearly equal size sit far back on the body. There is no anal fin.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The tail fin is large, with a long lower lobe.

body.lede: The cookiecutter's 'bite' is really a suction, spin and slice, made possible by an unusual set of teeth.

systems.title: Two kinds of teeth
systems.text: The upper jaw holds 30–37 small, erect, thorn-like teeth that grip, while the lower jaw has 25–31 much larger, triangular blades that cut. Larger sharks have more teeth.

systems.title: Teeth as one blade
systems.text: The lower teeth are joined at their bases, so touching one moves the whole row, so the whole row acts as one cutting edge.

systems.title: Light organs
systems.text: Countless minute photophores give the belly an even glow, which hides the shark's silhouette from animals looking up from below.

mind.lede: No one has watched a cookiecutter hunt in the deep, so its behaviour is pieced together from wounds and rare encounters.

studies.title: Biting a great white
studies.text: Researchers documented a cookiecutter shark attacking a white shark, one of the largest predatory fishes in the sea.

studies.title: Scars on dolphins and whales
studies.text: Crater-shaped bite wounds from cookiecutter sharks have been catalogued on cetaceans in the Gulf of Mexico, a sign of how widely it feeds.

studies.title: Dark nights, more bites
studies.text: Of seven known bites on living people worldwide, six were in Hawaiʻi. Analysis of channel swims there from 1961 to 2023 found that swimmers were far more likely to be bitten when neither moon nor sun was in the sky.

survival.lede: A small shark that feeds on giants has to hide from them as well.

tactics.title: Counter-illumination
tactics.text: The glowing belly matches the faint light from above, making the shark hard to see from below.

tactics.title: Deep by day
tactics.text: It spends the day below about 1,000 m and rises towards the surface only at night to feed.

tactics.title: Hit and run
tactics.text: By taking a single plug of flesh and letting go, it can feed on large, dangerous animals without having to kill them.

threats.title: Night-time catches
threats.text: Its deep habitat makes it hard to target, but it is sometimes caught at night during its migration to the surface. Populations could fall if fishing pressure grows.

life.lede: Like many deep-sea sharks, the cookiecutter gives birth to live young that hatch from egg cases inside the mother.

stages.name: Embryo
stages.text: Pups develop in egg cases inside the mother's uterus, living on their yolk. Litters of 6 to 12 live young have been recorded.

stages.name: Birth
stages.text: The pups hatch inside the mother and are born live at about 14 cm long.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Males mature at about 38 cm and females at about 40 cm long. Females grow larger, reaching up to 56 cm.

tagline: A pale yellow hunter whose venom is both feared and medically useful
summary: The deathstalker is a slender, straw-yellow scorpion of the deserts along the Nile, active at night and among the most medically important scorpions in its region. Its venom is a cocktail of nerve toxins, one of which, chlorotoxin, has been turned into a 'tumour paint' that makes cancer cells glow during surgery.

stats.size: Adults about 69–90 mm long
stats.habitat: Stony and gravel desert, hiding under rocks and in burrows; not in sand dunes
stats.range: Egypt and Sudan, as revised in 2014; older records across North Africa and the Middle East now partly belong to other species
stats.diet: Insects, spiders, centipedes and other scorpions
stats.conservation: Not evaluated by the IUCN Red List

facts.title: One name, several species
facts.text: A 2014 revision of the genus Leiurus split the old, wide-ranging deathstalker into several species. L. quinquestriatus in the strict sense is now confirmed from Egypt and Sudan, while scorpions from Israel and the Levant became L. hebraeus and several Arabian populations were described as new species.

facts.title: Dangerous, especially to children
facts.text: Its venom is very potent and it causes deaths every year. Most stings cause only local pain, but symptoms depend on body weight, so the venom is most dangerous to small children.

facts.title: A toxin that blocks chloride channels
facts.text: In 1993 researchers purified chlorotoxin from deathstalker venom: a small peptide that blocks chloride channels in cells and is toxic to arthropods.

facts.title: Tumour paint
facts.text: Chlorotoxin binds to many kinds of cancer cell. Linked to a near-infrared dye, it lit up brain tumours and other cancers in mice, down to clusters of a few hundred cells — the basis of 'tumour paint' for guiding surgeons.

facts.title: Hunter of the night
facts.text: It spends the day under stones or in burrows, sometimes digging its own about 20 cm down, and comes out at night to hunt — a way of saving water as well as avoiding the heat.

facts.title: Born alive
facts.text: Females give birth to live young rather than laying eggs. Older records report broods averaging about 60 after a gestation of several months, though these may include scorpions now placed in other Leiurus species.
