notes: Taxonomy: Lowe, Yağmur & Kovařík 2014 (Euscorpius 191) restored L. brachycentrus, raised L. hebraeus to species and described L. arabicus, L. haenggii, L. heberti and L. macroctenus from Arabia. Their treatment gives L. quinquestriatus s.str. distribution as 'Egypt, Sudan' (69–90 mm adults) and explicitly leaves records from Libya, Algeria and southern Sinai unrevised. So range is stated as Egypt and Sudan, with regions only sahara-arabia; the Scorpion Files page still lists a broad pre-revision range (Algeria to Saudi Arabia), and ADW's 80–110 mm size and brood data are pre-revision, hence the 'uncertain' birth fact. Chlorotoxin (DeBin 1993) was purified from venom sold as 'L. quinquestriatus' before the split; the exact population is not stated. Charybdotoxin and agitoxin come from L. q. hebraeus (now L. hebraeus), so they are deliberately not credited here. No 'apex-predators' category. Images: many Commons photos labelled L. quinquestriatus were taken in the Negev, Israel — after 2014 those are L. hebraeus, so none were used. The hero and alt-1 are captive animals labelled L. quinquestriatus by their photographers with no locality, so identity follows the uploaders' labels and cannot be checked against the 2014 diagnosis; the hero's 'captive' setting is inferred (no locality, studio-style shot). alt-2 is Koch's 1841 engraving, which predates the revision. LD50 figures (0.16–0.50 mg/kg per Scorpion Files) were not used because test route and species concept are unclear. No IUCN evaluation (ADW: not evaluated by IUCN or CITES).

anatomy.lede: A deathstalker is built like every scorpion — pincers, eight legs, a segmented body and a tail ending in a sting — in a slender, straw-yellow form that ranks among the most dangerous scorpions on Earth.

hotspots.label: Median eyes
hotspots.text: A pair of eyes sits on top of the head, with two to five more pairs at its front corners. Even so, scorpions do not see well.

hotspots.label: Pincers
hotspots.text: The slim pincers seize prey, crush it and draw it towards the mouth.

hotspots.label: Keeled back plates
hotspots.text: The first two plates on the back carry five raised keels each, a feature that sets this species apart from most other scorpions.

hotspots.label: Darker tail segment
hotspots.text: The fifth segment of the tail, just before the sting, is marked with brown, in contrast to the yellow body.

hotspots.label: Venom bulb and sting
hotspots.text: The swollen last part of the tail ends in a curved, dark-tipped sting that delivers the venom.

hotspots.label: Leg tip
hotspots.text: Tiny slit-shaped sense organs near the tips of the legs pick up vibrations in the ground.

senses.lede: A scorpion hunts in the dark by feel, reading the ground through its feet.

senses.name: Vibration
senses.text: Slit organs near the tips of the legs detect vibrations in sand or soil and can tell the scorpion both the direction and the distance of prey.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: Deathstalkers find their way and catch prey mainly by touch, using the comb-like pectines under the body as well as other organs.

senses.name: Pectines
senses.text: In experiments on two other scorpion species, the pectines and pincers worked as touch and chemical sensors: with either impaired, the scorpions could no longer judge a shelter's size or scent.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Despite having several pairs of eyes, scorpions have poor vision.

body.lede: The deathstalker's venom is a mixture of small proteins aimed at the nerves and cells of its prey.

systems.title: A potent venom
systems.text: Its LD50, the dose that kills half of test animals, is 0.16–0.50 mg per kilogram of body weight. In a study from Israel (where the scorpions are now classed as Leiurus hebraeus), 97% of people stung had only local reactions, but severity depends on body weight.

systems.title: Chlorotoxin
systems.text: The chloride-channel blocker in the venom is a small peptide of about 4,070 daltons. Its amino-acid sequence is similar to that of a group of short toxins thought to act on insects, and it is toxic to arthropods.

systems.title: Medicine from venom
systems.text: Besides chlorotoxin's use in cancer research, other venom components are being studied for diabetes, because the channels they act on help to regulate insulin. This work is at an early stage.

systems.title: Nourished before birth
systems.text: Most scorpions are viviparous: the young develop inside the mother, fed through the uterine wall or by membranes around the embryo, and are relatively large at birth.

survival.lede: Even a scorpion this venomous is food for other animals — above all, for other scorpions.

tactics.title: Night shift
tactics.text: Being active only at night helps it manage both its temperature and its water balance in the desert.

tactics.title: Under stones
tactics.text: By day it shelters under rocks or in the abandoned burrows of other animals, or digs its own about 20 cm down beneath a rock.

tactics.title: Ambush
tactics.text: It waits under stones or other cover for prey to pass, then seizes it with its pincers.

threats.title: Collecting and habitat loss
threats.text: Scorpions in general are increasingly threatened by habitat destruction and by collection for souvenirs and the pet trade, and their small broods and long generation times make recovery slow.

life.lede: Scorpions court in a dance, give birth to live young and carry them on their backs. Much of what is known for the deathstalker predates the 2014 revision that split it into several species.

stages.name: Courtship
stages.text: The male grasps the female's pincers in his own and leads her in a dance, the promenade à deux, before depositing a packet of sperm on the ground and guiding her over it.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Gestation averaged about 185 days in older records, followed by the birth of dozens of young.

stages.name: First instar
stages.text: In close relatives, newborn scorpions climb onto their mother's back and stay there until their first moult, protected and kept from drying out. High mortality follows soon after birth.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Young scorpions moult several times before becoming adult, looking like small adults at every stage.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Mortality is higher in adults than in scorpions of intermediate age.

tagline: The one-humped camel that lets itself heat up to save water
summary: The dromedary, or Arabian camel, has carried people and goods across hot deserts for about 3,000 years. Its secret is not a water tank in the hump, which is fat, but a body that tolerates extreme dehydration, refills fast and lets its temperature rise by day rather than sweat water away.

stats.size: About 1.8–2 m at the shoulder; males 400–600 kg
stats.habitat: Hot deserts and dry scrub, almost entirely with people
stats.range: North Africa and the Horn of Africa through Arabia to north-western India; feral herds in central Australia
stats.diet: Almost any desert vegetation, including dry, thorny and salty plants
stats.conservation: Not assessed by the IUCN: a domesticated animal whose wild ancestor is extinct; only feral herds live free

facts.title: Running on empty
facts.text: A dromedary can tolerate losing more than 30% of its body water. For most mammals, losing about 15% is fatal.

facts.title: A hundred litres in ten minutes
facts.text: When it does reach water, a thirsty dromedary can drink about 100 litres in just ten minutes.

facts.title: Running hot to stay wet
facts.text: Its body temperature can swing between about 34 °C and 41.7 °C in a day. Classic experiments by Knut Schmidt-Nielsen and colleagues showed that storing heat by day and losing it in the cool night saves water that would otherwise be spent on sweating.

facts.title: Fat, not water
facts.text: The hump stores fat, not water, as an energy reserve. When food is scarce it shrinks and can lean or droop.

facts.title: Born of a vanished wild camel
facts.text: Ancient and modern DNA show that wild dromedaries from the south-east Arabian Peninsula were among the founders of today's domestic herds. Those wild populations are now extinct.

facts.title: Wild again, in Australia
facts.text: Free-living dromedaries survive today only as feral herds in Australia, descended from camels introduced there in the 19th century.

notes: No iucnId: the IUCN Red List does not assess the domestic dromedary (ADW: 'not evaluated'/no special status); the only camel assessed is the wild Bactrian, Camelus ferus. Water figures (>30% loss tolerated vs ~15% lethal for most mammals; ~100 L in 10 min; 34–41.7 °C daily swing) are from ADW. The 1957 Schmidt-Nielsen paper (dated 1956 in its DOI) is the primary source for heat storage saving water; its full text was not accessible, so the specific numbers are attributed to ADW. San Diego Zoo quotes 145 L per drinking session and a 40% weight-loss tolerance — not used, as it is less specific. Shoulder height 1.8–2.0 m for males per ADW (San Diego gives 1.6–1.8 m). '3,000 years' of use is from Almathen et al. 2016; ADW says domestication evidence dates to ~4,000 years ago. Regions: sahara-arabia, indian-subcontinent (Thar/Rajasthan) and australian-outback (feral, introduced). The Horn of Africa holds very large herds but has no matching region slug; african-savanna was not used. Images are domestic/feral animals, labelled so; there are no wild dromedaries to photograph.

anatomy.lede: Almost every part of a dromedary's head and body is shaped by sand, sun and scarcity — from the lashes over its eyes to the broad pads beneath its feet.

hotspots.label: Eye and lashes
hotspots.text: A double row of eyelashes shields each eye from blowing sand and dust.

hotspots.label: Nostrils
hotspots.text: When a sandstorm begins, the camel can close its nostrils to keep the sand out.

hotspots.label: Thick lips
hotspots.text: The lips are thickened so the camel can grasp coarse, thorny plants. It chews each bite 40–50 times, keeping its mouth open while chewing thorny food.

hotspots.label: Throat and shoulder hair
hotspots.text: The coat is longer on the throat, shoulders and hump than elsewhere on the body.

hotspots.label: Padded foot
hotspots.text: The broad, pad-shaped feet spread the camel's weight on sand, but they are easily injured on sharp stones and slip in mud.

body.lede: The dromedary does not store water in its hump. Its secret is a body that spends water as sparingly as possible and can survive running very low.

systems.title: A body that warms up by day
systems.text: Instead of sweating to hold a steady temperature, the camel lets heat build up in its body during the day and gives it off in the cool night. In the 1950s, Knut Schmidt-Nielsen's team showed that this saves water that would otherwise be lost in sweat.

systems.title: Keeping the blood flowing
systems.text: When a dromedary dehydrates, the water it loses comes mainly from the fluid between and inside its cells. This helps explain how it can lose more than 30% of its body water and survive.

systems.title: A hump of fat
systems.text: The hump is fat bound together by fibrous tissue, a food store for hard times. Dromedaries also need six to eight times as much salt as other animals to absorb and hold water, so about a third of what they eat must be salty plants.

systems.title: Antibodies without light chains
systems.text: In 1993 researchers found that camel blood contains large amounts of antibodies made only of heavy chains, with no light chains, which still recognise a wide range of targets. The discovery opened new ways of engineering antibodies.

genome.lede: Camels carry 74 chromosomes, a karyotype that cytogeneticists describe as difficult to work with. A chromosome-level reference genome for the North African dromedary followed in 2019.

findings.title: Genes for desert living
findings.text: Comparing the genomes of the dromedary, Bactrian camel and alpaca, researchers found genetic features linked to fat and water metabolism and to coping with heat, aridity, strong ultraviolet light and dust. They proposed that changes in the kidneys underpin the camels' water economy.

findings.title: A well-mixed herd
findings.text: DNA from 1,083 living dromedaries showed little geographic structure: centuries of caravan trade have mixed the herds almost everywhere except East Africa, where populations have stayed more isolated.

findings.title: Restocked from the wild
findings.text: Models of the same data support the idea that after the first domestication, herders kept adding animals from wild populations that are now extinct.

mind.lede: Dromedaries live in small groups with clear roles, and they choose what they eat with care.

studies.title: Led from the front, guarded from the rear
studies.text: Groups of 2 to 20 are usually a family of one male, one or more females and their young. The females take turns to lead while the male directs from the back, keeping stray males away.

studies.title: A display of the throat
studies.text: Rutting males threaten rivals with low noises, stand as tall as they can and bend their necks back. Males also have an inflatable soft palate, used to attract females.

studies.title: A few leaves from each plant
studies.text: Foraging camels spread out and take only a few leaves from each plant. This eases the pressure on desert vegetation and may limit how much of any one plant toxin a camel swallows.

life.lede: Dromedaries breed slowly: usually one calf at a time, after a pregnancy that lasts more than a year.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Breeding happens in the winter rainy season, and the female carries a single calf for over a year.

stages.name: Calf
stages.text: Calves are born well developed and can move about freely by the end of their first day.

stages.name: Young camel
stages.text: The mother feeds and cares for her calf for one to two years, and it gains about 0.2–0.3 kg a day in its first year.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature at about three and first mate at four or five; males start to rut at three but are not fully mature until six. Females calve about once every two years.

lifespan.value: about 40–50 years

tagline: The deepest-living octopus, flapping on ear-like fins
summary: Dumbo octopuses are a genus of soft, jelly-like deep-sea octopuses named for the two ear-like fins above their eyes. They hover and 'hop' over the abyssal seafloor, and one was filmed nearly 7 km down, deeper than any other octopus or squid ever seen.

stats.size: Hadal individuals filmed at about 35–43 cm total length
stats.depth: Mostly about 1,000–7,000 m
stats.range: Probably worldwide in deep, cold water
stats.diet: Small seafloor animals: worms, copepods, amphipods, isopods
stats.conservation: Not evaluated by IUCN as a genus; most species are poorly known

facts.title: Deepest octopus on record
facts.text: In 2019 a baited camera lander in the Java Trench, Indian Ocean, filmed a Grimpoteuthis at 6,957 m: the first unequivocal sighting of any cephalopod in the hadal zone (below 6,000 m).

facts.title: Fins, not jets
facts.text: Unlike most octopuses, which jet water through a siphon, dumbos swim mainly by flapping their two fins, which helps them save energy in the food-poor deep sea.

facts.title: Hop, spread, repeat
facts.text: Filmed individuals foraged in short 'hops' across the mud, landing with arms and web spread before lifting off again. One picked up a tiny isopod, then dropped it.

facts.title: Eggs left on their own
facts.text: Dumbo octopuses attach large, tough-cased eggs to deep-sea corals and do not guard them. Hatchlings emerge as fully formed juveniles able to fend for themselves.

facts.title: A tangled family tree
facts.text: Telling species apart is hard: specimens are rare and often damaged, and many key features are internal, so photos alone rarely pin down a species.

anatomy.lede: Dumbo octopuses are soft, jelly-like and built for hovering: two fins for flying, and webbed arms fringed with tiny fingers.

hotspots.label: Ear-like fin
hotspots.text: One of two fins on the mantle, set above each eye, that give the genus its 'dumbo' nickname. Cushioning cartilage at the fin base supports the muscles that drive it.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Each fin sits above an eye, one on each side of the head.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The body is soft and gelatinous, quite unlike the muscular body of a shallow-water octopus.

hotspots.label: Web
hotspots.text: A web of skin joins the arms. When a dumbo lands on the seafloor it spreads its arms and web, then lifts off again a few seconds later.

hotspots.label: Cirri
hotspots.text: The fringe along each arm is made of cirri, small finger-like projections that are thought to help move food towards the mouth.

stats.label: Water temperature at the deepest sightings

body.lede: Life in cold, food-poor water favours an octopus that spends as little energy as possible.

systems.title: Fin power
systems.text: Dumbos rest on the seafloor with arms and web spread, crawl slowly, or lift off by contracting the web and arms and then swim with their fins. Jet propulsion, once proposed, is now thought unlikely.

systems.title: No ink, no colour change
systems.text: Like other finned (cirrate) octopuses, they have no ink sac and lack the nerve-controlled colour cells that let other octopuses change colour.

systems.title: A rare internal shell
systems.text: Some species have an internal shell. In one species, G. angularis, it has a shape distinct from the rest of the genus.

mind.lede: Almost all that is known about how dumbos behave comes from a few minutes of deep-sea video.

studies.title: Unbothered by cameras
studies.text: Two dumbos filmed in the Java Trench, at 5,760 m and 6,957 m, largely ignored the bait and the lander. The lights seemed neither to scare them off nor to draw them in.

studies.title: Short visits
studies.text: The shallower octopus stayed in view for 23 minutes, left for 6 and came back for 7 more. Neither animal appeared to be resting or dying.

survival.lede: Living at 1,000 m and deeper keeps dumbo octopuses far from most dangers, and from people.

tactics.title: Lift off and fly
tactics.text: When disturbed, a resting dumbo pulls in its web and arms to lift off, then flaps its fins to swim away.

tactics.title: The deepest refuge
tactics.text: Octopuses able to live down to about 7,000 m could reach about 99% of the seafloor, compared with about 75% for those limited to 5,145 m.

life.lede: Dumbos and their relatives do not breed in seasons. Females carry eggs at many stages and lay them a few at a time.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: Mating has never been seen. Males lack the modified arm other octopuses use and are thought to place sperm packets in the female's mantle with their enlarged suckers; she stores the sperm until she lays.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Females lay one or two large, tough-cased eggs at a time, attached to deep-sea corals, and leave them unguarded. This continuous spawning is best documented in a related genus.

stages.name: Hatchling
stages.text: The young hatch as fully competent juveniles, ready to fend for themselves.

lifespan.value: unknown; probably several years, judging by related octopuses

tagline: The biggest teeth for its size of any fish
summary: A small, ultra-black fish with a gaping mouth full of fangs—proportionally the largest teeth of any fish. Growing to only about 18 cm, it drifts through the twilight and midnight zones waiting for prey to come close, sensing movement rather than seeing it.
ability: oversized fangs that fold into sockets in its head

stats.size: Up to about 18 cm
stats.depth: Mostly 500–2,000 m; young near the surface, adults recorded to about 5,000 m
stats.range: Tropical and temperate seas worldwide
stats.diet: Crustaceans when young; mainly fishes as adults

facts.title: Teeth with their own garage
facts.text: Relative to its size, the fangtooth has the largest teeth of any fish. When it shuts its mouth, the huge lower fangs slide up into sockets on either side of its brain.

facts.title: Feeling, not seeing
facts.text: Its eyes are small and its eyesight is thought to be poor. Instead it relies on the dark lateral line along its side, a row of sensors that detects tiny movements in the water.

facts.title: Ultra-black skin
facts.text: Its skin is packed with pigment that absorbs about 99.5% of the light hitting it, helping it hide in plain sight.

facts.title: A baby in disguise
facts.text: Juveniles look like a different fish: pale, big-eyed, with long horn-like spines on the head and small teeth. The name cornuta, 'horned', refers to those juvenile spines.

facts.title: Rarely seen alive
facts.text: Despite living worldwide, it is elusive: MBARI's remotely operated vehicles have spotted a fangtooth on average less than once every two years since the institute opened.

notes: Hero is a dead specimen on ice (Commons Category:Anoplogaster cornuta; North Atlantic, where only A. cornuta occurs). Rejected: NOAA Photo Library 'Fis01058' (sharper, fresh, but only categorised to genus Anoplogaster and from a Pacific Cobb trawl, so A. cornuta vs A. brachycera cannot be confirmed; also shows a hand and wristwatch). Size: MBARI/FishBase give max 18 cm; Monterey Bay Aquarium says up to 15.2 cm and WHOI says adults average 16 cm. The fang-socket detail: Fishes of Australia says sockets 'on either side of its brain'; WHOI describes them as on the roof of the mouth—same function, different wording. WHOI also lists 'bioluminescence: yes, on the sides', which is not supported by other sources and was not used. Order follows WoRMS (Trachichthyiformes); older sources place it in Beryciformes.

anatomy.lede: A fangtooth is little more than a head and a mouth wrapped in a black body: a palm-sized ambusher built to grab whatever drifts close in the dark.

hotspots.label: Fangs
hotspots.text: The jaws carry huge fang-like teeth, and adults are dark even inside the mouth, so the teeth are the only thing that stands out.

hotspots.label: Small eye
hotspots.text: The eyes are small and are not thought to be very powerful, so the fish leans on other senses to find prey.

hotspots.label: Lateral line
hotspots.text: The lateral line runs as an open groove along the side, bridged at intervals by scales. It picks up tiny movements in the water.

hotspots.label: Pectoral fin
hotspots.text: When its mouth is stuffed with large prey, the fangtooth is reported to fan water over its gills with its pectoral fins.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: A single long-based dorsal fin carries 17–20 soft rays and no spines.

hotspots.label: Prickly tail
hotspots.text: The skin of the tail fin carries small, prickly scales.

senses.lede: In water where sunlight never reaches, the fangtooth seems to feel its way to food rather than look for it.

senses.name: Lateral line
senses.text: The lateral line along each side senses even small movements nearby, which is how the fish is thought to detect prey.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: Scientists at MBARI believe the fangtooth has poor eyesight but an excellent sense of touch.

senses.name: Temperature
senses.text: The lateral line is also described as sensing changes in water temperature.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Its small, milky-blue eyes are not very powerful, and how much it uses them has not been documented.

body.lede: Cold, dark, oxygen-poor water shapes how the fangtooth looks and how it breathes.

systems.title: Skin that swallows light
systems.text: A continuous layer of tightly packed pigment granules in the skin, with none of the gaps found in ordinary black fish, absorbs more than 99.5% of the light that hits it. The granules are close to the ideal size and shape for trapping light.

systems.title: Built for the cold
systems.text: The fangtooth is adapted to a narrow band of cold water, around 4–6 °C.

systems.title: Breathing tested
systems.text: In a 1976 study, ten fangtooths swam at controlled speeds at 3, 7 and 10 °C while the oxygen in their water was lowered towards zero, to learn how the species might survive the oxygen-poor layers of the eastern Pacific.

systems.title: Living with little oxygen
systems.text: How it copes with the oxygen-poor layers it passes through is unsettled. It may visit them only briefly and pay back an 'oxygen debt' later, or switch to metabolism that needs no oxygen while there.

survival.lede: Small as it is, the fangtooth is both hunter and hunted in the open midwater.

tactics.title: Lurk and wait
tactics.text: Its gaping mouth, stubby fins and mottled body suggest a predator that hangs in the water and waits for prey to come close rather than chasing it.

tactics.title: Invisible in the beam
tactics.text: In the deep sea, the main threat is being lit up by another animal's bioluminescence. Ultra-black skin can cut the distance at which a predator spots it more than six-fold compared with a fish reflecting 2% of light.

tactics.title: Big mouthfuls
tactics.text: Adults have been seen eating fish about a third of their own size, and most prey is swallowed whole.

life.lede: A fangtooth starts life near the surface and sinks into the dark as it grows, changing so much on the way that the young were once thought to be another species.

stages.name: Egg and larva
stages.text: Eggs are spawned into open water with no parental care, and the larvae drift in the plankton, nearer the surface than the adults.

stages.name: Horned juvenile
stages.text: Juveniles are pale, with long head spines, large eyes and small teeth in several rows. They feed on crustaceans and start to look like adults at about 8 cm.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults turn uniformly blackish-brown, grow their great fangs and switch mainly to fish. They are thought to mature at about 13 cm.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: Spawning has been reported from June to August. Where it happens is unknown, and there seem to be no special spawning grounds.

tagline: The smallest fox, with the biggest ears for its size
summary: The fennec is the smallest of all the dog family, a sand-coloured fox of the Sahara that spends the hot day in a burrow and hunts at night. Its enormous ears do two jobs at once: they shed body heat, and they pick up the sound of insects and rodents moving beneath the sand.
ability: giant ears for cooling and listening

stats.size: Body about 36–41 cm plus an 18–30 cm tail; about 0.8–1.5 kg
stats.habitat: Sandy desert and arid scrub; shelters in burrows by day
stats.range: Throughout the Sahara, east to Sinai and Arabia
stats.diet: Insects, small rodents, lizards, birds and eggs, plus roots, fruits and leaves

facts.title: All ears
facts.text: The fennec has the largest ears relative to its body size of any member of the dog family. They can reach 10–15 cm long on an animal that weighs little more than a kilogram.

facts.title: Radiators and radar
facts.text: Those ears dissipate heat, and they are sensitive enough for the fox to hear prey moving under the sand. Once it has located a meal, the fennec digs with all four feet to reach it.

facts.title: The smallest canid
facts.text: The fennec is the smallest of all canids. Adults weigh roughly 0.8–1.5 kg, smaller than many pet cats.

facts.title: No need to drink
facts.text: Fennecs can go for long periods, possibly indefinitely, without drinking free water. Much of their moisture comes from food, including fruit, leaves and roots.

facts.title: Fur-lined slippers
facts.text: The soles of the feet are thickly furred, protecting the pads from hot sand and giving grip on loose dunes.

facts.title: Night shift
facts.text: Fennecs spend the hottest hours in burrows they dig themselves and come out to hunt at night. A reflective layer behind the retina, the tapetum, helps them see in the dark.

anatomy.lede: A fennec is mostly ears and fur: a kilogram of fox built to lose heat by day, hear through sand by night and walk on ground too hot to touch.

hotspots.label: Ear
hotspots.text: Each ear can be 10–15 cm long, and does two jobs: shedding body heat and gathering sound.

hotspots.label: Pale ear lining
hotspots.text: The fur on the face, legs and ear linings is white, while the back is buff. Fennecs are the palest of all foxes, which camouflages them on sand.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: A reflective layer behind the retina, the tapetum, gathers extra light for hunting at night and makes the eyes seem to glow.

hotspots.label: Whiskers
hotspots.text: The whiskers, nose pad and eyes are all black, set in a pale face.

hotspots.label: Nose
hotspots.text: Smell, with hearing, is one of the two senses the fennec relies on most.

hotspots.label: Furred paw
hotspots.text: Thick fur covers the soles, giving grip on loose sand and protecting the pads from the heat.

senses.lede: The fennec lives by its ears. Hearing and smell lead it to food buried in sand on moonless nights.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Besides the huge outer ears, the bony chambers of the middle ear, the auditory bullae, are enlarged. Together they let the fox hear prey moving through many centimetres of sand.

senses.name: Voices of the family
senses.text: Fennecs can tell apart subtle differences between the whines and whimpers of other fennecs, and their own calls include barks, shrieks, squeaks, growls, howls and chatters.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: A highly developed sense of smell helps the fox find prey and read the urine and droppings that mark the edges of each family's territory.

senses.name: Night vision
senses.text: The tapetum behind the retina reflects light back through it a second time, improving vision in the dark.

body.lede: Life in the Sahara means coping with searing days, cold nights and almost no drinking water.

systems.title: Ears as radiators
systems.text: The ears are massive in proportion to the skull, and one of their main jobs is to get rid of body heat.

systems.title: Water from food
systems.text: Fruit, leaves and roots supply almost all of a fennec's water, so it can go indefinitely without drinking.

systems.title: Kidneys under selection
systems.text: Whole genomes from Saharan foxes revealed repeated signs of natural selection on genes that control water balance in the kidneys, in both the fennec and Rüppell's fox, backed by differences in gene activity and physiology.

genome.lede: The fennec has been sequenced as part of a study of how foxes adapted, again and again, to the Sahara.

findings.title: Four foxes, one desert
findings.text: Researchers sequenced 82 whole genomes from four fox species living in the Sahara, which arrived there at different times in their evolution, including the fennec.

findings.title: Borrowed genes
findings.text: Newer arrivals in the desert appear to have adapted partly by inheriting stretches of DNA from older desert species through interbreeding, including a 25-million-letter region that may be adaptive.

mind.lede: Fennecs are sociable, playful and vocal — unusual for a fox — though each still hunts alone.

studies.title: Families with helpers
studies.text: Family groups of up to ten usually include a breeding pair, their pups and some older siblings, who help to raise the young.

studies.title: Stalk, spring, pounce
studies.text: The fennec hunts alone by stalking, springing and pouncing. It can kill prey larger than itself: fully grown rabbits have been recorded.

studies.title: Hidden stores
studies.text: Fennecs cache spare food and are said to remember the hiding places from one season to the next.

studies.title: Born to dig
studies.text: Fennecs raised in the laboratory often dig, or try to dig, inside their cages, which suggests that digging is instinctive rather than learned.

survival.lede: Little is recorded about what hunts the fennec. Its defences are a sand-coloured coat, sharp ears and a burrow with more than one way out.

tactics.title: Tunnels with escape hatches
tactics.text: Burrows can grow into tunnel systems up to 10 m long with several entrances, so the fox can flee if an enemy arrives. They are often dug under bushes whose roots hold the walls up.

tactics.title: Sand-coloured
tactics.text: The pale coat that helps the fennec stalk prey probably also hides it from larger predators.

tactics.title: Out of the sun
tactics.text: By spending the day underground and hunting at night, the fox avoids the hottest hours and saves water.

threats.title: Trapping for sale
threats.text: The main threat is people: fennecs are commonly trapped for exhibition or for sale to tourists, and they are also hunted in parts of the Sahara.

threats.title: Settlements
threats.text: In some places, new human settlements have spread into fennec habitat, though so far only on a limited scale.

life.lede: Fennecs pair for life and raise one litter a year, with both parents caring for the pups.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Mating takes place in January and February, and the female is in heat for only a day or two.

stages.name: Newborn pup
stages.text: Usually two to four pups are born, sometimes five or six, each weighing about 50 g and blind. The mother stays with them in the den while the father brings her food.

stages.name: Growing pup
stages.text: Eyes open after 8–11 days and pups walk at about two weeks. They play inside the den at four weeks, outside it at five, and nurse for around ten weeks.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Young fennecs reach adult size and sexual maturity at between six and eleven months, depending on the source.

lifespan.value: up to 10 years in the wild; 12 in captivity

tagline: A walking light show on the seafloor
summary: A small cuttlefish of tropical sand and mud flats that walks rather than swims, ambling on its arms and fin flaps. When disturbed, it stays put and ripples with waves of dark brown, white, yellow and red: a bold display long said to warn of toxic flesh, though the evidence is mixed.

stats.size: Mantle up to about 6–8 cm
stats.depth: About 3–86 m
stats.range: Northern Australia and southern New Guinea to Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines
stats.diet: Crustaceans and small fishes
stats.conservation: IUCN: Data Deficient (assessed as Metasepia pfefferi, 2012)

facts.title: A cuttlefish that walks
facts.text: Its cuttlebone (the buoyant internal shell) is small and lets it float only briefly, so it mostly ambles over the bottom on two arms and flaps of its fin.

facts.title: Standing its ground
facts.text: Unlike most cuttlefish, it does not dart away when threatened. It stays still, pulses its fins and flashes vivid colour waves, with red arm tips, that may warn predators off.

facts.title: Toxic? Not proven
facts.text: It is often called the only poisonous cuttlefish, based on an unpublished toxicology result. Later tests found only trace tetrodotoxin, too little to harm vertebrates, so its toxicity remains unconfirmed.

facts.title: A daytime hunter
facts.text: While most cephalopods hunt at night, it is active by day, using shifting camouflage to stalk crustaceans and small fishes.

facts.title: Eggs left to hatch
facts.text: Females cement single eggs into crevices and leave them. The eggs turn see-through as they develop, and hatchlings can already make adult colour patterns.

Reference index 1 (Lupše) supports the name change only; facts 0, 1 and 3 cite the Monterey Bay Aquarium (index 2) and facts 2 and 4 cite Wikipedia (index 3). MBA still states the flesh is 'highly poisonous ... as lethal as blue-ringed octopuses' (Mark Norman, unpublished); Wikipedia reports later work finding only trace TTX. Treated as uncertain; 'venomous' category NOT assigned. Size: sources differ (6 vs 8 cm mantle). Commons file title begins with a Cyrillic 'С' (sourceUrl percent-encoded accordingly). IUCN assessment (2012) used the old name Metasepia pfefferi.

anatomy.lede: A flamboyant cuttlefish is a small, broad body with blade-like arms, fleshy flaps and a skin that never stops changing colour.

hotspots.label: Red arm tips
hotspots.text: The broad, blade-like arms carry four rows of suckers. Their tips often flush bright red, which may help ward off predators.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Like other cuttlefish, it is probably colour-blind, yet it can still produce colour patterns of great complexity.

hotspots.label: Papillae over the eye
hotspots.text: Fleshy papillae rise above the eyes, part of the skin texture it can raise and lower.

hotspots.label: Mantle flaps
hotspots.text: Three pairs of large, flat flaps stand up from the top of the very broad, oval mantle.

hotspots.label: Fin
hotspots.text: The fins edging the mantle pulse during its warning display, and help it 'walk' along the bottom together with its arms.

hotspots.label: Walking arms
hotspots.text: Two arms act like legs. Its cuttlebone is too small to keep it afloat for long, so it ambles over sand and mud instead of hovering.

senses.lede: Its senses are barely studied; what is known comes mostly from its better-known relatives.

senses.name: Colour-blind vision
senses.text: Tests on the common cuttlefish show that cuttlefish cannot tell colours apart, although they are sensitive to contrast. Researchers assume the flamboyant cuttlefish sees in the same way.

senses.name: A daytime hunter's eyes
senses.text: Unlike most cephalopods, it is active by day, when it can be seen hunting crustaceans and small fish in full light.

body.lede: Its body is built for walking rather than swimming, and for showing off rather than hiding.

systems.title: A cut-down cuttlebone
systems.text: The cuttlebone is a small rhombus, two-thirds to three-quarters the length of the mantle, and lacks the central ridge and outer cone found in most other cuttlefish.

systems.title: A skin of many parts
systems.text: In one aquarium study, researchers counted 7 texture, 14 posture and 7 movement components, plus 42–75 colour components, which combine into 11 distinct body patterns.

systems.title: Poisonous or not?
systems.text: Its muscle has been described as highly toxic, based on unpublished work. Preliminary later tests found only trace amounts of tetrodotoxin, too little to harm vertebrates.

mind.lede: Though described in 1885, this cuttlefish was not reported alive until 1988, and its behaviour is still poorly known.

studies.title: First seen alive
studies.text: The first report of living animals described an 'extremely rich' set of body-pattern components, but only as a preliminary inventory.

studies.title: Waves that never stop
studies.text: In five aquarium-bred adults, 8 of the 11 body patterns included waves of colour travelling across the mantle. In other cuttlefish such waves mostly appear during hunting, but these animals used them in many situations.

studies.title: Dark, not hidden
studies.text: Almost all the patterns recorded in the aquarium were dark, even over pale gravel, and the animals hardly tried to blend in. The authors suggest this may be a side effect of captivity, since wild animals are reported to camouflage well.

studies.title: Dens and duels
studies.text: Males fight over mating dens, and females visit a den to mate with the male living there.

survival.lede: Instead of fleeing, the flamboyant cuttlefish stands its ground and puts on a show.

tactics.title: Warning colours
tactics.text: When disturbed, it switches from its usual dark brown to black, dark brown and white with yellow patches, often with red arm tips.

tactics.title: An honest warning?
tactics.text: The display is often said to advertise poisonous flesh, but no significant toxin has yet been isolated, so what the warning protects remains unclear.

tactics.title: Camouflage on the hunt
tactics.text: It uses complex, changing camouflage to stalk its prey.

threats.title: Trawling and pollution
threats.text: Pollution, overfishing and habitat destruction threaten cephalopods like this one, and bottom trawling churns up the seafloor sediment it lives on.

life.lede: A flamboyant cuttlefish lives fast: it mates, lays a few eggs, and the female dies soon afterwards.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: Pairs mate face to face, and the male uses a special arm to pass a sperm packet into the female's mantle cavity.

stages.name: Eggs
stages.text: Eggs are laid singly in crevices or under ledges in coral, rock or wood; about a dozen were once found under half a coconut husk. Fresh eggs are white and slowly turn see-through.

stages.name: Hatchling
stages.text: Hatchlings are fully independent, receive no care, and can already make the same camouflage patterns as adults.

stages.name: End of life
stages.text: The female dies shortly after laying her eggs.

tagline: A glowing lure-tipped hat that rests by day and hunts by night
summary: A hydromedusa, not a true jellyfish, from shallow coastal waters off Japan and Korea. Its tentacles curl up over the outside of its striped bell and end in fluorescent green bands and pink tips. Experiments suggest these glowing tips may lure the small fish it eats.

stats.size: Bell up to about 15 cm across
stats.depth: Shallow coastal waters, less than about 30 m
stats.range: Northwestern Pacific: central and southern Japan, Jeju Island (South Korea)
stats.diet: Mainly small fish

facts.title: Tentacles worn on top
facts.text: Unusually, its tentacles grow up along the outside of the bell. Each one ends in a green fluorescent band and a pink-pigmented tip.

facts.title: Fluorescent fishing lures
facts.text: In lab trials, juvenile rockfish were strongly attracted to the tentacles under blue light, which makes the tips fluoresce, but not under yellow or white light. This suggests the glow works as prey bait.

facts.title: Fluorescent, not bioluminescent
facts.text: The glow is fluorescence: proteins absorb blue light and re-emit it as green. The jelly makes no light of its own.

facts.title: Day rester, night hunter
facts.text: Adults spend the day resting on the bottom among rocks or algae and rise at night to hunt. They are seen mainly from December to July, and each adult lives only a few months.

facts.title: Tentacles placed by maths
facts.text: New tentacles are added at a near-constant angle of about 137.5°, the same rule seen in plant leaf spirals. Mathematicians liken this to 'Fibonacci hashing', which spreads tentacles evenly as their number grows.

references.title: Olindias formosus (Goto, 1903)

image.alt: A dome-shaped translucent jelly on a black background. Its bell is pinstriped with dark lines and shows a peach interior, and it is ringed by many cream-coloured, pink-tipped tentacles that curl upward over the bell and trail below.
image.caption: Flower hat jelly in an aquarium. The pink-tipped tentacles curl up over its striped bell.
image.creator: Σ64

notes: The name was formerly spelled O. formosa; it was changed to formosus to correct a gender mismatch with the genus. Many popular sites also list Brazil and Argentina in its range, but sources consulted here give only Japan and Korea. South American records likely refer to a congener (e.g. O. sambaquiensis), so we left them out. Wikipedia mentions a single reported human fatality in Japan. We did not include it as a fact because it rests on a single case. Adult seasonality and day/night behaviour come from Wikipedia, which cites Patry et al. 2014 (JMBA). The setting is an aquarium; no correctly identified in situ photo was found at good resolution.

anatomy.lede: The flower hat jelly wears its tentacles like a bonnet: many of them curl up over the bell, each ending in a glowing band and a pink tip.

hotspots.label: Bell
hotspots.text: The bell is translucent and pinstriped with opaque bands, and can grow to about 15 cm across.

hotspots.label: Pinstripes
hotspots.text: Dark lines run down the bell from top to rim, giving the jelly its striped look.

hotspots.label: Upturned tentacles
hotspots.text: Unusually, many tentacles grow up along the outside of the bell.

hotspots.label: Pink tips
hotspots.text: Each tip holds a pink pigment that absorbs blue light and looks dark under it, which may sharpen the contrast with the glowing band just behind it.

hotspots.label: Trailing tentacles
hotspots.text: Other tentacles trail below the bell. New tentacles are added around the rim at a steady angle, spreading them evenly as their number grows.

body.lede: Much of what makes this jelly remarkable is chemistry: a glowing protein, a dark pigment and a precise growth rule.

systems.title: Green protein, pink pigment
systems.text: The tentacle tips contain a green fluorescent protein next to a non-fluorescent pink chromoprotein. Together they make a bright band beside a dark tip under blue light.

systems.title: A protein for the lab
systems.text: A green fluorescent protein from this jelly, named Gamillus, stays bright in acidic conditions. Biologists now use it as a tag to follow molecules inside cells.

systems.title: Glowing from the start
systems.text: The fluorescence appears very early in life: the jelly's tiny polyp stage was first found in an aquarium by spotting the glow of medusa buds developing on it.

mind.lede: A jelly has no brain, but the flower hat's daily routine and hunting posture are well documented.

studies.title: Lures that need blue light
studies.text: Juvenile rockfish attacked the barrier in front of a medusa nearly seven times more often under blue light than without it. Under yellow or white light, which do not make the tips glow, the medusa had no significant effect.

studies.title: Fishing posture
studies.text: In experiments, the medusa settled on the bottom bell-up, with its tentacles stretched out, a stance the researchers called a 'fishing' posture.

studies.title: Rest by day, rise by night
studies.text: Adults spend the day on the bottom among rocks or algae and float up at night to hunt.

life.lede: Like many hydrozoans, the flower hat jelly lives two lives: a tiny polyp fixed to the seabed and a free-swimming medusa.

stages.name: Polyp
stages.text: The bottom-living polyp went undescribed for over a century, until one was found in an aquarium in November 2012. No polyps have yet been reported from the wild.

stages.name: Budding medusa
stages.text: In an aquarium, polyps grew in small clusters and released medusae about 1 mm across. Budding happened at 15 °C, and warmer water seemed to trigger the switch to medusae.

stages.name: Young medusa
stages.text: Wild medusae first appear around December at about 2 cm across.

stages.name: Adult medusa
stages.text: Adults grow to about 15 cm and are seen until about July, most often in April and May.

lifespan.value: a few months as an adult medusa

tagline: A 'flying' fish that never leaves the seabed
summary: Despite its name — volitans means 'flying' — this bottom-dwelling Atlantic fish cannot fly or even glide. It walks over sand on its pelvic fins, probing for crabs and clams, and when disturbed it suddenly fans out enormous, blue-edged pectoral fins like a pair of wings.

stats.size: Commonly about 38 cm; up to about 50 cm
stats.depth: About 1–100 m
stats.range: Both sides of the Atlantic, incl. the Mediterranean; Canada to Argentina in the west
stats.diet: Bottom-living crustaceans (especially crabs), clams and small fishes

facts.title: It can't fly
facts.text: Despite both its common and scientific names, the flying gurnard cannot fly or glide through the air — which is why some prefer the name 'helmet gurnard'.

facts.title: Wings as a warning?
facts.text: When excited, it spreads its huge, semi-transparent pectoral fins, edged in bright blue. Scientists suggest the sudden flash may startle predators.

facts.title: Walking the seabed
facts.text: Flying gurnards have been seen 'walking' along sandy seafloors on their pelvic fins while they search for food.

facts.title: A drumming fish
facts.text: Flying gurnards make sounds with a special drumming muscle that beats against their two-lobed swim bladder.

facts.title: Digging for dinner
facts.text: It feeds mainly on bottom-living crustaceans — especially crabs — plus clams and small fishes, using a stiff front fin ray to dig into the sediment.

image.caption: Fins fully fanned: a flying gurnard over sand off Menorca, Mediterranean Sea
image.creator: Encarna Sáez Goñalons & Víctor Martínez Moll

gallery.alt: Side view of a red-brown flying gurnard on sand, covered in turquoise spots, with large golden eyes, wing-like pectoral fins folded back and two tall separate spines rising from its head
gallery.caption: Wings folded: a flying gurnard propped on its fins on the seabed
gallery.creator: Barry Peters

notes: Hero location: Commons description says only 'Xoriguer' (Cala en Xoriguer, Menorca) — caption assumes Menorca. IUCN Least Concern (assessed 2013) per FishBase. Digging fact comes from Wikipedia, citing Davenport & Wirtz 2019. No allowed category clearly fits, so categories is empty.

anatomy.lede: Folded up, a flying gurnard is a heavy-scaled bottom fish with big eyes. Its secret is in the pectoral fins, which work as shovels and as a sudden pair of wings.

hotspots.label: Large eye
hotspots.text: The eyes are large, and the body colour is very variable: brown or greenish with reddish or yellowish patches.

hotspots.label: Front of the pectoral fin
hotspots.text: The front part of each pectoral fin is used to explore the seabed and to dig. Its stiff, unsegmented leading ray forms a digging edge.

hotspots.label: Folded 'wing'
hotspots.text: The back part of the pectoral fin, folded here, opens into a huge semi-transparent fan with bright blue tips when the fish is excited.

hotspots.label: Pelvic fin
hotspots.text: Flying gurnards have been seen 'walking' over sand on their pelvic fins while searching for food.

hotspots.label: Armoured scales
hotspots.text: The body is covered in heavy, protective scales.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: Adults can reach about 50 cm and 1.8 kg, though about 38 cm is more usual.

body.lede: Each pectoral fin is really two tools in one, and the whole fish is wrapped in armour.

systems.title: A fin with two halves
systems.text: Each pectoral fin has a digging part, with flexible segmented rays behind a stiff front ray, and a larger rear part supported by unsegmented rays that forms the 'wing'.

systems.title: Digging, then sucking
systems.text: Once the fin has uncovered prey, the fish catches it by suction, drawing it into the mouth with a rush of water.

systems.title: Colour on demand
systems.text: It can shift from very dark brown or grey to almost white depending on the ground beneath it and other conditions.

mind.lede: Close watching of how the flying gurnard feeds has shown a careful, repeated digging routine.

studies.title: Digging with 'hands'
studies.text: Usually only one pectoral fin digs at a time. It sweeps forward and inwards, twists and presses down so the stiff front ray bites into the sediment, then pulls back and out to stir it up.

studies.title: Short bursts
studies.text: Each dig lasts from one to seven strokes, made at between about one and four strokes a second.

survival.lede: A slow walker on open sand, the flying gurnard relies on armour and a surprise.

tactics.title: The sudden flash
tactics.text: Spreading the brightly coloured pectoral fins may startle a predator long enough for the fish to escape.

tactics.title: Armour
tactics.text: Heavy, protective scales cover the body.

threats.title: Caught with shrimp
threats.text: Off south-eastern Brazil, many flying gurnards are taken as bycatch by shrimp trawlers. Most of the catch are juveniles, and the shrimp closed season does not protect the spawning fish.

threats.title: Fished and kept
threats.text: It is also of minor commercial importance, caught as a gamefish, and sold for aquariums.

life.lede: Flying gurnards begin life adrift in open water and settle to the seabed only later.

stages.name: Floating larva
stages.text: Many species of flying gurnard have an extended larval stage that floats freely in the ocean, while the adults live on the bottom.

stages.name: Growing up
stages.text: In one study of 592 fish caught off Brazil, lengths ranged from about 7 to 35.5 cm, and fish of around 10 cm were the most common.

stages.name: Maturity
stages.text: Half of females were mature at 17.4 cm and half of males at 19.3 cm.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: Off Brazil, the ovaries and testes grew heavier between November and February, which points to that being the spawning season.

tagline: A round, spiny angler with a glowing, tasselled lure
summary: A deep-sea anglerfish shaped like a lumpy ball. Females, up to about 60 cm long, dangle a fleshy lure lit by glowing bacteria to draw prey within reach. Males are tiny, under 5 cm, and—unlike many anglerfish—they latch on only temporarily rather than fusing for life.

stats.size: Females up to about 60 cm (standard length); males about 4 cm
stats.depth: Usually 200–800 m; recorded to about 1,830 m
stats.range: Mainly the Atlantic, from Greenland and Norway to South Africa; scattered records elsewhere
stats.diet: Fishes, squids and crustaceans

facts.title: A living lantern
facts.text: The lure (esca) on the female's head 'fishing rod' glows because it hosts light-producing bacteria. In the darkness, the light draws prey within striking distance of her mouth.

facts.title: Teeth like a trap
facts.text: Its teeth point inward, so whatever swims into the mouth struggles to get back out. Recorded prey includes fishes, squids and crustaceans.

facts.title: Tiny, independent males
facts.text: Males reach only about 4 cm, against roughly 60 cm for females. In this family males apparently do not become permanently fused 'parasites' on females, as happens in some other anglerfishes.

facts.title: A temporary grip
facts.text: Males sniff out females with large nostril organs and clamp on with special bony teeth. One female carried a scar probably left by a male that later let go.

facts.title: Prey for whales
facts.text: Despite its spines, it is eaten by sperm whales: several footballfish have been found in the stomachs of whales caught off the Azores.

image.caption: A preserved female Atlantic footballfish on display at the Port of Nagoya Public Aquarium, Japan.
image.creator: KKPCW (Wikimedia Commons)

notes: Catalogue slot 'Anglerfish'. Image is the only licence-compatible Commons photo of this species: a preserved museum specimen labelled 'チョウチンアンコウ' (the Japanese standard name for H. groenlandicus) at the Port of Nagoya Public Aquarium, filed in Category:Himantolophus groenlandicus; ID rests on the aquarium label. Lure-bacteria and inward-teeth facts are from NHM LA describing the family (Pacific footballfish, H. sagamius) and apply to footballfishes generally; male non-parasitism is stated for this species by FishBase ('apparently') and for the family by NHM. Wikipedia used for range, diet, temporary-attachment and Azores sperm-whale records (it cites Pietsch 2009, Oceanic Anglerfishes). Distribution: FishBase lists 'tropical and temperate parts of all oceans' while Wikipedia/IUCN emphasise the Atlantic; editor may wish to verify. Note: the familiar 'ball-shaped anglerfish with lantern' image in Japan (chōchin-ankō) refers to this species.

anatomy.lede: The female footballfish is a round, spiny body with a vast mouth and a glowing rod on its head. This preserved specimen shows her lure, but not its light.

hotspots.label: Fishing rod
hotspots.text: The rod, or illicium, is a modified fin spine. In this species it measures 28–54% of the body length.

hotspots.label: Lure
hotspots.text: The bulb at the tip, the esca, holds glowing bacteria. Its size and shape vary more than in other deep-sea anglerfishes.

hotspots.label: Lure appendages
hotspots.text: Branched and unbranched tentacle-like appendages sprout from the bulb, with light-guiding appendages at its tip.

hotspots.label: Tiny eye
hotspots.text: Females have small to tiny eyes, unlike the well-developed eyes of the males.

hotspots.label: Mouth
hotspots.text: The large, slanting mouth has a stout lower jaw that juts beyond the upper, lined with slender, curved teeth that fold inwards.

hotspots.label: Skin spines
hotspots.text: Large conical spines are scattered over the head and body. The bumps are the bases of these spines, which may put off predators.

hotspots.label: Pectoral fin
hotspots.text: Footballfishes have no pelvic fins at all. The short dorsal and anal fins sit far back, near the tail.

senses.lede: Males and females are built for different jobs. Females wait in the dark; males must search it for a mate.

senses.name: A male's nose
senses.text: Males have large smelling organs with nostrils facing sideways, and are thought to find females by smell.

senses.name: A male's eyes
senses.text: Males have well-developed eyes, 5.5–8.7% of their body length across, and directed to the sides.

senses.name: A female's eyes
senses.text: Females have small to tiny eyes; instead of searching for food, they lure it to them.

body.lede: Everything about the female is designed to bring food to her mouth and keep it there.

systems.title: Borrowed light
systems.text: The lure does not make its own light. It glows because of living light-producing bacteria, Photobacterium, housed inside it.

systems.title: A fluorescent lure?
systems.text: In a Pacific footballfish, the lure also showed fluorescence, the first recorded in a deep-sea anglerfish. Whether this helps attract prey or mates is unknown.

systems.title: Gripping without teeth
systems.text: Males have no jaw teeth. Instead, bony plates on the snout and chin carry 16–31 and 20–50 hooked denticles, used to grip a female temporarily.

survival.lede: Footballfishes are rarely seen alive; most of what is known comes from specimens caught in nets or found inside whales.

tactics.title: A trap of teeth
tactics.text: Prey is whatever fits into the mouth, and backward-curving teeth stop it escaping.

tactics.title: Spiny skin
tactics.text: The spines scattered over the body may deter predators.

life.lede: Footballfishes start as tiny, round larvae near the surface and change shape completely before descending.

stages.name: Egg and larva
stages.text: Eggs and larvae drift in open water. The larvae are short and almost spherical, with puffed-up skin, and reach 17–22.5 mm.

stages.name: Metamorphosis
stages.text: Even as larvae, females can be told apart by a small club-shaped stub of the future rod on the head. Larvae transform into their adult shape at about 20–33 mm.

stages.name: Free-living male
stages.text: Males are free-living and never parasitic. They are thought to cling to a female only briefly, though no male has yet been found attached to one.

stages.name: Female
stages.text: Females keep growing long after the males stop. The largest known female of this species, from south-west Greenland, measured about 46.5 cm in standard length; some sources give up to about 60 cm.

tagline: An eel-shaped shark with a collar of frills
summary: A slender, eel-like shark with six frilly gill slits—the first pair meeting across the throat like a ruff—and a mouth lined with rows of small, three-pointed teeth. A primitive-looking deep-water hunter, it swallows squid, fishes and even other sharks, and may carry its young for more than a year.
ability: needle-trap jaws and an extremely long pregnancy

stats.size: Females up to almost 2 m
stats.depth: Typically 500–1,000 m; recorded from about 20 to 1,500 m
stats.range: Patchy in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, on outer shelves, slopes and seamounts
stats.diet: Deep-water squid, bony fishes and other sharks

facts.title: Where the name comes from
facts.text: It has six gill slits with frilly edges, and the lower ends of the first pair join across the throat, forming a ruff-like collar.

facts.title: Teeth that point inward
facts.text: Its large mouth holds groups of small, sharp, three-pointed teeth that point inward. It can swallow relatively large prey, including other deep-water sharks.

facts.title: A very long pregnancy
facts.text: Young hatch from eggs inside the mother and feed on large yolky eggs; litters of 2–15 pups are born at about 40–60 cm long. Gestation is thought to last more than a year.

facts.title: First filmed in 2004
facts.text: In August 2004, scientists reviewing submersible video off the south-eastern USA spotted a frilled shark gliding over sandy seafloor—thought to be the first time one was seen alive in its natural habitat.

facts.title: A 'living fossil'?
facts.text: Often called a 'living fossil', it shares many physical features with shark ancestors from the age of dinosaurs, and is described as a primitive deep-water shark.

Gallery: NOAA 2004 in-situ video frame (low quality, burnt-in data overlay; depth 2,866 ft as shown on the frame). Rejected: 'Frill shark - Australian Museum 2022.png' (credited to ChatGPT—AI-generated), 'Deania hystricosa.jpg' (other species). 'Living fossil' is a popular label; the NatGeo source is a photo caption.

anatomy.lede: Long, eel-like and dark brown, the frilled shark has a head unlike any other living shark: a mouth at the very tip of the snout and gills edged with frills.

hotspots.label: Snout-tip mouth
hotspots.text: Unlike most sharks, whose mouths sit underneath the head, the frilled shark's mouth is at the front of the snout.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: The eyes are moderately large horizontal ovals and have no protective third eyelid.

hotspots.label: Three-pronged teeth
hotspots.text: About 300 trident-shaped teeth line the jaws in 19–29 rows. The small, sharp teeth point inwards.

hotspots.label: Long jaws
hotspots.text: The jaws hinge directly to the skull behind the eyes. This is thought to give it a relatively weak bite.

hotspots.label: Frilled gills
hotspots.text: There are six gill slits on each side, not the usual five, and their frilly edges give the shark its name.

senses.lede: How a frilled shark finds food in the dark is mostly inferred from its anatomy.

senses.name: Open lateral line
senses.text: Its lateral line is an open groove, with sensory hair cells exposed directly to the water, which helps it sense movement, vibration and pressure.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: The eyes are moderately large, but how well it sees has not been studied.

body.lede: Many features of the frilled shark look like those of very early sharks.

systems.title: A simple backbone
systems.text: The skeleton is cartilage, and the spinal column is a notochord with only poorly defined vertebrae.

systems.title: An oily liver
systems.text: A large liver full of oil helps it control its buoyancy.

systems.title: Slow digestion?
systems.text: Of 139 sharks examined from Suruga Bay, Japan, 73% had empty stomachs, an unusually high share for a deep-water shark, and the food that was found was heavily digested.

mind.lede: Almost nothing has been watched directly; its hunting style is pieced together from stomachs, captives and its body shape.

studies.title: A squid specialist
studies.text: Squid and other cephalopods were found in 60% of stomachs that held food, and fish in about 10%. Beaks showed it eats both deep-water and near-surface squid.

studies.title: Strike like a snake
studies.text: It may bend its body, brace with its rear fins and lunge forward to seize prey, like a striking snake.

studies.title: A gleaming lure
studies.text: Captive frilled sharks have been seen swimming with their mouths open. Their white teeth against the dark mouth may attract prey.

survival.lede: A slow-breeding shark is easily harmed by even modest fishing.

tactics.title: Living deep
tactics.text: It usually stays between 500 and 1,000 m, on outer shelves, slopes and seamounts.

threats.title: Bycatch
threats.text: It is not targeted, but is caught by accident in deep-water bottom trawls and other fishing gear, and sometimes used for fishmeal or food.

threats.title: Very slow to recover
threats.text: With few young and a very long pregnancy, its population is estimated to take more than 14 years to double.

life.lede: The frilled shark breeds extremely slowly, carrying its young for years.

stages.name: Egg capsule
stages.text: Eggs develop inside the mother in capsules, which are shed when the embryos reach 6–8 cm. Early development is slow.

stages.name: Embryo
stages.text: The embryos live on yolk inside the uterus. Based on 264 sharks from Suruga Bay, Japan, gestation was estimated at three and a half years or more.

stages.name: Birth
stages.text: Pups are born at about 55 cm long and 380 g, in litters of 2–10, with an average of six.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Males mature below about 1.1 m long and females at 1.4–1.5 m. Females have no fixed breeding season.

tagline: An angler with a worm on a stick and a lightning gulp
summary: A lumpy, slow-moving anglerfish that sits motionless on the seabed, blending in, while it twitches a lure made from its first dorsal fin spine. When curious prey comes close, the frogfish's mouth snaps open and sucks it in within milliseconds — even prey nearly twice its own size.

stats.size: Commonly about 10 cm; up to about 25 cm
stats.depth: From under 1 m to over 200 m; often around 40 m
stats.range: Tropical and warm-temperate Atlantic and Indo-Pacific waters
stats.diet: Fishes and other small animals drawn in by its lure

facts.title: A fin turned fishing rod
facts.text: Its front-most dorsal fin spine has become a rod, the illicium, tipped with a bait called the esca. In this species the esca bears 2–7 worm-like appendages that wriggle like tempting prey.

facts.title: Gone in six milliseconds
facts.text: Its jaws open so suddenly that prey is sucked in along with water in about six milliseconds. High-speed filming has shown frogfishes have one of the fastest feeding mechanisms of any vertebrate.

facts.title: Eyes bigger than its stomach
facts.text: A huge mouth and stretchy stomach let it swallow prey up to twice its own size.

facts.title: Slow-motion chameleon
facts.text: Its colour is extremely variable, and over a few weeks a striated frogfish can completely change colour to match its surroundings.

facts.title: Eggs on a raft
facts.text: Its eggs are released wrapped in a ribbon-like, floating mass of mucus known as an 'egg raft'.

anatomy.lede: A striated frogfish is a lumpy, scaleless ball of a fish, with an upturned mouth, limb-like fins and a fishing rod growing from its head.

hotspots.label: Lure (esca)
hotspots.text: The bait at the tip carries 2–7 worm-like appendages, which grow back if they are lost.

hotspots.label: Fishing rod
hotspots.text: The rod, or illicium, is the front-most dorsal fin spine. When not fishing it rests against the head, and is swung forward over the mouth to tempt prey.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Prominent lines radiate out from the eyes, which it uses to follow prey before striking.

hotspots.label: Upturned mouth
hotspots.text: The mouth points upwards and the palate carries teeth. It can expand up to twelve times in size as it opens.

hotspots.label: Skin filaments
hotspots.text: The bumpy skin is covered in forked spinules, and males have longer skin appendages than females.

hotspots.label: Stripes
hotspots.text: The species name striatus means 'striped'. Individuals from the same place can look completely different, from red to black, striped or plain.

hotspots.label: Limb-like fins
hotspots.text: Its pectoral fins are arm-like. Small, tube-shaped gill openings sit behind and below them.

stats.label: Largest prey, relative to its own size

body.lede: The frogfish's body is a trap: it sits still, breathes without seeming to move, and swallows in an instant.

systems.title: Breathing in secret
systems.text: Rhythmic pumping draws water in through the mouth and out through the small gill openings, so the fish can breathe while looking completely motionless.

systems.title: A one-way gulp
systems.text: After a strike, the water rushes out through the gills while a special muscle closes the gullet to keep the prey inside.

systems.title: Inflatable
systems.text: Like a puffer fish, it can inflate its body. A gas bladder controls its buoyancy.

mind.lede: Frogfishes are patient hunters whose lures and lightning strikes were first revealed by careful filming in the 1970s.

studies.title: A lure that looks like a fish
studies.text: In one Antennarius frogfish, the lure was found to mimic a small fish, giving prey both a tempting sight and probably a low-frequency pressure cue, at very little energy cost to the angler.

studies.title: Filmed at 1,000 frames a second
studies.text: High-speed filming showed frogfishes create enormous suction by rapidly expanding the mouth and gill chambers, engulfing prey faster than any other fish then recorded.

studies.title: Stalk, then strike
studies.text: It watches approaching prey with its eyes, and may stalk it or shift the angle of its mouth before it strikes.

survival.lede: Being hard to see protects the frogfish as well as feeding it.

tactics.title: Stillness
tactics.text: Its camouflage and lack of movement make it hard for prey and predators alike to notice.

tactics.title: Seldom eaten
tactics.text: Other frogfish and moray eels do prey on adults, but this is thought to be uncommon. Young frogfish are more at risk from opportunistic fishes.

life.lede: Spawning is a short, dramatic event that ends with the eggs drifting away in a raft of mucus.

stages.name: Courtship
stages.text: Before spawning, the pair walks over the seabed with the female in front and the male close behind, his snout touching her vent. She swells with eggs, often to twice her normal size.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: The pair dashes up towards the surface, where the female releases her eggs and the male his sperm. A pair may spawn several times over the following weeks.

stages.name: Egg raft
stages.text: The eggs float in a buoyant, ribbon-like mass of mucus, which may carry them long distances.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults commonly reach about 10 cm and live on rock, sand, rubble or coral, usually shallower than 40 m.

tagline: A pill bug the size of a dinner plate, scavenging the deep slope
summary: A distant, ocean-dwelling cousin of the garden woodlouse, scaled up enormously. Giant isopods patrol the muddy continental slopes of the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean, scavenging whatever dead animals sink from above. Adults commonly measure 19–36 cm, and the largest documented is about 50 cm.

stats.size: Typically 19–36 cm; largest documented about 50 cm
stats.depth: Typically 310–1,800 m
stats.range: Western Atlantic: Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean, and north to Georgia (USA)
stats.diet: Scavenger of dead animals sinking to the seafloor

facts.title: The largest isopod
facts.text: It is the largest known isopod. The biggest individual documented in scientific literature was about 50 cm; a widely shared 76 cm claim from the press has never been confirmed.

facts.title: Males run larger
facts.text: An analysis of historical records found that adult males are on average about 5 cm longer than females.

facts.title: Big because it's deep?
facts.text: Its large size is often explained by 'deep-sea gigantism', the tendency of some cold-water invertebrates to grow larger and live longer. The exact causes are still debated.

facts.title: Mini-adults, no larva
facts.text: Females brood eggs in a pouch called a marsupium. The young hatch as miniature adults (mancae), up to about 6 cm long, skipping a larval stage entirely.

facts.title: Eyes that shine
facts.text: Its widely spaced compound eyes have more than 4,000 facets and a reflective layer, the tapetum lucidum, that makes them seem to glow in a camera light.

notes: We chose NOAA Gulf of Mexico images because records of 'B. giganteus' from the Indo-Pacific are now treated as other species (McClain 2015, citing Lowry & Dempsey 2006). Many Japanese and Taiwanese aquarium photos on Commons labelled B. giganteus may therefore show other Bathynomus species and were not used. Depth: McClain 2015 gives 310–1,800 m (one record at 80 m); Wikipedia gives 310–2,140 m for the genus in the West Atlantic. Facts 3–5 come from Wikipedia (last resort), which cites Briones-Fourzán & Lozano-Alvarez 1991 (J. Crust. Biol.). The popular story of an aquarium isopod that 'starved for five years' was deliberately not used. NOAA's swimming-isopod note (ref 1) says the animal filmed was nearly 30 cm.

anatomy.lede: Built on the same plan as a garden woodlouse, the giant isopod is an armoured box of segments and legs, enormously scaled up.

hotspots.label: Antenna
hotspots.text: Every isopod has two pairs of antennae, along with compound eyes and four sets of jaws.

hotspots.label: Head shield
hotspots.text: The two triangular compound eyes sit at the front of the head, about 25 mm apart.

hotspots.label: Mouthparts
hotspots.text: Fish, squid and crabs were the most common foods found in the guts of giant isopods caught off Yucatán, Mexico.

hotspots.label: Walking legs
hotspots.text: Each of the seven segments of the thorax carries its own pair of walking legs.

hotspots.label: Body segments
hotspots.text: Overlapping armoured plates cover the seven thorax segments; behind them, the short abdomen has segments of which one or more fuse into a tail.

senses.lede: The giant isopod has large eyes in a world with almost no light, and they are badly damaged by sunlight.

senses.name: Light-gathering eyes
senses.text: Each eye is about 18 mm along its top edge and holds roughly 3,500 facets. Cells packed with tiny clear vesicles behind the light-sensitive parts are thought to reflect light back through them.

senses.name: Forward-facing view
senses.text: The eyes face forwards and slightly down, and their fields of view may overlap a good deal.

senses.name: Blinded by daylight
senses.text: Isopods brought up from the deep and exposed to daylight suffered severe damage to their light-sensitive cells, which did not recover even after two months in darkness.

body.lede: Beneath the armour, the giant isopod breathes and swims with the same limbs.

systems.title: Gills that paddle
systems.text: Under the abdomen, branched limbs called pleopods do two jobs: they exchange gases like gills and beat to swim. Giant isopods are seldom seen swimming, though one has been filmed coming in to land.

systems.title: Large eggs, not more eggs
systems.text: Although far bigger than other isopods, a female carries about the same number of eggs. Instead, egg size seems to grow almost in step with body size.

systems.title: Ordinary on the inside
systems.text: The male reproductive organs look much like those of smaller isopod species.

survival.lede: A slow scavenger on the dark seafloor, the giant isopod eats what falls from above and whatever cannot get away.

tactics.title: Scavenging
tactics.text: Gut contents support the idea that it is mainly a scavenger of dead animals, especially fish, squid and crustaceans.

tactics.title: Easy prey
tactics.text: It also feeds on fixed or slow-moving animals, such as echinoderms and sea squirts.

life.lede: Giant isopods skip the larval stage entirely: the young leave their mother's pouch looking like small adults.

stages.name: Brooded egg
stages.text: Females lay eggs into a brood pouch, the marsupium, on the underside of the body and carry them until the young are ready to emerge.

stages.name: Manca
stages.text: The young, called mancae, look like miniature adults but lack the seventh pair of legs.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Isopods trapped off Yucatán, at 349–733 m, ranged from 4.4 to 36.5 cm long.

stages.name: Breeding
stages.text: Far more males and females were mature in February than in August, suggesting that reproduction is seasonal.

tagline: The real kraken, finally caught on camera
summary: The giant squid is one of the largest invertebrates on Earth, with tentacles longer than any other cephalopod's and eyes the size of dinner plates. Known for centuries only from carcasses and sea-monster tales, it was first photographed alive in the deep sea in 2004.

stats.size: Females up to about 12–13 m total length, males about 10 m (tentacles included)
stats.depth: Possibly about 300–1,000 m
stats.range: Worldwide in temperate oceans; rare in the tropics and polar seas
stats.diet: Deep-sea fishes and squids

facts.title: First photos in the wild
facts.text: In 2004 a Japanese team's deep-sea camera photographed a giant squid attacking bait at 900 m off the Ogasawara Islands. A tentacle it left behind confirmed its identity and showed the animal was over 8 m long.

facts.title: Not 20 metres long
facts.text: Tales of 20 m giants are not backed by any measured specimen. Mantles are not known to exceed about 2.25 m; much of the length is two stretchy feeding tentacles.

facts.title: Eyes like dinner plates
facts.text: Its eyes reach at least 27 cm across, among the largest of any animal. One proposed reason is spotting the faint glow stirred up by approaching sperm whales, its main predator.

facts.title: Seen alive, and active
facts.text: Rather than a sluggish drifter, the 2004 images suggest an active predator that strikes and tangles prey with its long feeding tentacles.

facts.title: One species worldwide
facts.text: Several species were once proposed, but DNA from giant squid around the globe shows remarkably little variation, suggesting there is just one species.
