Commons spells the vessel 'Godon Gunter' (typo for Gordon Gunter). Diet from Animal Diversity Web (based on stomach contents of dead specimens). Size, eye, single-species and IUCN (Allcock & Barratt 2014, LC) facts via Wikipedia, which cites O'Shea, Nilsson et al. 2012 and Winkelmann et al. 2013. The 'spotting sperm whales' explanation for the eyes is a hypothesis (Nilsson et al. 2012).

anatomy.lede: Laid out on a ship's deck, a giant squid is mostly reach: eight thick arms, two far longer feeding tentacles, and behind them a torpedo-shaped mantle that holds the organs.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: A photographed giant squid eye measured about 27 cm across, with a 9 cm pupil — the largest eyes known in any animal apart from the colossal squid's.

hotspots.label: Eight arms
hotspots.text: Each of the eight arms carries two rows of suckers, which hold prey once the tentacles have caught it.

hotspots.label: Tentacle club
hotspots.text: The two feeding tentacles end in broadened clubs. Their suckers are ringed with sharp, finely serrated chitin teeth that grip slippery prey.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The muscular mantle encloses the internal organs. Measured mantles are not known to exceed about 2.25 m.

hotspots.label: Fins
hotspots.text: A pair of fins sits at the rear tip of the mantle; body length is measured from here to the tentacle tips.

senses.lede: Almost everything known about the giant squid's senses comes from dead specimens, and it centres on one organ: the eye.

senses.name: Giant eyes
senses.text: Modelling suggests that below about 600 m an eye this size could pick out a sperm whale at more than 120 m, by the glow of bioluminescent plankton the whale disturbs. Such eyes would be poorly suited to spotting small prey or mates far away.

senses.name: A modest visual brain
senses.text: An MRI scan of one male's optic lobe found a well-developed outer layer for processing images, but a relatively small inner region that links vision to movement. Its brain may not have grown in step with its huge eyes.

body.lede: Inside, the giant squid is built like other squids, only larger — with a few features that hint at life in cold, dark water.

systems.title: Blood suited to the cold
systems.text: Research on its oxygen-carrying blood suggests it binds oxygen poorly at higher temperatures, so warm water may leave a giant squid short of oxygen. That could explain why it lives in cool, deep water.

systems.title: Closed circulation
systems.text: Like other squids it has a closed circulatory system, with blood pumped through vessels rather than washing loosely around the organs.

systems.title: A terminal organ for mating
systems.text: Most male cephalopods pass sperm packets with a modified arm. Two dying males found in shallow water were seen moving a penis-like terminal organ out through the funnel, supporting the idea that giant squid transfer sperm packets with it directly.

genome.lede: A draft genome assembled in 2020 from a specimen tissue sample gave the first look at the giant squid's DNA.

findings.title: Brain-building genes
findings.text: The genome holds about 135 protocadherin genes, many in clusters. This family, linked to wiring nerve cells, is greatly expanded in cephalopods compared with other molluscs.

findings.title: Reflectin genes
findings.text: It has seven reflectin genes and three reflectin-like genes, which in other cephalopods make the light-reflecting proteins of the skin and eyes.

findings.title: Very little variation
findings.text: Mitochondrial genomes from 43 giant squid across the world showed no regional structure and exceptionally low diversity, consistent with a single, widely dispersing global species.

mind.lede: Its behaviour has been glimpsed only a handful of times, each sighting rewriting what was assumed about it.

studies.title: Attacking bait off Japan
studies.text: An automated camera at about 900 m off the Ogasawara Islands photographed a giant squid wrapping its tentacles around a baited line, showing it to be an active predator.

studies.title: Stalking a fake jellyfish
studies.text: In the Gulf of Mexico, a camera with a ring of lights mimicking a glowing jellyfish filmed a juvenile about 3–3.7 m long. It stalked the lure, seized it with its tentacles, then pulled back into the dark.

studies.title: Probably a loner
studies.text: No two giant squid have been caught together in fishing nets, which has led researchers to suggest they hunt alone.

survival.lede: Adult giant squid have very few enemies, but one of them is the largest toothed predator on Earth.

tactics.title: Early warning
tactics.text: Seeing a sperm whale's glowing wake at long range may give a giant squid time to mount a powerful escape before the whale closes in.

tactics.title: Strike from a distance
tactics.text: Its long feeding tentacles let it seize prey well away from its body, then pull it in to the arms and beak.

tactics.title: Grip that holds
tactics.text: Toothed sucker rings on the arms and clubs grip struggling fish and squid that would slip from smooth suckers.

life.lede: How giant squid mate, where they spawn and how long they live are still largely unknown; what follows is pieced together from specimens.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: A female can carry more than 5 kg of eggs — well over a million — each only about 0.5–1.4 mm long.

stages.name: Drifting young
stages.text: Low genetic variation across the oceans suggests young giant squid disperse widely, possibly as drifting larvae carried by currents.

stages.name: Rapid growth
stages.text: One study suggests giant squid may reach adult size within about three years, an extraordinary growth rate for an animal of several hundred kilograms.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: Males mature at a smaller size than females and store sperm packets in a Needham's sac before passing them to a female.

tagline: The tallest animal on Earth, browsing where no one else can reach
summary: With legs and a neck that lift its head more than five metres off the ground, the giraffe feeds on leaves that other browsers cannot reach, plucking them from thorny acacias with a long, dark tongue. Giraffes are still officially one species, but genetic studies suggest there may be four.

stats.size: Males stand up to 5.7 m tall to the tips of their horns and weigh up to 1,930 kg; females up to 1,180 kg
stats.habitat: Dry savanna, grassland and open woodland
stats.range: Africa south of the Sahara; now gone from most of West Africa
stats.diet: Leaves, especially from acacia trees; an adult male can eat up to 66 kg of food a day

facts.title: Seven bones, very long
facts.text: A giraffe's neck has the same number of vertebrae as a human's — seven — but each one is greatly elongated.

facts.title: A 45 cm tongue
facts.text: Its black tongue, about 45 cm long, grasps prickly food from the very tops of trees. Acacia leaves are its main food.

facts.title: A two-metre drop
facts.text: A newborn calf drops about 2 m to the ground at birth — and already stands around 2 m tall at the shoulder.

facts.title: A coat for life
facts.text: Each giraffe's pattern of patches stays the same throughout its life. The 'horns', called ossicones, are bony knobs covered in skin and fur.

facts.title: One species, or four?
facts.text: Traditionally giraffes are one species with nine accepted subspecies. A 2016 study of 190 giraffes from across Africa, using several genetic markers, found at least four separate lineages and proposed recognising them as four species.

facts.title: A silent extinction
facts.text: Giraffe numbers fell by about 40%, from around 157,000 in 1985 to 97,500 in 2015, through illegal hunting, habitat loss, expanding farms and mines, conflict with people and civil unrest. In 2016 the IUCN moved the giraffe from Least Concern to Vulnerable.

notes: Taxonomy: follows the IUCN Red List and GBIF backbone (both accept a single species, Giraffa camelopardalis, which IUCN divides into nine subspecies). Fennessy et al. 2016 (ref 2) proposed four species (northern G. camelopardalis, reticulated G. reticulata, Masai G. tippelskirchi and southern G. giraffa); some authorities and Commons now use that split, e.g. Commons files these photos under 'Giraffa giraffa'. The four-species fact is marked 'hypothesis' because it is not yet the IUCN treatment. Images: hero is the South African subspecies (G. c. giraffa), gallery the Angolan (G. c. angolensis) and Kalahari giraffes; under the four-species view all three would be southern giraffe, G. giraffa. Conservation: Muller et al. 2016 assessment, amended 2018 (e.T9194A136266699), Vulnerable per GBIF's IUCN checklist (July 2026); iucnredlist.org returns 403 to scripted requests, so that URL was confirmed via the GBIF API. Some subspecies have separate, more threatened assessments, not covered here. Decline figures are from Mongabay's report of the 2016 IUCN update (other outlets gave 151,702–163,452 in 1985 and 97,562 in 2015); I could not fetch the original IUCN release. Lifespan (ADW: 10–15 years in the wild) left out as it conflicts with other commonly quoted figures. Categories: none fit (IUCN VU, not EN). Regions: namib-kalahari for the Angolan giraffes of Namibia and the Kalahari populations (gallery). No elevation given: no source checked gives one.

anatomy.lede: The tallest animal alive is a feat of engineering: a two-metre neck on seven bones, a heart that must pump blood uphill to the brain, and legs sheathed in tight skin that keeps blood from pooling in the feet.

hotspots.label: Ossicones
hotspots.text: The 'horns' are bony knobs covered in skin and fur. Males' are thick and worn bald on top from sparring; females' are thin and tufted.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Very large eyes, held high above the savanna, let a giraffe keep watch on its herd and spot predators far away.

hotspots.label: Neck
hotspots.text: A bull's neck is about 2.4 m long. Males swing their necks and heads at each other in fights known as necking.

hotspots.label: Chest
hotspots.text: Near the heart, arterial blood pressure is about twice that of a human — enough to push blood up the long neck to the brain.

hotspots.label: Coat
hotspots.text: Patch patterns differ between giraffe populations and stay the same throughout an individual's life, helping to camouflage it in scrub.

hotspots.label: Legs
hotspots.text: Tight skin on the legs, together with narrowing blood vessels, stops blood and fluid pooling in the feet.

hotspots.label: Hooves
hotspots.text: A kick from the front hooves can kill. Adults can run fast, but also stand and defend themselves.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The tail, 76–101 cm long, ends in a black tuft that whisks away flies.

senses.lede: Height is a giraffe's greatest sense organ. From up to 5.7 metres, it keeps watch over a scattered herd and the land around it.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Keen eyesight and great height let giraffes stay in visual contact with herd-mates at long distances and spot predators early.

senses.name: Smell and taste
senses.text: A courting bull tests a female's urine, curling his lip in a gesture called flehmen, to judge whether she is ready to mate.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Giraffes are often said to talk in infrasound like elephants, but over 947 hours of zoo recordings found no infrasonic calls — only snorts, grunts and a low night-time hum.

body.lede: Being tall poses problems no other mammal faces, from pumping blood two metres uphill to digesting tough, thorny leaves.

systems.title: High-pressure circulation
systems.text: Giraffes have about twice a human's arterial blood pressure at heart level. Tight skin, constricting small arteries and leak-resistant capillaries stop fluid building up in the legs.

systems.title: Four stomachs
systems.text: Giraffes are ruminants with a four-chambered stomach. They chew the cud, even while walking, which lets them make the most of feeding time.

systems.title: Thorn-proof mouth
systems.text: A 45 cm tongue, narrow muzzle and flexible upper lip strip leaves from thorny acacias, and the molars crush the thorns.

genome.lede: The giraffe genome was published in 2016 alongside that of its closest relative, the short-necked okapi, so that the two could be compared gene by gene.

findings.title: Neck and heart evolved together
findings.text: Genes with changes unique to the giraffe include some in the HOX, NOTCH and FGF pathways, which shape both the skeleton and the cardiovascular system. The long neck and the powerful heart may therefore have evolved in parallel through a small number of genes.

findings.title: Built for a toxic diet
findings.text: Genes for mitochondrial metabolism and for transporting fatty acids have diverged in the giraffe, perhaps linked to a diet that includes poisonous plants.

findings.title: One species or several
findings.text: Genetic markers from 190 giraffes across Africa revealed at least four distinct lineages, which some researchers propose are separate species.

mind.lede: Long thought silent and simple, giraffes are turning out to have richer social and vocal lives than once believed.

studies.title: Under five hours of sleep
studies.text: Video of zoo giraffes over 152 nights found they slept about 4.6 hours a day, in short bouts, both standing and lying down. Deep sleep, with the head resting on the rump, made up under 5% of that time.

studies.title: A hum in the night
studies.text: Night-time recordings in three European zoos picked up sustained, harmonic 'humming' calls that may carry information about the caller.

studies.title: Sizing each other up
studies.text: Males settle rank by sparring: walking side by side, intertwining necks and leaning on each other to test strength, before swinging blows if it escalates.

survival.lede: A healthy adult giraffe is a formidable opponent. Predators mostly target calves and the old or sick.

tactics.title: Lethal kicks
tactics.text: Adults stay vigilant and can run fast or deliver deadly blows with their front hooves.

tactics.title: Watching from above
tactics.text: Herds spread out to feed and gather together when threatened, keeping in sight of one another from their great height.

tactics.title: Hidden calves
tactics.text: For its first week a calf lies hidden on the ground, with its mother feeding within 25 m.

threats.title: Illegal hunting
threats.text: Giraffes are poached for their meat, skin and tail.

threats.title: Losing ground
threats.text: Habitat loss, expanding farms and mines, conflict with people and civil unrest cut giraffe numbers by about 40% between 1985 and 2015.

life.lede: A giraffe begins life with a two-metre fall and is on its feet within minutes.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Mothers give birth standing up or walking, usually to a single calf. Females breed every 20–30 months.

stages.name: Newborn
stages.text: The 50–55 kg calf is standing and suckling about 15 minutes after birth, then spends much of its first week hidden.

stages.name: Crèche
stages.text: Calves join a nursery group watched over by mothers in turn, so each mother can roam up to 200 m away to feed.

stages.name: Weaning
stages.text: Females wean at 12–16 months and stay in the herd; young males tend to become solitary.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature at 3–4 years but breed a year or more later; males mature at 4–5 years and start to breed at about seven.

lifespan.value: 10–15 years in the wild; 20–27 years in zoos

tagline: An octopus you can see straight through
summary: A gelatinous, almost colourless octopus that drifts through the dim midwaters of tropical and subtropical oceans. Only its eyes, optic nerves and digestive organs are easy to see. It is so rarely encountered that most specimens have come from the stomachs of predators.

stats.size: Mantle up to about 11 cm; total length up to about 45 cm
stats.depth: Mesopelagic to bathypelagic (twilight and midnight zones); filmed alive at 680 m
stats.range: Tropical and subtropical seas worldwide
stats.diet: Not well known; young are thought to shift to softer-bodied prey as they grow

facts.title: Glass body
facts.text: Its body is gelatinous and transparent, so in the open ocean there is little for a predator to see except the compact eyes and gut.

facts.title: Rectangular eyes
facts.text: Seen from the side its eyes look rectangular. The narrow, upright shape is thought to shrink the eye's shadow when seen from below, helping the octopus stay hidden.

facts.title: Rarely seen alive
facts.text: Records are extremely rare; many come from the stomachs of predators such as northern bottlenose whales. In 2021 a remotely operated vehicle filmed two living glass octopuses near the Phoenix Islands, one at 680 m.

facts.title: Mother as nursery
facts.text: Females brood hundreds of eggs, each about 4 mm long, inside the mantle cavity. The mother dies soon after the young are born, leaving them to fend for themselves.

facts.title: Moving deeper with age
facts.text: Tiny young live near the upper layers; as they grow, these octopuses gradually move away from the surface into deeper water.

Hero is Joubin's public-domain drawing (inverted, white on black; portrait 1265×1920) because it shows the transparent form; the museum specimen photo (alt) is opaque, damaged and has a scale bar, so it ranks lower editorially despite the brief's specimen>illustration order — swap if preferred. Brooding details via Wikipedia (citing WoRMS). depthRange 200–1000 m is approximate; trawl records extend deeper (Joubin's specimen came from a net fished to 5,300 m, depth of capture uncertain).

anatomy.lede: Joubin's 1918 drawing shows a female from below: a glassy bell of a mantle over eight long, slender arms. In life almost nothing but the eyes and gut would be visible.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The mantle is gelatinous and nearly colourless. In adults it reaches about 11 cm long; in brooding females it holds the eggs.

hotspots.label: Arms
hotspots.text: The upper three pairs of arms are about as long as the mantle in juveniles and two to three times longer in adults; the lowest pair is slightly shorter.

hotspots.label: Suckers
hotspots.text: Its suckers are small, widely spaced and set in a single row along each arm.

senses.lede: The one organ a transparent animal cannot hide is its eye — and the glass octopus's eyes seem shaped around that problem.

senses.name: Elongated eyes
senses.text: Examined in two specimens caught at 200 m, its eyes are cylindrical with the lens in the middle, which narrows their field of view sideways.

senses.name: A smaller shadow
senses.text: The upright shape is argued to minimise the eye's silhouette as seen by a predator looking up from below, at the cost of a wider view.

body.lede: Transparency shapes the whole body, but a few internal features are distinctive.

systems.title: Glass tissues
systems.text: Its body is transparent, gelatinous and almost colourless, so that in open water mainly the compact eyes and digestive organs stand out.

systems.title: A mating arm
systems.text: In males the third left arm is modified as a hectocotylus, which delivers sperm to the female and can detach during mating.

mind.lede: Its behaviour is almost unknown; most records come from nets and from the stomachs of whales.

studies.title: Found inside a whale
studies.text: Beaks of glass octopuses were among the remains in the stomach of a northern bottlenose whale stranded on the Danish island of Tåsinge in 1997.

studies.title: Filmed alive
studies.text: A remotely operated vehicle exploring seamounts near the Phoenix Islands filmed two living glass octopuses, one at 680 m.

survival.lede: In open water there is nowhere to hide, so the glass octopus hides in plain sight.

tactics.title: Transparency
tactics.text: Scientists think its near-transparency is largely a defence, making it hard for predators to spot and helping it approach prey.

tactics.title: Shadow-shrinking eyes
tactics.text: Narrow, upright eyes may cast less of a silhouette against the faint light from above.

life.lede: The glass octopus carries its young inside its own body until they hatch.

stages.name: Brooded egg
stages.text: The female broods hundreds of eggs, each about 4 mm long, inside her mantle cavity.

stages.name: Paralarva
stages.text: Newborn young have a mantle about 2.2 mm long. The mother dies soon after they are born, leaving them to fend for themselves.

stages.name: Growing deeper
stages.text: Tiny young live in the upper layers; as they grow, they move away from the surface into deeper water.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults reach about 11 cm in mantle length and up to 45 cm overall, living in the dim twilight and midnight zones.

tagline: A pink, flabby shark with slingshot jaws
summary: A rarely seen deep-water shark with a long, flat, blade-like snout and pinkish skin coloured by blood vessels showing through. Its jaws can shoot forward from under its head faster and farther than those of any other shark, snatching fish, squid and crustaceans.

stats.size: Up to about 3.9 m; possibly larger
stats.depth: Mostly 270–960 m; recorded to about 1,300 m
stats.range: Scattered records in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans; most from Japan
stats.diet: Bony fishes, squids and crustaceans

facts.title: Slingshot jaws
facts.text: Filmed feeding in 2016, goblin sharks swung the lower jaw down and back, then shot both jaws forward at up to 3.1 m/s—the fastest, farthest jaw protrusion known among sharks.

facts.title: An electric snout
facts.text: The underside of the long snout is peppered with pores leading to the ampullae of Lorenzini, organs that sense electric fields. It most likely finds prey by detecting their electrical signals.

facts.title: Pink from blood
facts.text: Its pinkish-white colour comes from blood vessels visible through the skin; young are ghostly white and grow pinker with age. Preserved specimens fade to brown.

facts.title: A trade-off for weak swimming
facts.text: Its body is soft and flabby. Researchers suggest the lightning jaws evolved to suit food-poor deep water, possibly compensating for the loss of strong swimming ability.

facts.title: Last of an old lineage
facts.text: It is the only living member of its family, which also includes extinct sharks known only from fossils, such as Scapanorhynchus.

Not used, pending editor verification: 'Goblin shark (Mitsukurina owstoni).jpg' (public domain via fws.gov, credited 'Michigan State University', described as 'underwater image') — editorially the best picture, but its provenance is unexplained and it has the look of a digital composite of a dead specimen on a seabed, so it was not presented as an in-situ photo. Museum Victoria juvenile photos are too small (≤1500×312). Size: Australian Museum gives 3.9 m; Florida Museum notes photo-based estimates of 5.4–6.2 m are unconfirmed. 'Ancient' category is based on the family's fossil members (Florida Museum); the 'living fossil' label is popular rather than technical. AphiaID per WoRMS is 105842 (the brief's example showed 105826).

anatomy.lede: The goblin shark's head is a hunting tool: a long, flat, sensor-studded snout above jaws that sit tucked away until the instant they are flung forward.

hotspots.label: Blade-like snout
hotspots.text: The long, flattened snout is heavily pored underneath. The pores open into the ampullae of Lorenzini, organs that sense electric fields.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Its eyes are tiny for a shark of its size.

hotspots.label: Protrusible jaws
hotspots.text: At rest the mouth sits back under the eye. To feed, the jaws shoot forward beneath the snout, as in this museum mount.

hotspots.label: Needle-like teeth
hotspots.text: Long, slender front teeth snag slippery prey; smaller, flattened teeth further back are suited to crushing.

hotspots.label: Gill openings
hotspots.text: Five short gill openings run along each side of the head.

stats.label: Jaw reach, as share of body length

senses.lede: With tiny eyes in near-darkness, the goblin shark is thought to rely on a sense humans lack.

senses.name: Electric sense
senses.text: Pores packed along the underside of the snout lead to the ampullae of Lorenzini. The shark most likely uses them to find prey by the weak electric fields their bodies give off.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Its eyes are tiny, and how well it sees in the dim water it lives in has not been studied.

body.lede: Its body is soft and weakly muscled; most of its specialisation is concentrated in the jaws.

systems.title: Double-ligament jaw launcher
systems.text: A double set of ligaments at the jaw joints powers the rapid forward thrust of the jaws, which are otherwise held tightly closed while it swims.

systems.title: Speed over force
systems.text: Three-dimensional lever analysis found the goblin shark has the least efficient biting jaws of the lamniform sharks studied, because its jaw-closing muscles sit far back.

systems.title: A soft, flabby body
systems.text: Its body is soft and flabby and the lower lobe of the tail is weakly developed — not the build of a fast-cruising hunter.

mind.lede: For more than a century the goblin shark was known only from dead specimens; filmed behaviour is very recent.

studies.title: Slingshot feeding on film
studies.text: Five strikes by two goblin sharks, videotaped at sea, showed the lower jaw swinging down and back, then both jaws shooting forward. The mouth opened and closed again as the jaws retracted, a feeding pattern not described in other sharks.

studies.title: What 121 stomachs held
studies.text: Stomach contents of 121 goblin sharks from Tokyo Submarine Canyon contained bony fishes, squids and crustaceans.

studies.title: First sightings in the wild
studies.text: Deep-sea cameras recorded live goblin sharks in their habitat for the first time, on a seamount near Jarvis Island in 2019 and on the slope of the Tonga Trench in 2024, extending the species' known depth range.

studies.title: Hard to keep
studies.text: One goblin shark taken to an aquarium in Yokohama survived only a week.

survival.lede: Rarely met and barely fished, the goblin shark survives in the deep by ambush rather than pursuit.

tactics.title: Ambush, not chase
tactics.text: Rather than outswimming prey, it closes the last gap with its jaws. Researchers suggest this suits food-poor deep water and may compensate for weak swimming.

tactics.title: Detecting hidden prey
tactics.text: Its electrosensory snout may let it locate prey it cannot see in the dark.

threats.title: Bycatch
threats.text: It is caught only incidentally, in deep-water trawls, longlines and deep-set gill nets, and its meat is rarely sold. The IUCN lists it as Least Concern.

life.lede: No pregnant female goblin shark has ever been caught, so how it breeds is inferred from its relatives.

stages.name: Birth
stages.text: It is thought to give birth to live young that develop from eggs inside the mother, but no pregnant female has ever been captured.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: The smallest specimen on record measured 107 cm. Young are ghostly white, and smaller individuals are occasionally seen near the surface in open water.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Mature males measure about 2.6–3.8 m and mature females about 3.4–3.7 m. Photo-based estimates of 5.4–6.2 m have been suggested but not confirmed.

lifespan.value: possibly up to about 55 years, maturing at about 16.5 (growth model from one specimen; unconfirmed)

tagline: A bat that hunts with one long, pure note
summary: The largest horseshoe bat in Europe hangs wrapped in its wings by day and hunts low over pasture and woodland edges at night. Instead of the short chirps most bats use, it sends out long calls held at almost a single pitch, about 82 kHz, through a fleshy horseshoe-shaped noseleaf, and listens for the flutter of insect wings in the echoes.

stats.size: Head and body 57–71 mm; wingspan 35–40 cm; 17–34 g
stats.habitat: Pasture, woodland edge and hedgerows; roosts in old buildings and caves, hibernates underground
stats.range: North Africa and Europe through the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Himalaya to China, Korea and Japan
stats.diet: Large insects: chafers, dung beetles, noctuid moths, craneflies and caddis flies
stats.conservation: IUCN: Least Concern (2016 assessment); rare and much reduced in Britain

facts.title: A horseshoe on the nose
facts.text: Horseshoe bats are recognised by a complex, horseshoe-shaped noseleaf. It is tied to their particular kind of echolocation: the calls are sent out through the nose rather than the mouth.

facts.title: One long note
facts.text: The greater horseshoe's call is held at an almost constant frequency of about 82 kHz, far above human hearing. Through a bat detector it comes out as a series of continuous warbles.

facts.title: Correcting for the Doppler shift
facts.text: At rest the bat calls for about 50 ms at around 83 kHz. In flight it lowers the pitch by just enough that the echoes, raised by its own movement, come back close to that resting note, the frequency to which its hearing is most sharply tuned.

facts.title: A mother's note
facts.text: Recordings of 386 wild bats aged 1–28 years in south-west England showed that each bat's resting note rises in youth, falls in old age and dips in midwinter. Young bats' notes closely matched their mothers'.

facts.title: Perch and pounce
facts.text: Greater horseshoes often hunt like flycatchers, watching from a regular perch and flying out to take passing insects. Large prey is carried back to a feeding perch, where discarded wings and wing-cases pile up beneath.

facts.title: Long lives, steep decline
facts.text: Individuals have lived for up to 30 years, and females may not breed until their third year. In Britain the species is now confined to south-west England and south Wales, and its numbers are estimated to have fallen by over 90% in a century.

The doi.org links for Jones & Ransome also return 403 to scripts; the paper's metadata was confirmed via Crossref and the full text was read from the Plazi/Zenodo copy (doi:10.5281/zenodo.13447367). signatureData: callKhzMin/Max 82–84 kHz is the band of resting constant-frequency (CF) values in Jones & Ransome (1993) — text: CF 'at about 83 kHz'; Figure 1 group means of British bats run from about 82.0 to 83.5 kHz with standard deviations reaching about 84 kHz; Figure 3 values for mothers and infants lie between 82 and 84 kHz. This is a British population at rest. Other sources differ: Bat Conservation Trust gives 'about 82 kHz'; Schuchmann & Siemers (2010) give a mean of 80 kHz for flying bats in Bulgaria (emitted CF is lowered in flight to compensate for Doppler shift); ADW quotes 77–81 kHz (Schober & Grimmberger 1997); Wikipedia's 69–83 kHz is for the whole call including the FM sweeps; East Asian populations call much lower. Ref 3 (Schuchmann & Siemers) is kept to document the in-flight value. Size, diet, hunting behaviour, lifespan and UK decline from BCT; ADW gives the same measurements, citing Schober & Grimmberger. Regions: europe first; china-mongolia (China, Korea; Japan lies just off that region) and himalaya-tibet (the IUCN account and Wikipedia note montane Himalayan populations). North African (Maghreb) populations exist but were not mapped to sahara-arabia because they are in the Mediterranean mountains, not the desert. Images: hero (Slovakia, 2024) and alt-2 (Japan, show-cave area, 2019) are wild bats in situ. alt-1 (Klaus Krahn, 2004) is described on Commons only as a day roost with occasional flight inside the roost; the location is not stated. Its file is in the species category and the bats match the species, but the individual flying bat cannot be confirmed separately.

anatomy.lede: The largest horseshoe bat in Europe, about the size of a small pear, with a face shaped around the sound it makes.

hotspots.label: Ear
hotspots.text: The large, pointed ears have no tragus, the small flap that stands inside the ear of many other bats.

hotspots.label: Ear tuned to one note
hotspots.text: Hearing is sharply tuned to frequencies close to the bat's own resting call.

hotspots.label: Pointed upper noseleaf
hotspots.text: The upper part of the noseleaf rises to a point, while the lower part is shaped like a horseshoe.

hotspots.label: Horseshoe
hotspots.text: The bat calls through its nostrils, which sit inside the horseshoe. This complex noseleaf is tied to the horseshoe bats' particular kind of echolocation.

hotspots.label: Fur
hotspots.text: Adults are buff- or greyish-brown with a reddish tint, paler beneath; young bats are uniformly grey.

hotspots.label: Wrapped wing
hotspots.text: At rest, and through hibernation, the bat hangs free with its wing membranes wrapped around its body.

senses.lede: Horseshoe bats hunt with one long, pure note and listen for the flicker of insect wings in its echoes.

senses.name: Constant-frequency sonar
senses.text: Instead of brief sweeps, the greater horseshoe sends out long calls held at almost one frequency, emitted through the nose. A moving bat adjusts the pitch so that the returning echoes land on the note its ears hear best.

senses.name: An acoustic fovea
senses.text: In the bat's auditory midbrain, a disproportionate share of neurons responds to a narrow band of frequencies around the echo frequency, much as the fovea of the human eye packs in receptors for sharp central vision.

senses.name: Listening to rivals
senses.text: Among European horseshoe bats, differences in call loudness change how far away each species can detect prey, and may help them share out food. Loudness might also carry information about a bat's condition.

body.lede: A long-lived bat that spends half the year in hibernation and controls exactly when its single pup is conceived.

systems.title: Hibernation
systems.text: From about October to April the bats hibernate in caves, mines, cellars and tunnels, often in clusters. They wake at frequent intervals and may move up to 30 km between sites in search of the right temperature.

systems.title: Delayed fertilisation
systems.text: Mating happens mostly in autumn, but the female stores the sperm and fertilisation is delayed until later. After mating, a plug secreted by the male closes the female's reproductive tract.

systems.title: Teeth lost before birth
systems.text: Greater horseshoe bats shed their milk teeth before they are even born.

genome.lede: The greater horseshoe bat was one of the first six bats to receive a reference-quality genome, assembled with long-read sequencing.

findings.title: Small genomes
findings.text: At about 2 billion letters, bat genomes are generally smaller than those of other placental mammals, which typically run to 2.5–3.5 billion. Smaller genomes contain fewer transposable elements.

findings.title: Hearing genes
findings.text: Signs of selection on hearing-related genes in the ancestor of all bats suggest that echolocation using the larynx was present from the start.

findings.title: Living with viruses
findings.text: Lost and altered immunity genes, extra copies of antiviral APOBEC3 genes and fragments of old viruses in bat genomes point to a long history of tolerating viral infection.

mind.lede: Long-term studies of a few colonies in south-west England have revealed an intricate social life.

studies.title: Faithful partners
studies.text: Genetic studies showed that most females return to breed with the same male year after year, so their pups from different years are full siblings. Mothers and daughters also share mates more often than chance would predict, without raising inbreeding.

studies.title: A note learned from mother
studies.text: Young bats' call frequencies closely match their mothers', suggesting that the calls are shaped by maternal effects, possibly learned while young.

studies.title: Noisy nurseries
studies.text: Maternity colonies are noisy places, full of continuous chattering, chirping and scolding calls.

survival.lede: The greatest threats to this bat come from people disturbing its roosts and changing the countryside where it feeds.

tactics.title: Warm summer roofs
tactics.text: Breeding females gather in sun-warmed roof spaces of large old houses, churches and barns, but need a cave or tunnel nearby to retreat to when bad weather cuts off their food.

tactics.title: Saving energy in the cold
tactics.text: The bats do not hunt in winter unless it is warm enough for insects to fly, and they hunt less in cold or wet weather.

threats.title: Roost disturbance
threats.text: The bats are particularly sensitive to disturbance at nursery and winter roosts, which need protection and unobstructed entrances.

threats.title: Farming and pesticides
threats.text: Loss of permanent pasture and the use of pesticides have reduced the large beetles, especially cockchafers, and moths that the bats depend on.

life.lede: A female raises at most one pup a year, and may wait years before her first.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: Mating takes place mainly in autumn, sometimes in late winter or spring, with fertilisation delayed until the spring.

stages.name: Birth
stages.text: Maternity colonies gather from May, and each female gives birth to a single pup after a gestation of about 80 days.

stages.name: Pup
stages.text: Eyes open at about seven days and pups fly at three to four weeks. By seven to eight weeks they are ready to leave the roost.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Males can breed at two. Females usually mature in their third year, often do not have young until their fifth, and one known female did not breed until her tenth year.

lifespan.value: up to 30 years

tagline: A giant constrictor that lives in the water
summary: A massive, olive-green boa of South American swamps and slow rivers, and one of the heaviest snakes on Earth. It lies almost hidden in shallow water, with only its eyes and nostrils showing, then seizes passing animals and squeezes them until they suffocate.

stats.size: Females average about 6 m and males about 3 m; reported up to 250 kg
stats.habitat: Swamps, marshes, slow-moving rivers, flooded grasslands and rainforest waterways
stats.range: Tropical lowlands of South America east of the Andes, especially the Amazon and Orinoco basins and the Llanos; also Trinidad
stats.diet: Fish, birds, caimans, capybaras, deer and other animals, swallowed whole
stats.conservation: IUCN Red List: Least Concern (2021 assessment)

facts.title: A heavyweight with disputed records
facts.text: Green anacondas have been reported at up to 250 kg, which makes them among the heaviest snakes alive — though the true maximum size is still argued over, and many giant-snake stories are exaggerated.

facts.title: Females are the giants
facts.text: Females are far bigger than males: on average about 6 m long against about 3 m for males, and much heavier.

facts.title: Periscope eyes
facts.text: Its eyes and nostrils sit on top of its head, so it can watch and breathe while the rest of its body stays hidden underwater.

facts.title: Breeding balls
facts.text: Up to 13 males may coil around a single female in a writhing 'breeding ball', competing to mate with her for as long as a month. Afterwards she may eat one or more of her much smaller suitors.

facts.title: Born alive and ready to swim
facts.text: Females do not lay eggs; they give birth in shallow water to live young, usually 20–40 of them, with a record of 82. Each newborn is about 68 cm long, and a pregnant female may go without food for up to seven months.

facts.title: Two anacondas in one?
facts.text: In 2024 researchers named a Northern green anaconda, Eunectes akayima, arguing that genetic data show the 'green anaconda' is really two species that split about 10 million years ago. The proposal is still debated and has not yet been adopted by major checklists.

notes: Taxonomy: GBIF's backbone places Squamata at class rank; the record uses class Reptilia, order Squamata (ITIS convention). Rivas et al. 2024 split off Eunectes akayima (northern green anaconda: Ecuadorian Amazon through Colombia and Venezuela to the Guianas); the split is disputed (e.g. by Dubois et al., reported second-hand, not checked) and E. akayima does not resolve in the GBIF backbone (checked Nov 2026), so this record treats E. murinus in the broad sense. Photos were deliberately chosen from the southern part of the range (Amazonas and São Paulo, Brazil; Beni, Bolivia), which is E. murinus under either taxonomy. The alt-1 location (Ilha Solteira, upper Paraná basin) is identified on iNaturalist as E. murinus; the round spots and lack of yellow ground colour rule out the yellow anaconda. Regions: only 'amazon' — green anacondas are reported from Paraguay, but I found no solid source for the Pantanal, where the yellow anaconda dominates. Biome set to 'wetland' because the species is aquatic, although the region is rainforest. The 250 kg maximum is from Smithsonian and ADW; ADW notes maximum size is 'the subject of much dispute'. IUCN DOI and GBIF links resolve in a browser but return 403 to scripted requests; IDs were checked via the GBIF API and Wikidata.

anatomy.lede: A snake built for life half-submerged: eyes and nostrils on top of the head, loose skin that can soak for long periods, and a body heavy enough to overpower a caiman.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: The small eyes sit high on the head, so an anaconda can watch the surface while the rest of its body stays hidden underwater.

hotspots.label: Nostrils
hotspots.text: The nostrils open on the top of the snout, letting the snake breathe with only the tip of its head above water.

hotspots.label: Eye stripe
hotspots.text: A prominent black stripe runs back from each eye to the angle of the jaw.

hotspots.label: Spots
hotspots.text: Dark oval blotches on an olive body make a submerged anaconda almost invisible from a short distance away.

hotspots.label: Belly
hotspots.text: The olive back gradually shades to yellow on the underside, which is covered in narrow belly scales.

hotspots.label: Skin
hotspots.text: The skin is soft and loose, with small smooth scales, and can withstand long periods of soaking in water.

stats.label: Growth in mass, birth to adult

senses.lede: An anaconda finds prey and mates mainly by scent and vibration; sight and hearing matter less.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Flicking its forked tongue, the snake picks up chemical traces from the air and passes them to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of its mouth. Males track the scent of females this way in the breeding season.

senses.name: Vibration
senses.text: Anacondas detect approaching animals through vibrations.

senses.name: Heat
senses.text: Some sources describe pit organs along the upper lip that sense the body heat of prey, but how well anacondas detect heat has been little studied.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Anacondas can see and hear, but these senses are less well developed than their senses of smell and vibration.

body.lede: Swallowing huge meals whole demands a slow metabolism, a crushing grip and a body that can go months without food.

systems.title: Death by coils
systems.text: An anaconda grips prey with needle-sharp, curved teeth and coils around it, tightening each time the victim struggles. Death comes from failure of breathing and circulation — or from drowning, as most attacks happen near water.

systems.title: A slow metabolism
systems.text: Apart from breeding females, anacondas need to eat only once every few weeks, and after a big meal a large snake can go weeks or months without food.

systems.title: Leftover legs
systems.text: Like other boas, anacondas have small horny claws near the vent — remnants of hind limbs. Males' spurs are larger, about 7.5 mm, whatever the female's size.

systems.title: Head-first swallowing
systems.text: Prey is swallowed whole and head first, so the limbs fold back rather than snagging. Prey usually weighs 14–50% of the snake's own mass.

mind.lede: Field observations show anacondas adjusting their behaviour closely to the wet and dry seasons.

studies.title: Sleeping out the drought
studies.text: In seasonally flooded savannas, anacondas must find water in the dry season or bury themselves in mud and become dormant until the rains return.

studies.title: Coming home
studies.text: Anacondas keep well-defined home ranges. In the wet season some move to higher ground, then return to their original range when the dry season comes.

studies.title: Basking for the brood
studies.text: Pregnant females bask regularly in the sun, on raised ground or dense vegetation, while non-breeding snakes are rarely seen basking.

survival.lede: Fully grown females have few enemies. Young and small anacondas are another matter.

tactics.title: Ambush in the water
tactics.text: Anacondas rely on stealth, lying submerged and camouflaged until prey comes close.

tactics.title: Coiled defence
tactics.text: When attacked, an anaconda rolls into a ball that protects its head while letting it strike back. It may also release a foul smell from glands near the vent.

tactics.title: Escape route
tactics.text: Juveniles and males escape predators by burrowing into mud or retreating into water.

threats.title: Habitat loss
threats.text: Deforestation continues, and protected areas are not always well regulated.

threats.title: Trade and fear
threats.text: Anacondas are killed out of fear or to protect livestock, sold for their body parts and caught for the international pet trade, which is regulated under CITES but continues illegally.

life.lede: Anaconda young are born alive in the water and are on their own from the first day.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: In the dry season several males coil around one female in a breeding ball; mating can last for weeks.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: The female carries her eggs inside her body and moves and feeds as little as possible to protect the developing young.

stages.name: Birth
stages.text: She gives birth in shallow water, usually to 20–40 young; bigger females have larger litters. Newborns weigh about 200 g and get no parental care.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Anacondas mature at about 3–4 years. Females usually breed only every other year, recovering the energy that pregnancy costs.

lifespan.value: About 10 years in the wild; over 30 in captivity

tagline: Mostly mouth, with a glowing tail tip
summary: Also called the pelican eel, this black, whip-tailed fish is built around an enormous, loosely hinged mouth that can balloon open to scoop up prey and water together. Its tiny eyes sit near the tip of its snout, and the end of its long tail carries a light organ.

stats.size: Up to about 80 cm; some records to about 1 m
stats.depth: About 500–3,000 m
stats.range: Tropical and temperate seas worldwide
stats.diet: Mainly crustaceans; also fishes, squids and other invertebrates

facts.title: A mouth like a net
facts.text: Its jaws extend far back along the body, so the gape makes up half or more of the length in front of the vent. The mouth cavity can stretch enormously.

facts.title: Big mouth, small meals
facts.text: Despite the huge gape, it mainly eats crustaceans. It is thought to gulp prey along with a mouthful of water, then push the water out through its gill openings.

facts.title: Caught on camera
facts.text: In 2018 the E/V Nautilus team filmed a young gulper eel off Hawaiʻi inflating its mouth like a black balloon, then deflating and swimming away. Why it did so is unknown; some researchers suspect a reaction to threat.

facts.title: A glowing tail tip
facts.text: The long, tapering tail ends in an expanded light-producing organ. What it is used for has not been established.

facts.title: Males transform
facts.text: At maturity males change: their smell organs enlarge while their teeth and jaws degenerate. Degeneration in both sexes suggests they may spawn only once and then die.

Pelican Eel, Eurypharynx pelecanoides

image.caption: A freshly caught gulper eel, its oversized jaws hanging open.
image.creator: Alexei Orlov

notes: Image is a fresh specimen (Commons Category:Eurypharynx pelecanoides, VRTS-confirmed CC BY 3.0); location not stated. Rejected: NHM London display models; Hong Kong market 'Gulpers' photo (unidentified, not this species). WoRMS currently places Eurypharyngidae in Anguilliformes; the Australian Museum and older sources use Saccopharyngiformes. Size: Australian Museum says 80 cm, FishBase 100 cm TL; depth: Australian Museum 500–3,000 m, FishBase gives an implausibly wide 500–7,625 m (usually 1,200–1,400 m), so the museum range was used. The tail light organ's function is not established in sources fetched (popular sources often call it a lure; omitted).

anatomy.lede: The gulper eel has stripped its body down to a huge, loosely hinged mouth and a long, whip-thin tail, with very little in between.

hotspots.label: Snout
hotspots.text: Its tiny eyes sit close to the tip of the snout, far from the hinge of the enormous jaws.

hotspots.label: Lower jaw
hotspots.text: The jaws extend far back along the body, enlarging the mouth enormously. They carry several rows of small teeth.

hotspots.label: Expandable mouth
hotspots.text: The mouth cavity is greatly distensible, opening like a net to take in prey together with a large volume of water.

hotspots.label: Whip-like tail
hotspots.text: The body tapers into a very long, thin tail with no tail fin. In intact specimens it ends in an expanded light-producing organ.

senses.lede: Its senses have barely been studied, but its anatomy offers clues — especially in mature males.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: At maturity males' smell organs enlarge while their jaws and teeth degenerate, suggesting that finding a mate by scent becomes their main task.

senses.name: Lateral line
senses.text: Instead of a line of pores along its sides, its lateral line — the system fishes use to sense water movement — is made of groups of raised tubules.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Its eyes are tiny; how much it relies on them in the near-darkness where it lives is not known.

body.lede: Much of the usual fish anatomy is missing: the gulper eel has no scales, no tail fin and no fin spines.

systems.title: Mouth as a scoop
systems.text: Prey is taken in along with water, which is then pushed out through the gill openings.

systems.title: A pared-down body
systems.text: It lacks scales, a tail fin and dorsal or anal fin spines, and its body is long and eel-like behind the head.

mind.lede: Almost everything known about its behaviour comes from a few chance encounters with underwater cameras.

studies.title: The black balloon
studies.text: Near a mile down off Hawaiʻi, a remotely operated vehicle filmed a young gulper eel inflating its mouth like a balloon, then deflating it and swimming off.

studies.title: A threat response?
studies.text: After seeing a gulper eel inflate in the Gulf of Mexico, some researchers suggested the display happens when the fish feels threatened.

studies.title: Mapping where it lives
studies.text: Modelling of museum records predicted a near-worldwide range, with gaps such as the Southern Ocean and Bering Sea. The gulper eel is not known to migrate up and down the water column each day.

life.lede: Its life cycle is pieced together from preserved specimens and from what is known of related eels.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Eggs are released into the open water and drift as plankton.

stages.name: Leptocephalus larva
stages.text: Eggs hatch into leptocephalus larvae, the drifting larval form of eels, which live in the plankton.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: At maturity males change shape: their smell organs grow while their teeth and jaws shrink. Females remain relatively unchanged.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: Degenerative changes in both sexes suggest gulper eels may spawn only once and then die.

tagline: The rainforest eagle that snatches sloths from the treetops
summary: One of the largest and most powerful eagles in the world, the top aerial predator of the Amazon canopy. Using its huge talons, it plucks sloths and monkeys from the branches, and a pair raises only one chick every two to three years.

stats.size: About 1 m long with a wingspan up to 2 m; 4–9 kg, females up to twice the weight of males
stats.habitat: Tall, unbroken lowland rainforest
stats.range: Southern Mexico through Central America to northern Argentina, with its stronghold in the Amazon
stats.diet: Sloths, monkeys and other canopy mammals, plus birds and reptiles

facts.title: Talons up to 10 cm long
facts.text: The rear talons on each foot are about 8–10 cm long — the weapons it uses to seize and crush animals as heavy as an 8-pound (3.6 kg) sloth.

facts.title: A sloth specialist
facts.text: A three-year study of five breeding pairs in the central Amazon found their diet was dominated, by number and by weight, by two species of sloth — including the brown-throated three-toed sloth.

facts.title: An owl-like face for hearing
facts.text: It is one of the few daytime birds of prey with a facial disc. By raising or lowering the feathers around its face it can funnel sound towards its ears to pinpoint hidden prey.

facts.title: Nests in the giants
facts.text: Pairs build a nest about 40 m up in the fork of one of the tallest trees in the forest. It can be nearly 2 m across and made of more than 300 branches.

facts.title: One chick at a time
facts.text: The female lays two eggs but raises only one chick. The young eagle stays dependent on its parents for a year or more, so a pair breeds only every two to three years.

facts.title: Starved by deforestation
facts.text: A study of 16 nests in Brazil's 'Arc of Deforestation' found that where more than half the forest had been cleared, parents could not bring in enough prey: three fledglings starved, and no nests were found where over 70% of the forest was gone.

notes: Talon length: the Peregrine Fund gives rear talons of about 3–4 inches (8–10 cm); ADW gives up to 12.5 cm. The more conservative figure is used. Weight (4–9 kg) follows the Peregrine Fund and ADW; the summary's 'among the largest eagles' is supported by Miranda et al. 2021 ('Earth's largest eagle'). The sloth fact comes from the Aguiar-Silva et al. 2014 abstract (via the DOI page and FAO AGRIS record); the full text was not read, so no percentages are given. alt-2 is a figure extracted from Miranda et al. 2021 (CC BY 4.0), credited there to Jiang Chunsheng; the study nests were in the Amazon 'Arc of Deforestation' in Mato Grosso, but the exact place is not stated. The hero is from iNaturalist (Pará); it appears wild but the setting is not confirmed by the uploader. Elevation is omitted because sources only say 'low elevations'. Pantanal not included as a region: no solid source found. IUCN DOI and GBIF links resolve in a browser but return 403 to scripted requests; IDs were checked via the GBIF API and Wikidata.

anatomy.lede: The harpy eagle is built to hunt inside the forest rather than above it: short, broad wings and a long tail for steering between trees, an owl-like face for listening, and feet strong enough to seize a sloth.

hotspots.label: Crest
hotspots.text: A crest of long feathers can be raised and lowered at will, for example when the eagle feels threatened.

hotspots.label: Facial disc
hotspots.text: A ring of feathers around the face can be lifted to funnel sound towards the ears on the sides of the head — a trait shared with owls.

hotspots.label: Bill
hotspots.text: The hooked black bill tears meat; a mother feeds her tiny chick small pieces with it.

hotspots.label: Chest band
hotspots.text: Adults have a dark band across the chest above a white belly. This colouring may help eagles recognise mates that are ready to breed.

hotspots.label: Wing
hotspots.text: Harpies are not built for soaring. Their relatively short wings let them fly from tree to tree with surprising agility for their size.

hotspots.label: Legs
hotspots.text: Thick, powerful legs let the eagle snatch prey from the canopy and carry it off to a perch.

hotspots.label: Talons
hotspots.text: The rear talons are about 8–10 cm long — the size of a grizzly bear's claws.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The long, barred tail acts like a rudder for steering through dense vegetation.

senses.lede: Under the canopy, even at midday, the forest is dim. The harpy hunts with both eyes and ears.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Harpies use keen eyesight to find prey in thick rainforest, sometimes dropping below the canopy to search.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Because little light reaches the forest interior, harpies also use hearing to pinpoint prey, raising the feathers of the facial disc to direct sound to their ears.

body.lede: A predator of monkeys and sloths needs immense grip, precise flight in cramped spaces and a gut that copes with irregular meals.

systems.title: Feet for heavy prey
systems.text: Powerful legs and long, sharp talons let harpies catch animals that are out of reach for most birds, including howler monkeys, sloths and even young deer.

systems.title: Steering, not soaring
systems.text: Short wings and a long tail suit slow travel from tree to tree rather than long flights over open country.

systems.title: Feast and wait
systems.text: Harpies do not hunt every day. They may feed on one kill for several days and tolerate slightly rotten meat.

genome.lede: A chromosome-level harpy eagle genome was produced by the Vertebrate Genomes Project in 2022. Its chromosomes had already shown how unusual birds of prey are.

findings.title: A reshuffled karyotype
findings.text: Most birds have a few large chromosomes and many tiny 'microchromosomes'. Painting harpy chromosomes with chicken probes showed this pattern has been lost: they are mostly medium-sized, with only four pairs as small as chicken microchromosomes.

mind.lede: Long-lived and slow-breeding, harpies form stable partnerships and invest heavily in a single chick.

studies.title: Partners for life
studies.text: Pairs build the nest together, chirping to each other, and occasionally rub their bills together for a few seconds — behaviour thought to strengthen their bond.

studies.title: Fresh greenery
studies.text: Adults keep bringing green twigs to the nest after the chick hatches. Some researchers think this keeps insects and parasites away or cools the nest.

studies.title: Patient hunters
studies.text: A harpy can stay perched for up to 23 hours while watching for prey.

survival.lede: As an apex predator, an adult harpy has no natural enemies. Its fate is tied to the forest.

tactics.title: Careful with dangerous prey
tactics.text: Monkeys and sloths can fight back with teeth and claws, and young eagles in particular risk injury while learning to hunt.

tactics.title: Guarding the nest
tactics.text: Parents defend the nest and their territory of about 30 km², driving out competing eagles.

threats.title: Forest loss
threats.text: Logging and farming destroy the tall forest harpies need; where too much forest is cleared, parents cannot feed their young.

threats.title: Shooting
threats.text: Harpies are shot by people who fear them or think they take livestock. A 2002 survey in Panama found most killings stemmed from misunderstanding the bird's behaviour.

life.lede: Raising one harpy takes so long that a pair usually breeds only every two to three years.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays one or two eggs and does most of the incubating, but only one chick is raised; the second egg may be a back-up.

stages.name: Nestling
stages.text: A hatchling fits in the palm of a hand, yet reaches adult size in five or six months, when it fledges.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: The young eagle stays dependent on its parents for one to two years, then disperses to find its own territory.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Young birds are pale grey and white, darkening with each moult until they reach adult plumage at about five years old.

lifespan.value: Estimated 25–35 years

tagline: A silver blade that hides with its own light
summary: A thin, mirror-sided fish no longer than a finger, shaped like the blade of a hatchet. Rows of light organs along its belly glow to match the faint daylight filtering down from above, erasing its silhouette from hunters looking up from below.
ability: counter-illumination (belly lights that erase its shadow)

stats.size: Up to about 8 cm
stats.depth: Mostly 200–600 m by day; rises to about 80–300 m at night
stats.range: Tropical and temperate oceans worldwide, except the eastern North Pacific
stats.diet: Ostracods and copepods; larger fish also take pteropods, krill and small fishes

facts.title: Invisible from below
facts.text: Light organs (photophores) along the belly shine a pale blue light matching daylight from above. This 'counter-illumination' hides the fish from predators that hunt by looking up for silhouettes.

facts.title: A dimmer switch
facts.text: Hatchetfish can adjust the intensity and colour of their belly lights to keep matching the light filtering down as conditions change.

facts.title: Lights aimed at its eyes
facts.text: Its eyes point upward, so how does it check its belly glow? Researchers propose that small light organs facing into its own eyes act as a reference for setting brightness.

facts.title: A nightly commute
facts.text: By day it stays mostly at 200–600 m. Early at night it climbs to about 80–200 m to feed, then sinks back down by day.

facts.title: Mirror armour
facts.text: Its flattened, silvery sides add a second layer of disguise, helping it vanish in the dim, downward light of the twilight zone.

notes: Species chosen: Argyropelecus aculeatus (best image: NOAA SEFSC public-domain specimen photo, Gulf of Mexico). Common names vary: 'Atlantic silver hatchetfish' (NOAA), 'Lovely hatchetfish' (Fishes of Australia, FishBase). WoRMS authority date 1850; Fishes of Australia cites 1849. Monterey Bay Aquarium's page and the Duke/Davis et al. study cover hatchetfishes generally, not this species specifically. Depth gauge 100–600 m reflects day/night range; FishBase records to about 2,056 m.

anatomy.lede: Seen side-on it is a deep, flattened blade of silver, edged below with rows of light organs.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: A light organ aimed at the eye shines into it through a dip in the iris, possibly so the fish can compare its own glow with daylight from above.

hotspots.label: Jaws
hotspots.text: The jaws are large, with long, backward-curving teeth and two enlarged canines in the lower jaw.

hotspots.label: Dorsal spine and fin
hotspots.text: A tall spine stands in front of the dorsal fin, which has 9 soft rays.

hotspots.label: Silver flank
hotspots.text: The mirror-like sides, with diffuse dark pigment on the trunk, help it blend into the dim light filtering down through the twilight zone.

hotspots.label: Belly light organs
hotspots.text: Rows of photophores along the belly give off a pale blue light, in a pattern particular to each species.

hotspots.label: Tail light organs
hotspots.text: A separate cluster of photophores sits under the tail, with spines below and in front of them and dark pigment concentrated above.

senses.lede: Its eyes do two jobs: looking up for food and, it seems, checking its own disguise.

senses.name: Sharp eyes for the twilight
senses.text: Measurements of its lens optics suggest it can resolve details about 0.08 degrees apart.

senses.name: A built-in light meter
senses.text: Light from the eye-facing photophore passes through clear tissue, the iris dip and the lens, and probably lands as an unfocused spot on an accessory retina. This may let the fish set its belly lights to match the light it sees above.

body.lede: Its camouflage depends on light organs that are carefully shielded, positioned and timed to develop.

systems.title: A shielded reference light
systems.text: The eye-facing photophore is wrapped on its front and outer sides by a layer of melanin, so its light goes into the eye instead of out into the water where it could give the fish away.

systems.title: Found wherever counter-shading lights exist
systems.text: Across three families of related fishes, every species with belly lights capable of counter-illumination had an eye-facing photophore. Two species that cannot counter-illuminate lacked one.

systems.title: A spiny keel
systems.text: Well-developed spines sit on the rear of the belly, the hind one much larger, and the keel there juts below the line of the body.

survival.lede: It hides by day and feeds by night, using light, silver and timing.

tactics.title: Erasing its shadow
tactics.text: The belly lights match the colour and brightness of daylight from above, hiding its silhouette from midwater hunters looking up.

tactics.title: Feeding at dusk
tactics.text: It rises towards the surface early at night and is a selective feeder, mainly on tiny shelled crustaceans called conchoecid ostracods, with some copepods and larval crabs, shrimps and fishes.

tactics.title: Quick to recover
tactics.text: FishBase rates its resilience as high, with a population thought able to double in less than 15 months, though this estimate is preliminary.

life.lede: A short life, lived between the twilight zone by day and shallower water at night.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Fertilisation is external. Eggs are scattered in open water and the parents give no care.

stages.name: Young fish
stages.text: The adult pattern of light organs develops at about 15 mm in length.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Young fish have a clear, unpigmented bar just in front of the tail stalk.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Sexes are separate. Females spawn in repeated batches, and half are mature by about 39 mm in standard length.

lifespan.value: About 2 years

group: Horseshoe crab (chelicerate arthropod, not a true crab)
tagline: Not a crab, and older than the dinosaurs
summary: Despite its name, the horseshoe crab is not a crab at all but a relative of spiders and scorpions, from a lineage far older than the dinosaurs. Each spring and summer, crowds of them crawl onto Atlantic beaches to spawn, laying eggs that feed migrating shorebirds. Their blue, copper-based blood is used to keep medicines safe.

stats.size: Females up to about 30 cm across the shell and 60 cm long with tail; males 25–30% smaller
stats.depth: Shallow coasts to more than 200 m; mostly shallower than about 30 m
stats.range: Atlantic coast of the Americas, from Maine to the Yucatán Peninsula and the Gulf
stats.diet: Marine worms and other small invertebrates living in the seabed

facts.title: Not a true crab
facts.text: Horseshoe crabs are not crustaceans. They belong to an ancient group of arthropods more closely related to spiders and scorpions than to crabs.

facts.title: Living fossil
facts.text: Their body plan has changed relatively little for around 350 million years, and their lineage predates the dinosaurs by more than 200 million years.

facts.title: Beach-wide spawning parties
facts.text: On spring and early-summer high tides around full and new moons, females crawl ashore with a male clasped to their shell, often trailed by several more males. One female may lay 100,000 or more eggs over several nights.

facts.title: Blood that guards medicine
facts.text: Their copper-based blood clots on contact with bacterial toxins. An extract called Limulus Amoebocyte Lysate is used to check that vaccines, drugs and medical devices are free of contamination.

facts.title: A feast for birds
facts.text: More than 20 species of migratory birds, as well as loggerhead turtles and many fishes, rely on horseshoe crab eggs. Delaware Bay hosts the largest population in the world.

notes: NOT A TRUE CRAB: a chelicerate (relative of spiders and scorpions), stated in tagline, group and fact 1. WoRMS class is Merostomata, order Xiphosurida. Fact refs: 0-based index 1 = NOAA NOS, 2 = USFWS. NOAA NOS says bled crabs are returned 'relatively unharmed'; ASMFC management now counts biomedical mortality, so that claim was deliberately omitted. Date-like phrasing: FWS gives ~350 million years unchanged; NOAA says lineage predates dinosaurs by >200 million years. IUCN Vulnerable via Wikipedia infobox (2016 assessment, not fetched directly). depthRange 0–30 m reflects preferred depths; adults range deeper than 200 m. Fact 5 ref is NOAA NOS (index 1). The 'reproduction' category reflects mass beach spawning with satellite males (FWS).

anatomy.lede: Seen from above, a horseshoe crab is a domed shield, a hinged rear plate and a spike of a tail. Almost everything else — legs, gills, mouth — is tucked away underneath.

hotspots.label: Compound eye
hotspots.text: Two large compound eyes sit on the sides of the shell. Their main job is finding mates during the spawning season.

hotspots.label: Head shield
hotspots.text: The front, horseshoe-shaped shield covers the head and the six pairs of appendages used for feeding and walking.

hotspots.label: Hinge
hotspots.text: A hinge joins the head shield to the spiny rear section, which shelters the book gills underneath.

hotspots.label: Tail (telson)
hotspots.text: The long tail is harmless. It works as a rudder in the water and as a lever to flip the animal upright when a wave turns it over.

senses.lede: The horseshoe crab's eyes are among the most studied in biology, and they work almost as well at night as by day.

senses.name: Compound eyes
senses.text: Each lateral eye is made of large units with individual photoreceptors big enough to record from. Linked photoreceptors dampen their neighbours' signals, sharpening edges before the image reaches the brain.

senses.name: Night vision
senses.text: A clock in the brain sends signals to the eyes at night that greatly raise their sensitivity, so horseshoe crabs can see at night nearly as well as by day.

senses.name: Extra eyes
senses.text: Besides the compound eyes, it has a pair of median eyes on top of the shell and three pairs of small 'rudimentary' eyes — larval eyes that persist into adulthood. Each type changes its light sensitivity over the day.

body.lede: Its body plan has barely changed in hundreds of millions of years, and some of its parts are unlike anything in a true crab.

systems.title: Copper-based blood
systems.text: Its blood carries oxygen with copper rather than iron. It is straw-coloured and turns blue when exposed to oxygen; its blood cells clot around bacterial toxins.

systems.title: Book gills
systems.text: Six page-like gills under the rear section each carry about 150 thin flaps, like the pages of a book. Beating them also lets the animal swim in an emergency.

systems.title: A tube-shaped heart
systems.text: The heart is a long tube running down the middle of the head shield and abdomen.

genome.lede: Sequencing shows that the horseshoe crab's ancestors copied their entire genome more than once — a rare event among invertebrates.

findings.title: Whole-genome duplications
findings.text: A 2025 chromosome-level assembly supports three whole-genome duplications unique to horseshoe crabs, none shared with spiders and scorpions.

findings.title: Doubled toxin detectors
findings.text: The genome carries tandem copies of Factors C and G, proteins in the pathway that detects bacterial toxins — the pathway behind the medical blood test.

findings.title: ZW sex chromosomes
findings.text: Females carry a ZW pair of sex chromosomes. The genome also records a steep population decline over the last 5 million years.

mind.lede: Horseshoe crabs have taught neuroscience more than their simple behaviour might suggest.

studies.title: One nerve fibre at a time
studies.text: Using the horseshoe crab's long, easily isolated optic nerve, H. Keffer Hartline and colleagues became the first to record nerve impulses from single optic nerve fibres.

studies.title: Lateral inhibition
studies.text: Hartline showed that excited photoreceptors suppress their neighbours, boosting contrast at edges. The discovery earned him a share of the 1967 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

studies.title: Courting a cement crab
studies.text: On a Massachusetts mating beach, males approached a cement model of a female from about 0.9 m away — about as well at night as in daylight. Females avoided it.

survival.lede: Adults are well armoured, but their eggs feed a whole coastline, and people take adults for bait and blood.

tactics.title: Righting itself
tactics.text: Flipped onto its back by the surf, a horseshoe crab uses its long tail to turn itself back over.

tactics.title: Spawning on the tides
tactics.text: Spawning usually coincides with high tides around full and new moons, when females come ashore to lay their eggs on the beach.

tactics.title: Many eggs
tactics.text: Females lay roughly 90,000 eggs a year in clusters, spread over repeated spawning visits.

threats.title: Bait harvest
threats.text: Horseshoe crabs are caught as bait for conch and eel fisheries; reported coastwide bait landings in 2024 were about 551,000 crabs.

threats.title: Biomedical bleeding
threats.text: In 2024 about 1.07 million crabs were collected for their blood, and an estimated 185,000 of them died as a result.

threats.title: Lost beaches
threats.text: Habitat loss and over-harvest leave the species vulnerable to local extinction, especially in New England and the Gulf of Maine.

life.lede: A horseshoe crab sheds its shell more than a dozen times and spends roughly a decade growing up before it spawns.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Females lay tiny green eggs in clusters of about 4,000 on spawning beaches. Some larvae overwinter in the nest and emerge the next spring.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: Hatchlings are about 3 mm across and have no tail. They swim in the plankton before settling on the bottom and starting to moult.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Young crabs stay on intertidal flats near their home beaches, then move into deeper water as they grow.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Males mature after about 16 moults at 8–9 years; females after 17 moults at 10–11 years. Adults live offshore and return to beaches to spawn.

lifespan.value: more than 20 years

tagline: A fist-sized ambush with a glowing lure
summary: Also called the black seadevil, this small, velvety-black anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of a cavernous, needle-toothed mouth. The light comes from bacteria living inside the lure. Females reach about 18 cm; the dwarf males are under 3 cm and live independently.
ability: bacterial light lure and an expandable stomach

stats.size: Females up to about 18 cm; males about 3 cm
stats.depth: Usually 100–1,500 m; recorded to about 4,500 m
stats.range: Tropical to temperate waters of all oceans
stats.diet: Small fishes and crustaceans; can swallow prey longer than itself

facts.title: Borrowed light
facts.text: The female's 'fishing rod' is the first ray of her dorsal fin. Its tip, the esca, is a sac packed with light-producing bacteria, so the fish doesn't make the glow itself—its microbial partners do.

facts.title: Fishing, not chasing
facts.text: Rather than spending energy hunting, the angler hangs in the dark with its lure lit and waits. When a small fish or crustacean comes close, the huge mouth and sharp teeth snap shut.

facts.title: A stretchy stomach
facts.text: Its stomach stretches enormously. A 6.6 cm humpback anglerfish was found with a roughly 24 cm viperfish inside it—prey more than three times its own length.

facts.title: Dwarf, but not a parasite
facts.text: Males are tiny and, like other dwarf anglerfish males, find females by following their scent. Unlike some anglerfish whose males fuse permanently to the female, Melanocetus males are non-parasitic and stay free-living.

facts.title: Black as ink
facts.text: Deep-sea anglerfishes have dark skin that absorbs light—an ultra-black camouflage that helps mask their presence.
