notes: Hero is a historical scientific illustration (Günther 1864 type description, PZSL) because the only real photograph on Commons (NOAA trawl specimen, used as gallery alt-1) is cluttered and does not show the lure. Rejected: NHM London display models (Commons 'Hal - Melanocetus johnsonii' and 'Melanocetus johnsonii.00x' files — these are models, not specimens) and 'Rape abisal, Greg Dykstra' (an artwork of a different-looking anglerfish). Lure/bioluminescent-bacteria and ultra-black-skin facts come from MBARI's order-level page and apply to deep-sea anglerfishes generally. The 2014 MBARI ROV video of a live Melanocetus in Monterey Canyon is often cited as a first; sources only identify it to genus, so it is not used. Common names also include 'black seadevil' and 'humpback blackdevil'.

anatomy.lede: The female is little more than a lure, a mouth and a stomach, wrapped in a rounded black body.

hotspots.label: Esca (lure)
hotspots.text: The glowing bulb at the tip is simple, usually with a rounded or conical extension, and has small crests at front and back.

hotspots.label: Illicium (rod)
hotspots.text: In females the rod measures from about a third to more than half of the body length.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: The mouth is huge and opens almost vertically, but the gape does not extend back past the eye.

hotspots.label: Teeth
hotspots.text: The teeth are slender, curved backwards and can fold down. There can be up to about 178 in the upper jaw and 142 in the lower.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: Behind the rod, the soft dorsal fin has 13 to 17 rays.

hotspots.label: Tail fin
hotspots.text: The small tail fin has 8 rays.

hotspots.label: Deep body
hotspots.text: The body is very deep, 60 to 75% as deep as it is long (excluding the tail fin).

senses.lede: The sexes sense the world differently: the female waits, while the male must search the darkness for her.

senses.name: The male's eyes
senses.text: Adult males have well-developed eyes that face sideways, elliptical in shape and with a pupil larger than the lens.

senses.name: The male's nose
senses.text: Dwarf anglerfish males have a strong sense of smell and follow chemical signals (pheromones) to find a female.

body.lede: The humpback anglerfish relies on partners and on cheap, watery tissue to make a living in the dark.

systems.title: Bacteria with shrinking genomes
systems.text: The light in its lure comes from a bacterium named 'Candidatus Enterovibrio escacola' ('esca-dwelling'). Its genome is about half the size of free-living relatives and full of broken genes and jumping DNA, a sign that it is becoming dependent on its host.

systems.title: Light caught from the sea
systems.text: Most anglerfish species studied share this same symbiont, and its family tree does not match that of its hosts. This suggests each fish picks up its bacteria from the surrounding water, not from its parents.

systems.title: A watery layer
systems.text: It is one of many deep-sea fishes with a gelatinous layer under the skin. Such tissue is mostly water, cheap to grow and lighter than seawater, so it may help with buoyancy.

systems.title: Males built for searching
systems.text: Adult males have large, inflated nostrils on the sides of the snout and no jaw teeth. Instead they carry bony plates in front of the jaws studded with strong, hooked denticles.

survival.lede: It saves energy by letting prey come to it, and hides by reflecting almost no light.

tactics.title: Lure and wait
tactics.text: Instead of chasing, it hangs in the dark with its lure lit and snaps shut on small fishes and crustaceans that come close.

tactics.title: Ultra-black skin
tactics.text: Deep-sea anglerfishes have dark skin that absorbs light, so the glow of other animals barely shows them up.

tactics.title: Swallow anything
tactics.text: It can swallow prey longer than itself: one 6.6 cm fish held a viperfish of about 24 cm.

threats.title: Seabed mining
threats.text: Mining the abyssal plain for metals would release sediment plumes that cloud the water, and anglerfishes depend on clear water for their lures to work.

life.lede: It begins life near the surface and sinks into the deep as it matures.

stages.name: Egg raft
stages.text: Eggs are probably released in a floating gelatinous raft or veil, as in other deep-sea anglerfishes.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: Larvae have short, almost spherical bodies and live mainly in the upper 100 m. Even then, young females show a small club-shaped rudiment of the rod on the head.

stages.name: Metamorphosis
stages.text: The larva transforms into its adult form at a standard length of 8 to 10 mm.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females keep growing to about 18 cm, while males stay under 3 cm. Males are free-living and never become parasitic; only two cases of temporary coupling with a female are known.

tagline: A jellyfish that can run its life cycle backwards
summary: A hydrozoan jellyfish only a few millimetres across. When starved, injured or ageing, its adult form can collapse into a cyst and regrow as a polyp, the stage it began as. That reversal earned it the nickname “immortal”, though in the wild most individuals are simply eaten or die of disease.

stats.size: Bell up to about 4.5 mm across
stats.depth: Coastal waters; polyps on docks, hulls and the seabed
stats.range: Temperate to tropical seas; first described from the Mediterranean
stats.diet: Zooplankton, fish eggs, small molluscs

facts.title: Life cycle in reverse
facts.text: When damaged, starved or senescent, the medusa shrinks into a cyst (a ball of poorly differentiated cells). The cyst then grows into a polyp, the attached stage that normally comes before the jellyfish.

facts.title: Cells that change jobs
facts.text: During the reversal, cells transdifferentiate: specialised cells switch to entirely different cell types. That differs from dedifferentiation, where cells only step back to a less specialised state within their own lineage.

facts.title: Rejuvenates even after breeding
facts.text: In laboratory studies, sexually mature medusae can revert at rates up to 100%, with no apparent limit on how many times one individual can repeat the cycle.

facts.title: Immortal, with limits
facts.text: It still dies. Reversal has not been observed in the wild, and most medusae probably fall to predators or disease first. New medusae budded from the polyp are clones, not the original animal.

facts.title: Clues in the genome
facts.text: Comparing its genome with the non-rejuvenating Turritopsis rubra revealed extra copies or variants of genes for DNA replication, DNA repair and telomere maintenance. These may help explain the ability, but this is not proven.

anatomy.lede: A medusa smaller than a fingernail, built from a thin jelly bell, a central stomach and a fringe of tentacles.

hotspots.label: Bell
hotspots.text: The bell is made of mesoglea, a jelly-like layer, and is about as tall as it is wide. Its walls are thin, thickening slightly at the top.

hotspots.label: Manubrium (stomach)
hotspots.text: The central tube that carries the mouth holds a large population of interstitial cells, the stem-like cells that help cnidarians regenerate.

hotspots.label: Marginal tentacles
hotspots.text: Tentacles are added around the rim as the medusa grows. Researchers use their number, with the shape of the bell's top, to tell apart four stages of development.

hotspots.label: Outer bell skin
hotspots.text: Cutting experiments showed that a medusa can turn back into a polyp only if cells of this outer skin and part of the gut system are present.

stats.label: Size when released from the polyp

body.lede: Its body plan is ordinary for a hydrozoan. What is extraordinary is what its cells can turn into.

systems.title: Not powered by stem cells alone
systems.text: When the stomach tube, rich in stem-like cells, was cut out and kept alone, it could not become polyp tissue. The outer bell skin, which has none of those cells, could. That points to fully specialised cells being reprogrammed into new types.

systems.title: Parts that exist only in the jellyfish
systems.text: Striated swimming muscles under the bell, nerve rings and simple light-sensitive spots (ocelli) are found only in the medusa. During reversal they disappear, and cells that make a protective chitin coat, found only in polyps, appear instead.

systems.title: A cyst with no recognisable parts
systems.text: A reverting medusa shrinks, stops swimming and settles into a cyst wrapped in a thin chitin envelope. Over the next 24 to 36 hours it grows a creeping root-like stolon from which new polyps sprout.

systems.title: Polyps regrow from fragments too
systems.text: In a laboratory study at 25 °C, cut pieces of polyp first rounded up into a 'dumpling' and, within about two days, grew a new stolon.

genome.lede: Two genome projects have compared the immortal jellyfish with a close relative that cannot rejuvenate after breeding.

findings.title: A bigger genome than its mortal cousin
findings.text: The genome is estimated at about 390 million base pairs, against about 210 million in Turritopsis rubra. About 17,500 genes were predicted, compared with about 9,300 in T. rubra, though the T. dohrnii assembly was more fragmented.

findings.title: Switching genes back to an early state
findings.text: During reversal, genes normally kept silent by a regulator called polycomb repressive complex 2 were switched off, while targets of pluripotency factors were switched on. The authors propose these as key drivers of rejuvenation.

findings.title: A long-read assembly from Japan
findings.text: A 2023 draft genome, built from one clonal line using long DNA reads, totalled about 436 million base pairs with 23,314 high-confidence genes, giving researchers a reference for future work.

survival.lede: Its one great trick is to go backwards when life turns hostile.

tactics.title: Reverse instead of die
tactics.text: Medusae at every stage, from newly released to fully mature, were shown to turn back into colonial polyps, either directly or after a resting period.

tactics.title: Many triggers
tactics.text: In the laboratory, reversal was set off by starvation, sudden temperature changes, lower salinity and physical damage.

tactics.title: Built for long journeys
tactics.text: Because starved or damaged medusae can revert to polyps, they may survive long voyages in ships' ballast water.

threats.title: Spread by people, not threatened by them
threats.text: Near-identical genes in animals from Japan, Panama, Florida, Spain and Italy point to a worldwide, human-assisted introduction. Medusae looked different in tropical and temperate waters, which helped the spread go unnoticed.

life.lede: A typical hydrozoan cycle, with one extra path: from adult back to polyp.

stages.name: Planula larva
stages.text: Fertilised eggs become short-lived, feeding larvae that do not travel far before settling on the seabed.

stages.name: Polyp colony
stages.text: The larva becomes a colonial polyp that spreads by budding and releases new medusae, each a clone of the colony.

stages.name: Medusa
stages.text: Released medusae about 1 mm across feed in the plankton and mature in a few weeks: about 25–30 days at 20 °C and 18–22 days at 22 °C. Development is faster in warmer water.

stages.name: Cyst (reversal)
stages.text: A damaged, starved or ageing medusa shrinks into a cyst, which within 24 to 36 hours develops polyp features and starts the cycle again.

lifespan.value: No fixed limit seen in the lab; unknown in the wild

tagline: The big cat that kills with a bite to the skull
summary: The largest cat in the Americas, a powerfully built hunter of rainforest, river and swamp. Rather than simply gripping the throat, a jaguar will often drive its canines straight through its prey's skull, and its jaws can crack turtle shells and pierce the armoured hide of a caiman.

stats.size: Head and body 1.5–1.8 m plus a 70–90 cm tail; usually 68–136 kg
stats.habitat: Dense lowland rainforest, flooded forest, swamps and wetlands, nearly always close to water
stats.elevation: Mostly below 2,000 m; recorded up to 3,800 m in Costa Rica
stats.range: Mexico to northern Argentina, across 18 countries; rare wanderers reach Arizona and New Mexico
stats.diet: Over 85 prey species, from peccaries, capybaras and deer to caimans, turtles and fish
stats.conservation: IUCN Red List: Near Threatened (2017 assessment)

facts.title: Straight through the skull
facts.text: A jaguar may kill with a suffocating neck bite, but it often drives its canines through the back of its prey's skull instead. The same jaws can bite through thick reptile skin and turtle shells.

facts.title: Pound for pound, the strongest jaws
facts.text: A 2012 study of the jaw muscles of nine cat species found that the jaguar — the most bone- and shell-crunching cat in the sample — had relatively greater bite-force capacity than the others. A tiger bites harder in absolute terms, but for its size the jaguar comes out ahead.

facts.title: A cat that loves water
facts.text: Jaguars are excellent swimmers. In the flooded forests of the Amazon they swim from tree to tree to hunt monkeys and sloths, and they regularly catch caimans, turtles and anacondas.

facts.title: A menu of 85 species
facts.text: More than 85 kinds of prey have been recorded in the jaguar's diet. One jaguar was seen dragging a 34 kg sea turtle 91.5 m into the cover of the forest.

facts.title: Black jaguars are not a separate species
facts.text: All-black jaguars are fairly common, especially in forest. Their colour comes from a single dominant gene, and the rosettes are usually still faintly visible against the dark coat.

facts.title: Half its kingdom lost
facts.text: Jaguars have been wiped out from nearly half of their historic range, mainly through habitat loss, conflict with ranchers and the hunting of their prey.

notes: All three photographs are wild jaguars from the Brazilian Pantanal (no licensed in-situ Amazon photo of comparable quality was found); the record is still filed under 'amazon' first as briefed. Commons labels the alt-2 animal with the subspecies name P. o. palustris, but jaguar subspecies are not generally recognised, so species is given as Panthera onca. The bite-force fact rests on Hartstone-Rose et al. 2012, whose abstract says the jaguar 'appears to have relatively higher force production capabilities' among nine felids; the tiger comparison is from the lead author's comments reported by BBC Wildlife (discoverwildlife.com), not cited here. Size: ADW notes Pantanal males average 100 kg while Honduran males average 57 kg, so the 68–136 kg range is typical rather than absolute. Elevation minimum (10 m) follows ADW. The IUCN DOI and GBIF links resolve in a browser but return 403 to scripted requests (bot protection); IDs were checked through the GBIF API and Wikidata. IUCN year is the publication year of the assessment (2017).

anatomy.lede: The jaguar is built for power, not speed: a stocky, muscular cat with a broad head, short limbs and, for its size, the strongest bite of the cats measured.

hotspots.label: Ear
hotspots.text: Jaguars communicate mainly by voice. A typical call is a series of seven to a dozen grunts, more powerful in males than in females.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Jaguars are most active around dawn and dusk, hunting by pouncing on prey from a hidden spot.

hotspots.label: Jaws
hotspots.text: Large, square jaws and prominent cheeks anchor huge muscles. For its size, the jaguar has a greater bite-force capacity than the other cats studied.

hotspots.label: Forelimbs
hotspots.text: Lean bodies and muscular limbs let a jaguar drag heavy prey into cover — one hauled a 34 kg sea turtle 91.5 m.

hotspots.label: Rosettes
hotspots.text: Jaguars' rosettes have distinct spots inside them, unlike the leopard's smaller spots and rosettes.

hotspots.label: Paws
hotspots.text: Large, rounded paws help jaguars swim long distances in rivers and flooded forest.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The tail measures 70–90 cm, against a head-and-body length of 1.5–1.8 m.

senses.lede: Jaguars are secretive and solitary, and much of their communication is by sound and scent left for others to find.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Females in season call in the early morning and late at night, and males answer and travel to find them. Hunters exploit this by mimicking the call with a hollow gourd.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Jaguars mark their home ranges by spraying urine, leaving droppings in prominent places and scraping trees and the ground.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Two genes involved in optic nerve development, DOCK3 and COL4A5, show signs of positive selection in jaguars, possibly linked to vision.

body.lede: Where other big cats rely on speed or size, the jaguar relies on raw strength concentrated in its head and forequarters.

systems.title: A crushing bite
systems.text: Measurements of jaw muscles from nine cat species found the jaguar had relatively the greatest bite-force capacity, suiting a diet that includes caimans and turtles.

systems.title: A throat built to roar
systems.text: Like other big cats, jaguars cannot purr. They roar instead, thanks to a hyoid bone in the throat attached to a stretchy ligament.

systems.title: Size follows the prey
systems.text: Jaguars in the open Pantanal average 100 kg for males, while those in Honduran forest average 57 kg — perhaps because big hoofed prey is more plentiful in open habitats.

genome.lede: The jaguar genome was first sequenced and published in 2017, alongside comparisons with all the other living big cats.

findings.title: Big cats that interbred
findings.text: The genomes of the Panthera cats show tangled family trees, caused partly by hybridisation between species after they split.

findings.title: Borrowed genes, put to use
findings.text: Some genes that jaguars seem to have picked up through ancient hybridisation also show signs of natural selection within the species, suggesting interbreeding helped big cats adapt.

findings.title: The black jaguar gene
findings.text: Black jaguars carry a small deletion in the MC1R gene, one of at least four separate genetic origins of black coats in the cat family.

mind.lede: The jaguar has long been described as a strict loner. Camera traps and GPS collars are revealing more flexible behaviour.

studies.title: Male partnerships
studies.text: Studies in the Venezuelan Llanos and Brazilian Pantanal recorded 70 cases of cooperation or coalition between males, including joint patrolling and marking. Two coalitions lasted more than seven years.

studies.title: But not hunting together
studies.text: Unlike lions and cheetahs, coalition jaguars spent less time together and were not seen hunting cooperatively. Coalitions were most likely where females lived at high density.

studies.title: An escort out
studies.text: Jaguars have occasionally been seen following people, perhaps to 'escort' them out of their territory. They do not attack humans without provocation.

survival.lede: As top predator of the American tropics, an adult jaguar has no natural enemies — only people.

tactics.title: Ambush from cover
tactics.text: Jaguars stalk on the ground through thick vegetation and pounce from a concealed spot, then drag the kill somewhere secluded to eat.

tactics.title: Hidden in plain sight
tactics.text: Cryptic colouring and secretive habits help jaguars avoid detection by both prey and people.

tactics.title: Up and away
tactics.text: Jaguars climb trees for safety or to hunt, and in flood season may be forced to rest in them.

threats.title: Conflict with ranchers
threats.text: Jaguars occasionally kill cattle and are often shot on sight in ranching areas, despite legal protection.

threats.title: Lost and broken habitat
threats.text: Habitat loss and fragmentation, and overhunting of the jaguar's prey, threaten it across its range.

threats.title: Poaching
threats.text: Jaguars are still illegally killed for their pelts, paws and teeth.

life.lede: Jaguar cubs depend on their mother for almost two years, learning to hunt at her side.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Most births come in the wet season, when prey is plentiful. A litter is usually two cubs, but can be one to four.

stages.name: Newborn cub
stages.text: Cubs are born with their eyes closed and are completely dependent on their mother; their eyes open at about two weeks.

stages.name: Learning to hunt
stages.text: Cubs nurse until 5–6 months old, then begin hunting with their mother, staying with her until they are almost two.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature at 12–24 months and males at 24–36 months. Male home ranges usually overlap those of two or three females.

lifespan.value: 11–12 years in the wild; over 20 in captivity

tagline: The widest-reaching arthropod on Earth
summary: Called taka-ashi-gani, 'tall-legged crab', in Japan, it has the greatest leg span of any known arthropod: up to about 3.7 m from claw to claw. It walks the seafloor off southern Japan, scavenging and picking at plants and shellfish, and disguises its bumpy shell with living sponges and other animals.

stats.size: Leg span up to about 3.7 m; body up to about 40 cm wide; up to about 19 kg
stats.depth: Adults usually about 50–600 m
stats.range: Pacific coast of Japan (mainly southern Honshū); outlying records off Iwate and Taiwan
stats.diet: Omnivore and scavenger: dead fish, molluscs, small invertebrates, algae

facts.title: Record-breaking reach
facts.text: Guinness World Records lists it as the longest marine crustacean. One specimen had a claw span of 3.7 m and weighed 18.6 kg, though average spans are closer to 2.4–2.7 m.

facts.title: Wears living disguises
facts.text: It tears sponges, worm tubes and other organisms from the seabed, shapes them with its mouthparts and sticks them onto its shell, where they keep growing as camouflage.

facts.title: Larvae near the surface
facts.text: Females carry up to about 1.5 million eggs per season. The hatchlings drift as plankton near the warmer surface through several larval stages before settling to the cold depths.

facts.title: A fragile 100-minute moult
facts.text: Moulting takes about 100 minutes. The crab becomes immobile, backs out of its shell starting at the rear, and frees its long walking legs last.

facts.title: Half a century old?
facts.text: Guinness says specimens live 50+ years, but crabs are hard to age and no peer-reviewed lifespan estimate was found.

notes: WoRMS currently places the genus in its own family, Macrocheiridae; older sources use Inachidae. No acceptable in situ photo was found on Commons, so both images are aquarium shots. The gallery file's title is just 'Spider Crab', but it is filed in Category:Macrocheira kaempferi, is from the Aquarium of the Pacific, and is unmistakably this species. Depth varies by source: Wikipedia gives 50–600 m, while Guinness says 30–50 m. We used Wikipedia's range, which matches regular occurrence at about 300 m in Suruga Bay. No IUCN assessment was found. Wikipedia mentions fishery conservation measures, but we found no primary source for them.

anatomy.lede: A body no bigger than a large dinner plate hangs from legs that reach across a room. Most of a Japanese spider crab is limb.

hotspots.label: Carapace
hotspots.text: The pear-shaped shell is covered in small, spike-like bumps. Young crabs have long spines for their size; on adults they are short and curve outwards.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Its eyestalks and antennae are reduced, and its senses seem less developed than those of many related crabs.

hotspots.label: Claw
hotspots.text: The claws sit on the first pair of legs. Females' are much shorter than males', and even shorter than the next pair of legs.

hotspots.label: Walking legs
hotspots.text: The legs keep growing after the crab reaches maturity, which is why old crabs reach such extraordinary spans.

hotspots.label: Leg tip
hotspots.text: It cannot swim. It walks slowly over the seafloor on its pointed leg tips, searching for food.

mind.lede: Little is known about how this giant lives day to day. Aquariums and divers describe a calm, solitary crab.

studies.title: Calm loners
studies.text: Japanese spider crabs spend much of their time slowly searching the seafloor for food. Even when kept together, they interact very little.

studies.title: Disguise is for the young
studies.text: Juveniles often camouflage themselves with sponges and other debris. Adults rarely bother, perhaps because their size already deters most predators.

survival.lede: For a young spider crab, safety means looking like the seabed; for an adult, being too big to bother with.

tactics.title: Living camouflage
tactics.text: Young crabs cover their shells with sponges and debris to blend in with the bottom.

tactics.title: Size and claws
tactics.text: Large adults are avoided by most predators and can fend off smaller attackers with their claws.

threats.title: Fishing
threats.text: It is caught as a delicacy in Japan, and catches have declined over the past 40 years. Data are too few to assess its conservation status.

threats.title: Protecting the breeding season
threats.text: Japanese law bans catching the crabs from January to April, their mating season, and restocking with farmed juveniles has been proposed.

life.lede: The world's longest-legged crab starts life as a speck of plankton, passing through four larval forms before it settles to the seabed.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Mating takes place in early spring, and the female carries her fertilised eggs on her body until they hatch.

stages.name: Prezoea
stages.text: The newly hatched larva is a prezoea, a stage that lasts only minutes before it moults.

stages.name: Zoea
stages.text: Two zoeal stages follow, swimming with the plankton near the surface.

stages.name: Megalopa
stages.text: The last larval stage, the megalopa, has the longest gap between moults. The planktonic stages together can last one to three months; 15–18 °C suits them best.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Young crabs settle on the seafloor, where they hide under sponges and other debris as they grow.

lifespan.value: Unverified; often said to exceed 50 years

tagline: A fish that dresses as drifting seaweed
summary: A relative of seahorses found only in southern Australia, the leafy seadragon is draped in leaf-shaped skin flaps that make it look like a scrap of kelp. It glides on tiny, nearly invisible fins, sucks up minute crustaceans — and, as in seahorses, it is the father who carries the eggs.

stats.size: Up to about 35 cm long
stats.depth: About 4–50 m
stats.range: Southern Australia, from Kangaroo Island (SA) to south-western Western Australia
stats.diet: Mysids and other tiny crustaceans

facts.title: Leaves for hiding, not swimming
facts.text: The leafy flaps are camouflage, letting it sway like kelp in the swell. It actually moves by rapidly fluttering small, almost transparent fins, steering with its tail.

facts.title: Dad carries the eggs
facts.text: The female deposits 250–300 eggs onto a spongy patch under the male's tail, and he carries them for 6–8 weeks until they hatch. Males may raise two broods a season.

facts.title: A cup for every egg
facts.text: The male's skin is soft when the eggs are first pressed in, then hardens to form a small cup around each one.

facts.title: Toothless pipette feeder
facts.text: With no teeth, it feeds by suction, slurping tiny crustaceans such as mysids whole through its long, tube-like snout.

facts.title: A state emblem
facts.text: Found nowhere but southern Australia, it is protected throughout its range and is the official marine emblem of South Australia.

IUCN Red List site itself returned 403, so not cited directly. Gallery photo location not stated on Commons (photographer is Sydney-based; species occurs only in southern/western Australia).

anatomy.lede: Under the leaves is a seahorse-like fish: an armoured body of bony plates, a tube for a mouth, and fins so small and clear that it seems to drift rather than swim.

hotspots.label: Snout
hotspots.text: The long, thin, pipe-like snout has no teeth. It sucks in tiny prey whole, working much like a pipette.

hotspots.label: Face
hotspots.text: Markings on the face differ between individuals. Divers have used photographs of them to recognise the same seadragon for at least 11 months.

hotspots.label: Leafy appendages
hotspots.text: The leafy appendages are bony and stand away from the body, so scientists have been able to attach tracking tags to them without harming the fish.

hotspots.label: Spines
hotspots.text: Each bony plate of the body carries a long, sharp spine that may help defend the seadragon.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: A small, transparent dorsal fin on the back ripples to push the fish along. Seadragons have lost the tail fin and the pelvic fins.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The tail makes up about half the total length. In males, eggs are carried attached to its underside.

body.lede: Seadragons feed, defend themselves and breed in ways shared only with their seahorse and pipefish relatives.

systems.title: No teeth, no stomach
systems.text: Leafy seadragons have neither teeth nor a stomach, so they feed almost constantly on mysid shrimps, other small crustaceans and larval fish.

systems.title: A suit of bony plates
systems.text: The body is covered in bony plates, each bearing a long, sharp spine, giving this fragile-looking fish a suit of armour.

systems.title: Male pregnancy
systems.text: It is the male who carries the eggs, attached to a brood area on the underside of his tail, for the six to eight weeks until they hatch.

genome.lede: In 2022 researchers published chromosome-scale genomes of a male leafy seadragon and a female weedy seadragon, the first major genetic resources for these fish.

findings.title: Missing growth-factor genes
findings.text: Seadragons, seahorses and pipefishes have lost the genes fgf3 and fgf4, which other vertebrates use in forming teeth, limbs and skin outgrowths. This may be linked to their toothless jaws and unusual bony armour.

findings.title: A genome full of repeats
findings.text: Seadragon genomes are unusually dense in repetitive DNA, with recent bursts of 'jumping genes' (transposable elements). They also have divergent non-coding DNA near a developmental gene involved in skin outgrowths.

findings.title: Two separate populations
findings.text: DNA from 71 wild seadragons shows two main groups, one in Western Australia and one in South Australia. Genetic diversity is moderate to low, and especially low in the west.

mind.lede: Tracking and photo-identification show the leafy seadragon is a homebody, spending most of its time standing still in a small patch of reef and seagrass.

studies.title: Tracked by sound
studies.text: Nine adults fitted with ultrasonic tags mostly stayed within home ranges of up to 5 ha. Short bursts of movement were separated by long still spells, by day or by night.

studies.title: Known by their faces
studies.text: Over 14 months, divers identified nine individuals from their facial markings and resighted them months apart in the same area, about 57 seadragons per hectare.

studies.title: Seasonal gatherings
studies.text: Seadragons are usually solitary and move into deeper water in winter. In late winter they gather in shallow bays to pair and mate.

survival.lede: A slow, fragile fish with few defences, the leafy seadragon survives by not being noticed.

tactics.title: Hiding as seaweed
tactics.text: Leafy appendages, the ability to change colour and a gentle swaying motion make it look like drifting weed.

tactics.title: Spines
tactics.text: Sharp spines on the bony plates may deter a predator that sees through the disguise.

threats.title: Losing kelp and seagrass
threats.text: The kelp and seagrass habitats seadragons need have been retreating throughout their range.

threats.title: Pollution and fishing
threats.text: Coastal development, pollution and fertiliser runoff damage their habitat, and some are taken as bycatch or by poachers.

threats.title: Warming seas
threats.text: Rising water temperatures from climate change may also affect them.

life.lede: Seadragon life begins on the father's tail, and the young emerge looking nothing like their leafy parents.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays 250–300 eggs, each about 4 mm across, onto the underside of the male's tail.

stages.name: Brooding
stages.text: The male carries the eggs, each held in its own small cup in his skin, until they are ready to hatch.

stages.name: Hatching
stages.text: He releases only a few young at a time, so a whole brood can take hours or days to hatch.

stages.name: Fry
stages.text: Newborn fry have very short snouts and no leafy appendages, and stay close to the bottom for about two days.

lifespan.value: Possibly 7–10 years in the wild

tagline: The spotted hunter of the Antarctic pack ice
summary: A long, sinuous, spotted seal with a huge head, at the top of the Antarctic food web. It eats almost anything from krill to penguins and young seals, sieving small prey through interlocking cheek teeth, and it roams thousands of kilometres between the pack ice and the subantarctic islands.
ability: teeth that both seize penguins and sieve krill

stats.size: Females up to about 3.8 m and over 500 kg; males smaller, about 3 m and 300 kg
stats.depth: Usually short, shallow dives (on average about 30 m and 3 minutes); one dive recorded to 1,256 m
stats.range: Around Antarctica's pack ice and the Southern Ocean, reaching the subantarctic islands, especially in winter
stats.diet: Krill, fish, squid, penguins and other seabirds, and seals, including crabeater and fur seal pups

facts.title: Bigger females
facts.text: Adult females measured at Cape Shirreff, Antarctic Peninsula, averaged 454 kg against 302 kg for males, about 50% heavier. That makes the leopard seal one of the most extreme cases of females outsizing males among marine mammals.

facts.title: Two ways to eat
facts.text: Captive leopard seals catch small prey by suction, then force the water back out through their cheek teeth, whose cusps interlock to form a sieve. The same jaws seize and shake penguins.

facts.title: A shallow diver, with one surprise
facts.text: Tagged adults at Cape Shirreff made dives averaging about 29 m and 3 minutes. One male, however, dived to 1,256 m for 25 minutes, far deeper than the previous record of 425 m.

facts.title: Penguin specialists, sometimes
facts.text: Leopard seals are generalists, eating krill, fish, seals and penguins. At Bird Island, South Georgia, they have been estimated to take 16–20% of the small local gentoo penguin population.

facts.title: Long-distance wanderers
facts.text: Seals tracked from Bird Island for an average of 294 days made trips of 100–500 km, some heading south to the pack ice, and travelled up to 1,950 km from the island. They spent about a quarter of their time hauled out.

facts.title: Slender-clawed water-worker
facts.text: Its scientific name Hydrurga leptonyx translates as 'slender-clawed water-worker', fitting an animal far more agile in the water than on the ice.

notes: Taxonomy per WoRMS (AphiaID 231417). The IUCN page blocks scripted access; the 2015 assessment (Hückstädt, assessed 20 January 2015) was confirmed through Crossref and the Least Concern category through SeaLifeBase and other secondary sources. The British Antarctic Survey's own leopard seal page could not be loaded (bot protection), so the BAS-led tracking study at Bird Island (Staniland et al. 2018) is cited instead. The 1,256 m dive is a single record from one adult male; typical dives are shallow. Size: ADW gives females up to 3.8 m and 500 kg; Kienle et al. weighed a 540 kg female. The filter-feeding evidence comes from captive seals in Australia. Leopard seals also wander further north (Commons holds photographs from Petone Beach, New Zealand, and from southern Chile and Argentina), but only the Southern Ocean is mapped as their range. The hero photo's Commons page gives no location. Category shelves left empty: none of the ocean shelves fits without forcing.

anatomy.lede: The leopard seal is built like no other Antarctic seal: long and slender for speed and agility in the water, with an outsized head and jaws made for handling large prey.

hotspots.label: Huge head
hotspots.text: The large head carries a long snout, well suited to catching and handling prey as big as penguins and young seals.

hotspots.label: Jaws and cheek teeth
hotspots.text: Behind the lips, the many-cusped cheek teeth interlock when the mouth closes, forming a sieve that strains small prey from the water.

hotspots.label: Spotted coat
hotspots.text: The back is dark grey and the underside silvery grey, both scattered with dark and light spots, the 'leopard' pattern behind its name.

hotspots.label: Foreflipper
hotspots.text: Its species name leptonyx means 'slender-clawed', after the claws on its flippers.

hotspots.label: Slender body
hotspots.text: The long, slender body makes the leopard seal very agile in the water, where it spends most of its time.

stats.label: Heaviest female weighed at Cape Shirreff

body.lede: A predator that can tackle a penguin one day and krill the next needs versatile equipment.

systems.title: A two-way mouth
systems.text: Captive seals drew small prey in by suction and expelled the water through their cheek teeth. Wear on the front teeth but not the cheek teeth suggests the cheek teeth act mainly as a sieve.

systems.title: Short, flat-bottomed dives
systems.text: Most tagged dives at Cape Shirreff lasted about 3 minutes and averaged about 29 m; around two-thirds had a square, flat-bottomed profile.

systems.title: Heavier females
systems.text: Adult females averaged 454 kg and 196 cm around the girth, against 302 kg and 156 cm for males.

genome.lede: A reference genome was published only in 2025, from a seal that stranded in New Zealand.

findings.title: A nearly complete map
findings.text: Long-read sequencing of a stranded adult male from Kaitorete Beach, Christchurch, produced a 2.4-billion-base-pair assembly in just 203 pieces, judged about 98% complete for genes expected in carnivores.

findings.title: Lining up with relatives
findings.text: The assembly covers about 95% of the Hawaiian monk seal genome, and its pieces map onto that seal's 18 chromosomes, including the Y chromosome.

mind.lede: Leopard seals are solitary and hard to watch, so much of what is known about their behaviour comes from sound recordings, tags and captive animals.

studies.title: Songs with a signature
studies.text: Recordings of adult males in Prydz Bay, East Antarctica, showed each male sang his calls in a distinctive order; a sequence could be matched to the right seal 83% of the time.

studies.title: Switching techniques
studies.text: Captive leopard seals hunting small prey underwater sucked it into the mouth and then expelled the water through the sieve of their cheek teeth, the first direct observations of filter feeding in the species.

studies.title: Midday rests
studies.text: Seals tracked at South Georgia hauled out most often around midday from October to April, with haul-outs spread more evenly through the day in winter.

survival.lede: As an apex predator, an adult leopard seal has little to fear except killer whales and a changing climate.

tactics.title: Eat what is in season
tactics.text: At Cape Shirreff, adult females switch in spring and summer to warm-blooded prey such as penguin chicks and fur seal pups, while males feed lower in the food web.

tactics.title: Roam widely
tactics.text: Tracked seals made long trips north to the Polar Frontal Zone and south to the pack ice, rather than staying near one colony.

threats.title: Shrinking sea ice
threats.text: Leopard seals give birth and nurse on pack ice, so a decline in Antarctic sea ice is likely to affect them.

life.lede: Leopard seals breed on the drifting pack ice, which makes them among the least studied seals in the world.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Mating takes place in the water in December and early January, shortly after pups are weaned.

stages.name: Pup
stages.text: Pups are born on ice floes between late October and November, about 120 cm long, and are nursed and guarded by the mother alone.

stages.name: On the ice
stages.text: Satellite tags on three females that stayed on the ice for more than ten days probably captured birth and nursing for the first time.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature at about 4 years and males at about 4.5; they breed once a year.

lifespan.value: Recorded up to about 30 years in the wild

tagline: The only big cat that lives and hunts as a family
summary: Lions live in prides built around related females, which do most of the hunting and often work together to bring down animals far bigger than themselves. Once found across much of Africa and into Asia, wild lions now survive mainly in Africa south of the Sahara, with a single Asian population in India's Gir Forest.

stats.size: 1–1.2 m at the shoulder; males weigh 150–250 kg
stats.habitat: Savanna, grassland, open woodland and semi-desert
stats.elevation: From lowlands up to 4,240 m in Ethiopia's Bale Mountains
stats.range: Africa from the southern edge of the Sahara to South Africa, plus the Gir Forest in north-west India
stats.diet: Mainly large animals weighing about 45–450 kg

facts.title: A sisterhood
facts.text: Lions live in prides of related females and their young, which may number from several to as many as 40 animals. The females raise the cubs and do most of the hunting, though males sometimes join in.

facts.title: Better together
facts.text: Several lions may stalk prey from different directions to within about 30 m before charging. In the Serengeti, lions hunting alone succeeded 17% of the time, while group hunts succeeded 30% of the time.

facts.title: A roar heard 8 km away
facts.text: Lions roar to mark their territory and keep in touch with pride members, and a roar can be heard up to about 8 km (five miles) away.

facts.title: Twenty hours of rest
facts.text: Where prey is plentiful, lions spend about twenty hours a day sleeping or resting.

facts.title: The last Asian lions
facts.text: Asiatic lions survive as a single wild population in and around the Gir Forest of north-west India, where they face inbreeding, limited habitat and frequent conflict with people.

facts.title: Holding on in the south
facts.text: An analysis of 47 lion populations found lions declining everywhere in Africa except in four southern countries — Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe — partly thanks to small, fenced, intensively managed reserves.

notes: Conservation: IUCN 2025 assessment (Nicholson et al., e.T15951A280792135), category Vulnerable per GBIF's IUCN checklist (July 2026 release); iucnredlist.org returns 403 to scripted requests, so the URL was confirmed via the GBIF API, not a page fetch. Regions: african-savanna; namib-kalahari for the Kalahari lions (e.g. Kgalagadi, Tswalu) and Etosha; indian-subcontinent for the Gir population (Smithsonian, ADW). No population totals given: Smithsonian's figures (about 20,000 in Africa; about 250 in Gir) look dated against the 2023 Green Status figures reported in the press (~23,000 in Africa, ~670 in India), so I left numbers out rather than mix sources. Diet range '45–450 kg' converts Smithsonian's '100 to 1,000 pounds'. Elevation max 4,240 m is ADW's Bale Mountains population; the minimum is set at sea level (approx: true) as no source gives a lower limit. The 17%/30% hunting success figures are ADW's summary of Serengeti research. The hero shows the male with mouth open (Commons does not say whether yawning, roaring or flehmen), so the alt text describes it without guessing.

anatomy.lede: Strip away the coat and a lion is almost indistinguishable from a tiger. What sets it apart is its social life — and the male's mane, a signal read by friend and rival alike.

hotspots.label: Jaws and canines
hotspots.text: Powerful jaws and teeth pull down and kill prey often much larger than the lion itself. Adults have 30 teeth.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Lions use visual cues to recognise one another — including reading the size and colour of a male's mane from a distance.

hotspots.label: Mane
hotspots.text: Only male lions grow manes, from about age three. A dark mane signals good nutrition and high testosterone.

hotspots.label: Forelegs
hotspots.text: Strong, compact bodies and powerful forelegs let lions wrestle large animals to the ground.

hotspots.label: Body
hotspots.text: Adult males typically weigh about 189 kg and females about 126 kg; the heaviest male on record weighed 272 kg.

hotspots.label: Tail tuft
hotspots.text: The long tail ends in a black tuft; cubs are born with spotted coats that fade as they grow.

senses.lede: Living in groups that come and go across a large territory, lions keep track of each other — and of rivals — by sound, sight and scent.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Lions listen closely to strangers' roars. In playback trials, pride females could judge how many intruders were calling and compared that with how many companions they had.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Manes are read visually: their length signals fighting ability to other males, and their darkness affects which males females choose.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Resident males regularly spray vegetation with urine and scuff the ground to mark territory, and females spray occasionally.

body.lede: The lion's body reflects its role as a heavy, cooperative predator — and the costs of male showmanship.

systems.title: A hot coat
systems.text: Manes come at a price: dark-maned males run hotter, have more abnormal sperm and eat less in the hottest months. Males grow lighter or shorter manes in hotter seasons, years and places.

systems.title: Living with a virus
systems.text: In the Serengeti, Ngorongoro Crater and Kruger, 92% of lions tested carried feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV). It does not seem to harm lions, though it kills domestic cats.

systems.title: Built for big prey
systems.text: Lions mainly eat animals weighing about 45–450 kg, such as zebra and wildebeest. In lean times they switch to rodents, reptiles and other small animals.

genome.lede: A chromosome-level lion genome was published in 2020. Ancient and modern lion DNA now traces how the species spread and shrank.

findings.title: Cave lions split long ago
findings.text: Lions and the extinct cave lions of Ice Age Eurasia shared an ancestor about 500,000 years ago, and probably did not interbreed afterwards.

findings.title: Two modern lineages
findings.text: Living lions fall into two main lineages that split about 70,000 years ago, with later gene flow between them.

findings.title: Indian lions lack variety
findings.text: The lions of India's Gir Forest have almost no genetic diversity, the legacy of extremely small populations in the recent past.

mind.lede: The Serengeti lions have been studied continuously since 1966, making them among the best-understood social carnivores on Earth.

studies.title: Wings and centres
studies.text: In 486 group hunts in Etosha, Namibia, lionesses took set roles: some circled the prey as 'wings' while others waited as 'centres'. Each lioness tended to keep the same position, and hunts went best when they did.

studies.title: Counting the opposition
studies.text: When recorded roars of strange females were played in 21 pride territories, residents were less likely to approach when they were outnumbered — and roared to recruit absent pride members.

studies.title: What a mane says
studies.text: Dark-maned males in the Serengeti had longer reproductive lives and their cubs survived better. Females preferred dark manes, while rival males paid attention to mane length.

studies.title: Shared nurseries
studies.text: Related lionesses often give birth at the same time and nurse each other's cubs in a crèche, which lowers cub deaths.

survival.lede: Adult lions have no natural predators. Their dangers come from other lions, from hunger and from people.

tactics.title: Defending the territory together
tactics.text: Lions live at higher densities than other big cats, so pride members must defend their territory together against takeovers by other lions.

tactics.title: Coalitions of brothers
tactics.text: Young males leave home at about 2.5 years and team up, usually with brothers, to take over a pride. Coalitions of three or four tend to hold a pride for longer than pairs.

tactics.title: Stealing a meal
tactics.text: Lions scavenge actively, following hyenas and vultures, and steal kills from hyenas and leopards.

threats.title: Poison and snares
threats.text: Lions are killed with snares, rifles and arrows, and because they scavenge they are especially vulnerable to poisoned carcasses.

threats.title: Disease from dogs
threats.text: Many lions have died from diseases such as canine distemper, spread by domestic dogs from villages near their habitat.

threats.title: Declines across Africa
threats.text: Lion populations are falling across most of Africa; only some intensively managed southern populations are holding up.

life.lede: A lion's life is shaped by the pride: cubs are raised communally, and their survival depends on how long their fathers hold power.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: One to six cubs are born, each weighing 1–2 kg. Females usually have a litter every two years.

stages.name: Hidden cub
stages.text: Eyes open by about 11 days and cubs can run at a month old, but their mother keeps them hidden until about eight weeks.

stages.name: Pride cub
stages.text: Cubs are weaned at 7–10 months and depend on the pride until at least 16 months. Up to 80% die in their first two years, many from starvation or from males taking over the pride.

stages.name: Nomad or pride member
stages.text: Young females usually stay in their mother's pride for life. Young males are driven out and roam for two to three years before trying to win a pride of their own.

lifespan.value: Females 15–16 years in the wild; few males live past 10

tagline: A cold-water giant trailing a mane of stinging hair
summary: One of the largest jellyfish known, drifting through cold northern seas with a bell that can reach about 1.8 m across and a curtain of more than a thousand sticky, stinging tentacles. It hunts fish and other jellies, and its sting is painful but rarely dangerous to people.

stats.size: Bell up to about 1.8 m across; usually far smaller
stats.depth: Mostly near the surface, rarely below about 20 m
stats.range: Cold and temperate waters of the Arctic, North Atlantic and North Pacific
stats.diet: Fish, zooplankton, smaller jellyfish

facts.title: A mane of tentacles
facts.text: More than 1,000 tentacles hang beneath the bell, each armed with nematocysts (stinging cells). The bell itself is split into eight lobes, giving it the outline of an eight-pointed star.

facts.title: The 36-metre record
facts.text: The often-quoted 36.6 m (120 ft) tentacles come from a single 1865 account by Alexander Agassiz, with no details of how they were measured. That animal may even have been a different, undescribed Cyanea species.

facts.title: Sinks onto its prey
facts.text: It positions itself above fish, spreads its tentacles, then slowly sinks, catching prey in a living net and stunning it with stinging cells.

facts.title: Stings long after detaching
facts.text: In experiments with Icelandic specimens, detached tentacles kept their full ability to catch prey for 24 days, a risk for nearby fish farms.

facts.title: Bigger in the far north
facts.text: Lower-latitude individuals are usually smaller, with bells around 50 cm. Juveniles are tan or light orange and darken to red and purple with age.

notes: Hero cropped slightly top and bottom to remove a mooring rope in the lower-left corner. Size figures vary by source: Oceana gives a bell up to 1.8 m; Wikipedia says 'over 2 m'. We used the more conservative figure. The famous 36.6 m tentacle length is marked uncertain. McClain et al. 2015 trace it to Agassiz's 1865 Nahant (Massachusetts) specimen and say western Atlantic 'C. capillata' may be a genetically distinct Cyanea sp. Cyanea taxonomy is unsettled (some workers lump the genus), and Japanese populations are sometimes treated as C. nozakii. No IUCN assessment found; Oceana says the population has not been assessed. Depth (≤20 m) is from Wikipedia.

anatomy.lede: A lion's mane has no brain, heart or bones: just a lobed bell of jelly, a mass of frilly arms around the mouth, and a curtain of stinging tentacles.

hotspots.label: Bell
hotspots.text: Slow pulses of the bell push the jellyfish only weakly forward, so it relies on currents to travel long distances.

hotspots.label: Bell margin
hotspots.text: In each of the eight notches between the bell's lobes sits a small balance organ that helps the jellyfish keep itself the right way up.

hotspots.label: Tentacles
hotspots.text: The tentacles hang in clusters, about 70–150 under each of the eight lobes, around 1,200 in all.

hotspots.label: Oral arms
hotspots.text: Beneath the bell, broad, frilly oral arms armed with stinging cells surround the mouth.

mind.lede: Without a brain, the lion's mane still hunts other jellies, and its prey reacts to the touch of its tentacles.

studies.title: A jellyfish that eats jellyfish
studies.text: In a Swedish fjord, lion's manes caught moon jellies, and larger lion's manes caught more of them. One moon jelly took about 38 hours to digest.

studies.title: The prey fights back
studies.text: Moon jellies that brushed a lion's mane pulled in their tentacles and pulsed 46% faster, rising away from the predator.

studies.title: Shoals
studies.text: Unusually for jellyfish, lion's manes sometimes gather in shoals up to a kilometre long.

survival.lede: A big lion's mane has little to fear, except one animal that seeks it out: the leatherback turtle.

tactics.title: A wall of stings
tactics.text: More than a thousand tentacles, each armed with stinging cells, stun prey and deter most attackers.

tactics.title: Size
tactics.text: Adults have very few natural predators because of their size, but juveniles are eaten by seabirds and larger fish such as ocean sunfish.

tactics.title: Turtle food
tactics.text: Cameras on leatherback turtles off Nova Scotia showed lion's manes made up 83–100% of their prey. Each turtle ate about 261 jellyfish a day on average.

threats.title: No major known threats
threats.text: The species is not known to face any major threats, though its population has never been assessed.

threats.title: Warming seas
threats.text: During periods of warming, some individuals may drift outside their usual range.

life.lede: The giant medusa is only one part of a life that alternates between a free-swimming bell and a tiny polyp fixed to the seabed.

stages.name: Egg and larva
stages.text: Medusae reproduce sexually. The female carries her fertilised eggs in her tentacles.

stages.name: Polyp
stages.text: The larvae settle and grow into small polyps, which multiply asexually.

stages.name: Ephyra
stages.text: Each polyp buds off a stack of tiny, immature medusae called ephyrae, which break away and swim off.

stages.name: Medusa
stages.text: The ephyrae grow into adult medusae, which are seen most often in late summer and autumn.

lifespan.value: About a year for the four stages

tagline: The fastest bat ever measured, from the largest bat colonies on Earth
summary: Also called the Brazilian free-tailed bat, this small, narrow-winged bat roosts in caves and under bridges in colonies that can number in the millions. At dusk the colonies pour out in dark ribbons, climbing to hunt moths and other insects in open sky. Radio-tracked from an aeroplane, individual bats reached ground speeds of 160 km/h.

stats.size: Wingspan about 28 cm; adults weigh roughly 7–13 g
stats.habitat: Caves, mines, bridges and buildings; hunts high over desert, scrub and farmland
stats.range: Southern United States and Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to south-western South America, including Brazil, Chile and Argentina
stats.diet: Flying insects, mainly moths and beetles, plus flies, true bugs and others

facts.title: 160 km/h, tracked from the air
facts.text: Seven bats from Frio Cave, Texas, were fitted with radio tags and followed at night by a light aircraft. All of them exceeded ground speeds of 25 m/s, and their individual top speeds ranged from 27.2 to 44.5 m/s (160 km/h), the fastest ever documented for a bat.

facts.title: Flap, pause, glide
facts.text: The faster the bats flew, the more often they paused between wingbeats. The researchers suggest that this flap-gliding helps the bats reach their high speeds.

facts.title: Built like a swift
facts.text: Free-tailed bats have long, narrow wings and high wing loading, like swifts. They hunt insects in open airspace well above the ground rather than among trees.

facts.title: The largest bat colony in the world
facts.text: Bracken Cave, near San Antonio in Texas, holds up to 20 million Mexican free-tailed bats in summer, the largest bat colony in the world. Bat Conservation International bought the cave in 1992 to protect it.

facts.title: Carlsbad's evening flight
facts.text: Each bat weighs about 13 g, about as much as three nickel coins, and has a wingspan of about 28 cm. The resident colony in Carlsbad Cavern, New Mexico, was about 400,000 in summer 2005, and counts during spring and autumn migration reached 793,000.

facts.title: Hunting high and far
facts.text: Free-tailed bats have been recorded flying above 3,300 m, the highest flight altitude recorded for any bat. A bat may travel 25 km or more to forage in an evening, and some have been recorded up to 65 km from their roost.

notes: IUCN Least Concern per Barquez et al. (2015), e.T21314A22121621. iucnredlist.org, gbif.org and doi.org/royalsocietypublishing.org return 403 to automated requests. The category and IUCN taxon ID were confirmed via the GBIF API (iucnRedListCategory: LC, iucnTaxonID 21314) and the assessment DOI 10.2305/IUCN.UK.2015-4.RLTS.T21314A22121621.en, which redirects to the cited page. McCracken et al. (2016) was read in full via Europe PMC (PMC5180116). Speeds are ground speeds: the authors modelled the wind but did not convert every value to airspeed, and they removed one 60.1 m/s outlier. Mass: NPS gives about 13 g (½ oz); ADW gives 7–12 g, varying with season and age. Wingspan 28 cm from both. The 3,300 m altitude and 25 km / 65 km foraging distances are from ADW, which does not give primary sources inline. The Bracken Cave figure is BCI's 'up to 20 million'. Other sources quote 15–20 million, and colony counts are estimates. Regions: north-american-deserts first (Carlsbad Caverns, the Chihuahuan Desert); central-america and andes-patagonia because ADW and IUCN place the range through Central America to south-western South America (Chile, Argentina). The migrations shelf is justified because northern populations migrate seasonally (ADW; NPS notes spring and autumn migration counts at Carlsbad). Images: all USFWS (Ann Froschauer), public domain as US federal government works. alt-2's Commons date (18 Sept 2012) matches the Bracken Cave emergence series, but the file itself does not name the location, so the 'Bracken Cave' in its caption is an inference from that same-day series. alt-2 shows a bat being handled (setting 'in hand'). A Carlsbad outflight photo by Nick Hristov was considered and rejected because its public-domain status rests only on NPS hosting.

anatomy.lede: A bat built for open sky: long narrow wings, a tail that sticks out beyond its membrane, and a body that weighs about as much as three coins.

hotspots.label: Broad ear
hotspots.text: The ears are large for the bat's size, 8–15 mm long, and broad.

hotspots.label: Ear
hotspots.text: Echolocation is its main sense for finding its way and catching insects in the dark.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Sight still matters: bats recognise one another by visual, chemical and vocal cues as well as by echolocation.

hotspots.label: Short snout
hotspots.text: A short, pug-like snout is one of the features that identify the species.

hotspots.label: Wrinkled lips
hotspots.text: The upper lips are deeply wrinkled, typical of free-tailed bats.

hotspots.label: Folded wing
hotspots.text: Folded here, the long, narrow, pointed wings are made for rapid, direct flight in open air.

senses.lede: Free-tailed bats find their prey by sound, and their pups by sound and smell.

senses.name: Echolocation
senses.text: Cruising bats give brief calls at a nearly constant frequency, usually between 49 and 70 kHz. When they detect food or an obstacle they switch to sweeping calls from about 75 down to 40 kHz.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Pups learn their mother's scent early in life, and mothers use their pups' smell and calls to find them in the crowded crèche.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Beyond echoes, the bats listen to a rich vocal repertoire, including complex songs sung by males.

body.lede: A small bat with a high-performance body, fuelled by milk richer than that of any other bat.

systems.title: Rich milk
systems.text: Mothers produce milk with over 28% fat, the highest recorded for any bat, which lets the pups grow quickly.

systems.title: Torpor
systems.text: Like other bats of temperate regions, it can let its body temperature drop into daily torpor to save energy, and it may hibernate.

systems.title: Climbing legs
systems.text: Its legs are powerful, and it climbs well.

genome.lede: A chromosome-level genome assembly of the species was released in 2023, about 2.3 billion letters long.

mind.lede: Life in colonies of millions has produced some unusual behaviour, from sonar sabotage to song.

studies.title: Jamming the competition
studies.text: Field recordings showed that bats chasing the same insect emit a special call that interferes with a rival's echolocation. Played back, the jamming call made bats miss their targets.

studies.title: Not quite indiscriminate nursing
studies.text: Genetic tests on nursing pairs in Texas showed that mothers mostly nurse their own or related pups, not any pup at random. Even so, about 17% of females were feeding pups that could not be theirs.

studies.title: Songs with syntax
studies.text: Males sing songs built from the same four syllable types and three phrase types, ordered by shared rules, yet each bat varies its song from one rendition to the next.

survival.lede: Owls, hawks and snakes all take free-tailed bats, but against a population in the tens of millions their toll is very small.

tactics.title: Safety in numbers
tactics.text: With a total population of around 100 million, the number of bats lost to predators is very low.

tactics.title: Fast and high
tactics.text: Quick, straight flight takes them far from the roost, often 25 km or more, to forage high in the open air.

threats.title: Roosts and pesticides
threats.text: Populations have fallen over the past century, probably through the disturbance and destruction of roosts and indirect poisoning by pesticides in the insects they eat.

life.lede: Mothers leave their pups in vast nurseries, returning to find and feed their own.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: Males call and scent-mark territories to attract females. Females have a single oestrous cycle each spring.

stages.name: Birth
stages.text: A single pup is born while its mother hangs upside down; the birth takes about 90 seconds, and the newborn finds a nipple within 10–15 minutes.

stages.name: Crèche
stages.text: Pups are left in dense clusters while their mothers feed, and are nursed daily until they reach adult size and independence.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females can breed at nine months, males at about two years. Adults have a 70–80% chance of surviving each year.

lifespan.value: over 8 years in the wild; 12 in captivity

tagline: One octopus, many costumes
summary: A slender, long-armed octopus of tropical sand and silt flats that forages in daylight, in full view of predatory fish. Instead of just hiding, it reshapes its body and colours to impersonate other animals, including venomous ones, and appears to choose its disguise to suit the threat.

stats.size: About 60 cm long including arms
stats.depth: Mostly shallower than about 15 m
stats.range: Indo-West Pacific, from the Red Sea to New Caledonia and the Great Barrier Reef; most records from Indonesia
stats.diet: Small fishes, crabs and worms

facts.title: Found on film first
facts.text: Scientists filming in Sulawesi and Bali described it as an octopus new to science in 2001; its formal scientific name followed in 2005.

facts.title: Dynamic mimicry
facts.text: Nine individuals were seen switching between postures and colour patterns, several clearly impersonating venomous animals that share its habitat. Biologists call this shape-shifting repertoire 'dynamic mimicry'.

facts.title: A cast of characters
facts.text: Reported guises include a lionfish (arms fanned out like spines), a banded sea snake (two arms stretched out, the rest hidden) and a flat, banded sole gliding over the sand.

facts.title: Choosing the right disguise
facts.text: Observers suggest the octopus picks a model to fit the threat: one harassed by damselfish turned into a 'sea snake', a predator of damselfish. How deliberate this choice is remains under study.

facts.title: Mud, not reef
facts.text: Unlike most octopuses that shelter on reefs, it lives on open sand and silt, often near river mouths, jetting just above the bottom to search burrows for prey.

notes: Specific mimicry models (lionfish, sea snake, sole), size, depth, range and IUCN status come from Wikipedia, which cites Norman & Hochberg 2005, Hanlon et al. 2008 and IUCN (Allcock 2019); the primary papers and IUCN site could not be fetched (403/JS). The 'choice of disguise' fact is framed as a hypothesis, as in Norman et al. 2001 ('our observations suggest'). Close relative Wunderpus photogenicus looks similar; the chosen photo is labelled T. mimicus by the photographer.

anatomy.lede: Long, thin arms and a boldly banded skin are the raw materials of the mimic octopus's disguises. The features that tell it apart from other octopuses are small details of pattern and sucker.

hotspots.label: Eye horns
hotspots.text: A small horn sticks up above each eye, which sits high on the head.

hotspots.label: Mantle markings
hotspots.text: Distinctive base markings include a white teardrop-shaped ring in the middle of the back and a white 'U' patch towards the rear of the mantle.

hotspots.label: Arms
hotspots.text: The arms are long and narrow, and can be shed at a set point near the base, an escape trick known as autotomy.

hotspots.label: Bands
hotspots.text: The high-contrast brown-and-white bands may copy a toxic sole, break up the animal's outline, or warn predators off.

hotspots.label: Suckers
hotspots.text: Unlike many octopuses, neither males nor females have any enlarged suckers.

mind.lede: Field studies are trying to separate the mimic octopus's legend from what it actually does, and why.

studies.title: Mimicry when moving
studies.text: Divers filmed mimic octopuses copying the shape, swimming style, speed and sometimes colour of local flounders, but only while moving across open sand, where movement would give away their camouflage.

studies.title: Hunting by touch
studies.text: Octopuses foraged twice a day, using two feeling-and-probing tactics to find hidden prey in the sand.

studies.title: Where flatfish swimming came from
studies.text: A family-tree study found that flatfish-style swimming appeared alongside very long arms in a group of sand-dwelling octopuses. The bold colours may have been added later.

studies.title: The mimic gets mimicked
studies.text: Video from Indonesia showed a black-marble jawfish, coloured like the octopus's arms, swimming close beside a mimic octopus, probably to forage safely away from its burrow.

survival.lede: Foraging by day on open sand, with nowhere to hide, the mimic octopus defends itself mainly by not looking like an octopus.

tactics.title: Still: a sponge
tactics.text: When motionless it takes on shapes and patterns resembling small sponges, tube-worm tubes or sea squirts, among the few objects on the open sand.

tactics.title: Moving: a flatfish
tactics.text: When it must travel, it switches to flounder mimicry as its first line of defence.

tactics.title: Plan B
tactics.text: When fishes and mantis shrimps actually confronted it, the octopus used ordinary octopus defences rather than mimicry.

tactics.title: Dropping an arm
tactics.text: Its arms can break off at a set point near the base, which may let it escape a predator's grip.

tagline: A butterfly weighing under a gram that flies up to 4,800 km to a mountain forest
summary: Every autumn, monarchs from across eastern North America fly south to a handful of fir-clad mountains in central Mexico, while those west of the Rockies head for the California coast. The butterflies that make the journey have never been there before. They steer by a sun compass timed by clocks in their antennae, and their descendants take three or four generations to get back north.

stats.size: Adults weigh less than a gram; caterpillars grow to about 5 cm
stats.habitat: Open fields, meadows and roadsides with milkweed; winters in mountain fir forest in Mexico and coastal groves in California
stats.range: Breeds across the United States and southern Canada; eastern monarchs winter in central Mexico, western monarchs on the California coast
stats.diet: Caterpillars eat only milkweed; adults drink nectar from flowers
stats.conservation: IUCN Red List: species Least Concern; the migratory subspecies was listed Endangered in 2022 and moved to Vulnerable in December 2023

facts.title: Up to 4,800 km to a winter home
facts.text: Some monarchs fly as far as 3,000 miles (about 4,800 km) to reach their wintering grounds, travelling 50–100 miles (80–160 km) a day. The journey can take up to two months.

facts.title: A mountain forest of butterflies
facts.text: Eastern monarchs spend the winter in 11 to 12 mountain areas in the Mexican states of Mexico and Michoacán, clustering in oyamel fir forests between 2,400 and 3,600 m. Western monarchs roost in eucalyptus, Monterey pine and Monterey cypress groves on the California coast.

facts.title: Two weeks, or nine months
facts.text: In summer, adult monarchs live for 2 to 5 weeks. The generation that migrates south can live as long as 9 months. On the way back north, it takes 3 to 4 generations to repopulate the northern United States and Canada.

facts.title: Clocks in the antennae
facts.text: Migrating monarchs steer with a time-compensated sun compass. Experiments showed that the antennae are needed for this compass to work and that they contain their own circadian clocks, which probably provide its main timing signal.

facts.title: A magnetic back-up
facts.text: In flight-simulator tests, autumn migrants also used an inclination magnetic compass to head towards the equator. It works only in ultraviolet-A or blue light (380–420 nm), and the light-sensitive magnetic sensors appear to sit in the antennae.

facts.title: Endangered, then Vulnerable
facts.text: The IUCN listed the migratory monarch as Endangered in 2022, then moved it to Vulnerable from 11 December 2023. This change came after a petition questioned the population models used, not because monarch numbers had recovered.
