notes: IUCN status history: the species Danaus plexippus is Least Concern (Walker, Oberhauser, Pelton & Pleasants 2022, DOI 10.2305/IUCN.UK.2022-1.RLTS.T159971A219149911.en; taxon ID 159971, confirmed via the GBIF IUCN checklist because iucnredlist.org returns 403 to scripts). The migratory subspecies D. p. plexippus was listed Endangered in the July 2022 Red List update (press coverage, July 21, 2022; the Monarch Joint Venture post dates the assessment 30 December 2021). After a petition, the IUCN Standards and Petitions Committee announced on 27 September 2023 that it would downlist it to Vulnerable, effective 11 December 2023 (Monarch Joint Venture). The species is therefore not shelved under 'endangered'. US Endangered Species Act: USFWS proposed listing as Threatened in December 2024; secondary sources say the final rule was moved to 'long-term actions' and a lawsuit over the delay was filed in February 2026. I found no final rule, but this was not checked against the Federal Register, so it is left out of the facts. Science (doi.org/10.1126/science.1176221) returns 403 to scripts; the abstract and metadata were read via Europe PMC. Regions: north-american-forests first. The western population breeds through the Rockies and the interior West, and eastern monarchs breed and migrate through the Dakotas/Prairies edge of the polygon. north-american-deserts is included because Xerces Society sources describe breeding habitat in Arizona and western Nevada, and monarch breeding at Great Basin milkweed sites. The Mexican overwintering sanctuaries (Michoacán/State of Mexico, around 19.2–19.7 N, 100 W) fall outside every mapped polygon (central-america starts at about 97 W), so they are described in the text, not mapped. Most of the eastern breeding range (east of about 95 W) is unmapped. Introduced/vagrant populations (Australia, New Zealand, Pacific islands, Iberia) are not mapped. Biome: temperate-forest, following the first region and the oyamel fir winter forest; much summer breeding is in open grassland/fields. Mass (under a gram) and caterpillar length (about 5 cm) are from USFS. That adults drink nectar is general knowledge and not in the cited USFS text. The USFS biology page gives the migration as 2,000–3,000 miles, and the migration page as 'as far as 3,000 miles'. Images: hero and alt-1 by Charles J. Sharp at Piedra Herrada (State of Mexico, February 2023; the hero is a Commons Featured Picture). alt-2 is a Featured Picture of a male in Brooklyn Botanic Garden (August 2025, geotagged). Its flower is a Tithonia, described in the caption as a Mexican sunflower.

anatomy.lede: Less than a gram of butterfly, carrying a sun compass, a magnetic compass and a dose of plant poison across a continent.

hotspots.label: Antennae
hotspots.text: The antennae house circadian clocks that time the sun compass, and appear to contain light-sensitive magnetic sensors.

hotspots.label: Compound eye
hotspots.text: Photoreceptors in the topmost row of the eye are arranged to detect the polarisation of skylight, one of the cues the sun compass uses.

hotspots.label: Thorax
hotspots.text: The black, white-spotted thorax holds the flight muscles. Genes for muscle function show the strongest signs of selection linked to migration.

hotspots.label: Orange forewing
hotspots.text: Bright orange is a warning to predators that the butterfly is poisonous. Variation in this colouring is controlled by a single myosin gene.

hotspots.label: Black veins
hotspots.text: Females have thicker black veins than males. Males can also be recognised by a small swollen pouch on each hindwing.

hotspots.label: Spotted border
hotspots.text: Black borders with white spots frame the wings in both sexes.

senses.lede: Getting to a few mountain forests in Mexico from as far away as Canada takes more than one way of finding direction.

senses.name: Sun and polarised light
senses.text: In outdoor flight simulators, turning a polarising filter above migrating monarchs changed their flight direction in a predictable way, showing that the angle of polarised skylight feeds into their sun compass.

senses.name: Magnetic sense
senses.text: An inclination compass, which senses the angle of the Earth's magnetic field rather than its polarity, may guide migrants when the sun is hidden and fine-tune the sun compass on clear days.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: The monarch genome contains monarch-specific expansions of chemoreceptor genes, which may matter for long-distance migration.

body.lede: A monarch is poisonous because its caterpillar eats poisonous plants, and has evolved a body that can tolerate them.

systems.title: Borrowed poison
systems.text: Caterpillars take up cardiac glycosides from the milkweeds they eat and store them, which makes monarchs poisonous to vertebrate predators.

systems.title: A resistant sodium pump
systems.text: Cardiac glycosides attack the sodium pump in animal cells. Monarchs carry three amino-acid changes in this pump; when the same changes were edited into fruit flies, the flies became as insensitive to the toxins as monarchs.

systems.title: Delayed breeding
systems.text: The last generation of the year does not become reproductive. These butterflies migrate and overwinter in reproductive diapause, maturing only in February and March as they head north.

genome.lede: A draft monarch genome was published in 2011: 273 million letters of DNA containing 16,866 protein-coding genes.

findings.title: Clock and compass genes
findings.text: The genome revealed a complete set of molecular parts for the monarch's circadian clock, a vertebrate-like opsin, and microRNAs that differ between summer and migratory butterflies.

findings.title: Born to migrate
findings.text: Sequencing 101 Danaus genomes from around the world showed that the monarch was ancestrally migratory and spread out of North America to its present worldwide range.

findings.title: Efficient flight muscles
findings.text: Migratory monarchs carry a distinctive form of the collagen IV α-1 gene, used in flight muscle, and fly more efficiently than non-migratory populations.

mind.lede: Much of what is known about monarch navigation comes from tethering butterflies in flight simulators and seeing which way they try to fly.

studies.title: Reading the sky
studies.text: Butterflies tested in the morning or the afternoon responded in the same way to a rotated polarising filter, suggesting that polarised light helps them stay on course even under varied skies.

studies.title: A compass for cloudy days
studies.text: In flight-simulator tests, migrants oriented towards the equator using an inclination magnetic compass, but only in ultraviolet-A or blue light between 380 and 420 nm, a detail earlier studies had overlooked.

studies.title: Courtship in two acts
studies.text: Courtship has an aerial phase, in which the male chases, nudges and brings down the female, and a ground phase, in which they mate. Monarchs rely less on chemical signals than their relatives.

survival.lede: Warning colours and stored poison deter most predators, but a few birds have learned to get around them.

tactics.title: Advertised poison
tactics.text: The orange and black pattern warns predators that the butterfly is distasteful, a defence built on toxins carried over from caterpillar to adult.

tactics.title: Safety in the middle
tactics.text: In wintering colonies, monarchs on the edges and in thinned patches of forest are at much greater risk from birds, which may explain why they gather in dense clusters.

threats.title: Bird predation in winter
threats.text: In one 2.25-hectare colony in Mexico, orioles and grosbeaks killed an average of about 15,000 monarchs a day, around 9% of the colony over the winter. They took more males, perhaps because of their fat or because females carry more toxin.

threats.title: Wintering forests
threats.text: The migration itself has been called a threatened phenomenon. In California, introduced eucalyptus trees now hold most wintering sites, standing in for native trees reduced by logging.

life.lede: The monarch goes through complete metamorphosis — egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult — several times over in a single summer.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Females lay their eggs on milkweed plants, the caterpillars' only food.

stages.name: Caterpillar
stages.duration: egg and caterpillar together about 2 weeks
stages.text: The caterpillar grows by shedding its skin several times. How fast it develops depends on temperature.

stages.name: Chrysalis
stages.text: The caterpillar stops growing and forms a case around itself. Inside, its body is rebuilt into a butterfly.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Summer adults live a few weeks, mating and laying eggs for the next generation. The late-season generation migrates and can live for as long as nine months.

lifespan.value: 2–5 weeks in summer; up to 9 months for the migratory generation

tagline: A swimming millstone that dives for jellies
summary: One of the heaviest bony fishes on Earth: a huge, flattened disc with towering fins and no proper tail, able to top 2.5 tonnes. Once thought to be a lazy drifter, it is an active swimmer that dives hundreds of metres to hunt jellies and siphonophores, then returns toward the surface.
ability: wing-like fin flapping and deep dives

stats.size: Up to about 3.3 m long and 4.2 m tall fin-to-fin; over 2.5 tonnes
stats.depth: Mostly the top 200 m; dives beyond 800 m, possibly 1,000 m
stats.range: Tropical and temperate oceans worldwide
stats.diet: Jellyfish, siphonophores, salps and comb jellies; also small crustaceans, squids and fishes

facts.title: A fish without a tail
facts.text: Instead of a tail fin it has a clavus—Latin for 'rudder'—a stiff lobe formed from extensions of the dorsal and anal fins. Its name Mola is Latin for millstone, after its round shape.

facts.title: Flying underwater
facts.text: It swims by flapping its tall dorsal and anal fins in unison, like a pair of wings. This is thought to be an efficient stroke that lets it dive repeatedly to great depths.

facts.title: Not just a lazy drifter
facts.text: Tagged sunfish in the north-west Atlantic spent over 80% of their time in the top 200 m but dived as deep as 844 m, making regular forays to feed on deep-water siphonophores and jellies.

facts.title: Why bask at the surface?
facts.text: Sunfish are often seen lying flat at the surface. One idea is that they warm up after cold dives; but a tagging study found no link between cold-water time and surface time, so the reason remains debated.

facts.title: 300 million eggs
facts.text: A single adult female can produce up to 300 million tiny, buoyant eggs, yet sunfish larvae are rarely collected.

Commons lists the file under both PD-USGov-NOAA and CC BY 2.0 (NOAA Flickr); public domain recorded. Divers appear in the frame (gives scale). 'Heaviest bony fish' is avoided: the sources call M. mola the heaviest/largest bony fish, but the heaviest recorded individual (Azores, 2021) has been reported as Mola alexandrini (from memory of Sawai et al. 2022; not re-verified in this session)—worded as 'one of the heaviest'. Fact refs: 'not a lazy drifter' combines the Potter & Howell (2010) tagging figures quoted by the Australian Museum with Fishes of Australia's note on siphonophore-feeding dives. Depth gauge max uses the 844 m tagging record; Fishes of Australia mentions records beyond 1,000 m. 'Reproduction' category based on extreme fecundity.

anatomy.lede: A sunfish is a fish that seems to have stopped halfway: a deep, flattened body ending abruptly in a stiff rudder, driven by two tall fins that work like a pair of wings.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: The tall dorsal fin and the anal fin below it are a matched pair, with the same shape, the same area and the same mass of swimming muscle.

hotspots.label: Pectoral fin
hotspots.text: The small, rounded pectoral fin behind the head is supported by just 11–13 fin rays.

hotspots.label: Skin
hotspots.text: There are no scales. The skin is covered in tiny denticles and mucus, feels as rough as sandpaper and can be up to 7.3 cm thick on the belly.

hotspots.label: Clavus
hotspots.text: The rudder-like clavus is supported by about 12 fin rays, 8–9 of which carry small bony knobs called ossicles.

hotspots.label: Anal fin
hotspots.text: Tags show the dorsal and anal fins beating together, about 0.3–0.6 times a second, to give lift-based thrust, much as a penguin uses its flippers.

body.lede: Inside, the sunfish is built light: a skeleton largely of cartilage, no swim bladder, and a thick layer of jelly that keeps it afloat at any depth.

systems.title: Floating without a swim bladder
systems.text: Sunfish have no swim bladder, yet they are neutrally buoyant at every depth. A thick, low-density gelatinous layer under the skin does not compress as the fish dives.

systems.title: A bony fish made of cartilage
systems.text: Although it belongs to the bony fishes, its skeleton is mostly cartilage. This lighter skeleton may help the giant fish stay buoyant.

systems.title: Warming up at the surface
systems.text: Body temperature drops during deep feeding dives and recovers at the surface. Heat-budget models suggest the fish gains heat 3–7 times faster than it loses it, perhaps by controlling blood flow.

systems.title: A beak for jellies
systems.text: The teeth in each jaw are fused into a single plate, and the mouth is small compared with the huge body.

genome.lede: In 2016 the sunfish genome was sequenced and compared with those of other bony fishes, including its relative the pufferfish, to look for the genetic roots of its size, speed of growth and missing tail.

findings.title: Genes for growing big
findings.text: Several genes in the growth hormone and IGF-1 signalling pathway show signs of positive selection or fast evolution. This may help explain the sunfish's rapid growth and huge size.

findings.title: Cartilage genes under selection
findings.text: Several collagen genes involved in forming cartilage have evolved quickly in the sunfish, which may be linked to its largely cartilaginous skeleton.

findings.title: Losing the tail without losing a Hox gene
findings.text: Sunfish have the same seven Hox gene clusters as the tailed pufferfish, and even more Hox genes. Losing the tail fin was therefore not caused by losing a particular Hox gene.

mind.lede: Tags carrying accelerometers, thermometers and cameras have changed our picture of the sunfish, from a lazy drifter to a diving forager working to a daily routine.

studies.title: A swimmer, not a drifter
studies.text: Multi-sensor tags showed sunfish swimming continuously and diving often, at speeds similar to salmon, marlin and open-ocean sharks.

studies.title: Cameras on the hunt
studies.text: Animal-borne cameras filmed sunfish catching prey. Siphonophores were the commonest prey, taken mostly at 100–200 m during the day, in water below 12 °C.

studies.title: Dive, then warm up
studies.text: Body temperature fell during deep dives and rose again at the surface, suggesting that basking at the surface lets sunfish rewarm and so feed longer in cold water. Not all tagging studies agree.

studies.title: Visiting the cleaners
studies.text: Sunfish carry more than 40 kinds of parasites. They are reported to visit cleaner fish around drifting kelp and to let seabirds pick at their skin while lying at the surface.

survival.lede: Sheer size protects an adult sunfish from most hunters, but the young are bite-sized, and people now pose the greatest risk.

tactics.title: Too big to tackle
tactics.text: Adults have few natural predators, though sea lions, orcas and sharks will eat them.

tactics.title: Safety in numbers
tactics.text: Young sunfish swim in schools for protection, a habit they give up as they grow.

threats.title: Bycatch
threats.text: Sunfish are often caught in huge numbers by accident in gillnet, driftnet, longline and midwater trawl fisheries, which are largely unregulated for this species.

threats.title: A declining population
threats.text: The IUCN lists the ocean sunfish as Vulnerable, with drift gillnets its main threat.

threats.title: Ships and plastic
threats.text: Sunfish are sometimes struck by ships. Floating debris such as plastic bags may also be a threat.

life.lede: No vertebrate starts smaller and ends bigger. A sunfish begins as one of hundreds of millions of tiny drifting eggs and passes through a spiny, pufferfish-like stage before it loses its tail.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Eggs and sperm are released into the open sea, where the tiny, buoyant eggs are fertilised and drift.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: A newly hatched larva is only about 2.5 mm long and weighs less than a gram.

stages.name: Spiny fry
stages.text: The young first look like miniature pufferfish, with large pectoral fins, a tail fin and body spines.

stages.name: Transformation
stages.text: In a second, highly transformed stage the tail is completely absorbed and the clavus takes its place.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Survivors may grow to up to 60 million times their hatching weight. How fast wild sunfish grow is still not known.

lifespan.value: Unknown in the wild; up to about 10 years in captivity

tagline: The ocean's top predator, with family dialects and hunting traditions
summary: The largest member of the dolphin family and the most widely distributed whale or dolphin, found in every ocean. Orcas live in tight family groups led by older females, and each population has its own learned calls and hunting methods, from chasing salmon to washing seals off ice floes.
ability: cooperative hunting techniques passed down through families

stats.size: Up to about 9.8 m and 10 tonnes; adult males are larger than females
stats.depth: Often shallow; a tagged whale dived to 1,087 m
stats.range: Every ocean, from polar seas to the tropics; most abundant in cold waters such as the Antarctic, North Atlantic and North Pacific
stats.diet: The most varied of any cetacean, including fish, squid, seals and other whales; each population specialises
stats.conservation: IUCN: Data Deficient (2017); some populations, such as the Southern Residents, are endangered

facts.title: The biggest dolphin
facts.text: Despite its name, the killer whale is the largest member of the dolphin family, Delphinidae. It is found in every ocean, making it the most widely distributed of all whales and dolphins.

facts.title: Diet by tradition
facts.text: Neighbouring populations can eat completely different food. Off the US Pacific Northwest, 'Resident' killer whales eat only fish, mainly salmon, while 'Bigg's' (transient) killer whales hunt mainly marine mammals. NOAA attributes this mostly to culture: learned hunting tactics.

facts.title: Family dialects
facts.text: Among 16 pods of Resident killer whales off British Columbia, each pod used 7–17 types of call. Calls are learned, can stay almost unchanged for more than 25 years, and group the pods into four clans with no calls in common.

facts.title: Making waves
facts.text: Pack-ice killer whales off the Antarctic Peninsula swim side by side towards an ice floe to raise a wave that washes a seal into the water. They took 12 of 14 seal kills this way, choosing Weddell seals almost every time.

facts.title: A dive for stolen fish
facts.text: A satellite-tagged killer whale taking toothfish from fishing lines off South Georgia dived to 1,087 m. After each very deep dive it spent hours making only shallow dives.

facts.title: Long-lived grandmothers
facts.text: Females typically live about 50 years in the wild, but some reach at least 90. Killer whales are among the few animals known to go through menopause.

notes: Slug 'orca'; common name given as 'Orca (Killer Whale)' since NOAA, IUCN and most sources use 'killer whale'. Taxonomy and AphiaID from the WoRMS REST API. IUCN: Data Deficient (Reeves, Pitman & Ford 2017), confirmed via Crossref, GBIF's IUCN category and the IUCN SSC Cetacean Specialist Group status page; several ecotypes may be separate species or subspecies, and the Strait of Gibraltar subpopulation is assessed separately. NOAA gives 32 ft and 11 tons (US), converted to about 9.8 m and 10 tonnes. Depth: the 1,087 m record (Towers et al., published online 2018, in print 2019) was made while the whale was depredating longlines; the paper notes each deep dive was followed by 3.9–4.6 h of shallow (<100 m) diving; no general depth-use figure was sourced. Not shelved as a 'giant'. Pitman & Durban (2012) was published online in 2011. A striking NOAA photo of three killer whales (anim1102) was not used because its Commons record has no description or location.

anatomy.lede: The orca's black-and-white pattern is one of the most recognisable in the sea. Its markings, fins and flippers also show differences between individuals and between the sexes.

hotspots.label: Head
hotspots.text: Hunting killer whales scan for prey with very broadband echolocation clicks, mostly centred between 45 and 80 kHz.

hotspots.label: Eye patch
hotspots.text: A white patch sits just above and behind each eye. Like all the markings, its shape varies between individuals and populations.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: Adult males grow much taller dorsal fins than females, along with larger flippers and flukes and a thicker body.

hotspots.label: Saddle patch
hotspots.text: A grey or white 'saddle' lies just behind the dorsal fin. Natural markings like these let researchers recognise individual whales and their pods.

hotspots.label: White underside
hotspots.text: Killer whales are mostly black on top and white underneath, a pattern seen here as this whale clears the water.

hotspots.label: Pectoral flipper
hotspots.text: The second whale shows a broad, paddle-like flipper. Adult males develop disproportionately large flippers.

senses.lede: Killer whales rely on underwater sound to feed, communicate and navigate. Different populations use their voices in very different ways.

senses.name: Echolocation
senses.text: Fish-eating Resident killer whales hunting along cliffs off Vancouver Island produced clicks of 195–224 dB (re 1 µPa). A model suggests a chinook salmon's echo would still be clearly audible at about 100 m.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Noise from vessels, industry and military activity interferes with their use of sound for feeding, communication and orientation. Southern Residents call louder near noisy boats, which costs them energy.

senses.name: Family calls
senses.text: Besides clicks and whistles, killer whales make pulsed calls that are learned and passed on within each population. NOAA describes them as 'family badges' that help hold groups together.

body.lede: A long life at the top of the food chain brings particular strains: polluted blubber, cold skin and the physical cost of deep dives.

systems.title: Blubber that stores pollutants
systems.text: Because they live long, eat at the top of the food web and carry a lot of blubber, killer whales build up unusually high levels of contaminants. These can harm their immune, nutritional and reproductive systems.

systems.title: Trips to warm water for the skin?
systems.text: Tagged Antarctic killer whales made fast, non-stop trips to subtropical waters off Uruguay and Brazil, one covering about 9,400 km in 42 days. The authors suggest the warmer water lets them renew their skin without losing too much body heat.

systems.title: The price of deep dives
systems.text: A tagged killer whale dived beyond 750 m five times while taking fish from longlines, but each deep dive was followed by 3.9–4.6 hours of only shallow diving. This suggests such dives push it close to its physical limits.

genome.lede: Killer whale genomes help show how different ways of life, passed on by learning, can leave marks in DNA.

findings.title: Convergence, but rarely adaptive
findings.text: Comparing the killer whale, walrus and manatee genomes found that matching amino-acid changes are common across the genome. Few of them are linked to the shared features of a marine lifestyle.

findings.title: Culture shaping genes
findings.text: Killer whale ecotypes spread around the world in less than about 250,000 years. Their genetic differences line up with learned diets and habitats, which suggests culture has helped steer their evolution.

mind.lede: Long-term studies of known individuals have made killer whales a key example of animal culture.

studies.title: Pod dialects
studies.text: Each of 16 Resident pods off British Columbia had its own set of calls, and pods sharing calls formed four clans. Small changes in learned calls over generations probably produced each pod's dialect.

studies.title: Wave-washing and 'butchering'
studies.text: Pack-ice killer whales made 120 waves in 22 attacks on seals resting on ice floes, catching 75% of the Weddell seals they targeted. They also took the carcasses apart so carefully that the authors called it 'butchering'.

studies.title: Grandmothers lead the way
studies.text: Among Resident killer whales, females past breeding age led the group through salmon foraging grounds, especially in years when salmon were scarce. This supports the idea that older females pass on ecological knowledge.

survival.lede: As the ocean's top predator, an adult killer whale has no natural enemies. Its strength lies in its family group.

tactics.title: Hunting as a team
tactics.text: Killer whales often hunt cooperatively, working together like a pack of wolves to catch prey.

tactics.title: Specialised diets
tactics.text: Taken together, killer whales eat a wider range of food than any other whale or dolphin, but each population usually specialises in particular prey and learned hunting methods.

tactics.title: Close-knit pods
tactics.text: Most live in pods of maternally related whales, from a few to 20 or more individuals, and stay closely tied to their mother's group.

threats.title: Shortage of prey
threats.text: Overfishing and habitat loss have reduced food for some populations. This is a serious problem for Southern Residents, whose main prey, chinook salmon, is itself threatened.

threats.title: Oil spills
threats.text: After the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill in Alaska, the AT1 Transient group fell from 22 whales to 6.

threats.title: Disturbance and capture
threats.text: Near vessels, killer whales hunt less and travel more. Capture for aquariums no longer happens in the United States but still threatens killer whales elsewhere.

life.lede: Killer whales mature slowly and breed infrequently, and females can live for decades after they stop breeding.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: A single calf is born. There is no fixed calving season, so births can happen in any month.

stages.name: Calf
stages.text: Calves feed only on milk for at least a year and stay close to their mother for at least the first two years.

stages.name: Maturity
stages.text: Females become sexually mature between 10 and 13 years old.

stages.name: Breeding years
stages.text: In some populations females are estimated to give birth about every 5 years over a breeding life of around 25 years.

stages.name: After menopause
stages.text: Killer whales are one of the few species known to go through menopause. Older females go on leading their family groups.

lifespan.value: Females typically about 50 years (up to at least 90); males about 30 (up to at least 60)

tagline: A rainbow-coloured boxer with a spring-loaded punch
summary: This vividly coloured reef crustacean smashes snails and crabs with club-like forelimbs that strike faster than almost any other animal movement. Its eyes are among the most complex known — though, contrary to popular belief, that doesn't mean it sees colours better than we do.

stats.size: About 3–18 cm long
stats.depth: About 3–40 m
stats.range: Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to the Mariana Islands
stats.diet: Snails, crabs and other crustaceans, clams

facts.title: A punch with a spring
facts.text: A saddle-shaped spring in each striking limb stores energy, then releases it in a blow reaching 14–23 m/s with accelerations of 6,300–8,000 times gravity — one of the fastest feeding strikes known.

facts.title: Every strike hits twice
facts.text: The club moves so fast that it creates cavitation bubbles — pockets of vapour that collapse violently. Force sensors recorded a second peak from the collapsing bubbles a fraction of a millisecond after the impact itself.

facts.title: Up to 16 kinds of light sensors
facts.text: Mantis shrimp eyes contain between 12 and 16 types of photoreceptor (light-sensing cells), with about 12 devoted to colour, spanning ultraviolet to far red. Humans have four types.

facts.title: Myth: they see more colours
facts.text: Despite all those receptors, colour tests found mantis shrimps are surprisingly poor at telling similar colours apart — worse than humans. More receptors does not mean a richer palette.

facts.title: Colour by scanning?
facts.text: Researchers proposed that mantis shrimps recognise colours quickly by sweeping their eyes across a scene, rather than finely comparing them as we do. This idea is still being tested and debated.

anatomy.lede: The peacock mantis shrimp carries two hammers folded under its head and a pair of eyes unlike any other animal's.

hotspots.label: Compound eye
hotspots.text: The band across each eye is the mid-band. In two of its rows, small ultraviolet-sensitive cells respond to polarised ultraviolet light, set at right angles to each other.

hotspots.label: Eyestalk
hotspots.text: Each eye can swivel, tilt and roll on its stalk, largely independently of the other.

hotspots.label: Striking limb
hotspots.text: A saddle-shaped spring in the exoskeleton of this limb stores energy and then releases it in an extremely fast strike.

hotspots.label: Dactyl club
hotspots.text: The heel of the folded limb is the club, a mineral-packed hammer of crystalline hydroxyapatite and amorphous calcium phosphate and carbonate over a spiralling chitin framework.

stats.label: Peak impact force of one strike
Gap between impact and bubble-collapse force peaks

senses.lede: Mantis shrimp eyes do not just see colour; they read polarised light and move constantly to sample the scene.

senses.name: Narrow colour channels
senses.text: Some mantis shrimps have 12 photoreceptor types, each sampling a narrow band of wavelengths from deep ultraviolet to far red, 300 to 720 nanometres.

senses.name: Ultraviolet polarisation
senses.text: Recordings from single cells showed that this species has ultraviolet-sensitive receptors that respond to the angle of polarised light.

senses.name: Rolling eyes for contrast
senses.text: It rolls its eyes to line up particular receptors with the angle of polarised light, making an object stand out from its background. This was the first known case of an animal doing so.

body.lede: Hitting hard-shelled prey thousands of times takes a spring to power the blow and a hammer that does not shatter.

systems.title: A spring-loaded strike
systems.text: The strike is too fast for muscle alone. Energy is stored in a saddle-shaped spring and released all at once.

systems.title: Two blows in one
systems.text: On average, the force from collapsing cavitation bubbles is half the force of the impact itself, and sometimes up to 280% more.

systems.title: A hammer that resists cracking
systems.text: The club's layered mix of minerals and spiralling chitin fibres gives it several lines of defence against breaking under repeated high-energy blows.

genome.lede: Mantis shrimp genomes are giants, and only a first survey of this one exists.

findings.title: An enormous genome
findings.text: Survey sequencing estimated the genome at about 11,068 million base pairs, with high heterozygosity and roughly 83–86% repeated sequences across the three species studied.

findings.title: A missing mitochondrial gene
findings.text: Its mitochondrial genome is 16,110 base pairs long and lacks the ATP8 gene found in a related Odontodactylus species.

mind.lede: Lab studies of how the peacock mantis shrimp moves its eyes show a visual system that works unlike ours.

studies.title: Recognising rather than comparing
studies.text: Mantis shrimps did poorly at telling close wavelengths apart, so researchers proposed they recognise colours by scanning their eyes over a scene instead.

studies.title: Eyes that sometimes work together
studies.text: When tracking a moving scene, its two eyes were only weakly linked; when startled, the uncovered eye drove a covered one. How independent the eyes are depends on the task.

studies.title: No steadying for a rolling eye
studies.text: It steadies its gaze against sideways motion, but shows no response to keep the eye from rolling. The researchers suggest its motion-sensing brain circuits may be arranged in a circle to cope.

survival.lede: A burrow at the reef's edge and a punch that can break glass keep this small crustacean safe.

tactics.title: A U-shaped burrow
tactics.text: It digs U-shaped holes in loose sediment near the base of coral reefs, about 3 to 40 metres down.

tactics.title: Smashing its way in
tactics.text: It strikes a shell again and again until it reaches the soft tissue inside. The largest can break aquarium glass.

threats.title: Aquarium trade
threats.text: The peacock mantis shrimp is especially colourful and in demand among aquarium keepers.

tagline: The falcon that hunts by falling out of the sky
summary: A powerful, sharp-winged falcon that catches other birds in mid-air, often at the end of a steep, wing-folded dive called a stoop. Its top speed is famous but hard to pin down: radar has tracked wild stoops at up to 39 m/s (140 km/h), while models suggest a long vertical dive could go far faster. Wiped out across much of its range by DDT, it has since made one of conservation's great comebacks.

stats.size: 33–50 cm long with a wingspan of 78–122 cm; 0.4–1.5 kg
stats.habitat: Cliffs, crags, coasts and open country, and increasingly tall buildings in cities
stats.range: Breeds on every continent except Antarctica; northern populations migrate long distances
stats.diet: Mainly birds, from songbirds to pigeons and ducks, caught in the air
stats.conservation: IUCN Red List: Least Concern (2021 assessment)

facts.title: Clocked by radar: 39 m/s
facts.text: A tracking radar followed a peregrine through stoops lasting 40–110 seconds, at dive angles of 13–64° and losing 450–1,080 m of height. Average speeds were about 25 m/s, and the fastest 10-second stretches reached 31–39 m/s (up to about 140 km/h).

facts.title: Faster on paper
facts.text: Estimates of a peregrine's top diving speed run as high as 157 m/s, but none this high has ever been accurately measured. A physics model of 'ideal falcons' found that, given enough time, a vertical dive could reach 89–112 m/s. Whether real falcons ever go that fast remains to be shown.

facts.title: Cruising, not racing
facts.text: Radio-tracked migrating peregrines flapping in straight, level flight below about 100 m averaged an airspeed of just 43.7 km/h (about 12 m/s), the fastest 53.5 km/h. The researchers note that their top speeds are certainly higher, but that these are the speeds they normally travel at.

facts.title: A spiral attack
facts.text: A peregrine sees prey most sharply by turning its head about 40° to one side, but that slows it down. Wild peregrines watched through telescopes and a tracking device kept their heads straight and closed on prey along curved paths from up to 1,500 m away, a route that keeps the prey in their sharpest line of sight.

facts.title: Back from the brink
facts.text: The pesticide DDT left peregrine eggs thin-shelled and weak, and by the 1960s the falcon had vanished from the eastern United States. Captive breeding released more than 4,000 young birds, and in 1999 the species was removed from the US Endangered Species List.

facts.title: At home on skyscrapers
facts.text: Peregrines live and breed on every continent except Antarctica. What their homes have in common is good nesting habitat, and more and more of them now find it on the buildings of cities.

notes: signatureData: stoopSpeedMs 39 is the upper end of 'maximum speeds during 10-s intervals were between 31 and 39 m s-1' for the peregrine in Alerstam 1987 (abstract, via Crossref/OpenAlex; tracking radar, four stoops of a peregrine and a goshawk). I used this as the highest reputably measured stoop speed for a peregrine. Not used: the 389 km/h (108 m/s) and '200+ mph' figures from Ken Franklin's trained falcon diving with skydivers, which are not peer-reviewed. Also not used: a radar figure of about 51 m/s (114 mph) attributed to Peter & Kestenholz 1998 (Ornithologischer Beobachter), which I saw only quoted second-hand (Hedenström 1998 TREE, mailing lists) and could not read in the original; if confirmed, it would replace 39. A trained gyrfalcon (a different species) reached 52–58 m/s with optical tracking (Tucker, Cade & Tucker 1998, J Exp Biol 201: 2061). Ponitz et al. 2014 (PLoS ONE) measured only 22.5 m/s for a trained bird diving from a dam, so it is not used. levelSpeedMs 12.1 is the mean airspeed of 43.7 km/h for six radio-tracked migrating peregrines in level flapping flight (Cochran & Applegate 1986, Table 1; read from a scanned PDF of the original via the Wayback Machine copy of SORA). Their maximum was 53.5 km/h, their gliding airspeeds were 62–64 km/h, and the mean groundspeed was 48.8 km/h. The column headers were partly lost in OCR, so the airspeed/groundspeed columns were assigned from the text ('both the mean and the maximum peregrine airspeeds exceed those of the Merlin'). Chase speeds are higher, but I found no direct measurement: Mills et al. 2018 (PLoS Comput Biol) model a maximum sustained level speed of about 29 m/s. Fact 2 is marked 'hypothesis' because it is a model. Regions: the Peregrine Fund gives every continent except Antarctica; Animal Diversity Web notes tundra breeders in Alaska and Canada that migrate to Argentina and Chile (hence arctic-tundra and andes-patagonia). Biome 'mountain' was chosen for the cliff-nesting habit; the first region's own biome is temperate-forest. apex-predators: an aerial bird-hunter with few predators of its own. Sizes are from the Peregrine Fund. Images: the hero is an urban wild bird at Winchester (Flickr via Commons). alt-1 (Featured Picture) gives no location, so none is stated; 'La Cañada' in its file name is not explained. alt-2 is a Commons Featured Picture from Bavaria, described as 'approaching the nest'. The IUCN DOI resolves through the DOI handle API, and the IUCN ID and LC status were confirmed via GBIF's IUCN checklist. allaboutbirds.org returned 403 to scripted requests, so Cornell is not cited.

anatomy.lede: Seen from below, the peregrine is all purpose: long pointed wings, a compact barred body, a dark 'moustache' and eyes built to lock on to flying birds.

hotspots.label: Bill
hotspots.text: Peregrines usually kill with the bill, by severing the prey's neck vertebrae.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Peregrines have extraordinarily keen vision, able to spot small objects at great distances.

hotspots.label: Cheek stripe
hotspots.text: A black stripe runs down each cheek of the otherwise pale face.

hotspots.label: Barred underparts
hotspots.text: Adults are finely barred below. Females are typically 15–20% larger than males.

hotspots.label: Feet
hotspots.text: In a stoop the falcon closes its feet and uses them to knock prey out of the sky. Even as nestlings, peregrines have very large feet for their size.

hotspots.label: Pointed wing
hotspots.text: To stoop, the falcon folds these long wings and falls into a nose dive.

stats.label: How much heavier females are than males

senses.lede: A peregrine's world is mostly visual: it must find a bird far away, then keep it in sight at very high speed.

senses.name: Distant sight
senses.text: Peregrines have extraordinarily keen vision and hunt by spotting prey from high vantage points.

senses.name: Sideways sharp spot
senses.text: A peregrine's sharpest vision lies about 40° to one side of its head. Holding its head straight while diving, it curves its flight path to keep prey in that sharp spot.

body.lede: Speed is only part of the story. Peregrine bodies are also shaped by how they kill and how the two sexes share the work.

systems.title: Knock, then bite
systems.text: The falcon strikes prey with closed feet, often in mid-air, then kills it with a bite to the neck. Prey may be eaten in flight or stored for later.

systems.title: Bigger females
systems.text: Females are 15–20% larger and 40–50% heavier than males. Simulations suggest males are better at catching very agile prey in level flight, while females can carry up to 50% heavier loads.

systems.title: Bird-eating specialist
systems.text: Birds make up 77–99% of prey items, from starlings and pigeons to shorebirds and ducks; a few peregrines specialise in bats.

genome.lede: The peregrine was one of the first birds of prey to have its genome sequenced, alongside the saker falcon, in 2013.

findings.title: Fast-evolving genomes
findings.text: Comparing about 8,400 genes with those of chicken, turkey and zebra finch showed that falcon genomes have evolved rapidly across the board.

findings.title: Beaks and smell
findings.text: Falcons showed distinctive changes in genes linked to beak development and to smell, which the authors relate to their predatory lifestyle.

findings.title: Fused chromosomes
findings.text: Most birds have about 80 chromosomes, but the peregrine has 50. Chromosome painting shows that many small chromosomes have fused with larger ones in falcons.

mind.lede: Cameras and GPS loggers carried by falcons have shown that their attacks follow surprisingly precise rules.

studies.title: Steering like a missile
studies.text: Footage from falcon-mounted cameras and GPS showed that peregrines close on targets using the same guidance rule as most guided missiles: turning in proportion to how fast the line of sight to the target swings round.

studies.title: Why stoop?
studies.text: Computer simulations suggest a high, fast dive raises catch success against erratically dodging prey, because speed gives the falcon more force to manoeuvre. The best-performing settings matched what real peregrines do.

studies.title: Sky dances
studies.text: Courting pairs perform power dives, tight turns, high soaring and rolls, and gently grip each other's bills at the nest ledge.

survival.lede: Even a peregrine has enemies, especially when young, and its recovery from pesticides is one of conservation's great successes.

tactics.title: Height is an advantage
tactics.text: Peregrines usually hunt from a high perch, which gives them more height from which to begin a stoop.

tactics.title: Many ways to hunt
tactics.text: Besides diving, peregrines chase prey in level flight, sometimes hunt in pairs, and have been seen using ships as perches to hunt seabirds far out at sea.

threats.title: Pesticides still in use
threats.text: Organochlorine pesticides such as DDT and dieldrin thin eggshells. They are restricted in North America but not everywhere in Central and South America, where many peregrines spend the winter.

life.lede: Peregrines grow up fast: a chick can fly about six weeks after hatching.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays 2 to 6 eggs about two days apart. She does most of the incubating.

stages.name: Nestling
stages.text: Chicks are fed by their parents until they are fully feathered and fledge at five to six weeks old.

stages.name: Fledgling
stages.text: After fledging, young falcons stay near their parents while learning to hunt, becoming independent after about six weeks.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females first breed at 1 to 5 years old; males start later, at 2 to 8 years.

lifespan.value: Wild records of 16–20 years; 25 years in captivity

tagline: A shrimp that fires bubbles hot enough to glow
summary: A small shrimp with one enormous claw. When it snaps shut, it shoots out a water jet so fast that a vapour bubble forms and then collapses with a bang loud enough to stun prey — and, for an instant, a flash of light.

stats.size: Up to about 5.5 cm; most adults much smaller
stats.depth: Shallow coastal waters
stats.range: Western Atlantic from Cape Hatteras to Brazil, incl. the Gulf of Mexico, West Indies and Bermuda
stats.diet: Worms, small crustaceans and small fishes such as gobies

facts.title: The bang is a bubble
facts.text: High-speed filming with underwater microphones showed the snap's sound comes not from the claw halves hitting, but from the collapse of a cavitation bubble — a vapour cavity torn open by the fast water jet.

facts.title: A weapon made of water
facts.text: The claw snaps shut so quickly that it fires a jet of water fast enough to boil it into vapour at low pressure. The snap can stun or kill small prey animals.

facts.title: 'Shrimpoluminescence'
facts.text: As the bubble collapses it emits a brief flash of light, implying temperatures of at least 5,000 K inside — the first known case of an animal making light this way.

facts.title: One claw rules
facts.text: The snapping claw, which can be on either the left or right side, is half as long as the shrimp's body; the other claw is ordinary-sized.

facts.title: Living in pairs
facts.text: Bigclaw snapping shrimps mostly live as monogamous pairs, sheltering in crevices, burrows and reef holes in shallow water.

notes: Kept the brief's slug 'pistol-shrimp'; entry is Alpheus heterochaelis because both landmark cavitation papers (Versluis 2000, Lohse 2001) studied this species. Commons has no in-situ photo of it; hero is a fresh specimen on black (very wide 2.6:1 aspect — may crop tightly in full-screen frames). Searched other Alpheus spp. — only goby-partnership shots of other species or watermarked images. Depth: sources say only 'shallow water'; depthRange 0–10 m is an approximation for the gauge. No allowed category fits, so categories is empty.

anatomy.lede: A small shrimp built around one oversized weapon, with a helmet over its eyes to survive its own blasts.

hotspots.label: Snapper claw
hotspots.text: When this claw snaps shut it fires a water jet fast enough to tear open a cavitation bubble. The bubble's collapse makes the bang that stuns or kills prey.

hotspots.label: Small claw
hotspots.text: The other claw is ordinary-sized. Young shrimps start with two equal claws; one enlarges later, on either side.

hotspots.label: Orbital hood
hotspots.text: A clear, helmet-like extension of the shell covers the eyes. It damps the shock waves from snaps, protecting the shrimp's brain.

hotspots.label: Antennules
hotspots.text: These short feelers sense both chemicals and water movement. Rivals aim fast currents from their gills straight at them during encounters.

hotspots.label: Swimmerets
hotspots.text: Beating the swimmerets drives strong currents backwards, one of several kinds of current the shrimp makes when meeting others.

hotspots.label: Eggs
hotspots.text: This is a female with eggs. In females, a bigger snapper claw comes at a cost: fewer, smaller eggs.

senses.lede: Long thought to be half-blind under its hood, the bigclaw snapping shrimp turns out to see well and to read the water around it.

senses.name: Fast, clear sight
senses.text: Its compound eyes look out through a hood almost as transparent as seawater, resolve detail to about 8 degrees, and have at least two colour classes of photoreceptor.

senses.name: The fastest eyes in water
senses.text: Its eyes sample at least 160 times a second, the fastest yet measured in an aquatic animal, and work from late twilight to direct sunlight.

senses.name: Feeling the jet
senses.text: Hairs on the snapper claw sense the water jet of a rival. When researchers coated them with lacquer, shrimps that were hit retreated instead of approaching.

senses.name: Smelling the current
senses.text: Slow sideways currents from the gills most probably help the shrimp sample odours, and its antennules pick up both chemical and mechanical cues.

body.lede: The snap is a feat of engineering: a spring, a latch and the physics of a collapsing bubble.

systems.title: A spring-loaded claw
systems.text: The snapper claw works by a spring-and-latch mechanism. It develops gradually and starts snapping about a month after hatching, when the claw is only millimetres long.

systems.title: Body armour against blasts
systems.text: Shrimps whose orbital hoods were removed slowed down and lost motor control after shock waves; those with intact hoods did not. It is the first known biological armour that damps shock waves.

systems.title: A costly weapon
systems.text: In three snapping shrimp species, a bigger claw came with a smaller abdomen, suggesting the weapon is paid for with the rest of the body.

mind.lede: Snapping shrimps settle disputes with ritualised shots, water currents and signals rather than all-out fights.

studies.title: Aimed warning shots
studies.text: In staged encounters, a shrimp cocked its claw for about half a second, and over half its snaps were aimed at the rival, usually striking its snapper claw from under a centimetre away. Males held the cock longer and hit more often than females.

studies.title: Talking with water
studies.text: Shrimps fire fast, focused gill currents at an opponent's antennules. Dominant animals released more of these currents and more water jets than subordinates, so the currents may carry information about status.

studies.title: Big claws win partners
studies.text: In males, but not females, a larger snapper claw went with a better chance of being paired and with a relatively larger partner.

survival.lede: Small and soft-bodied, the shrimp relies on its bang and on a good hiding place.

tactics.title: The bang
tactics.text: The snap deters predators as well as stunning prey, and is also used in displays.

tactics.title: Hiding by day
tactics.text: It often hides in a crevice or hole during the day, among reefs, seagrass, salt marshes and mud.

tactics.title: Living in pairs
tactics.text: Most bigclaw snapping shrimps live as monogamous pairs, sharing a shelter.

life.lede: The bigclaw snapping shrimp races through its larval life and starts snapping while still tiny.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: The female is only receptive for a short time just after she moults.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Eggs hatch about four weeks after being laid.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: The larvae do not feed but live on their yolk, passing through three larval stages in about five days.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Reared from eggs, young shrimps began snapping about a month after hatching, as the spring mechanism in the claw gradually developed.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults mostly live as monogamous pairs, hiding in crevices and burrows in shallow water.

tagline: Not a jellyfish but a colony sailing under one float
summary: It looks like a jellyfish but is a siphonophore: a colony of genetically identical zooids that each do one job. A gas-filled float acts as a sail, while stinging tentacles trailing many metres below catch small fish and crustaceans. It goes wherever wind and currents take it.

stats.size: Float rises up to about 15 cm above the water; tentacles average about 10 m, up to about 30 m
stats.depth: Floats at the surface; tentacles hang below
stats.range: Mostly tropical and subtropical seas; sometimes drifts to the coasts of Britain and Ireland
stats.diet: Small crustaceans and larval fish

facts.title: A colony, not a jellyfish
facts.text: Each man o' war is a colony of zooids, genetically identical clones specialised for floating, catching prey, feeding or reproducing. None can survive on its own.

facts.title: A float that sails
facts.text: The gas-filled float, called the pneumatophore, has a crest along its top that works as a sail. With no way to swim, the colony goes where the wind and currents take it.

facts.title: Digestion outside the body
facts.text: Prey is paralysed by the tentacles' stinging cells and hauled up to feeding polyps called gastrozooids, which release digestive juices onto it.

facts.title: Dangerous even when stranded
facts.text: Stings cause severe pain and welts and are rarely deadly to people. A man o' war washed up on the beach can still sting weeks later.

facts.title: Fleets of a thousand
facts.text: Men o' war sometimes drift in groups of 1,000 or more. Mass strandings on British and Irish coasts are rare, historically only a few times a century.

notes: Hero is a stranded animal (setting 'specimen'). No sharp, correctly identified in-water float photo was found on Commons. A set of five 8688px Flickr images titled 'Physalia physalis' (48740683238 etc.) shows pale, colourless fragments on black that do not look like the man o' war float, so they were rejected as doubtful. Tentacle length differs between sources: NOAA says an average of 10 m and up to 30 m; MarLIN says 10–20 m when extended. WoRMS lists P. physalis as accepted. A Europe PMC search also turned up a 2024 genomics study titled 'Global genomics of the man-o'-war (Physalia) reveals biodiversity at the ocean surface'. It was not read here, but the editor may want to check it for possible species splits. depthRange shows the tentacle reach below the surface float.

anatomy.lede: What looks like one animal is a colony: a gas-filled float on top, and beneath it clusters of specialised zooids that feed, sting and breed.

hotspots.label: Float
hotspots.text: The pneumatophore is filled with carbon monoxide and air. Gas-making cells in a gas gland inside the float produce the carbon monoxide.

hotspots.label: Sail crest
hotspots.text: The crest along the top of the float works as a sail. Muscles around the float squeeze it to raise the pressure inside and stand the sail up.

hotspots.label: Feeding zooids
hotspots.text: Under the float hang the gastrozooids, feeding polyps that spread over caught prey and digest it. Upwards of 50 have been seen covering a single 10 cm fish.

hotspots.label: Tentacle
hotspots.text: Each tentacle belongs to a tentacular palpon, a zooid found only in this genus and specialised for making stinging cells. Caught prey is hauled up to the feeding zooids near the float.

stats.label: Share of fish and fish larvae in the diet

body.lede: With no brain, heart or swimming muscles of note, the colony relies on a float, a sail and a curtain of stinging cells.

systems.title: A float that makes its own gas
systems.text: The float holds less carbon monoxide than the floats of other siphonophores, probably because its gas mixes with air through diffusion and exchange.

systems.title: One kind of sting
systems.text: Its stinging capsules are all of a single type, which can only pierce soft-bodied prey. The toxin paralyses fish.

systems.title: A division of labour
systems.text: Unlike other siphonophores, its feeding zooids have no tentacles of their own. Catching prey falls to the tentacular palpons, and eating to the gastrozooids.

genome.lede: Genomes from specimens collected around the world showed that the 'one' man o' war is really several species.

findings.title: A big, repetitive genome
findings.text: The first Physalia genome assembly, made for this global study, measured about 3.33 billion base pairs, with roughly 65% of it made of repeated sequences.

findings.title: Not one species but at least four
findings.text: Whole genomes of 151 samples fell into five distinct lineages that do not appear to interbreed even where they overlap. Four match recognisable body forms, including a newly named species, Physalia minuta.

findings.title: Populations follow the currents
findings.text: Within each species, populations are regional and persist from year to year, with boundaries that line up with prevailing currents and winds.

survival.lede: Drifting at the surface, the colony cannot flee, so its defence is its sting.

tactics.title: A curtain of stings
tactics.text: Tentacles towed by the wind trail far below the float, catching and paralysing fish that brush against them.

tactics.title: A fish that lives among the tentacles
tactics.text: The man-of-war fish, Nomeus gronovii, swims among the tentacles and even feeds on them. It tolerates the venom far better than other fish.

tactics.title: Stings that outlast the colony
tactics.text: The stinging cells stay active after the colony dies, so stranded animals remain dangerous to touch.

life.lede: Much of the man o' war's life cycle happens out of sight, below the surface, and has never been watched directly.

stages.name: Breeding clusters
stages.text: Each colony is either male or female. Its reproductive clusters, called gonodendra, are thought to break away when mature, perhaps swimming down with small jet-propelling bells.

stages.name: Egg and larva
stages.text: Fertilisation, the egg and the earliest larva have never been observed, and they develop at an unknown depth below the surface.

stages.name: Young larva
stages.text: The smallest larva described is 2 mm long, with a tiny float and a first feeding polyp bearing a tentacle. The sail's left- or right-handed set is fixed this early.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Once its float is big enough, the young colony can ride at the surface. Juveniles have floats about 8–10 cm long and immature breeding clusters.

tagline: A moray that changes colour as it grows
summary: A ribbon-thin moray with flared, leaf-like nostrils that peers from sand and rubble burrows near coral reefs. It is the only moray known to change colour abruptly as it ages — black as a juvenile, electric blue, then yellow — a sequence long thought to track a change of sex.

stats.size: Up to about 130 cm long
stats.depth: About 1–67 m
stats.range: Tropical Indo-West Pacific
stats.diet: Small fishes

facts.title: Black, then blue, then yellow
facts.text: Small juveniles are jet black with a yellow dorsal fin. Males are bright blue with a yellow snout and jaw, and females are yellow, sometimes with blue towards the tail.

facts.title: A one-off among morays
facts.text: It is the only moray eel known to go through abrupt colour changes as it grows.

facts.title: Male first, then female?
facts.text: Ribbon eels are widely described as switching sex from male to female (protandry). But this has been inferred from their colour changes and not yet confirmed directly.

facts.title: Enormous nostrils
facts.text: The tip of its snout carries enormous, flared nostrils — one of the features that makes this slender eel so striking.

facts.title: Head-out ambusher
facts.text: Secretive by nature, it usually hides in sand or rubble near reefs, often with only its head sticking out, and feeds on small fishes.

No allowed category clearly fits, so categories is empty. Depth: FishBase 1–67 m (Fishes of Australia gives 1–57 m). Gallery photo location not given on Commons.

anatomy.lede: A ribbon eel is almost all length: a whip-thin moray with a frilled snout, built to slip into narrow burrows and peer out at passing fish.

hotspots.label: Flared nostril
hotspots.text: The front nostrils are long tubes that end in fan-like expansions, flaring from the tip of the snout like small leaves.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Its retina differs markedly in structure from those of three other morays studied, a difference researchers link to its shallow, sunlit home.

hotspots.label: Chin tentacles
hotspots.text: Three small fleshy tentacles sit at the tip of the lower jaw, with a single pointed projection at the tip of the snout.

hotspots.label: Blue phase
hotspots.text: Bright blue with a yellow snout and jaw is the colour usually described for males. Juveniles are black, and the largest animals turn yellow.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: A high, yellow dorsal fin runs along the back. Like the anal fin, it has no spines.

body.lede: Inside, the ribbon eel is as unusual as it looks outside.

systems.title: A spine of hundreds of bones
systems.text: Its backbone has 270 to 286 vertebrae, which is what makes such a long, thin, flexible body possible.

systems.title: Organs behind the vent
systems.text: In ribbon eels the reproductive organs lie behind the anus rather than in front of it, as in other fishes. A 1990 study described Rhinomuraena as the first vertebrate genus known with this arrangement.

systems.title: Eyes for bright water
systems.text: Comparing two shallow-water and two deep-sea morays, researchers found that the light sensitivity of each species' eye cells closely matched the light in its habitat, with the ribbon eel's retina standing apart in structure.

survival.lede: A slender fish on an open reef survives by staying close to cover.

tactics.title: Never far from home
tactics.text: It lives in burrows in sand or rubble beside coral reefs, in lagoons and on seaward reefs, and rarely leaves them.

tactics.title: Only the head shows
tactics.text: Secretive by nature, it usually stays hidden with just its head out, waiting for small fishes to come within reach.

tactics.title: Larvae seeking shelter
tactics.text: Large moray larvae, probably of this species, have been filmed swimming near the bottom in shallow water and trying to enter small crevices — perhaps looking for a safe place to change into juvenile eels.

threats.title: Collected for aquariums
threats.text: It is caught commercially for the aquarium trade. FishBase rates its vulnerability to fishing as high to very high and its resilience as very low, with populations estimated to need more than 14 years to double.

life.lede: A ribbon eel's life is told in colours, though what each colour means is still being worked out.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: In 2014, fertilised ribbon eel eggs laid at the Vienna Zoo hatched into feeding larvae for the first time anywhere, and the larvae were kept alive for seven days.

stages.name: Leptocephalus larva
stages.text: Like all eels it begins as a transparent, leaf-like larva. Large, greenish moray larvae seen off Indonesia are thought to be ribbon eels, but this has not been confirmed.

stages.name: Black juvenile
stages.text: Small juveniles are jet black with a yellow dorsal fin.

stages.name: Blue adult
stages.text: Adults turn bright blue with a yellow snout, lower jaw and dorsal fin, a phase usually interpreted as male.

stages.name: Yellow adult
stages.text: The largest animals turn yellow, a phase usually interpreted as female. But the Vienna Zoo study found that, in captivity, colour did not reflect an eel's sex or maturity, and sex change has not been confirmed.

tagline: A three-gram bird that hangs in the air on a blur of wings
summary: The only hummingbird that nests in eastern North America, the ruby-throat hovers in front of flowers on wings beating about 53 times a second. Each autumn these tiny birds, which weigh less than a coin, fatten up and head south to Mexico and Central America, and many may cross the Gulf of Mexico on the way.
ability: hovering on a blur of wings

stats.size: About 3.4 g for males and 3.8 g for females
stats.habitat: Deciduous woodland, forest edges, meadows, orchards and gardens; dry forest and scrub in winter
stats.range: Breeds across eastern North America and the Canadian prairies; winters from southern Mexico to Costa Rica and in the West Indies
stats.diet: Nectar from red or orange tubular flowers, plus small insects and spiders
stats.conservation: IUCN Red List: Least Concern (2021 assessment)

facts.title: 53 wingbeats a second
facts.text: The ruby-throat beats its wings about 53 times a second. Like all hummingbirds, it can stop in an instant, hang motionless in mid-air and shift up, down, sideways and even backwards with fine control.

facts.title: Too short-legged to walk
facts.text: Its legs are so short that it cannot walk or hop; the best it can do is shuffle along a perch. To scratch its head it raises a foot up and over its wing.

facts.title: A nest the size of a thimble
facts.text: The female builds her nest on top of a slender branch from thistle or dandelion down bound with spider silk, and decorates the outside with lichen and moss. The cup is about 5 cm across, and its walls stretch as the chicks grow.

facts.title: Fuelled for the Gulf
facts.text: On the Alabama coast in autumn, older birds arrived with larger fuel loads and stayed for shorter stopovers than first-year birds. The researchers calculated that an average bird could fly the roughly 1,000 km across the Gulf of Mexico in still air, but they could not say whether the birds actually fly over the Gulf or around it.

facts.title: The East's only hummingbird
facts.text: It is the only hummingbird that breeds in eastern North America, and its breeding range covers a larger area than that of any other North American hummingbird.

facts.title: Common, but declining
facts.text: Partners in Flight estimates about 36 million breeding birds. But an analysis of Breeding Bird Survey data found that, after decades of increase, ruby-throats have been declining since about 2004 across most of their breeding range.

notes: signatureData: wingbeatHz 53 is Cornell All About Birds' 'Cool Facts' figure ('beats its wings about 53 times a second'). Cornell gives no sex or flight mode; Birds of the World (Weidensaul et al. 2020, paywalled, seen only in a search snippet) reportedly attributes ~53 beats/s for all flight types, including hovering, to Greenewalt (1960). ADW also gives 53 beats/s, but elsewhere gives 'the normal 90 beats per second' and up to 200 in courtship, which conflict, so ADW is not used for the figure. Peer-reviewed hovering kinematics papers on this species (Chai et al. 1997, 1998; Mahalingam & Welch 2013, JEB) report wingbeat frequency, but their numbers could not be read (paywalled; abstracts give trends only). heartRateBpm is omitted: the widely quoted 1,260 bpm figure appears to come from the blue-throated hummingbird (Lampornis clemenciae), and the only ruby-throat figure found (~614 bpm, at rest) is neither a maximum nor confirmed from the primary source. allaboutbirds.org and iucnredlist.org return 403 to scripted requests. Cornell text was read from Wayback Machine copies (Dec 2025 / Jan 2026), and the IUCN category and ID came from the GBIF IUCN checklist (BirdLife International 2021, DOI 10.2305/IUCN.UK.2021-3.RLTS.T22688193A186910664.en). Zenzal & Moore: fuel-load and age results are from the abstract; the '~1,000 km' Gulf crossing estimate and the authors' uncertainty about over-versus-around come from the Discussion. The fact is marked hypothesis because the range is a flight-simulation estimate and the authors say such models may overestimate it. Mass is from ADW. The nest width converts Cornell's 'about 2 inches'. Population (36 million) is Partners in Flight via Cornell, and the post-2004 decline is from the English et al. 2021 abstract. Regions: north-american-forests is first because Cornell notes the species 'across the Canadian prairies' (the polygon covers Alberta/Saskatchewan and the eastern Dakotas); most of the eastern breeding range lies east of every mapped polygon. central-america is wintering range (ADW: southern Mexico, Central America to Costa Rica, West Indies). Categories: migrations (Gulf of Mexico migration); not endangered (LC). Images: hero is an iNaturalist observation (138799680), New Brunswick, 2022. alt-1 is from Cullman County, Alabama, 2014 (geotagged). alt-2 is a Commons Featured Picture, Louisville, Kentucky, 2006 (geotagged); the uploader describes the bird as a male, but its gorget is patchy, so it may be a young male.

anatomy.lede: A ruby-throat weighs less than four grams, yet every part of it is tuned for hovering: a needle bill, a reflective throat, tiny feet and wings that hardly ever rest.

hotspots.label: Bill
hotspots.text: The long, straight bill reaches deep into tubular flowers. Inside, the tongue does the real work of gathering nectar.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Its eyes are sensitive to blue-violet and near-ultraviolet light as well as the colours we see, which may help it pick out flowers.

hotspots.label: Gorget
hotspots.text: Only males have the brilliant metallic red throat. Females have a dull greyish throat instead.

hotspots.label: Iridescent green
hotspots.text: The back and head are iridescent green and the underparts white in both sexes.

hotspots.label: Wing
hotspots.text: Normal flight takes about 53 wingbeats a second. In courtship displays a male's wings can beat up to 200 times a second.

hotspots.label: Feet
hotspots.text: The feet are tucked up in flight. They are used for perching and, in territorial fights, for striking intruders.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: Males have a forked tail; females have a square tail with white tips.

senses.lede: A hummingbird finds its food mainly by eye, scanning for red and orange flowers across a meadow.

senses.name: Colour and ultraviolet sight
senses.text: Ruby-throats can see into the blue-violet and near-ultraviolet range, roughly 370 to 570 nanometres. This may help them find and identify flowers worth visiting.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: They may also be able to find and tell apart food sources by smell, though this is less well established than their use of sight.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Their rapid, squeaky chips are used mostly as threats. A resident male answers an intruder with a single note repeated more and more loudly before he gives chase.

body.lede: Hovering is one of the most expensive ways to move. The ruby-throat's body runs close to its limits all day and has to switch itself down at night.

systems.title: A tongue that traps nectar
systems.text: The tip of the tongue splits into two fringed edges. As it leaves the nectar, the fringes curl inwards and trap the liquid. This works the same way in dead birds, so it costs the bird no energy and is not capillary action, as was long assumed.

systems.title: A furnace of a metabolism
systems.text: Hovering needs about 204 calories per gram of body weight an hour, around ten times the resting rate of 20.6. To keep this up, a ruby-throat eats about twice its body weight in food each day.

systems.title: Nightly torpor
systems.text: On cold nights it saves energy by entering torpor, a state like a short hibernation in which its body cools by several degrees and its body processes slow down.

systems.title: Fuel for migration
systems.text: Before migrating, ruby-throats often double their body mass, storing fat to fuel the long journey south.

genome.lede: The ruby-throat's genome was assembled to chromosome level in 2022, from a single female.

findings.title: A chromosome-scale assembly
findings.text: Researchers at Johns Hopkins University combined short-read and nanopore sequencing of brain and flight-muscle tissue from an adult female from Toronto. The resulting assembly, released in 2022, is about 1.1 billion base pairs long and is NCBI's reference genome for the species.

mind.lede: Ruby-throats live alone and meet mainly to mate or fight. Their behaviour is a constant balance between defending food and spending as little energy as possible.

studies.title: Defending a patch
studies.text: Males hold territories and warn intruders with escalating calls. If that fails, the resident chases the intruder and may jab it with his bill or strike it with his feet.

studies.title: The dive display
studies.text: A courting male flies in looping dives above a female. If she perches, he switches to very fast side-to-side arcs less than half a metre in front of her.

studies.title: Stopovers on the Gulf coast
studies.text: A study of birds stopping on the Alabama coast in autumn compared how much fuel adults and first-year birds carried and how long each stayed before moving on, giving a rare look at how these tiny migrants prepare for the Gulf of Mexico.

studies.title: Testing the tongue
studies.text: High-speed filming of hummingbird tongues, including the ruby-throat's, showed that the tongue tip changes shape as it leaves the nectar, overturning the long-held capillary model of how hummingbirds drink.

survival.lede: For a bird this small, the biggest dangers are running out of fuel and being caught by a quicker hunter.

tactics.title: Unmatched agility
tactics.text: Hummingbirds can hover and even fly backwards and upside down, manoeuvres few other birds can match.

tactics.title: Timing the return
tactics.text: The spring migration north is timed so that birds arrive as their food plants come into flower along the way.

tactics.title: Shutting down to survive the cold
tactics.text: Torpor lets a bird survive a cold night that would otherwise burn through its small energy reserves.

threats.title: Collected for their feathers
threats.text: In the 19th century, ruby-throats were hunted for collections because of their small size and brilliant plumage, though the species never became threatened.

threats.title: A recent decline
threats.text: Breeding Bird Survey data show that, after decades of increase, numbers have fallen since about 2004 across much of the breeding range. The causes are not yet clear.

life.lede: Males leave after mating, so the female raises each brood alone, and in a good year she may raise up to three.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays 1 to 3 eggs, usually 2, and incubates them alone.

stages.name: Nestling
stages.text: The chicks hatch helpless and are brooded and fed by their mother until they leave the nest.

stages.name: Fledgling
stages.text: After fledging, the young are still fed by their mother until they are about 22 to 25 days old.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Young birds can probably breed in their first year. Males arrive back on the breeding grounds before females and set up territories.

lifespan.value: At least 9 years (female) and 5 years (male) in the wild

tagline: A heat-proof ant in a mirrored coat that forages at midday
summary: While almost everything else in the Sahara hides from the noon sun, the silver ant comes out. A coat of tiny triangular hairs reflects sunlight and radiates heat away, and it is the fastest ant ever measured, sprinting across scorching sand to scavenge before its own heat limit is reached.

stats.size: Workers under about 1 cm long
stats.habitat: Sand dunes; nests underground
stats.range: Sand seas of the Sahara, North Africa
stats.diet: Scavenges insects and other small animals, many killed by the heat
stats.conservation: Not assessed by the IUCN Red List

facts.title: A coat of tiny prisms
facts.text: The silver sheen comes from a dense array of hairs with a triangular cross-section. They reflect visible and near-infrared sunlight strongly, and also boost the ant's emission of mid-infrared radiation, letting it dump heat back into the sky even in full daylight.

facts.title: Five to ten degrees cooler
facts.text: The researchers estimated that the hair coat keeps the ants' bodies 5 to 10 °C cooler than they would be without it, helping them stay below their critical thermal maximum of 53.6 °C.

facts.title: Walking a thermal tightrope
facts.text: Foragers pour out of the nest in a burst lasting only minutes during the hottest part of the day. Below that window, predatory lizards are still active; above it, the ants themselves would die of heat.

facts.title: The fastest ant
facts.text: Filmed at midday, when the sand can reach 60 °C, silver ants ran at up to 855 mm per second — about 108 body lengths every second, the fastest speed recorded for any ant.

facts.title: Short legs, flickering feet
facts.text: Its legs are shorter than those of related desert ants. It makes up for this with stride frequencies above 40 per second, feet touching the ground for as little as 7 milliseconds, and leg swings of up to 1.4 m per second.
