notes: Name: GBIF's backbone spells it Cataglyphis bombycinus (key 1319624, fuzzy match); the literature cited here (Shi 2015, Pfeffer 2019) uses bombycina, which is kept. No IUCN assessment found; conservation stated as not assessed. Wehner et al. 1992 (Nature) is paywalled: the 'thermal tightrope' fact follows its abstract (explosive midday outburst lasting a few minutes, thermal window bounded by predation and heat) as quoted in secondary sources; press coverage gives the emergence threshold as ~45–47 °C at ant height, not used as a number. The 53.6 °C critical thermal maximum and the 5–10 °C cooling figure are from the Columbia/Phys.org release on Shi et al. 2015 (CTmax originally from Gehring & Wehner 1995). Speed figures (855 mm/s, 108 body lengths/s, 60 °C sand) from the Company of Biologists release; stride/stance/leg-swing figures from the Pfeffer et al. abstract. Size: the paper's figures imply ~8 mm body length (855/108); stated loosely as under about 1 cm. Diet line ('many killed by the heat') reflects the scavenging habit described in Wehner's work and press coverage — treat as general. Images: wild ants photographed by the uploader in Erg Chebbi, Morocco (geotagged); the AntWeb specimen photo was rejected because its rubbed hairs don't show the silver coat.

anatomy.lede: A silver ant is less than a centimetre long, yet nearly every part of it is tuned for a few minutes of foraging on the hottest sand on Earth.

hotspots.label: Mandibles
hotspots.text: Workers search the midday dunes for insects and other small animals that have died of heat, and carry or tear them apart to take back to the nest.

hotspots.label: Head and eye
hotspots.text: Cataglyphis desert ants can wander hundreds of metres from the nest and still head home in a straight line, keeping track of direction and distance as they go.

hotspots.label: Wingless thorax
hotspots.text: Like all worker ants, silver-ant workers are females with a simplified, wingless thorax and a reduced reproductive system. Only queens are built for flight.

hotspots.label: Silvered abdomen
hotspots.text: Dense hairs with a triangular cross-section give the body its silver sheen, reflecting sunlight and radiating heat away.

hotspots.label: Legs
hotspots.text: The ant runs with a strict tripod gait, three legs at a time, with moments when all six feet are off the ground.

body.lede: Reflective hairs keep the heat out. Inside, the ant's cells are prepared for heat before it arrives.

systems.title: Ready before the heat
systems.text: Cataglyphis ants build up heat-shock proteins, molecules that protect other proteins from damage, before they are exposed to high temperatures. Their cells keep making proteins up to 45 °C, against 39 °C in a temperate Formica ant and in fruit flies.

systems.title: Guarding the power stations
systems.text: When heated, silver ants switch on chaperone proteins that work inside the mitochondria, the parts of the cell that supply energy. This seems to keep their muscles working during sudden bursts of extreme heat.

systems.title: A measured response
systems.text: Under heat stress the silver ant alters the activity of only about 0.6% of its genes, compared with 8–13% in two temperate ants. Desert ants seem to need far less of an emergency response.

mind.lede: Cataglyphis desert ants are famous navigators, and the silver ant manages the feat on shifting sand at a sprint.

studies.title: Counting steps on soft sand
studies.text: Researchers expected the silver ant's bouncing gait and the yielding dune sand to spoil its sense of distance. In fact it found its way back to the nest as accurately as a salt-pan relative, on sand or on a hard floor.

studies.title: A wider search
studies.text: When a silver ant misses its nest entrance, it searches in a spiral that spreads wider than that of its relative, perhaps allowing for greater uncertainty in its reckoning.

studies.title: Timing the rush
studies.text: Foragers leave the nest only once the sand is hot enough to drive their lizard predators into shelter, and must be back before they overheat themselves.

survival.lede: The silver ant's niche is a narrow window between being eaten and being cooked.

tactics.title: Speed
tactics.text: Feet that touch the sand for only milliseconds and very high stride frequencies make it the fastest ant known, which may help it to limit time spent on the scorching surface.

tactics.title: Soldiers
tactics.text: Some colonies contain a third caste: large individuals with sabre-shaped mandibles and big abdomens, which appear to serve both for defence and for storing fat.

tactics.title: Deep nests
tactics.text: Nests in the dunes are huge and deep, with several entrances metres apart.

life.lede: Like all ants, the silver ant grows through egg, larva and pupa. What a larva becomes depends on how large it grows.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: Larvae are fed by workers. When a larva reaches a critical size it pupates, and different growth rules produce workers, soldiers or queens.

stages.name: Worker
stages.text: Most adults are wingless workers of varying size, which forage, care for the brood, build and defend the nest.

stages.name: Soldier
stages.text: Fewer, larger adults with sabre-shaped mandibles combine some growth patterns of workers with some of queens.

stages.name: Queen
stages.text: Winged young queens leave on nuptial flights, recorded in Morocco in April. A colony has one queen, who sheds her wings after mating; queens come in both large and small forms.

tagline: A small fish with an enormous, combative mouth
summary: This feisty blenny from California and Baja California lives inside empty shells, clam burrows — even discarded bottles — and defends its home fiercely. When rivals meet, males fling open their huge, brightly lined mouths and press them together in a bizarre wrestling match.

stats.size: Up to about 30 cm long
stats.depth: About 3–73 m
stats.range: Eastern Pacific, from San Francisco to central Baja California
stats.diet: Not well documented in the sources consulted

facts.title: A mouth bigger than its head
facts.text: Males have extremely long jaws that extend well past the back of the head. A special hinge lets the upper jaw swing outwards, so the open mouth flares wide during a 'gaping display'.

facts.title: Mouth-wrestling
facts.text: Rival males swim at each other with mouths agape and lock together mouth to mouth. In observed contests, the bigger fish with larger jaws tended to win.

facts.title: Fighting for a home
facts.text: It usually lives inside objects — mollusc shells, clam burrows and even bottles. Males defend these shelters because without one, a male cannot breed.

facts.title: Dad on guard
facts.text: Females lay eggs in old clam holes, under rocks or in discarded containers such as beer cans, and the male guards them until they hatch.

facts.title: A glowing threat?
facts.text: The membrane lining its mouth is brightly coloured and partly fluorescent, and reflects ultraviolet light. Researchers suggest this may make the display even more striking to rivals.

Diet not given by FishBase species summary — editor may want to fill from another source. No allowed category clearly fits (male egg-guarding is common in blennies), so categories is empty.

anatomy.lede: Most of a sarcastic fringehead's personality is in its head: bulging eyes, feathery brows and a mouth that can open far wider than its face.

hotspots.label: Cirri
hotspots.text: Wavy, fringe-like flaps called cirri stand above the eyes and give the fringeheads their name.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Big, bulging eyes sit high on the head, just below the cirri — the source of its 'bug-eyed' look.

hotspots.label: Fleshy lips
hotspots.text: A blunt snout and prominent lips frame a mouth lined with numerous needle-like teeth.

hotspots.label: Long upper jaw
hotspots.text: The upper jaw bone (maxilla) runs back well past the eye, almost to the edge of the gill cover. It is longer in males.

hotspots.label: Pale cheek patch
hotspots.text: The body is usually brown to grey with a reddish tint, often with pale spots or patches on the cheeks.

body.lede: The fringehead's famous gape is the result of several changes to an ordinary blenny's skull, all amplified in this one species.

systems.title: A hinge in the face
systems.text: A joint not found in related fishes, between the front of the upper jaw and the bone below the eye, lets the upper jaw swing outwards so the mouth flares sideways.

systems.title: Jaws that keep growing
systems.text: The upper jaw is lengthened by a soft, uncalcified extension at its back end. Comparisons with two close relatives suggest it evolved by growing faster and for longer than in other fringeheads.

systems.title: A painted mouth
systems.text: The membrane lining the mouth is enlarged, brightly coloured and partly fluorescent, which may make the open-mouthed display even more conspicuous.

mind.lede: Fringehead contests have been watched both on dives off California and in aquarium tanks.

studies.title: Residents gape first
studies.text: When another male approached a resident's shelter, the resident gaped at it in nearly 70% of encounters. The intruder then either retreated or fought.

studies.title: A signal of size
studies.text: Because a gaping mouth shows off jaw size, researchers suggest the display lets rivals judge each other and avoid some fights. Contests that did turn physical ended when one fish bit the other, usually on the head.

studies.title: Different message for females
studies.text: Males gape at other males but not at females, which they court by shaking their heads instead.

studies.title: Backing in
studies.text: Fringeheads move in short, rapid darts and often back into their burrows tail first rather than swimming in head first.

survival.lede: A small fish on open sand and mud survives by owning a hiding place and defending it hard.

tactics.title: A borrowed fortress
tactics.text: It rests inside an empty shell, burrow, crevice or discarded can or bottle with only its head showing.

tactics.title: Ambush from the doorway
tactics.text: It leaps out of its shelter to seize passing prey. Its wild diet is not known, but related blennies mostly eat crustaceans.

tactics.title: Warn, then bite
tactics.text: Intruders get a warning first — flexing the body, spreading the gill covers and snapping the jaws. If that fails, it may chase and bite, even a diver.

tactics.title: No intruder too big
tactics.text: Fringeheads have been seen chasing other fish and even octopuses away from their shelters.

life.lede: For a fringehead, a home is the key to breeding: no shelter, no family.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: A receptive female lays her eggs in a male's shelter, such as an old clam burrow, the space under a rock or a discarded container.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Eggs are 0.9–1.5 mm across, each with an oil droplet and sticky filaments that fix it to the shelter wall and to its neighbours.

stages.name: Guarded nest
stages.text: The male fertilises the eggs and guards them until they hatch.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: The newly hatched larvae are only about 3 mm long.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adult males grow larger than females and have more brightly coloured mouths, the equipment they need to win and hold a shelter.

lifespan.value: Up to about 6 years

tagline: A winged snail with a ruthless appetite
summary: The sea angel is a shell-less snail that 'flies' through cold Arctic and North Atlantic waters by flapping two wing-like lobes of its foot. Its see-through body glows with orange-red organs. Gentle as it looks, it is a specialist hunter that pulls sea butterflies out of their shells.

stats.size: Up to about 7–8.5 cm in the north; much smaller further south
stats.depth: Surface to more than 500 m
stats.range: Arctic Ocean and cold North Atlantic, south at least to the Sargasso Sea
stats.diet: Almost exclusively sea butterflies (Limacina helicina and L. retroversa)

facts.title: Snail with wings
facts.text: Sea angels are snails without shells. They swim by beating two wing-like flaps of the foot, and use gravity-sensing organs to keep upright in the water.

facts.title: A one-dish diet
facts.text: Adults eat almost nothing but sea butterflies, their shelled pteropod cousins. In Svalbard, researchers describe the sea butterfly Limacina helicina as its only prey.

facts.title: Grab, hook, extract
facts.text: Three pairs of finger-like 'buccal cones' shoot out of its mouth to grip a sea butterfly's shell. Chitin hooks then pull the soft body out, and the sea angel swallows it whole.

facts.title: A year without food
facts.text: In a lab experiment, sea angels from Svalbard survived 356 days with no food at all, shrinking from about 22 to 12 mm while living off stored fats.

facts.title: Whale food
facts.text: Baleen whales and fishes eat sea angels, and sailors historically nicknamed them 'whale-food'.

notes: Both photos are of live/fresh animals photographed in containers (black background), not in situ — labelled 'specimen'. The NOAA photo is from Alaska (AFSC); Wikipedia notes North Pacific Clione are now often treated as C. elegantissima, so that ID follows the photographer's label. WoRMS order for Clionidae returned as Pteropoda. The Walla Walla Salish Sea page (also describing buccal cones) was not cited because it treats NE Pacific animals as C. limacina. Size, depth, range, buccal-cone and 'whale-food' facts via Wikipedia (citing WoRMS, Lalli & Gilmer 1989, Böer et al.).

anatomy.lede: A sea angel is a snail stripped down for open water: no shell, a foot reshaped into wings, and a head that hides a set of grappling tools.

hotspots.label: Head
hotspots.text: Folded inside the head are three pairs of buccal cones, which inflate in an instant to seize a sea butterfly, plus chitin hooks and a toothed radula that pull it from its shell.

hotspots.label: Wing
hotspots.text: Each wing is a flap of the snail's foot, called a parapodium. The pair beat up and down, driven by a rhythm-generating circuit of nerve cells in the pedal ganglia.

hotspots.label: Second wing
hotspots.text: The sea angel swims almost constantly to hold its place in the water, and beats its wings faster when hunting or escaping danger.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The tail works as a rudder. When the body tips away from upright, it bends the opposite way to correct it.

stats.label: Survived without food in the lab

senses.lede: With simple, large nerve cells, the sea angel's senses have been traced almost cell by cell.

senses.name: Gravity sense
senses.text: Two statocysts — tiny balance organs, each holding a stone-like statolith — tell it which way is up. Receptor cells fire when they lie beneath the statolith. With the statocysts removed, a sea angel can no longer hold any steady orientation.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: A touch on the head normally triggers a defensive shutdown. But contact with its prey, the sea butterfly, sets off the whole hunting sequence instead: cones out, faster wing-beats and swimming in circles.

body.lede: Its nervous system is simple enough to study in a dish, which has made the sea angel a classic model in neuroscience.

systems.title: A built-in metronome
systems.text: Two groups of interneurons, one for the upstroke and one for the downstroke, inhibit each other in turn. The length of each inhibition largely sets how fast the wings beat.

systems.title: Serotonin for speed
systems.text: Serotonin-releasing neurons in the brain speed up swimming by recruiting extra cells into the wing circuit and strengthening the wing muscles' contractions. Stimulating the tail also speeds swimming and raises the heart rate.

genome.lede: The sea angel's DNA has been sequenced only in rough draft.

findings.title: A first rough draft
findings.text: A draft assembly of about 1.26 billion base pairs was deposited in 2023 by Iridian Genomes. It is split into more than 500,000 short pieces, so it is not yet a finished reference genome.

mind.lede: Russian and American laboratories have studied how this little snail's nervous system runs its behaviour for more than four decades.

studies.title: Hunting on a switch
studies.text: Injecting a drug that boosts the nerve messenger acetylcholine made sea angels perform the full hunting routine in response to a simple touch, or even spontaneously.

studies.title: Head up or head down
studies.text: Sea angels usually swim head up, but hold a head-down posture in warmer water and at one stage of hunting. Postural control switches off entirely during vertical migrations, defence and the 'looping' of a hunt.

studies.title: A brain steering a motor
studies.text: Researchers wired an isolated sea angel nervous system, with its statocysts, to a motor that rotated it. When the loop was closed, the neurons kept the preparation upright on their own.

studies.title: A model for changing gear
studies.text: Because it changes swimming speed to feed and to avoid predators, and its neurons can be recognised from animal to animal, the sea angel is used to study how nervous systems control speed.

survival.lede: A slow, soft-bodied snail in open water has few defences beyond speed and stamina.

tactics.title: Shut down when touched
tactics.text: A touch on the head triggers a defence reaction: the main motor systems, including swimming, the tentacles and the feeding apparatus, are inhibited for a long time.

tactics.title: Sprint away
tactics.text: Sea angels accelerate their wing-beats to escape potential predators.

tactics.title: Living on reserves
tactics.text: Stored fats carry it through long periods without prey, and lab animals survived about a year without eating.

life.lede: In the high Arctic, a sea angel takes years to grow from a speck into a winged hunter.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Sea angels are hermaphrodites, probably carrying male and female organs at the same time. They breed in spring and summer and lay eggs about 0.12 mm across.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: Young larvae feed on phytoplankton, then switch to sea butterflies as they grow.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Northern animals mature at about 3 cm and can reach 7–8.5 cm, feeding almost entirely on sea butterflies.

lifespan.value: Life cycle of at least two years in Svalbard

tagline: A snail that flies like an insect
summary: The sea butterfly is a tiny swimming snail, its glassy shell often under a centimetre across, that 'flies' through Arctic and subarctic seas on two wing-like flaps. Hugely abundant and a key food for fish, whales and the sea angel, its fragile shell makes it an early warning sign of ocean acidification.

stats.size: Shell about 5–10 mm wide (up to about 13 mm)
stats.depth: Mostly upper 150 m
stats.range: Arctic and subarctic seas of the Atlantic and Pacific
stats.diet: Phytoplankton, tiny protozoans and small zooplankton caught in a mucus web

facts.title: Flying, not swimming
facts.text: It beats two wing-like flaps 4 to 10 times a second in a stroke resembling that of tiny flying insects, effectively flying through the water.

facts.title: A net made of mucus
facts.text: It hangs still beneath a large, spherical web of mucus that traps plankton, then eats the web and its catch and spins a new one.

facts.title: A shell that dissolves
facts.text: Its thin shell is made of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate that dissolves easily. In experiments, shell damage increased steadily as seawater became more acidic.

facts.title: Arctic food staple
facts.text: It can make up more than half of all zooplankton in polar waters and is eaten by herring, salmon, seals, whales, seabirds and sea angels.

facts.title: Male first, then female
facts.text: Each sea butterfly starts life as a male and later becomes female once it grows larger than about 5 mm.

Editor may prefer image: null or a licensed replacement. Antarctic animals formerly called L. helicina are now L. antarctica (Wikipedia, citing Hunt et al. 2010). anatomy.lede: A sea butterfly is a snail the size of a lentil, with a glassy shell and a foot turned into a pair of beating wings.

hotspots.label: Wing
hotspots.text: The wings are parapodia: flexible flaps that evolved from the snail's foot.

hotspots.label: Second wing
hotspots.text: During each stroke the wings clap together and fling apart, a 'clap and fling' trick also used by tiny flying insects.

hotspots.label: Shell
hotspots.text: The very thin shell coils to the left, with five to six whorls, and is made of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate that dissolves easily in acidic water.

hotspots.label: Soft body
hotspots.text: The soft body, dark purple to violet in life, can pull right back inside the shell when the animal is disturbed.

stats.label: Share of polar zooplankton at times

body.lede: Moving through water at the scale of a few millimetres is neither quite swimming nor quite flying, and the sea butterfly does a little of both.

systems.title: Rowing and flying at once
systems.text: High-speed filming showed a complex three-dimensional wing-stroke with elements of both rowing and flapping flight, plus a rotation of the whole body. Smaller animals beat their wings faster than larger ones.

systems.title: Sawtooth climbs
systems.text: Swimming sea butterflies rise along a zigzag, sawtooth path as each stroke rocks the body. When they stop, they sink smoothly at 5–45 mm per second.

systems.title: A shell that thickens with depth
systems.text: In the Barents Sea, living sea butterflies had denser, larger and thicker shells the deeper they were caught, down to about 300 m.

survival.lede: Almost everything in polar seas eats sea butterflies, and their main defence is a shell that is itself under threat.

tactics.title: Retreat and drop the net
tactics.text: When disturbed, it pulls back into its shell and abandons its mucus feeding web.

tactics.title: Growing out of danger
tactics.text: One specialist predator, the sea angel Paedoclione doliiformis, eats only young sea butterflies with shells under 1 mm across.

threats.title: Corrosive coastal water
threats.text: Off Washington, Oregon and California in 2011, 53% of sea butterflies caught near shore and 24% offshore had severe shell dissolution. Researchers estimate such damage near shore has doubled since pre-industrial times and is on track to triple by 2050.

threats.title: Dissolving in the lab
threats.text: In week-long experiments with Puget Sound animals, shell damage rose steadily as the water's aragonite saturation fell, and survival was lowest in the most corrosive water.

life.lede: A sea butterfly lives fast, changing sex as it grows and completing its life within a year or two.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Sperm is passed in packets called spermatophores, and eggs are laid in ribbon-like clusters, mostly in summer but some in winter.

stages.name: Veliger larva
stages.text: The eggs hatch into tiny swimming veliger larvae.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: The smallest young, 0.2–0.4 mm across, live mainly in the top 50 m; larger animals range down to about 150 m.

stages.name: Male
stages.text: Every sea butterfly matures first as a male.

stages.name: Female
stages.text: Once larger than about 5 mm, it becomes female.

lifespan.value: About 1–2 years

tagline: The otter that keeps the kelp forest standing
summary: The smallest marine mammal and the heaviest member of the weasel family, living along the rocky coasts and kelp forests of the North Pacific. With no blubber, it stays warm inside the densest fur of any animal, eats about a quarter of its body weight a day, and cracks shellfish open with stones.
ability: stone tools and the densest fur of any animal

stats.size: Males 1.2–1.5 m, females 1–1.4 m long; up to about 45 kg
stats.depth: Most foraging at 2–30 m; dives recorded to about 100 m
stats.range: Coastal North Pacific: the Kuril and Commander Islands, the Aleutians and Alaska to British Columbia and Washington, and central California
stats.diet: Sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels, snails, abalone and other seabed invertebrates; some populations also eat fish

facts.title: Warm without blubber
facts.text: Unlike other marine mammals, sea otters have no blubber. They rely on the densest fur of any animal, with more than a million hairs per square inch at its thickest, which traps a layer of air next to the skin.

facts.title: Always hungry
facts.text: To keep its body at about 38 °C (100 °F) in cold water, a sea otter eats about a quarter of its body weight every day.

facts.title: Guardian of the kelp
facts.text: Comparing Aleutian islands with and without sea otters, Estes and Palmisano (1974) found that otters keep plant-eating invertebrates such as sea urchins in check. Where otters had been removed, grazing increased and kelp beds were destroyed.

facts.title: A rock in its pocket
facts.text: Sea otters break hard-shelled prey with stones, either holding the rock on the chest and pounding the prey against it or striking the prey with the rock. A loose fold of skin under each forearm can hold a favourite stone and food collected on a dive.

facts.title: Shallow feeders
facts.text: Sea otters fitted with depth recorders in south-east Alaska did most of their foraging between 2 and 30 m. Males often fed deeper than females, and the deepest foraging dives ranged from 35 to 100 m.

facts.title: Hunted to the brink
facts.text: Hunting for their fur in the 18th and 19th centuries greatly reduced the sea otter's range. Today three subspecies are recognised, and northern sea otters have been reintroduced to coasts from Alaska to Oregon.

The southern sea otter is separately listed as Threatened under the US Endangered Species Act. Depth: the 100 m maximum is the deepest foraging dive in Bodkin et al. (2004); the Monterey Bay Aquarium states that sea otters can dive to 600 ft (183 m), which could not be traced to a primary source and is not used for the gauge. Fur density: the aquarium gives more than a million hairs per square inch; ADW gives about 100,000 per cm² (about 645,000 per square inch), so 'densest of any animal' is used without a precise number in the summary. 'Smallest marine mammal' follows Yeates et al. (2007), cited in the deep chapters. 'Intelligent' shelf based on habitual stone-tool use. The Morro Bay photograph carries the photographer's credit line in the bottom-left corner; its Commons title says Piedras Blancas but the description places it at Morro Rock. The raft photograph's USFWS caption gives no location.

anatomy.lede: A sea otter is a weasel remade for the sea: webbed hind feet for swimming, nimble forepaws for handling food, and a coat that does the job other marine mammals leave to blubber.

hotspots.label: Webbed hind feet
hotspots.text: The hind legs are long and the feet broad, flat and webbed. Swimming, the otter tucks in its forelimbs and drives itself with its hind feet and tail.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The flattened tail is less than a third of the body length, about 25–35 cm.

hotspots.label: Whiskers
hotspots.text: Long, sensitive whiskers help it find small animals among kelp and in rock crevices.

hotspots.label: Forepaws
hotspots.text: The short forelimbs have retractable claws and agile paws for grooming and for rubbing, twisting and pulling prey apart.

hotspots.label: Two-layer fur
hotspots.text: A dark underfur lies beneath longer, lighter guard hairs, which trap a layer of air that keeps the skin dry.

stats.label: Hairs per square inch, at the thickest
Of body weight eaten each day
Deepest foraging dive recorded in Alaska

senses.lede: Sea otters hunt on the seabed largely by feel, and know one another by smell and voice.

senses.name: Whiskers and paws
senses.text: It searches the dense kelp and crevices with its whiskers and forepaws, catching prey by touch.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Each otter has its own scent that conveys identity, age and sex. Yet its genome shows many olfactory receptor genes have decayed, as in other aquatic mammals.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Researchers have recognised nine calls, from the squeals pups use to reach their mothers to coos, growls, snarls and distress screams.

body.lede: Being a small, blubberless mammal in cold water makes life expensive.

systems.title: Fur instead of fat
systems.text: With no insulating fat, the sea otter depends entirely on its fur for warmth, so it grooms meticulously to keep the coat waterproof.

systems.title: A costly lifestyle
systems.text: Measured in captive males, a foraging dive cost nearly twice as much energy as predicted for a seal, partly because the buoyant otter has to work hard to swim down. Wild otters balance this with long rests on the surface.

systems.title: Built-in pockets
systems.text: Loose pouches of skin under the forearms carry a stone tool and food gathered on a dive, leaving the paws free.

systems.title: Water from food
systems.text: It gets most of its water from its prey but also drinks seawater.

genome.lede: Sea otter genomes record both its move into the sea and its brush with extinction.

findings.title: Genes for life at sea
findings.text: Comparisons with the giant otter found signs of natural selection on genes for limb development and hair follicles.

findings.title: Very little diversity
findings.text: Southern and northern sea otters have extremely low genetic diversity and signs of recent inbreeding, raising the burden of possibly harmful mutations.

findings.title: Older declines
findings.text: Population declines visible in the genome may predate the fur trade.

mind.lede: Sea otters are the only marine mammals known to use stones habitually when foraging.

studies.title: Otter archaeology
studies.text: Over ten years at Bennett Slough, California, otters pounded mussels on the same rocks, leaving distinctive wear and heaps of shells broken in a characteristic way.

studies.title: Personal menus
studies.text: Individuals specialise: one otter may eat mostly urchins and crabs while another eats mostly fish, depending on its skills and on what is available.

studies.title: Keeping a tool
studies.text: An otter often keeps the same stone for many dives, carrying it in its forearm pouch.

survival.lede: Life at the surface leaves sea otters exposed to sharks from below and eagles from above.

tactics.title: Anchored in kelp
tactics.text: Resting otters float on their backs and wrap themselves in kelp so they do not drift, often in groups called rafts.

tactics.title: Dive with the pup
tactics.text: At any sign of a predator a mother grips her pup by the neck and dives.

threats.title: Oil spills
threats.text: In California, oil from a single tanker spill could threaten the whole southern population of about 3,000 otters.

threats.title: Shark bites
threats.text: Shark bites are a major cause of death for California's sea otters.

threats.title: A genetic bottleneck
threats.text: Fur-trade hunting left today's populations with very low genetic diversity, which could hamper recovery.

life.lede: A sea otter pup spends its first months riding on its mother's belly.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Thanks to delayed implantation the embryo can pause before developing, so pregnancy length varies widely. Births peak in May–June in the Aleutians and January–March in California.

stages.name: Pup
stages.text: A single pup of 1.4–2.3 kg nurses on milk that is 20–25% fat. Its fluffy coat traps so much air that it floats, and the mother wraps it in kelp when she dives.

stages.name: Young otter
stages.text: Pups start diving at about 2 months but rely on their mothers for six to eight months.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature at about 4 years and males at 5–6, though males may not mate until much later. Females usually pup once every one to two years.

lifespan.value: Up to about 23 years in the wild

tagline: A feathery colony that glows, deflates and hides in the sand
summary: Shaped like an old quill pen, the orange sea pen is a colony of polyps, each with its own job: anchoring, feeding or pumping water. It stands in soft sand and mud off western North America, strains plankton from the current and, when disturbed, flashes greenish-blue light and shrinks into its base.

stats.size: Up to about 46–48 cm tall
stats.depth: Subtidal sand and mud; reported from about 14 m to 225 m
stats.range: Northeastern Pacific, from Alaska to southern California / northern Mexico
stats.diet: Zooplankton

facts.title: One animal, many polyps
facts.text: A single primary polyp forms the stalk and the bulb that anchors it. Thousands of secondary polyps then take on jobs: feeding polyps catch plankton and make eggs and sperm, while pumping polyps move water in and out.

facts.title: A pulse of blue-green light
facts.text: When it is touched, a greenish-blue glow runs up and down the stalk, which may startle predators. A disturbed pen that has withdrawn into the sediment can still be seen glowing in the dark.

facts.title: It knows who's touching
facts.text: The amount it retracts depends on the predator. It withdraws when touched by the leather star, which hunts sea pens, but does not react defensively to the ochre star, which does not eat them.

facts.title: Drifts to a new home
facts.text: Though it looks rooted, it can inflate with water and drift like a leaf to relocate.

facts.title: Slow-growing, long-lived
facts.text: Young sea pens take over a year to reach about 2.5 cm (1 in) tall. A single pen may produce about a million eggs over a lifetime of a decade or more.

notes: Predator recognition: Wikipedia, citing Weightman & Arsenault 2002 (Can. J. Zool.), is also supported by the Oregon Coast Aquarium. The glow-in-sediment detail is from VIU. A Flickr image titled 'Fleshy Sea Pen' from an aquarium in Dubai was rejected because its species ID is unverified. Depth reports vary widely: Wikipedia gives 14–225 m, the Oregon Coast Aquarium says subtidal to about 30 m (100 ft), and VIU gives no depth. We used the wider range, so treat it with caution. WoRMS currently places sea pens in order Scleralcyonacea (formerly Pennatulacea). The 10-year lifespan and million-egg figures come from a Washington Dept. of Ecology article and are approximate.

anatomy.lede: What looks like a single feathery animal is a colony: one founding polyp turned into a stalk and anchor, carrying thousands of smaller polyps that each do one job.

hotspots.label: Anchoring bulb
hotspots.text: The colony's first polyp grows into a fleshy, bulb-shaped base that anchors it in sand or mud, and into which the colony can partly withdraw.

hotspots.label: Rachis
hotspots.text: The central stalk is the rachis. Pumping polyps (siphonozooids) on its orange sides move water in and out, inflating or deflating the colony.

hotspots.label: Polyp leaves
hotspots.text: The ribbed 'leaves' along each side are lined with feeding polyps (autozooids), each with eight tentacles for catching drifting plankton.

hotspots.label: Feeding polyps
hotspots.text: The same feeding polyps also make the colony's eggs and sperm.

hotspots.label: Neighbour
hotspots.text: Young sea pens tend to settle in dense clumps, so colonies often grow close together.

stats.label: Burrowed after touch by a leather star

senses.lede: A sea pen has no eyes or brain, yet it can tell a dangerous sea star from a harmless one.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: Physical contact is what triggers its defences. Most sea pens burrowed quickly after touching a specialist predator, the leather star, but barely reacted to a harmless ochre star or a glass rod.

senses.name: Chemical cues
senses.text: In experiments, water carrying the scent of predatory sea stars caused no defensive response on its own, in the lab or in the field. The sea pen waits for contact before it reacts.

body.lede: A sea pen's body is a water-filled colony that can light up, swell or shrink as a whole.

systems.title: Hydraulic skeleton
systems.text: Water pumped in by the siphonozooids holds the colony upright. Letting it out lets the pen shrink into the sediment, and inflating lets it drift off to a new spot.

systems.title: Colony-wide light
systems.text: Contact with a predatory sea star set off bioluminescent flashes across the whole colony, whereas a harmless star or a glass rod produced only weaker, local glows.

systems.title: A borrowed glow
systems.text: The orange sea pen's green fluorescent protein, Pt-GFP, is used by biologists as a pH sensor because its glow changes with acidity and resists fading.

systems.title: Chemical defence
systems.text: It produces a mild toxin, ptilosarcone, whose role has not been well studied.

mind.lede: Decisions without a brain: the sea pen's responses are graded to the threat.

studies.title: A food web around one animal
studies.text: A Puget Sound study found the sea pen feeds at least seven predators — four sea stars and three sea slugs — and worked out how each one affects its numbers.

studies.title: Telling predators apart
studies.text: Leather stars made 73% of sea pens burrow, the generalist sunflower star only 23%, and the harmless ochre star little more than a glass rod did.

studies.title: Not the first after all
studies.text: The 2002 authors had called theirs the first evidence of predator classification in cnidarians. After colleagues pointed to earlier studies, they agreed that claim was incorrect.

survival.lede: Standing tall on open sediment, a sea pen is one of the largest meals on the seafloor.

tactics.title: Dive into the sand
tactics.text: Threatened, it deflates and pulls down into its base and the sediment, though some soft tissue may remain exposed.

tactics.title: Flash a warning
tactics.text: A greenish-blue light runs up and down the stalk when it is disturbed, which may startle predators.

tactics.title: Not enough on its own
tactics.text: Its refuges and escapes do not fully explain how it stays abundant. Adult-eating predators take about 3% of adults each year, picking the largest pens.

life.lede: A sea pen starts as a drifting egg and builds itself, polyp by polyp, into a colony that can live for well over a decade.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: Colonies breed in spring, releasing eggs that drift in the water.

stages.name: Planula larva
stages.text: The eggs develop into planula larvae, which settle on the seafloor and become a single tiny polyp.

stages.name: Young colony
stages.text: The first polyp clones itself again and again to build the colony. In dense patches, 97% of young pens die in their first year, mostly eaten by sea slugs and a sea star.

stages.name: Mature colony
stages.text: Sea pens take five or six years to reach sexual maturity, In the Puget Sound population studied, adults spanned about ten year classes.

lifespan.value: 15 years or more

tagline: A see-through sea cucumber that walks the abyss on stilts
summary: Sea pigs are plump, translucent sea cucumbers that roam muddy deep-sea plains. Most sea cucumbers have stubby tube feet hidden underneath, but sea pigs stand on long, leg-like ones as they hoover up organic bits from the mud. Large herds gather at sunken whale carcasses.

stats.size: Typically 4–15 cm long; up to about 17 cm
stats.range: Deep seafloors worldwide
stats.diet: Seafloor mud and detritus (organic particles sinking from above)

facts.title: Legs that are feet
facts.text: The 'legs' are enlarged tube feet. Sea pigs use these long, stilt-like tube feet to hold their bodies above the soft mud as they walk.

facts.title: Mud for dinner
facts.text: Like most sea cucumbers, sea pigs eat seafloor mud and detritus: bits of dead algae and animals that sink from the sunlit waters far above.

facts.title: Crab nurseries on legs
facts.text: In video of about 2,600 sea pigs off Monterey Bay, almost a quarter carried juvenile king crabs. Ninety-six percent of the young crabs seen on open mud were riding on or hiding under sea pigs.

facts.title: Shelter on bare mud
facts.text: Researchers think the crabs use sea pigs to hide from predators, since little else rises above the flat mud. What the sea pig gets out of the arrangement, if anything, is unknown.

facts.title: Herds at whale falls
facts.text: Sea pigs are among the most commonly seen deep-sea animals off Monterey Bay, and huge groups have been spotted feeding near sunken whale carcasses.

notes: This is a genus-level entry, Scotoplanes spp. (WoRMS AphiaID 123520). MBARI itself refers to its animals as Scotoplanes sp. The hero is a NOAA/MBARI ROV frame, filed on Commons as S. globosa and from the Monterey Bay sanctuary (SIMoN) photo archive; species-level ID from video is tentative. All other Commons 'Scotoplanes' images are preserved USNM museum specimens. 'Hooked-nosed Sea Pig' on Commons is actually a grey seal and was rejected. Ref [2]: the crab study is Barry et al. 2016, Marine Ecology 38:e12396. The MBARI animal page gives a maximum size of 17 cm and the crab article gives 4–15 cm for animals off Monterey Bay. 'Transparent' is based on MBARI calling them 'see-through sea cucumbers'.

anatomy.lede: A sea pig is a sea cucumber rebuilt for walking: its tube feet have become legs, its back sprouts tall flexible papillae, and a ring of tentacles at the front shovels up mud.

hotspots.label: Feeding tentacles
hotspots.text: Ten tentacles surround the mouth, their surface deeply folded. They gather mud and fresh detritus from the seafloor.

hotspots.label: Dorsal papilla
hotspots.text: The long projections on the back are papillae. Under the microscope they resemble tube feet, each with a large muscular water canal running through the middle.

hotspots.label: Papillae
hotspots.text: Papillae rise from the upper side of the body, giving the sea pig its odd, horned outline.

hotspots.label: See-through body
hotspots.text: The body is pale and translucent, which is why MBARI calls sea pigs 'see-through sea cucumbers'.

hotspots.label: Walking tube feet
hotspots.text: Six pairs of greatly enlarged tube feet grow from the sides of the body and point downwards for walking, holding the body above the soft mud.

hotspots.label: Juvenile king crab
hotspots.text: A young king crab sheltering underneath. Off central California, 22% of nearly 2,600 sea pigs observed had at least one juvenile crab with them.

body.lede: Very few sea pigs have ever been examined under a microscope. A 2021 study of two animals from Monterey Bay found a body similar to other sea cucumbers — with some surprises.

systems.title: Breathing through its feet?
systems.text: Many sea cucumbers breathe with internal 'respiratory trees', but none was found in sea pigs. The large tube feet may take over the job of gas exchange.

systems.title: Hydraulic limbs
systems.text: Like all echinoderms, sea pigs move their tube feet and papillae with a water vascular system: fluid-filled canals run through the centre of each projection.

systems.title: A picky mud-eater
systems.text: Sea pigs in the Santa Catalina Basin had more freshly settled particles in their guts than in the surrounding mud, suggesting they select food that reached the seafloor within roughly the previous 20 days.

systems.title: A skin full of bacteria
systems.text: In sea pigs from the north-west Pacific, a single newly described bacterium made up 76–99% of the microbes in the body wall, forming clusters on the skin's outer side. Its role is still unknown.

genome.lede: No reference genome for a sea pig has been published. A rough, highly fragmented draft for Scotoplanes globosa was deposited in NCBI in 2023 without an accompanying paper.

findings.title: Mitochondrial genomes
findings.text: The much smaller mitochondrial genome has been fully sequenced for an unnamed Scotoplanes species (2018) and for Scotoplanes clarki (2024).

tagline: The white owl that hunts the Arctic summer in daylight
summary: A large, mostly white owl of the open Arctic tundra that, unlike most owls, hunts largely by day. Its life is tied to lemmings: satellite-tagged females roam thousands of kilometres each spring in search of a lemming boom to breed on, and some spend the winter far out on the sea ice.

stats.size: 63–73 cm long; wingspan about 1.4–1.7 m; 0.7–2.9 kg, females larger and heavier than males
stats.habitat: Open, treeless Arctic tundra; in winter also coasts, prairies, marshes and sea ice
stats.elevation: Usually from sea level to below 300 m on the breeding grounds
stats.range: Circumpolar Arctic; in some winters irrupts far south into southern Canada, the northern United States, Europe and Asia
stats.diet: Mainly lemmings, voles and other small rodents; probably seabirds when wintering on the sea ice

facts.title: An owl of the daylight
facts.text: Unlike most owls, snowy owls are largely active by day — an advantage in an Arctic summer when the sun never sets.

facts.title: 1,600 lemmings a year
facts.text: A single snowy owl may eat more than 1,600 lemmings in a year. The number of eggs it lays, usually 3 to 11, depends on how much prey is around.

facts.title: Roaming in search of a lemming boom
facts.text: Nine breeding females tracked by satellite for up to three years searched for up to 108 days and travelled up to 4,093 km each spring before settling where lemmings were plentiful. On average they nested 725 km from where they had bred the year before.

facts.title: Wintering on the sea ice
facts.text: Most satellite-tracked adult females that breed in the Canadian Arctic stayed at high latitudes in winter and spent up to 101 days on the sea ice, gathering around patches of open water where seabirds also gather. The ocean, it seems, helps feed this tundra hunter through the winter.

facts.title: Wings that whisper
facts.text: Like other owls, the snowy owl has soft, fringed edges and a velvety surface on its flight feathers, which let it fly almost silently. A 2020 review argues that these features mainly reduce the sound of feathers rubbing together. It is not yet settled whether silence helps owls sneak up on prey or lets them hear it better.

facts.title: Dressed for the cold
facts.text: White feathers cover even the legs and feet, protecting them from the cold. Males can become almost completely white as they age, while females keep more dark markings.

notes: Size: length (63–73 cm) is from ADW. Wingspan sources differ (ADW gives an average of 170 cm, the Peregrine Fund 4.5 ft, about 1.4 m), so a range is given. Mass is the Peregrine Fund's 1.5–6.5 lb, converted to 0.7–2.9 kg. The ADW account is filed under the old name Nyctea scandiaca; the Bubo scandiacus URL returns a 404 page. Daytime hunting, 1,600 lemmings a year, clutch of 3–11, habitat below 300 m, feathered feet and plumage differences are from ADW. Sea ice (up to 101 days, December–April, around open water) is from the Therrien et al. 2011 abstract. Spring searching (up to 108 days and 4,093 km; dispersal averaging 725 km, range 18–2,224 km) is from the Therrien et al. 2014 abstract (9 satellite-tracked breeding females, Canadian Arctic). Silent flight: the Peregrine Fund describes the soft, feathery feather edges. Clark et al. 2020 is a review of owls in general, not of snowy owls specifically, so that fact is marked 'hypothesis'. Categories: apex-predators because Therrien et al. call it 'a top predator of the tundra'; migrations for its irruptive, nomadic movements (Therrien et al. 2014 call the owls 'irruptive migrants'). It is not shelved as nocturnal because it is largely diurnal, and VU does not meet the EN/CR bar. Regions: arctic-tundra (breeding), plus north-american-forests for winter irruptions into southern Canada and the northern US (Peregrine Fund). I added no Eurasian winter region because I had no specific source. elevationRange is approximate (ADW: 'sea level to less than 300 m'). Images: alt-1 (Jones Beach, a Quality Image) shows a heavily barred bird, typical of females and young, but its sex and age are not stated. alt-2 has a small photographer's signature ('Golden Bright') in the bottom-right corner, and its location is not given. The IUCN status (VU) and ID were confirmed via GBIF's IUCN checklist and the DOI handle API. rspb.org.uk's snowy-owl page now returns a 404 and allaboutbirds.org returns 403, so neither is cited.

anatomy.lede: A snowy owl is a heavy, round-headed owl wrapped in dense white feathers, with forward-facing yellow eyes and a neck that lets it scan the open tundra without moving its body.

hotspots.label: Head
hotspots.text: Like other owls it can swivel its head about 270 degrees, three-quarters of the way round, to scan for prey.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Bright yellow eyes face forwards. This owl hunts mostly in daylight, often watching from a post, rock or low rise.

hotspots.label: Bill
hotspots.text: The black, hooked bill is largely hidden in the feathers of the face.

hotspots.label: Dark barring
hotspots.text: White feathers are marked with dusky brown spots and bars. Females usually carry more markings, while some adults become almost pure white with age.

hotspots.label: Wing tips
hotspots.text: The ends of the flight feathers are very soft and feathery, which helps the owl fly almost silently.

senses.lede: On the treeless tundra, a snowy owl watches by day and listens for what it cannot see.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Unusually for an owl, it hunts mainly by day, scanning open ground from a perch before swooping on prey.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Sharp hearing lets it pinpoint a vole moving beneath the snow, then pounce and grab it without ever seeing it.

body.lede: Living year-round where winters are long and dark, the snowy owl's body is built for cold.

systems.title: Feathers to the toes
systems.text: The feathers on its legs and feet are more densely layered than in owls of warmer climates, insulating the feet against snow and ice.

systems.title: Quiet wings
systems.text: Owl flight feathers have soft fringes and a velvety surface. A 2020 review suggests these mainly reduce the noise of feathers rubbing together as the wings move.

systems.title: A big appetite
systems.text: An owl needs several lemmings or voles a day just to survive, and a family with chicks can eat dozens a day.

genome.lede: A chromosome-level snowy owl genome, from a captive-bred female, was shared as a preprint in 2024 and published in 2026. It turned out to be one of the most repeat-rich bird genomes known.

findings.title: Unusually full of repeats
findings.text: About 28% of the snowy owl genome is repetitive DNA, compared with an average of around 10% in other birds — among the highest share reported for any bird.

findings.title: Giant centromere arrays
findings.text: Most of these repeats are satellite DNA at the centromeres, forming large blocks on several chromosomes — one of the biggest centromere expansions found in birds.

findings.title: New centromeres, new species?
findings.text: The owl's centromeres sit in different places from the chicken's, at points where chromosomes have been rearranged. The authors suggest this rapid change may have helped the snowy owl become a separate species.

mind.lede: Mostly solitary outside the breeding season, snowy owls communicate with displays and a surprising range of calls.

studies.title: Courtship displays
studies.text: Males court and threaten with displays both in the air and on the ground.

studies.title: Many voices
studies.text: Males hoot, mainly to defend territory. Both sexes also give barking 'rick, rick, rick' and 'kre kre kre' calls, mews and hisses, especially when disturbed near the nest.

studies.title: Sit and wait
studies.text: Snowy owls usually hunt from posts, rocks or the ground, watching quietly. They also snatch fish from the water's surface and even catch prey while walking.

survival.lede: Adults have few enemies, but eggs and chicks on an open tundra nest are exposed.

tactics.title: A guard on duty
tactics.text: While the female incubates and broods, the male stands guard near the nest.

tactics.title: Dive-bombs and decoys
tactics.text: Both parents dive at approaching predators and use distraction displays to lure them away from the nest.

threats.title: Collisions and shooting
threats.text: Common causes of death include collisions with vehicles, power lines and aircraft, shooting, electrocution and entanglement in fishing gear.

threats.title: A warming Arctic
threats.text: Climate change may be one of the biggest threats, as the Arctic is warming almost twice as fast as the global average.

life.lede: A snowy owl's breeding year depends on lemmings: in good years a pair raises a large brood, in poor years it may not breed at all.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays an egg about every two days; a clutch can reach 16 eggs when prey is extremely abundant.

stages.name: Nestling
stages.text: Chicks hatch roughly a day or two apart, so a brood ranges widely in size. They leave the nest on foot at 14–26 days, before they can fly.

stages.name: Fledgling
stages.text: Young owls master flight at about eight weeks old, and parents keep feeding them for several weeks until they can hunt.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Young owls are thought to be ready to breed at about two years old.

lifespan.value: Oldest known wild bird at least 9 years 5 months; 28 years in captivity

tagline: A deep-diving hunter with the loudest voice on Earth
summary: The largest toothed whale, with a vast, square head that holds an oil-filled organ used to focus sound. It hunts squid and fish in dives that routinely pass 600 m and last around 45 minutes, finding prey by echolocation in total darkness, and lives in close-knit family groups of females and young.
ability: long-range biosonar from an enormous sound-making nose

stats.size: Males up to about 16 m and 40 tonnes; females up to about 12 m and 14 tonnes
stats.depth: Foraging dives usually about 600–1,000 m; tracked dives to 1,185 m and possibly 2,000 m
stats.range: All deep oceans, from the equator to the edges of the Arctic and Antarctic pack ice; females and young stay in warmer waters
stats.diet: Mainly deep-water squid; also sharks, skates and other fishes

facts.title: A head full of oil
facts.text: The head makes up about a third of the body. It contains spermaceti, a waxy oil once prized by whalers for lamps and candles, which helps the whale focus sound.

facts.title: The loudest animal sound
facts.text: Recorded on-axis off Norway, sperm whale clicks reached source levels of up to 236 decibels (re 1 µPa) in a narrow, forward beam: by far the loudest sounds measured from any animal.

facts.title: Hunting in the dark
facts.text: Digital tags on 37 whales in the Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico and Ligurian Sea showed average maximum dive depths of 644–985 m depending on region. A typical cycle was a 45-minute dive followed by about 9 minutes at the surface.

facts.title: Over a kilometre down
facts.text: Two males tracked by sonar off Dominica in 1991 regularly dived to 400–600 m, once to 1,185 m and possibly once to 2,000 m.

facts.title: Families of females
facts.text: Females and their young live in lasting social units, on average about 12 females with their calves. Young males leave at 4–21 years old to join bachelor groups, and the biggest males travel alone towards the poles.

facts.title: One calf every few years
facts.text: After a 14–16-month pregnancy a single calf about 4 m long is born. Females have a calf only about once every five to seven years, which is why whaling hit the species so hard.

The Mediterranean subpopulation has its own, separate listing. NOAA gives weights in US tons (45 and 15 tons), converted to about 40 and 14 tonnes; 13 ft calf ≈ 4 m. Depth gauge max uses the 1,185 m sonar-tracked dive (Watkins et al. 1993); the 'possibly 2,000 m' dive was not certain in the source. Arctic Ocean included because NOAA gives the range as reaching the edge of the Arctic pack ice (large males only). 'Intelligent' shelf based on documented vocal clans and culture (see deep chapter). anatomy.lede: A sperm whale is built around its head: a huge, blunt block that holds the machinery for the most powerful sounds in the animal kingdom.

hotspots.label: Head and spermaceti
hotspots.text: The head is about a third of the body's length. It holds spermaceti, a waxy oil in a sac that helps the whale focus sound.

hotspots.label: Lower jaw
hotspots.text: The narrow lower jaw carries 20–26 large teeth on each side. Teeth in the upper jaw rarely break through the gums.

hotspots.label: Wrinkled skin
hotspots.text: The skin just behind the head is often wrinkled, and the body is mostly dark grey.

hotspots.label: Dorsal hump
hotspots.text: Instead of a tall fin, the sperm whale has a low, thick, usually rounded dorsal fin.

hotspots.label: Flukes
hotspots.text: Broad triangular flukes power foraging dives that last about 45 minutes on average.

hotspots.label: Calf
hotspots.text: A calf is about 4 m long at birth. It starts eating solid food before its first birthday but keeps nursing for several years.

stats.label: Length of a fully grown male
Teeth on each side of the lower jaw

senses.lede: Hundreds of metres down there is no sunlight, so the sperm whale hunts, navigates and keeps in touch almost entirely through sound.

senses.name: Long-range biosonar
senses.text: Whales start regular clicking on the way down and descend about 390 m on average before the first 'buzz', a rapid click burst that marks an attempt to catch prey. This suggests the clicks work as long-range sonar; tagged whales made about 18 buzzes per dive.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Sperm whales depend on sound to communicate. Ship and industrial noise shrinks the distance over which they can hear each other and, if loud enough, can damage their hearing.

senses.name: Coda clicks
senses.text: Socialising whales exchange codas, short patterned sequences of clicks. A 2024 analysis found the codas vary in rhythm, tempo, 'rubato' and 'ornamentation', making nearly ten times more distinct codas than had been recognised.

body.lede: The sperm whale's body is shaped by two demands: making extremely powerful sounds, and spending most of its life on long, deep dives.

systems.title: A nose that makes sonar
systems.text: Clicks recorded head-on are single pulses about 100 microseconds long, focused in a narrow forward beam. This supports the idea that the whale's huge nose works as a sound generator.

systems.title: One blowhole, on the left
systems.text: It is the only living whale or dolphin with a single blowhole set off-centre, on the left side of the crown of the head.

systems.title: Built for endurance
systems.text: Tagged whales spent more than 72% of their time in foraging dive cycles, needing only about 9 minutes at the surface between 45-minute dives. The researchers credit efficient swimming and a large capacity to dive on stored oxygen.

systems.title: A big appetite
systems.text: A sperm whale eats about 3–3.5% of its body weight each day, mostly deep-water squid and fish.

genome.lede: The sperm whale was among the first whales to have its genome assembled, and a later chromosome-level assembly is now the standard reference.

findings.title: Skin genes and an Ice Age decline
findings.text: The first sperm whale genome pointed to genes for skin integrity as especially important in whales, and showed a steep fall in population size in the early Pleistocene.

findings.title: Chromosome-level genome
findings.text: The first chromosome-level genome for any marine mammal, from a stranded female sperm whale, showed many repeated LINE elements, expanded gene families and fewer genes in the immune MHC region.

findings.title: One global gene pool
findings.text: Whole genomes of 45 whales from the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans showed almost no genetic structure, suggesting a single, globally mixing population. The Mediterranean whales were the exception and form a distinct group.

mind.lede: Sperm whales live in long-lasting family groups whose calls differ in ways that look like culture.

studies.title: Vocal clans
studies.text: Coda repertoires recorded in the South Pacific and Caribbean between 1985 and 2000 split the whales into six acoustic 'clans'. These clans overlap in range across thousands of kilometres, and family units prefer to group with units of their own clan.

studies.title: Codas as building blocks
studies.text: Whales adjust the timing of their codas to the conversation and copy each other's adjustments, combining a few features into a large set of distinct codas. What the codas mean remains unknown.

studies.title: Stealing from fishing lines
studies.text: Some sperm whales pull fish off longlines by using their jaws to tension the line until fish shake off the hooks. Scientists think this behaviour may be learned from other whales.

studies.title: Following the fishing boat
studies.text: A satellite-tagged sperm whale off South Georgia followed a fishing vessel for more than 180 km over six days, repeatedly taking toothfish as the lines were hauled in.

survival.lede: Their size and deep habitat were once thought to make sperm whales safe from predators. Close observation showed otherwise.

tactics.title: The marguerite
tactics.text: Attacked by about 35 killer whales off California in 1997, nine sperm whales formed a rosette with their heads together and tails pointing out.

tactics.title: Rescuing the isolated
tactics.text: When a whale was pulled out of the formation, one or two others left the rosette to flank it and guide it back, putting themselves at greater risk.

tactics.title: Strength in families
tactics.text: Females and young live in stable social units of about 12 females with their calves, staying with the same unit for life.

threats.title: The legacy of whaling
threats.text: Sperm whales were a main target of commercial whaling from 1800 to the 1980s, which nearly wiped out many populations. They are still recovering.

threats.title: Ship strikes
threats.text: Between deep dives sperm whales rest at the surface, often for up to 10 minutes. This 'rafting' leaves them exposed to collisions as shipping increases.

threats.title: Fishing gear and debris
threats.text: They can become tangled in traps, pots and gillnets, and may swallow marine debris in the deep layers where they feed.

life.lede: Sperm whales grow slowly and breed rarely, and males and females follow very different paths through life.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: A single calf, about 4 m long, is born after a pregnancy of well over a year.

stages.name: Calf
stages.text: Calves eat some solid food before their first birthday but keep nursing for several years, growing up within their mother's social unit.

stages.name: Young males leave
stages.text: Young males leave their family and join 'bachelor' groups of males of similar age. As they grow, they move towards the poles and the largest end up alone.

stages.name: Adult female
stages.text: Females mature at about 9 years and then have a calf only about once every five to seven years. They reach full size, up to about 11 m, at around 30.

stages.name: Breeding male
stages.text: Males keep growing into their 30s and reach full size at about 50. They rarely breed before their late twenties, when they return to the tropics to mate.

lifespan.value: Up to about 60 years

tagline: A buried ambusher that stares up at the sky
summary: Stargazers spend most of their lives buried in sand with only their upward-facing eyes showing. The whitemargin stargazer of the Indo-Pacific waits beneath the seabed, can dangle a lure from its mouth to draw prey close, and carries a venomous spine on each shoulder.

stats.size: Up to about 45 cm long
stats.depth: About 5–350 m
stats.range: Indo-Pacific: Red Sea to Indonesia, Fiji, Samoa and Tonga; also Réunion
stats.diet: Small bottom-living fishes and invertebrates

facts.title: Eyes to the sky
facts.text: Stargazers are named for eyes set on top of the head. This species is rarely seen because it lies buried in sand or mud most of the time, with only its eyes showing.

facts.title: Built-in sand filter
facts.text: While buried, a fringe of small fleshy flaps (cirri) around the edge of its mouth keeps sand out as it breathes.

facts.title: Fishing with a lure
facts.text: It has a lure in its mouth, used to attract prey within striking range before it lunges up from the sand.

facts.title: Venomous shoulders
facts.text: A venomous spine sits on each shoulder (the cleithral spine). Wounds can be serious — a hazard for anyone stepping on or handling a buried stargazer.

facts.title: Shocking cousins
facts.text: Some stargazers in the genus Astroscopus, from the western Atlantic, can produce electric discharges from organs built from modified eye muscles. The whitemargin stargazer is not one of them.

anatomy.lede: A broad, flat head with eyes and mouth pointing upwards: the whitemargin stargazer is built to wait under the sand.

hotspots.label: Upward-facing eye
hotspots.text: The eyes sit on top of the head, the feature that gives the family its name. Buried, the fish leaves little but its eyes showing.

hotspots.label: Upturned mouth
hotspots.text: The fringe of small fleshy cirri along the edge of the mouth keeps sand out while the buried fish breathes. Inside is a lure that draws prey within striking range.

hotspots.label: Shoulder spine
hotspots.text: Behind the gill cover and above the pectoral fin sits a venomous cleithral spine, one on each side.

hotspots.label: Black first dorsal fin
hotspots.text: The black first dorsal fin, with four spines, is one of the marks that identify this species.

survival.lede: The stargazer hunts and hides in the same way: by staying buried and still.

tactics.title: Ambush from below
tactics.text: Stargazers bury themselves in sand and then leap up to seize fish and invertebrates passing overhead.

tactics.title: Hidden in plain sight
tactics.text: This species spends most of its time buried in sand or mud, which is why it is so rarely seen.

tactics.title: Two venomous spines
tactics.text: Stargazers carry two large venomous spines behind the gill covers, above the pectoral fins.

threats.title: Fishing
threats.text: FishBase rates this species as moderately vulnerable to fishing. Its status is Least Concern, last assessed in 2023.

tagline: A hunter with a secret red searchlight
summary: A slender black dragonfish that shines red light from an organ beneath each eye—a colour almost no other deep-sea animal can see. Its own eyes are tuned to red, giving it a private beam for spotting prey that never knows it is lit.

stats.size: Up to about 25 cm
stats.depth: About 500–3,900 m; thought to stay below 500 m
stats.range: All oceans, from about 66°N to about 30°S; not known from the Mediterranean
stats.diet: Fishes, crustaceans and large copepods

facts.title: Two kinds of light
facts.text: Like most deep-sea animals it has a blue light organ, just behind the eye. But a large organ beneath the eye glows far-red—the 'stoplight' that gives the fish its name.

facts.title: A private waveband
facts.text: Red light barely travels in seawater, so nearly all deep-sea animals have lost the ability to see it. A red beam may let the loosejaw illuminate prey and signal to its own kind without being noticed.

facts.title: Borrowed pigment for red vision
facts.text: Unusually, its retina holds a pigment derived from bacteriochlorophyll (a bacterial cousin of chlorophyll) that boosts sensitivity to red light. Its similarity to pigments in copepods the fish eats suggests a dietary origin.

facts.title: Where the pigment comes from
facts.text: A 2016 study looked for bacteria in the eye that might make the pigment and found none; the chemical was spread throughout the retina, and its origin remains unclear.

facts.title: A hinged head
facts.text: A flexible joint between the back of the skull and the first vertebra lets it tip its head far back, widening its gape to swallow large prey.

anatomy.lede: A long black fish with two kinds of headlight, an eye tuned to red, and a jaw that swings open like a trapdoor.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Its retina holds two visual pigments most sensitive at about 520 and 540 nm, plus a chlorophyll-derived pigment that boosts its sensitivity to red.

hotspots.label: Far-red light organ
hotspots.text: The light organ below the eye shines far-red, peaking above 700 nm. Far-red light organs like this may have evolved up to three times among the loosejaw dragonfishes.

hotspots.label: Postorbital light organ
hotspots.text: A smaller light organ behind the eye gives off blue light, like those of most deep-sea animals.

hotspots.label: Head joint
hotspots.text: Where the skull meets the spine, only a flexible notochord remains. It lets the head tip far up and back, opening the mouth to a gape of up to 120 degrees.

hotspots.label: Lower jaw
hotspots.text: Its jaws are long and its prey relatively large. Compared with its southern look-alike, Malacosteus australis, its jaws are somewhat larger.

stats.label: Peak wavelength of its red light

senses.lede: In a sea where almost every eye sees only blue, the loosejaw can see the red light it makes.

senses.name: A borrowed red boost
senses.text: It lacks the most red-sensitive visual pigments found in its relatives, and instead uses a mixture of altered bacteriochlorophyll c and d to extend its sensitivity into the red.

senses.name: A single opsin gene
senses.text: Molecular analysis found only one opsin gene in its genome, forming a pigment pair with two slightly different versions of the light-catching chromophore.

senses.name: Bigger eyes in males
senses.text: Males have larger eye lenses than females. A model suggests this lets them spot the light organs of the opposite sex from farther away.

body.lede: The loosejaw's head is built for two jobs: making unusual light and swallowing big prey.

systems.title: A true head joint
systems.text: In most bony fishes the shoulder girdle is braced against the skull. In loosejaws it is not, and a folded sheath of notochord forms a working joint between skull and spine.

systems.title: Lights wired to different nerves
systems.text: The far-red organ of Malacosteus is supplied by a different branch of the trigeminal nerve than the similar organs of related genera, evidence that red light evolved separately in each.

genome.lede: No nuclear genome has been published, but its mitochondrial genome is one of the odder ones known in fishes.

findings.title: A large, complex mitogenome
findings.text: Its mitochondrial genome is 21,263 base pairs long, with two copies of a 1,198 bp inverted repeat and a long run of short repeated elements.

mind.lede: No one has watched a stoplight loosejaw hunt or court, so its behaviour is inferred from its body.

studies.title: A private waveband
studies.text: Because other deep-sea animals are blind to far-red light, loosejaws may use it to light up prey and signal to their own kind unseen.

studies.title: Closing the detection gap
studies.text: Males have larger postorbital light organs, so females should see males first. Larger eyes in males may even out the distance at which each sex can find the other.

survival.lede: Living below the reach of sunlight, the loosejaw hunts with a light its prey cannot see.

tactics.title: An invisible searchlight
tactics.text: Red light does not penetrate deep water, so most deep-sea prey cannot see it, and the fish can light up its prey unseen.

tactics.title: Staying deep
tactics.text: It has been suggested that, unlike many deep-sea fishes, it does not migrate up towards the surface at night and stays below 500 m.

tagline: Neither vampire nor squid, but a gentle snow-eater
summary: Despite its name, the vampire squid is neither a vampire nor a squid but the last surviving member of an ancient cephalopod group. It drifts through the low-oxygen twilight zone, gathering 'marine snow', the sinking debris of the waters above, with two long sticky filaments.

stats.size: Up to about 30 cm total length
stats.depth: Mostly 600–900 m
stats.range: Worldwide in tropical and temperate seas
stats.diet: Marine snow (sinking organic debris); also small zooplankton
stats.conservation: No IUCN assessment found in sources checked

facts.title: A living fossil
facts.text: Its scientific name means 'vampire squid from hell', yet it is the only living member of its family and the last survivor of an ancient lineage, distinct from both squids and octopuses.

facts.title: Mucus dumplings
facts.text: It traps falling marine snow on two sticky filaments, pulls them through its arms, and wraps the particles in mucus before passing the 'dumpling' to its mouth. It is the only cephalopod known to feed mainly as a scavenger.

facts.title: The pineapple pose
facts.text: When threatened it flips its webbed arms up over its body like a cloak, showing spiky-looking fleshy cirri. If danger persists, its arm tips glow blue, and it can release a glowing cloud instead of ink.

facts.title: Built for low oxygen
facts.text: It thrives in the oxygen minimum zone, where few predators can follow. A very slow metabolism and blood with an unusually high affinity for oxygen help it get by.

facts.title: Many spawnings
facts.text: Unlike most cephalopods, which breed once and die, female vampire squid appear to spawn repeatedly, releasing a few eggs at a time.
