anatomy.lede: Carl Chun's 1903 plate shows the vampire squid as it looks when calm: a soft, dark body, one pair of fins, enormous eyes and eight arms joined by a deep web like an umbrella.

hotspots.label: Fins
hotspots.text: Adults have a single pair of fins on the mantle. Gentle fin strokes are often the only movement seen as the animal hangs almost still in the water.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The body is soft and gelatinous, only slightly denser than seawater, so the animal stays afloat with very little effort.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: About 2.5 cm across on a body up to 30 cm long, these are the largest eyes of any living animal in proportion to its size. They are clear, and only look blue when lit by a submersible's lamps.

hotspots.label: Web
hotspots.text: A wide web of skin links the eight arms. When startled, the animal turns it inside out over its body like a cloak.

hotspots.label: Arm tips
hotspots.text: A small light organ at the tip of each of the eight arms gives off blue light, usually when the animal is touched.

hotspots.label: Cirri
hotspots.text: Rows of soft, finger-like cirri line the inside of the arms. They help move mucus-bound food along to the mouth.

senses.lede: In water where almost no sunlight reaches, the vampire squid relies on huge eyes and on two long filaments that feel the water around it.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Its eyes are the largest of any animal relative to body size. Its keen sight probably lets it pick out the largest flakes of marine snow drifting past.

senses.name: Sensory filaments
senses.text: The two retractile filaments carry large, apparently sensory cells linked to a thick nerve that runs to the brain. They are thought to detect food and perhaps approaching predators.

body.lede: The vampire squid lives where oxygen is scarce and food arrives slowly from above. Its body is built to spend as little energy as possible.

systems.title: The slowest cephalopod metabolism
systems.text: Measured against 33 other open-ocean cephalopods, it had the lowest metabolic rate. One individual of about 1 kg used oxygen more slowly, for its weight, than any cephalopod ever measured.

systems.title: Blood that grabs oxygen
systems.text: Large gills and a copper-based blood pigment, haemocyanin, with the highest affinity for oxygen known in any cephalopod help it take up the little oxygen around it.

systems.title: Light instead of ink
systems.text: It produces no ink. Instead, its arm tips can release a sticky fluid full of tiny glowing particles that forms a luminous cloud, powered by the light-making chemicals coelenterazine and luciferase.

systems.title: No colour change
systems.text: Many cephalopods change colour using muscles around their pigment sacs. The vampire squid lacks these muscles, so it stays a dark reddish brown.

genome.lede: A 2025 study sequenced the genome of a vampire squid caught in the western Pacific, identified only as Vampyroteuthis sp. It is the largest cephalopod genome sequenced so far.

findings.title: A giant genome
findings.text: After duplicated stretches were removed, the assembly was 11.7 billion base pairs, close to the 11.5–11.8 billion estimated from DNA reads. At least 62% of it is repetitive DNA.

findings.title: Squid-like chromosomes
findings.text: Although it has eight arms like an octopus, its genome keeps much of the chromosome layout seen in squids and cuttlefish. This suggests that octopuses' fewer, more tangled chromosomes arose later through fusions and swaps.

mind.lede: Watched by remotely operated vehicles off California, the vampire squid turned out to behave unlike any other cephalopod.

studies.title: Lights on contact
studies.text: Live animals brought gently to a laboratory showed two kinds of light display: glowing arm tips, readily triggered by touch, and a luminous cloud released only under stronger provocation.

studies.title: Fishing with a thread
studies.text: Video from submersibles showed animals hanging still with one filament stretched out to collect drifting debris, rarely both at once. Laboratory feeding confirmed that the filaments, not the arms, capture the food.

studies.title: A diet that changes with age
studies.text: Chemical signatures in the beaks of 104 animals from three oceans showed that young vampire squid hunt small zooplankton, while larger ones drift and feed more on sinking organic particles — the reverse of the pattern in most cephalopods.

survival.lede: The oxygen-poor water it lives in keeps most hunters away. For the rest, the vampire squid relies on staying hidden and on confusing displays rather than speed.

tactics.title: A refuge in low oxygen
tactics.text: By feeding on marine snow, it can spend most of its life at depths where oxygen is very low but predators are few.

tactics.title: Hidden by colour
tactics.text: Its dark colouring makes it hard to see in the dim twilight zone, where red light does not reach.

tactics.title: Confusing displays
tactics.text: Rather than swimming hard to escape, it probably relies on its camouflage and its glowing arm tips and light clouds. Only short bursts of swimming are thought to be needed.

life.lede: Most cephalopods breed once and die. Female vampire squid appear to spawn many times, resting in between.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Females release their eggs one at a time into open water rather than guarding a clutch.

stages.name: Young juvenile
stages.text: Small young have a pair of fins near the front of the body and actively hunt small zooplankton.

stages.name: Older juvenile
stages.text: For a time, growing juveniles carry two pairs of fins before reaching the adult form with a single pair.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Mature females keep thousands of immature egg cells and ripen batches of about 100 at a time. Between spawnings the ovary returns to a resting state, which has not been seen in other soft-bodied cephalopods.

lifespan.value: Possibly up to a decade (estimated, not measured)

tagline: A spotted dragon drifting through the kelp
summary: Also called the common seadragon, this slender relative of seahorses lives on kelp reefs and seagrass beds along southern Australia. Its reddish body is sprinkled with yellow spots and trimmed with small leafy flaps, and — as with all seadragons — the male carries the eggs.

stats.size: Commonly about 30 cm; up to 45 cm
stats.depth: About 1–50 m
stats.range: Southern Australia, from about Newcastle (NSW) to Tasmania and west to about Geraldton (WA)
stats.diet: Tiny crustaceans, especially mysids

facts.title: Father as nursery
facts.text: Males carry and nourish up to 250 developing eggs on a special patch on the underside of the tail, and some raise two broods in a breeding season.

facts.title: Stealthy hunter
facts.text: Seadragons are ambush predators: relying on camouflage and slow, stealthy approach, they suck up mysids and other tiny crustaceans through a long, tube-like snout.

facts.title: Homebodies
facts.text: Seadragons are a little more mobile than seahorses, yet tend to stay within a home range of roughly 500 m throughout their lives.

facts.title: Victoria's sea emblem
facts.text: The weedy (common) seadragon is the official marine emblem of the Australian state of Victoria.

facts.title: A worrying trend?
facts.text: Citizen-science dive surveys suggested a 59% population decline between 2011 and 2021, and the species is now listed as Vulnerable — though some researchers argue the data are too sparse to be sure of the trend.

anatomy.lede: A weedy seadragon is a seahorse stretched out straight: a long tube of a snout, an armoured body and a slender tail, all decorated with small leafy flaps that mimic drifting weed.

hotspots.label: Snout
hotspots.text: The long, tube-like snout ends in a tiny mouth at the tip. Prey such as mysids are sucked in through it.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Seadragons are ambush predators. They rely on camouflage and a slow, stealthy approach to get close to tiny crustaceans.

hotspots.label: Leafy flap
hotspots.text: Flat, oval skin flaps grow on the enlarged spines of the head and body. They give the species its 'weedy' name.

hotspots.label: Armoured trunk
hotspots.text: The body is encased in rings of bony plates. The pattern of spots and blotches on each side is unique to each seadragon and does not change.

hotspots.label: Bars
hotspots.text: Bluish bars cross the sides of the trunk, while fine yellow spots dust the head and back. Colours vary from reddish orange to purplish.

hotspots.label: Belly flaps
hotspots.text: More leafy flaps hang below the body. With the seadragon's colours they help it vanish among kelp and seagrass.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: In males, the underside of the tail holds a special patch where the fertilised eggs are carried and nourished until they hatch.

body.lede: Seadragons share the strange body plan of the seahorse family: armour instead of scales, a jaw built for suction and a father who becomes the nursery.

systems.title: Toothless suction feeding
systems.text: Seahorses, pipefishes and seadragons have no teeth. An elongated face and an unusual set of throat bones are built for a specialised kind of suction feeding.

systems.title: A body in rings
systems.text: Instead of flexible scales, the body is wrapped in bony rings — 17 around the trunk and 31–37 along the tail — with flattened spines that carry the leafy flaps.

systems.title: A father's brood patch
systems.text: The eggs are fixed to a special area on the underside of the male's tail, where he broods and nourishes them until they hatch.

systems.title: Weak swimmers
systems.text: Seadragons swim slowly and poorly — which helps explain why they are often found stranded on beaches.

genome.lede: In 2022 researchers published chromosome-scale genomes of the weedy and leafy seadragons, looking for clues to their leafy flaps and other unusual features.

findings.title: Size and chromosomes
findings.text: The weedy seadragon's genome was estimated at about 597 million base pairs, holding about 22,000 protein-coding genes. The DNA appears to be arranged on 23 chromosomes, a number inferred from the assembly rather than counted under a microscope.

findings.title: Missing growth genes
findings.text: Seahorses, pipefishes and seadragons have all lost several fibroblast growth factor genes, including fgf3 and fgf4. In other vertebrates these genes help build teeth, jaws and skin structures, so the losses may be linked to the family's toothless snouts and armoured bodies.

findings.title: Clues to the flaps
findings.text: The seadragon genomes are dense with repetitive DNA and have unusual non-coding regions near a gene involved in skin outgrowths — a possible lead to how the leafy appendages evolved.

mind.lede: Divers and scientists have followed individual weedy seadragons for years, learning how faithful they are to one small patch of reef.

studies.title: Tagged and followed
studies.text: Over a year, 84 tagged seadragons were followed. Pregnant males were seen for more than six months, from June–July to early January, and some carried two broods.

studies.title: Faces in the crowd
studies.text: In Tasmania, 43 adults were told apart from photographs alone, because the spots and blotches on each animal's side are unique and stayed unchanged for 18 months.

studies.title: Staying put
studies.text: A seven-year mark–recapture study at five sites confirmed that seadragons are strongly attached to their home sites. It also found declines at several of those sites.

survival.lede: The weedy seadragon survives by looking like weed. Its habitat, rather than any predator, is its main worry.

tactics.title: Looking like weed
tactics.text: Leaf-shaped flaps and cryptic colouring hide it among kelp and seagrass while it creeps up on prey.

tactics.title: Slow and stealthy
tactics.text: As ambush predators, seadragons rely on camouflage and slow, careful approaches rather than speed.

threats.title: Shrinking habitat
threats.text: Kelp reefs and seagrass meadows have declined along parts of the southern Australian coast, raising fears that seadragon numbers are falling too. Range-wide counts are still lacking.

threats.title: Collecting
threats.text: Collecting for the aquarium trade has been named as a possible threat, though seadragons are hard to keep and breed in captivity. The species is protected in New South Wales and Tasmania.

life.lede: Seadragons breed from the southern winter into summer, and the father does the carrying.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: A mature female releases about 110 eggs per spawning, and a few females spawn more than once a season.

stages.name: Brooding
stages.text: The male carries an average of about 90 eggs on his tail. In one study they hatched 35–42 days after fertilisation; other sources give 30–38 days or about 8 weeks.

stages.name: Hatchling
stages.text: Most young already look like miniature juveniles when they hatch, or soon afterwards.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Some seadragons mature after a year, but most do not breed until their second summer.

lifespan.value: Possibly more than 10 years (estimated from survival rates)

tagline: A forager that tells its sisters where the flowers are by dancing
summary: Native to Europe, Africa and western Asia and now kept almost everywhere, the honey bee lives in colonies run by one queen, which may lay up to 1,000 eggs a day. Its workers fly kilometres from the nest to gather nectar and pollen, and a returning forager can tell its nestmates the direction and distance of a rich patch of flowers with the waggle dance.
ability: foraging flights guided by the waggle dance

stats.size: Workers 10–15 mm long; drones 15–17 mm; queens 18–20 mm
stats.habitat: Woodland, meadows, farmland and gardens with plenty of flowers; wild colonies nest in tree cavities
stats.range: Native to Europe, Africa and western Asia; introduced by people to every other continent except Antarctica
stats.diet: Nectar and pollen collected from flowers
stats.conservation: No global IUCN assessment; Data Deficient in Europe as a whole, while wild colonies in the EU were assessed as Endangered in 2025

facts.title: Directions, danced
facts.text: A forager that has found food far from the hive performs the waggle dance on the comb. The dance tells other workers the direction of the food, measured against the sun's position, and its distance.

facts.title: Following the dance by radar
facts.text: Researchers fitted bees recruited by the waggle dance with tiny transponders and tracked them with harmonic radar. This gave the first record of the paths they actually flew, testing Karl von Frisch's Nobel Prize-winning conclusion that recruits use the dance to find the food.

facts.title: A three-kilometre beat
facts.text: Workers usually forage within about 3 km of the hive, but they can fly 8 to 13 km when they need to.

facts.title: A sting that costs a life
facts.text: A worker's sting is barbed. When she stings, it tears away from her body along with the venom glands, and she dies.

facts.title: Still wild in Europe's beech woods
facts.text: Wild honey bee colonies were long assumed to be gone from Europe. A survey of two German beech forests found colonies living in tree cavities at densities of at least 0.11 to 0.14 per km², some deep inside the forest and a median 2.6 km from the nearest apiary. The authors estimated that German woodlands hold several thousand wild colonies.

facts.title: Out of Asia
facts.text: An analysis of 251 genomes from 18 native subspecies supported an Asian origin for the species, with at least three expansions that led to the African and European lineages.

notes: Conservation: I found no global IUCN assessment; Apis mellifera is absent from the GBIF IUCN checklist. iucnId 42463639 is the IUCN taxon ID of the European regional assessment. That assessment was Data Deficient in the 2014 European Red List of Bees (assessment ID 42463665). An October 2025 reassessment led by Honey Bee Watch, for the forthcoming European Red List, rated wild (free-living) colonies in the EU27 Endangered, and the pan-European status remains Data Deficient (assessment www.iucnredlist.org/species/42463639/277757621, per the press release; iucnredlist.org returns 403 to scripts, so it was not opened). Because the Endangered rating is regional and covers wild colonies only, the bee is not shelved under 'endangered'. 'venomous' is used for the barbed sting. The press release also cites 62% average losses of US commercial colonies (June 2024 – March 2025); this is not used. Range and introductions: ADW says the species is native to Europe, western Asia and Africa and was introduced to other continents from the 17th century. 'Every continent except Antarctica' is my wording of ADW's 'now occurs worldwide'. The worldwide introduced range is deliberately not mapped. Regions: europe first; African regions (african-savanna, sahara-arabia for North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, congo-basin, namib-kalahari, madagascar) reflect the native African range. Assigning them to particular subspecies (for example, scutellata, capensis, adansonii, unicolor, jemenitica) is general knowledge and was not checked against the cited sources. Western Asian native range (Middle East, Caucasus, Central Asian mountains) has no matching mapped region. Biome: temperate-forest, following europe and the beech-forest wild colonies. Riley et al. 2005 (Nature) is paywalled: the fact follows the abstract only, so no accuracy figures are given. Kohl & Rutschmann: the figures are from the abstract, and the study sites (Hainich National Park, Thuringia; Swabian Alb Biosphere Reserve) come from the full text via Europe PMC (PMC5890725). Dogantzis et al.: abstract via Europe PMC; marked hypothesis because the origin of the species has long been debated. doi.org for Science Advances and PeerJ returns 403 to scripts; both DOIs were confirmed through Europe PMC/Crossref. Size, foraging range, sting, worker biology and queen egg-laying (up to 1,000 eggs/day) are from ADW. Images: Ivar Leidus's Keila (Estonia) photos are Commons Featured Pictures; the hero is from 13 May 2018 and alt-2 from Niitvälja bog, 2016 (geotagged). alt-1 is from Torfbroek, Belgium, 2010 (geotagged). These are foragers in the field, but whether each came from a managed or a wild colony cannot be known.

anatomy.lede: A worker honey bee is a flying toolkit: eyes that see ultraviolet, antennae that read scent, a pollen basket on each hind leg and a barbed sting kept for emergencies.

hotspots.label: Antenna
hotspots.text: Most honey bee communication runs on scent and taste. Each hive has its own chemical signature that nestmates use to recognise one another.

hotspots.label: Compound eye
hotspots.text: The eyes detect ultraviolet light, revealing flower markings we cannot see, and part of each eye is sensitive to polarised light for navigation.

hotspots.label: Mouthparts
hotspots.text: Workers suck up nectar with their tongue and store it in the crop, the front part of the gut, to carry home.

hotspots.label: Wings
hotspots.text: Workers are smaller than drones but have longer wings. The flight muscles also act as a heater for the bee and the hive.

hotspots.label: Hairy thorax
hotspots.text: The thorax is covered in hair, while the abdomen has much less. Pollen caught in the hair is groomed off on to the hind legs.

hotspots.label: Pollen basket
hotspots.text: Pollen is packed into a special structure on each hind leg, the pollen basket, and flown back to the hive.

hotspots.label: Banded abdomen
hotspots.text: The orange and black bands work as warning colours: predators learn to link the pattern with a painful sting.

stats.label: Eggs a queen can lay in a day

senses.lede: A honey bee lives in a world of scent and vibration inside the dark hive, and of ultraviolet patterns and polarised skylight outside it.

senses.name: Ultraviolet sight
senses.text: Honey bee eyes detect ultraviolet wavelengths beyond the range we can see. This lets them see flower markings that show up only in ultraviolet and find the sun on cloudy days.

senses.name: Polarised light
senses.text: One part of each eye is sensitive to the polarisation of skylight, which bees use as a compass when navigating.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Bees locate flowers from a distance by scent, and foragers pass the smell of a rich patch to nestmates. The honey bee genome holds more genes for odorant receptors than other insect genomes sequenced at the time.

senses.name: Taste
senses.text: Compared with other insects sequenced by 2006, the honey bee has fewer genes for gustatory (taste) receptors, consistent with a diet of nectar and pollen.

senses.name: Vibration
senses.text: Workers and queens sense vibrations. Workers pick up the vibrations of a dancing forager, and newly emerged queens call to each other and to the workers.

body.lede: Much of a worker's body is given over to jobs for the colony: making wax, feeding young, storing food and defending the hive.

systems.title: Muscles as a heater
systems.text: Honey bees are partly warm-blooded. By working their flight muscles they warm themselves and the hive, and in cold weather workers and queen form a tight, shivering cluster.

systems.title: Glands that build and feed
systems.text: In their second week, workers' wax glands become active and they build comb. Glands in the head make royal jelly and worker jelly, and the food a female larva gets decides whether she becomes a queen or a worker.

systems.title: A sting made from an egg-laying tube
systems.text: The sting of workers and queens is a modified ovipositor, supplied with venom from glands in the abdomen. A stinging worker also releases an alarm pheromone that draws other bees to the target.

systems.title: Turning nectar into honey
systems.text: Foragers hand nectar to younger workers, who add enzymes and store it in open cells where water evaporates, concentrating the sugars into honey.

genome.lede: The honey bee was one of the first insects to have its genome read, and it remains a model for how genes shape social behaviour.

findings.title: Fewer defences, more noses
findings.text: The 2006 genome showed that honey bees have fewer genes for immunity, detoxification and taste than other sequenced insects, but more for smell, and new genes for using nectar and pollen.

findings.title: Sixteen chromosomes, end to end
findings.text: A 2019 assembly placed more than 98% of the sequence on the 16 chromosomes, each as a single scaffold. Females carry two sets (32 chromosomes); males hatch from unfertilised eggs and carry one.

findings.title: Surprisingly vertebrate-like genes
findings.text: For circadian rhythm, RNA interference and DNA methylation genes, the honey bee genome is more similar to vertebrates than the fruit fly's is.

mind.lede: Honey bees are a classic subject for studying learning and memory, and they keep surprising researchers with what they can grasp.

studies.title: Same or different
studies.text: Bees learned to choose a stimulus that matched, or differed from, one they had just seen. They then applied the rule to new stimuli, even switching from colours to scents.

studies.title: Placing zero
studies.text: Bees trained on 'less than' with images of one to six shapes went on to rank an empty image below one, an understanding of zero shared with some parrots, primates and young children.

studies.title: Dances checked by radar
studies.text: Harmonic radar tracking of recruited bees confirmed that they use the waggle dance's directions to fly towards the advertised food.

studies.title: Jobs that change with age
studies.text: Workers move through a sequence of jobs as they age: cleaning cells, nursing, building comb, guarding the entrance and finally, after about three weeks, foraging.

survival.lede: A colony is a fortress full of food, so it is defended with walls, guards and a sting that costs the defender her life.

tactics.title: A sealed home
tactics.text: Colonies prefer protected cavities such as tree hollows and seal small gaps with propolis, a mix of wax and plant resins, leaving one small entrance.

tactics.title: Guards at the door
tactics.text: Guard bees check every arrival by scent and attack any non-member that tries to get in.

tactics.title: A sting that stays in
tactics.text: The heavily barbed sting and its venom glands stay embedded in the target, which kills the worker but may make the sting more painful and discourage further attack.

tactics.title: Swarming
tactics.text: Healthy colonies reproduce by swarming: the old queen leaves with up to half the workers, who cluster nearby while scouts search for a new home.

threats.title: Varroa mites
threats.text: The Varroa mite jumped from the Asian honey bee to Apis mellifera and has spread worldwide except Australia. It feeds on developing bees, spreads viruses and often wipes out colonies.

threats.title: Losing local bees
threats.text: In Europe there is concern that large-scale commercial beekeeping is endangering locally adapted populations and subspecies.

threats.title: Colony collapse
threats.text: Colony Collapse Disorder, in which hives suddenly empty of workers, has struck mainly large commercial apiaries in North America. No single cause has been identified.

life.lede: Every bee in the hive passes through four stages in a wax cell. What it is fed as a larva decides whether a female becomes a worker or a queen.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The queen lays each egg in a wax cell. Fertilised eggs become females; unfertilised eggs become males.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: A white grub that stays in its cell, fed and groomed by nurse workers. Development is fastest at 33–36 °C.

stages.name: Pupa
stages.text: Workers seal the cell, the larva spins a silk cocoon and transforms. Workers take about 12 days as pupae.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults chew out of their cells and never grow again. Summer workers live 2 to 4 weeks, but workers that live through winter can last up to 11 months; drones survive 4 to 8 weeks.

lifespan.value: Queens usually 2–3 years, sometimes 5

tagline: A shark disguised as the seafloor
summary: Flattened, blotched and fringed with branching skin flaps around its mouth, the spotted wobbegong looks more like a patterned rug than a shark. It rests on Australian reefs by day and hunts fishes, octopuses and crabs at night.

stats.size: Up to about 1.7 m long
stats.depth: Usually 0–110 m; recorded to about 220 m
stats.range: Southern Australia, from Western Australia to southern Queensland
stats.diet: Fishes, octopuses, crabs and crayfish

facts.title: A fringed disguise
facts.text: Along each side of the head, in front of the eye, are 6–10 long, branching skin flaps called dermal lobes. With its blotched, ringed pattern they help this well-camouflaged shark blend into reef and sand.

facts.title: Night shift
facts.text: Spotted wobbegongs are nocturnal: they usually rest during the day and feed at night, mostly on fishes and octopuses, plus crabs and crayfish.

facts.title: Big litters
facts.text: Females give birth to live young — up to 37 pups — after a gestation of 10–11 months. Inside the mother, the embryos feed only on their egg yolk.

facts.title: A shark out of water
facts.text: It can be found in water barely deep enough to cover it, and has been seen climbing between tide pools with its back out of the water.

facts.title: Docile — until stepped on
facts.text: Though usually placid, it bites people who step on or provoke it, can cause severe cuts, and is often reluctant to let go.

anatomy.lede: A spotted wobbegong is a shark pressed flat against the reef. Its broad head, blotched skin and fringe of skin flaps break up its outline as it waits for prey to come close.

hotspots.label: Ringed saddles
hotspots.text: Dark saddles edged with whitish rings and blotches set this species apart from its close relative, the banded wobbegong.

hotspots.label: Pectoral fin
hotspots.text: Like angel sharks, wobbegongs have a flattened body that suits life lying on the bottom and ambushing prey.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: A band of densely packed cells across the retina gives sharper vision in the lower field of view — towards the reef and passing prey.

hotspots.label: Dermal lobes
hotspots.text: Six to ten long, coarsely branched skin lobes line each side of the head in front of the eye. There are none on the chin.

hotspots.label: Mouth
hotspots.text: The broad mouth sits at the front of the head. Stomach contents show it eats mainly bony fish, along with some octopuses and other cephalopods, and occasionally sharks and rays.

hotspots.label: Snout
hotspots.text: The snout carries an extra cluster of electrosensory pores not found in the angel shark, adding to the wobbegong's ability to sense prey.

senses.lede: Lying still in dim water, often at night, a wobbegong needs to detect prey that comes within striking distance — and predators that might approach from behind.

senses.name: Electric sense
senses.text: Pores on the head lead to electroreceptors that detect the faint electric fields of living animals. The spotted wobbegong has more pores than the angel shark, including a cluster on the snout.

senses.name: Watching its back
senses.text: A cluster of pores just behind the first gill slit, more typical of rays, may help bottom-living sharks detect approaching predators.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Its retina has both rods and cones. Its visual system is tuned for sensitivity and seems especially well suited to low light.

mind.lede: Long seen as solitary lumps on the reef, spotted wobbegongs turn out to have patterns in where they go and whom they spend time with.

studies.title: Empty stomachs
studies.text: Most wobbegongs caught by commercial fishers had empty stomachs, probably because they regurgitate when caught. Those with food had eaten mainly bony fish.

studies.title: Familiar neighbours
studies.text: Acoustic tags in a small marine reserve showed that some sharks preferred the company of particular others, and many of these pairings resumed after the sharks returned from seasonal migration.

survival.lede: The spotted wobbegong's disguise works both ways: it hides the shark from prey, and from anything that might want to eat it.

tactics.title: Living camouflage
tactics.text: Its blotched pattern and fringe of dermal lobes blend into reef, sand and seagrass, so prey swims close without noticing.

tactics.title: Resting by day
tactics.text: It is nocturnal, usually resting during the day and hunting at night.

tactics.title: A tenacious bite
tactics.text: Although placid, it bites when stepped on or provoked. Fishes of Australia notes 23 confirmed bites on people recorded by the International Shark Attack File.

threats.title: Fishing
threats.text: It is targeted and taken as bycatch in commercial and recreational fisheries, and is listed as Vulnerable in New South Wales.

threats.title: Slow breeding
threats.text: Females breed only once every three years, so populations take a long time to recover from fishing.

life.lede: Wobbegong breeding is slow and tightly timed. In New South Wales, a female's full cycle takes three years.

stages.name: Egg development
stages.text: Eggs grow slowly inside the mother for a year, then rapidly in the second, and are released from the ovary in November.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: The young develop inside the mother, feeding only on their egg yolk.

stages.name: Birth
stages.text: Litters average 21 pups, each about 21 cm long. Pregnant females were found mostly in northern New South Wales.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females start to mature at about 1.1 m long, and half of males are mature by about 1.3 m.

tagline: A blind, furry crab wearing a coat of bacteria
summary: Discovered in 2005 on hydrothermal vents in the South Pacific, the yeti crab is a pale squat lobster whose long arms are thickly furred with bristles. Those bristles host dense mats of bacteria that can draw energy from vent chemicals rather than sunlight.

stats.size: The described type specimen is 8.8 cm long; popular accounts give about 15 cm
stats.range: Hydrothermal vents on the Pacific–Antarctic Ridge, south of Easter Island
stats.diet: Probably omnivorous; may feed on bacteria grown on its bristles

facts.title: A 21st-century discovery
facts.text: The species was found in 2005 on the Pacific–Antarctic Ridge, about 1,500 km south of Easter Island, at roughly 2,200 m depth, living around hydrothermal vents.

facts.title: So new it needed a family
facts.text: It was so distinct from known crustaceans that scientists created a brand-new family, Kiwaidae, to hold it.

facts.title: A coat of microbes
facts.text: Its 'fur' is setae (stiff bristles) covered in dense filamentous bacteria. Their enzymes suggest they can fix carbon and process sulfur from vent fluids — chemosynthesis, making food from chemicals instead of light.

facts.title: Farmer or scavenger?
facts.text: Scientists suspect it eats the bacteria it grows, but this has not been directly observed in Kiwa hirsuta; its describers also saw it feeding on damaged mussel tissue.

facts.title: Nearly eyeless
facts.text: Yeti crabs' eyes are reduced to small, soft, unpigmented tissue — little use in the pitch-dark deep sea, and the animal is thought to be blind.

anatomy.lede: Seen from above, the yeti crab is a pale, smooth shell with two enormous 'furry' arms. It is not a true crab but a squat lobster, with its tail tucked beneath its body.

hotspots.label: Folded tail
hotspots.text: As in other squat lobsters, the abdomen is folded up against itself beneath the body rather than stretched out behind.

hotspots.label: Carapace
hotspots.text: The shell is calcified, smooth and slightly domed, about 1.3 times longer than wide, with only a sparse scattering of fine setae.

hotspots.label: Walking legs
hotspots.text: The stout walking legs end in claw-like tips lined with dense, horny spinules for gripping rock.

hotspots.label: Paired rigid setae
hotspots.text: Besides the soft 'fur', each arm carries rigid, barbed setae about 13 mm long, set in pairs. Unlike the soft setae, these carry no bacteria.

hotspots.label: Antennae
hotspots.text: The antennae lack the scale found in many relatives. The eyes, beside them, are reduced to small, soft patches of unpigmented tissue.

hotspots.label: 'Fur'
hotspots.text: The arms, legs and underside are covered with flexible setae about 15 mm long, carrying clusters of filamentous bacteria mostly towards their tips.

hotspots.label: Claw
hotspots.text: The long, strong pincers are almost equal in size. The horny tip of the movable finger fits between two horny tips on the fixed finger.

body.lede: The yeti crab's most remarkable feature is not its own tissue but the community of microbes it carries.

systems.title: A microbial coat
systems.text: Electron microscopy showed dense clusters of bacteria attached to the outer layer of the setae, with no special structures for holding them. Most belong to a group called epsilon-Proteobacteria.

systems.title: Chemical food factories
systems.text: Enzymes found in the bacterial mats point to carbon fixation and the processing of sulfur compounds — the basis of chemosynthesis in vent fluids. Whether the crab eats them has not been shown for this species.

systems.title: Eyes without sight
systems.text: The eyes are reduced to soft, uncalcified, unpigmented tissue. Its describers set this apart as one of the features that make the family unique.

mind.lede: Almost everything known about yeti crab behaviour comes from a handful of submersible dives in 2004 and 2005.

studies.title: Spaced out around the vents
studies.text: Crabs were seen more or less evenly spaced on the pillow basalt around active vents, and also at the base of black smokers among vent mussels, where shimmering milky water emerges.

studies.title: Opportunistic feeders
studies.text: Yeti crabs were watched eating the tissue of mussels damaged by the submersible's sampling. Like other vent crustaceans, they are probably omnivores.

tagline: The patient spear-fisher of the sand
summary: The largest of all mantis shrimps, this striped ambush hunter lives in a sandy burrow and waits with only its eyes showing. When a fish or shrimp passes, it lunges out and impales it on barbed, spear-like claws — a very different strategy from the hammer-fisted 'smasher' mantis shrimps.

stats.size: Up to about 40 cm long
stats.depth: Shallow sandy seabeds; reported to about 145 m
stats.range: Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to Hawaii and the Galápagos
stats.diet: Small fishes and crustaceans

facts.title: Spearer, not smasher
facts.text: Mantis shrimps come in two broad types: 'smashers' roam and hammer hard-shelled prey, while 'spearers' like this one hide in sandy burrows and snatch fast, soft-bodied prey such as fish.

facts.title: Eyes at the doorway
facts.text: Field observations show it hunts mainly at night, hidden in its burrow with just its eyes peeking out, then lunging to grab passing prey.

facts.title: Slower than you'd think
facts.text: Its strikes averaged about 2.3 m/s and lasted about 25 milliseconds — slower than smashers' blows, but similar to other predators that catch evasive prey. Speed, it seems, isn't everything for an ambusher.

facts.title: The biggest mantis shrimp
facts.text: Reaching up to about 40 cm, it is described as the largest mantis shrimp in the world.

facts.title: A couple that shares a home
facts.text: Zebra mantis shrimps are socially monogamous: a male and female share a burrow, and the female cares for the eggs.

Editor may wish to mention the alternative name. Depth range 6–145 m comes from SeaLifeBase (seen in search results only; site blocked direct fetch, so not listed as a reference). Size, range and monogamy come from Wikipedia, which cites Caldwell (UCMP) and Templin et al. 2017.

anatomy.lede: Out of its burrow, the zebra mantis shrimp is a long, boldly banded animal with stalked eyes and a pair of folded hunting limbs held beneath its head like a praying mantis.

hotspots.label: Stalked eyes
hotspots.text: The eyes sit on movable stalks. Before an attack, they are often the only part of the animal showing above the burrow.

hotspots.label: Raptorial claw
hotspots.text: The hunting limbs are modified second maxillipeds. In spearers like this one, the last segment is unfolded, elongated and lined with sharp spines for snagging fish.

hotspots.label: Banded body
hotspots.text: Dark and pale bands run across the long, segmented body, giving the animal its common name.

senses.lede: Mantis shrimps have some of the most complex eyes of any animal. Their young start life with far simpler ones.

senses.name: Colour vision
senses.text: Adult mantis shrimps have photoreceptors that detect up to 12 different colours, almost four times as many types as most animals. Why they need so many is still not understood.

senses.name: Larval eyes
senses.text: Zebra mantis shrimp larvae caught at Lizard Island had eyes with a single type of colour receptor, like other plankton. The complex adult eye is grown anew at metamorphosis.

body.lede: The zebra mantis shrimp carries the same strike machinery as its famous hammer-wielding relatives, but uses it differently.

systems.title: A spring it rarely uses
systems.text: Scans and dissections showed that it has the spring-and-latch structures other mantis shrimps use for spring-loaded strikes. Yet high-speed films suggest that it does not consistently use them.

systems.title: Reach over force
systems.text: Smashers need force to break shells, but a spearer needs reach to snatch fast prey. Its strikes are slower and longer than a smasher's, but match those of other predators of fast-moving prey.

systems.title: Bigger claws for males
systems.text: Males and females are similar in overall size, but males have larger raptorial claws.

genome.lede: No reference genome exists yet, but a 2025 'genome survey' estimated the size of the zebra mantis shrimp's DNA — and it is enormous.

findings.title: A giant genome
findings.text: Genome size was estimated at about 12.7 billion base pairs, the largest of the three mantis shrimps surveyed. More than 83% of the DNA in these species is repetitive.

findings.title: A missing mitochondrial gene
findings.text: Its mitochondrial genome is 16,204 base pairs long and lacks the ATP8 gene, as does that of the peacock mantis shrimp.

findings.title: An early branch
findings.text: Family trees built from several types of genetic data place the zebra mantis shrimp near the base of the group, though relationships among mantis shrimps remain disputed.

mind.lede: Watching mantis shrimps in the wild showed that they behave very differently from animals filmed in aquarium tanks.

studies.title: Variable strikes in the wild
studies.text: In the field, zebra mantis shrimps struck at passing prey with both longer and shorter strikes than those recorded in the laboratory.

studies.title: Sharing a burrow
studies.text: Pairs are socially monogamous and share a burrow. Building such a burrow is costly, and finding a mate is risky, which may explain why pairs stay together.

survival.lede: For a large but soft-bodied ambusher, the burrow is everything: a hiding place, a hunting blind and a home for two.

tactics.title: Hidden in the sand
tactics.text: It hides in a sandy burrow with only its eyes showing, then lunges out to seize prey with both claws.

tactics.title: Night hunting
tactics.text: In the field it ambushed evasive prey mainly at night.

threats.title: Fishing
threats.text: There is a small artisanal fishery for this species.

life.lede: Like other mantis shrimps, the zebra mantis shrimp begins life drifting in the plankton before settling into a burrow.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female looks after the eggs.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: Late-stage larvae have been caught at the sea surface at night. Mantis shrimp larvae can pass through up to 11 drifting stages, depending on the species.

stages.name: Metamorphosis
stages.text: In the final hours of larval life, a completely new adult retina grows beside the old larval eye, which is later pushed aside and reabsorbed.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults live in sandy burrows, usually as a male–female pair.
